docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This book grew out of a frustration I encountered repeatedly: existing resources on cryptography and cybersecurity either stay comfortably abstract or dive into a single topic without connecting it to the broader ecosystem. A practitioner building a secure system needs both — the mathematical foundations that tell you why a primitive is secure, and the adversarial perspective that tells you how it breaks in the real world.

Security Systems Engineering: From Cryptographic Primitives to Emerging Cyber Threats is my attempt to bridge that gap. It covers the full spectrum of the field — from the number theory underlying RSA to the eBPF syscall interception that powers runtime security in Kubernetes. Every chapter is written with the same goal: give you enough depth to reason about the problem yourself, not just recognise the answer.

The book is designed for practitioners, researchers, and advanced students who require both theoretical depth and practical applicability. If you’re preparing for a career in security engineering, red teaming, or cryptographic system design, this is the reference I wish I’d had.

The text is organized into ten major parts, each corresponding to a domain of security expertise:

  1. Foundations of Cryptography — Mathematical prerequisites, symmetric and asymmetric cryptography, hash functions, and key management.

  2. Network Security — Protocol vulnerabilities, firewalls, intrusion detection, and network architecture.

  3. Web Application Security — OWASP vulnerabilities, authentication mechanisms, API security, and secure development.

  4. Hardware Security — Side-channel attacks, fault injection, TPM, PUFs, and TEMPEST.

  5. Secure Communications — TLS, SSH, email security, VoIP, and network protocols.

  6. Malware Analysis — Dynamic and static analysis, reverse engineering, and countermeasures.

  7. Digital Forensics — Disk, memory, network, mobile, and cloud forensics.

  8. Vulnerability Research — Fuzzing, binary analysis, exploit development, and responsible disclosure.

  9. Security Architecture — Enterprise architecture, cloud-native security, and secure SDLC.

  10. Human Factor and Emerging Threats — Social engineering, phishing, AI security, IoT, quantum migration, and Web3.

Each chapter includes worked examples, attack scenarios with mitigations, and exercises for self-assessment. Reference implementations are provided in Python, C, Solidity, and shell scripts throughout.

Prerequisites: Readers should have familiarity with discrete mathematics (modular arithmetic, probability), computer architecture, operating systems, and basic networking.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput

def is_prime(n, k=10):
    """Probabilistic primality test, k rounds."""
    if n < 2: return False
    if n in (2, 3): return True

    # Write n-1 = 2^r * d
    r, d = 0, n - 1

docs.title: Appendix C: Selected Exercise Solutions
docs.text: This appendix provides complete solutions to selected exercises from each chapter.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Mathematical Foundations
docs.text:
Solution. [Exercise 1.1] Compute \(17^{-1} \bmod 31\):

Apply extended Euclidean algorithm to \((31, 17)\):

\[\begin{align*} 31 &= 1 \cdot 17 + 14 \\ 17 &= 1 \cdot 14 + 3 \\ 14 &= 4 \cdot 3 + 2 \\ 3 &= 1 \cdot 2 + 1 \\ 2 &= 2 \cdot 1 \end{align*}\]

Back-substituting:

\[\begin{align*} 1 &= 3 - 1 \cdot 2 \\ &= 3 - 1 \cdot (14 - 4 \cdot 3) = 5 \cdot 3 - 14 \\ &= 5 \cdot (17 - 14) - 14 = 5 \cdot 17 - 6 \cdot 14 \\ &= 5 \cdot 17 - 6 \cdot (31 - 17) = 11 \cdot 17 - 6 \cdot 31 \end{align*}\]

So \(17^{-1} \equiv 11 \pmod{31}\). Check: \(17 \times 11 = 187 = 6 \times 31 + 1 \equiv 1 \pmod{31}\). ✓

Solution. [Exercise 1.3] Compute \(2^{100} \bmod 13\):

By Fermat’s Little Theorem, \(2^{12} \equiv 1 \pmod{13}\) (since 13 is prime and \(13 \nmid 2\)).

Write \(100 = 8 \times 12 + 4\), so:

\[2^{100} = 2^{8 \times 12 + 4} = (2^{12})^8 \cdot 2^4 \equiv 1^8 \cdot 16 \equiv 3 \pmod{13}\]

Solution. [Exercise 1.6] (a) \(H = \log_2(26^8) = 8\log_2 26 \approx 8 \times 4.700 = 37.6\) bits.

(b) Exhaustive search: \(26^8 = 208{,}827{,}064{,}576 \approx 2.1 \times 10^{11}\) passwords. At \(10^9\) per second: average \(\approx 10^{11}\) attempts \(\div 10^9\)/sec \(= 100\) seconds.

(c) For \(\geq 80\) bits: need alphabet size \(|\Sigma|^n \geq 2^{80}\). With \(n = 12\): \(|\Sigma| \geq 2^{80/12} = 2^{6.67} \approx 102\). Use printable ASCII (95 characters) with \(n \geq 13\), giving \(95^{13} \approx 2^{85}\) — above threshold.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Symmetric Cryptography
docs.text:
Solution. [Exercise 2.2] GCM nonce reuse attack:

If nonces \(N\) are reused with the same key \(K\):

\[\begin{align*} C_1 &= M_1 \oplus \text{KS}_N, \quad T_1 = \text{GHASH}(H, C_1, \text{AAD}_1) \oplus E_K(\text{cnt}_0) \\ C_2 &= M_2 \oplus \text{KS}_N, \quad T_2 = \text{GHASH}(H, C_2, \text{AAD}_2) \oplus E_K(\text{cnt}_0) \end{align*}\]

Where \(H = E_K(0^{128})\) is the GHASH key.

From the two tag equations:

\[T_1 \oplus T_2 = \text{GHASH}(H, C_1, \text{AAD}_1) \oplus \text{GHASH}(H, C_2, \text{AAD}_2)\]

This is a polynomial equation in \(H\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{2^{128}}\). Since GHASH is polynomial with known coefficients (from known \(C_1, C_2, \text{AAD}_1, \text{AAD}_2\)), we can solve for \(H\) directly. With \(H\) known, we can forge authentication tags for any message. Also, \(M_1 \oplus M_2 = C_1 \oplus C_2\), revealing plaintext.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Hash Functions and MACs
docs.text:
Solution. [Exercise 4.4] Argon2id tuning:

(a) Target: \(\leq 500\)ms on server hardware. Benchmark Argon2id with different parameters on the target machine. On typical modern server hardware:

  • time_cost=3, memory_cost=65536 (64 MB), parallelism=4 gives \(\approx 200\)–\(400\)ms

  • Adjust time_cost to hit the \(\approx 500\)ms target

(b) GPU resistance for \(> 2^{50}\) iterations: With memory_cost=65536 (64 MB): GPU has limited VRAM; each GPU core needs 64 MB, severely limiting parallelism. Typical H100 GPU with 80 GB VRAM: \(80{,}000 / 64 = 1{,}250\) parallel hashes. At 500ms per hash on GPU (memory-hard): \(1{,}250 / 0.5 = 2{,}500\) H/s. To achieve \(2^{50}\) attempts: \(2^{50} / 2500 \approx 4.5 \times 10^{11}\) seconds \(\approx 14{,}000\) years.

Recommendation: time_cost=3, memory_cost=65536, parallelism=4.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Key Management
docs.text:
Solution. [Exercise 5.1] Shamir \((3,5)\) secret sharing over \(\mathbb{F}_{97}\), secret \(S = 42\):

Choose random polynomial \(f(x) = 42 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{97}\). Let \(a_1 = 13\), \(a_2 = 7\) (random).

Shares:

\[\begin{align*} f(1) &= 42 + 13 + 7 = 62 \\ f(2) &= 42 + 26 + 28 = 96 \\ f(3) &= 42 + 39 + 63 = 144 \equiv 47 \pmod{97} \\ f(4) &= 42 + 52 + 112 = 206 \equiv 12 \pmod{97} \\ f(5) &= 42 + 65 + 175 = 282 \equiv 88 \pmod{97} \end{align*}\]

Reconstruction from shares \((1,62), (2,96), (3,47)\): Lagrange interpolation to find \(f(0)\):

\[f(0) = 62 \cdot \frac{(0-2)(0-3)}{(1-2)(1-3)} + 96 \cdot \frac{(0-1)(0-3)}{(2-1)(2-3)} + 47 \cdot \frac{(0-1)(0-2)}{(3-1)(3-2)}\] \[= 62 \cdot \frac{6}{2} + 96 \cdot \frac{3}{-1} + 47 \cdot \frac{2}{2} = 186 - 288 + 47 = -55 \equiv 42 \pmod{97}\]

Recovered secret: \(42\). ✓

docs.title: Chapter 7: Post-Quantum Cryptography
docs.text:
Solution. [Exercise 7.4] AES-256 vs RSA-2048 against quantum computers:

RSA-2048: Security relies on the Integer Factoring Problem. Shor’s algorithm factors \(n\)-bit integers in \(O(n^3)\) quantum gate operations. For RSA-2048: approximately \(2^{11} \approx 2000\) logical qubits with error correction are needed—feasible on a CRQC. Security against quantum: 0 bits.

AES-256: Security relies on exhaustive key search. Grover’s algorithm provides a quadratic speedup: searches \(N\) items in \(O(\sqrt{N})\) quantum evaluations. For AES-256: \(\sqrt{2^{256}} = 2^{128}\) quantum AES evaluations needed. This is infeasible even with a quantum computer.

Key distinction: Shor’s algorithm provides exponential speedup (polynomial vs. exponential classical); Grover provides only quadratic speedup. AES-256 simply doubles key length to maintain security against Grover’s quadratic speedup.

docs.title: Chapter 24: Exploit Development
docs.text:
Solution. [Sample: Stack Overflow Offset] Finding return address offset using pwntools cyclic pattern:

from pwn import *

# Generate cyclic pattern
pattern = cyclic(200)

# After crash, read EIP/RIP value from crash dump
# e.g., EIP = 0x6161616e ("naaa" in little-endian)

# Find offset
offset = cyclic_find(0x6161616e)  # or cyclic_find(b'naaa')
print(f"Offset to return address: {offset} bytes")

# Construct exploit
padding = b'A' * offset
ret_addr = p64(0xdeadbeef)  # Target address
payload = padding + ret_addr

docs.title: Chapter 1: Mathematical Foundations of Cryptography
docs.text: Cryptography rests on carefully chosen mathematical problems that are easy to compute in one direction but infeasible to reverse. This chapter builds the mathematical toolkit required for the rest of the book: modular arithmetic, group theory, hardness assumptions, elliptic curves, and the information-theoretic concepts that underpin security definitions.

docs.title: 1.1 Modular Arithmetic
docs.text:
Definition 1.1 (Modular Congruence)

We write \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\) if \(n \mid (a - b)\), i.e., \(n\) divides \(a - b\). The set of integers modulo \(n\) is denoted \(\mathbb{Z}_n = \{0, 1, …, n-1\}\).

Think of \(\mathbb{Z}_n\) as arithmetic on a clock face: once you hit \(n\), you wrap around to zero. This wrapping is what makes reversal hard. Adding two numbers modulo \(n\) is trivial, but given only the result, you can’t tell whether the inputs were 3 and 5, or 8 and \(n\) (since \(8 \equiv 8 + n \pmod{n}\)), which creates a natural information barrier that cryptographic constructions exploit.

The fundamental operations in \(\mathbb{Z}_n\) are:

  • Addition: \((a + b) \bmod n\)

  • Multiplication: \((a \cdot b) \bmod n\)

  • Exponentiation: \(a^e \bmod n\) (computed by repeated squaring)

Exponentiation deserves special attention. Computing \(a^e \bmod n\) is efficient — the square-and-multiply algorithm takes only \(O(\log e)\) multiplications. Reversing this operation (finding \(e\) given \(a\), \(a^e\), and \(n\)) is the discrete logarithm problem, and no polynomial-time classical algorithm is known for it in general groups. That asymmetry is the engine of public-key cryptography.

Example 1.1 (Modular Exponentiation)

Compute \(3^{13} \bmod 7\) using the square-and-multiply algorithm.

Solution. Write \(13 = (1101)_2 = 8 + 4 + 1\).

\[\begin{align*} 3^1 &\equiv 3 \pmod{7} \\ 3^2 &\equiv 9 \equiv 2 \pmod{7} \\ 3^4 &\equiv 2^2 = 4 \pmod{7} \\ 3^8 &\equiv 4^2 = 16 \equiv 2 \pmod{7} \\ 3^{13} &= 3^8 \cdot 3^4 \cdot 3^1 \equiv 2 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 24 \equiv 3 \pmod{7} \end{align*}\]

docs.title: 1.1.1 The Extended Euclidean Algorithm
docs.text:
Theorem 1.1 (Bézout’s Identity)

For integers \(a\) and \(b\), there exist integers \(s, t\) such that \(\gcd(a,b) = sa + tb\).

The extended Euclidean algorithm computes \(\gcd(a,b)\) and the coefficients \(s, t\):

def extended_gcd(a, b):
    """Returns (gcd, s, t) such that gcd = s*a + t*b."""
    if b == 0:
        return a, 1, 0
    g, s1, t1 = extended_gcd(b, a
    return g, t1, s1 - (a // b) * t1

# Example: find inverse of 3 mod 7
g, s, t = extended_gcd(3, 7)  # g=1, s=... gives 3*s ≡ 1 (mod 7)
inverse = s

Definition 1.2 (Modular Inverse)

The modular inverse of \(a\) modulo \(n\) is an integer \(a^{-1}\) such that \(a \cdot a^{-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}\). It exists if and only if \(\gcd(a, n) = 1\).

Modular inversion is the building block for RSA key generation (finding \(d = e^{-1} \bmod \lambda(n)\)) and for ECDSA signature verification (computing \(s^{-1} \bmod n\)). The condition \(\gcd(a, n) = 1\) matters in practice: if you accidentally pick \(e\) that shares a factor with \(\phi(n)\) during RSA key generation, no valid decryption key exists, and the keygen step should fail loudly rather than silently produce a broken key.

docs.title: 1.1.2 Chinese Remainder Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem 1.2 (Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT))

Let \(n_1, n_2, …, n_k\) be pairwise coprime integers and \(M = \prod_i n_i\). For any \(a_1, …, a_k\), the system

\[x \equiv a_i \pmod{n_i}, \quad i = 1, …, k\]

has a unique solution \(x \in \mathbb{Z}_M\).

CRT says that working modulo a composite is equivalent to working modulo each prime factor simultaneously. This gives you a tool for decomposing hard-looking computations over large moduli into easier ones over smaller moduli, then recombining. In cryptographic engineering, that recombination step is what makes RSA fast enough to deploy at scale.

CRT in RSA

RSA decryption uses CRT to speed computation. Rather than computing \(m = c^d \bmod n\) directly, compute \(m_p = c^{d_p} \bmod p\) and \(m_q = c^{d_q} \bmod q\) separately (where \(d_p = d \bmod (p-1)\), \(d_q = d \bmod (q-1)\)), then combine via CRT. This yields approximately a \(4\times\) speedup.

docs.title: 1.2 Group Theory
docs.text:
Definition 1.3 (Group)

A group \((G, \cdot)\) is a set \(G\) with a binary operation \(\cdot\) satisfying:

  1. Closure: \(a, b \in G \Rightarrow a \cdot b \in G\)

  2. Associativity: \((a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)\)

  3. Identity: \(\exists\, e \in G: e \cdot a = a \cdot e = a\)

  4. Inverses: \(\forall a \in G, \exists\, a^{-1}: a \cdot a^{-1} = e\)

If additionally \(a \cdot b = b \cdot a\), the group is abelian.

The group axioms look abstract, but they’re encoding a very specific guarantee: every element has a unique inverse, and the operation is well-behaved. For cryptography, what matters is that groups can be large (making exhaustive search infeasible), structured (allowing efficient computation), yet hard to invert in the sense of the discrete log problem. The key insight is that multiplying group elements is easy — \(g^a \cdot g^b = g^{a+b}\) — but separating the exponents from the result is hard.

Example 1.2 (Cryptographic Groups)

  • \((\mathbb{Z}_n, +)\): additive group of integers mod \(n\) (always abelian)

  • \((\mathbb{Z}_n^*, \cdot)\): multiplicative group of units mod \(n\) (elements coprime to \(n\)); \(|\mathbb{Z}_n^*| = \phi(n)\)

  • Elliptic curve group \(E(\mathbb{F}_p)\): points on an elliptic curve over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) with chord-and-tangent addition; used in ECDSA, ECDH

Not every group works for cryptography. For DLP-based schemes, you need a group whose order has a large prime factor; otherwise the Pohlig-Hellman algorithm decomposes the problem into small subgroups and solves each part cheaply. This is why prime-order subgroups and prime-order elliptic curves are standard practice: a prime-order group has no exploitable subgroup structure.

docs.title: 1.2.1 Euler’s Totient Function
docs.text:
Definition 1.4 (Euler’s Totient)

\(\phi(n)\) counts integers in \([1, n]\) coprime to \(n\):

\[\phi(n) = n \prod_{p \mid n} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right)\]

For \(n = pq\) (distinct primes): \(\phi(pq) = (p-1)(q-1)\).

Theorem 1.3 (Euler’s Theorem)

If \(\gcd(a, n) = 1\), then \(a^{\phi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}\).

Corollary 1 (Fermat’s Little Theorem)

If \(p\) is prime and \(p \nmid a\), then \(a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}\).

Euler’s theorem is the mathematical glue holding RSA together. Because \(ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\phi(n)}\), we get \(m^{ed} = m^{1 + k\phi(n)} = m \cdot (m^{\phi(n)})^k \equiv m \cdot 1^k = m\). The private exponent \(d\) is effectively an undo-button for raising to the power \(e\), but only if you know \(\phi(n)\), which requires knowing \(p\) and \(q\). Factoring \(n\) into \(p\) and \(q\) is the hard step; once done, the rest is straightforward arithmetic.

docs.title: 1.3 Computational Hardness Assumptions
docs.text:
Cryptographic security reduces to the assumed hardness of mathematical problems. The next three subsections cover the three main families.

No mathematical proof exists that any of these problems are truly hard — that would imply \(\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP}\), one of the great open questions in computer science. What we have instead are decades of failed attacks, which builds empirical confidence. When a protocol is described as “secure under the DLP assumption,” it means that breaking the protocol is at least as hard as solving DLP; if someone ever efficiently solves DLP, the protocol breaks.

docs.title: 1.3.1 Integer Factoring Problem (IFP)
docs.text:
Definition 1.5 (IFP)

Given \(n = pq\) (product of two large primes), find \(p\) and \(q\).

Best known algorithm: General Number Field Sieve (GNFS) — sub-exponential time \(O\!\left(e^{c(\ln n)^{1/3}(\ln\ln n)^{2/3}}\right)\).

Current security levels:

RSA modulus Classical security Quantum security 1024 bits Broken (2009) Broken 2048 bits 112 bits Broken (Shor) 3072 bits 128 bits Broken (Shor)

The sub-exponential scaling of GNFS is why RSA keys must be so much larger than AES keys for equivalent security. For AES-128 you need a 128-bit key; for RSA at the same security level you need 3072 bits. This is not a bug in RSA — it’s a consequence of the structure of the integers. In practice, this size difference means RSA private-key operations are much slower than AES, which is why TLS uses RSA only to bootstrap a session and then switches to symmetric keys for bulk data.

docs.title: 1.3.2 Discrete Logarithm Problem (DLP)
docs.text:
Definition 1.6 (DLP)

Given a group \(G\), generator \(g\), and element \(h = g^x\), find \(x\).

The DLP underlies Diffie-Hellman, DSA, and ElGamal. In \(\mathbb{Z}_p^*\), the index calculus algorithm solves DLP in sub-exponential time. For elliptic curve groups (ECDLP), the best general algorithm is Pollard’s rho in \(O(\sqrt{p})\) — fully exponential, which is why ECC keys can be much shorter.

Why is the DLP hard intuitively? Given \(g\) and \(g^x\), you’re asking: how many times was the generator “applied”? In a large group with prime order \(q\), elements are spread uniformly across the group, and there’s no mathematical shortcut that lets you count the applications without trying them one by one. The group structure gives you efficient forward computation — repeatedly doubling a point, say — but no efficient backward path.

Why ECC?

The ECDLP is harder than the DLP in \(\mathbb{Z}_p^*\) because index calculus does not apply to generic groups. A 256-bit elliptic curve key provides  128-bit security, equivalent to RSA-3072.

docs.title: 1.3.3 Computational Diffie-Hellman (CDH) and DDH
docs.text:
Definition 1.7 (CDH Assumption)

Given \((g, g^a, g^b)\) in group \(G\), it is hard to compute \(g^{ab}\).

Definition 1.8 (DDH Assumption)

Given \((g, g^a, g^b, g^c)\), it is hard to distinguish whether \(c = ab\) or \(c \leftarrow_\$ \mathbb{Z}_{|G|}\).

DDH is stronger than CDH; CDH is stronger than DLP. Many protocols require only CDH; some require DDH.

The DDH assumption is what makes ElGamal encryption semantically secure. If an attacker could tell whether \(g^c = g^{ab}\) or not, they could distinguish encryptions of different messages. DDH fails in some groups — for example, in \(\mathbb{Z}_p^*\) you can use the Legendre symbol to test quadratic residuosity, breaking DDH. This is why careful protocol designers specify not just a group but the precise subgroup that their security argument depends on.

docs.title: 1.4 Elliptic Curve Cryptography
docs.text:
Definition 1.9 (Elliptic Curve)

An elliptic curve over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) (for prime \(p > 3\)) is the set of points \((x, y) \in \mathbb{F}_p^2\) satisfying:

\[y^2 \equiv x^3 + ax + b \pmod{p}\]

together with a point at infinity \(\mathcal{O}\), where \(4a^3 + 27b^2 \not\equiv 0\) (non-singular).

The non-singularity condition \(4a^3 + 27b^2 \neq 0\) ensures the curve has no cusps or self-intersections, which would make the group law ill-defined at those points. Over the integers this looks like an ordinary smooth cubic curve, but over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) the picture is a finite scattered set of points — no curves visible, just a cloud of coordinates that satisfy the equation. The group law doesn’t rely on visual geometry; it’s entirely algebraic and computes the same result either way.

docs.title: 1.4.1 Point Addition
docs.text:
Figure 1.1. Elliptic curve point addition \(P + Q\): draw chord through \(P\) and \(Q\); reflect intersection about \(x\)-axis.

For \(P = (x_1, y_1)\) and \(Q = (x_2, y_2)\) with \(P \neq Q\):

\[\begin{align*} \lambda &= \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \pmod{p} \\ x_3 &= \lambda^2 - x_1 - x_2 \pmod{p} \\ y_3 &= \lambda(x_1 - x_3) - y_1 \pmod{p} \end{align*}\]

and \(P + Q = (x_3, y_3)\).

For point doubling (\(P = Q\)): \(\lambda = (3x_1^2 + a)/(2y_1) \bmod p\).

The formula for \(\lambda\) is just the slope of the line through \(P\) and \(Q\), computed in \(\mathbb{F}_p\) arithmetic. The division becomes modular inversion, which is why the group law requires \(p\) to be prime (ensuring every nonzero element has an inverse). When implementing ECC, you almost never work with these affine coordinates directly — projective coordinates (Jacobian form) avoid the expensive modular inversions in the inner loop, roughly halving the number of field operations needed per point multiplication.

docs.title: 1.4.2 Standard Curves
docs.text:
Curve Field Security Use P-256 (secp256r1) \(\mathbb{F}_p\), 256-bit 128 bits TLS, ECDSA P-384 \(\mathbb{F}_p\), 384-bit 192 bits NSA Suite B Curve25519 \(\mathbb{F}_p\), 255-bit 128 bits X25519 DH, Ed25519 secp256k1 \(\mathbb{F}_p\), 256-bit 128 bits Bitcoin, Ethereum Ed448 (Curve448) \(\mathbb{F}_p\), 448-bit 224 bits High security

Curve selection matters beyond security level. P-256’s parameters were generated by NIST with a seed that was never publicly justified, which made some researchers uncomfortable — the fear being that a malicious generator could choose parameters that weaken the ECDLP in ways not publicly known. Curve25519 was designed by Bernstein with fully explained, publicly auditable constants derived from simple numeric criteria, which is why it’s widely preferred for new protocols. In practice, both are believed secure, but Curve25519 is also significantly faster on software implementations and harder to implement incorrectly.

Example 1.3 (ECDH Key Exchange)

Alice and Bob agree on curve \(E\) and generator point \(G\) with order \(n\).

  1. Alice picks secret \(a \leftarrow_\$ \mathbb{Z}_n^*\); computes \(A = aG\); sends \(A\).

  2. Bob picks secret \(b \leftarrow_\$ \mathbb{Z}_n^*\); computes \(B = bG\); sends \(B\).

  3. Shared secret: Alice computes \(aB = a(bG) = abG\); Bob computes \(bA = b(aG) = abG\). Both obtain the same point \(S = abG\); shared secret = \(S_x\) (x-coordinate).

An attacker seeing only \(G\), \(A = aG\), \(B = bG\) must solve the ECDLP to find \(a\) or \(b\) — computationally infeasible for 256-bit curves.

docs.title: 1.5 Probability and Information Theory
docs.text:
Definition 1.10 (Negligible Function)

A function \(f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^+\) is negligible if for every polynomial \(p(\cdot)\), there exists \(N\) such that for all \(n > N\): \(f(n) < 1/p(n)\). Written \(f(n) = \mathsf{negl}(n)\).

Negligibility is the formal way to say “vanishingly small as a function of the security parameter.” When a security proof says an adversary’s advantage is negligible, it means that even if the adversary runs for polynomial time (realistic), their probability of winning is smaller than any fixed fraction, for large enough security parameters. This is stronger than just saying “small” — it rules out advantages like \(1/n\) (which is small but not negligible since \(p(n) = n\) witnesses it).

Definition 1.11 (Statistical Distance)

The statistical distance between distributions \(X\) and \(Y\) over domain \(\mathcal{D}\) is:

\[\Delta(X, Y) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{d \in \mathcal{D}} |{\Pr}[X = d] - {\Pr}[Y = d]|\]

Distributions are statistically indistinguishable if \(\Delta(X, Y) = \mathsf{negl}(\lambda)\).

Definition 1.12 (Shannon Entropy)

For a discrete random variable \(X\) over \(\mathcal{X}\):

\[H(X) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \Pr[X = x] \log_2 \Pr[X = x]\]

Entropy is maximized at \(H(X) = \log_2 |\mathcal{X}|\) for the uniform distribution.

Entropy quantifies unpredictability, not password length. A 20-character password made of the same character repeated has zero entropy — an attacker tries it first. A 12-character truly random lowercase password has about 56 bits of entropy and is far stronger. This distinction matters when evaluating password policies: requiring length and special characters doesn’t guarantee high entropy if users respond with predictable patterns like Password1!.

Perfect Secrecy — Shannon’s Theorem

A cipher \((\mathsf{Enc}, \mathsf{Dec})\) achieves perfect secrecy if for all \(m_0, m_1 \in \mathcal{M}\) and all \(c \in \mathcal{C}\):

\[\Pr[\mathsf{Enc}_K(m_0) = c] = \Pr[\mathsf{Enc}_K(m_1) = c]\]

where \(K \leftarrow_\$ \mathcal{K}\). The One-Time Pad achieves perfect secrecy when \(|\mathcal{K}| \geq |\mathcal{M}|\). Shannon proved that perfect secrecy requires \(|\mathcal{K}| \geq |\mathcal{M}|\).

Perfect secrecy sounds ideal but the key-length requirement makes it impractical for most real-world use. If you need to encrypt a gigabyte of data with a one-time pad, you need a gigabyte of random key material, and you need to transport that key securely — which is the same problem you started with. Modern cryptography accepts computational security instead: a cipher is secure if no efficient attacker can distinguish ciphertexts, even though an unbounded attacker could always brute-force the key.

Example 1.4 (Entropy Calculation)

A 4-character PIN chosen uniformly from \(\{0,…,9\}^4\) has entropy:

\[H = \log_2(10^4) = 4\log_2 10 \approx 13.29 \text{ bits}\]

A 12-character password from lowercase+digits (\(36^{12}\)) has entropy \(\approx 62\) bits — much stronger.

docs.title: 1.6 Finite Fields
docs.text:
Definition 1.13 (Finite Field \(\mathbb{F}_{2^n}\))

The binary extension field \(\mathbb{F}_{2^n}\) contains \(2^n\) elements, represented as polynomials over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) of degree \(< n\), modulo an irreducible polynomial \(p(x)\) of degree \(n\).

Addition: XOR of polynomial coefficients. Multiplication: polynomial multiplication followed by reduction modulo \(p(x)\).

AES operates in \(\mathbb{F}_{2^8}\) with irreducible polynomial \(p(x) = x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1\).

Why do block ciphers need a field? Because a field gives you both addition (cheap in hardware: XOR) and multiplication (invertible, nonlinear): these two operations together let you build the confusion and diffusion that Shannon identified as the core requirements for a secure cipher. XOR alone is linear and easy to analyze algebraically; adding field multiplication (the S-box and MixColumns in AES) breaks that linearity in ways that resist known cryptanalytic attacks.

The choice of irreducible polynomial matters for implementation, not security. Different irreducible polynomials give isomorphic fields — the math is the same, but the hardware can be faster or slower. AES’s specific choice of \(x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1\) was selected partly because it enables efficient hardware implementations of the \(\mathtt{xtime}\) operation (multiply by \(x\)), which chains into the MixColumns step. This is a good example of how cryptographic standards balance theoretical soundness with engineering constraints.

Example 1.5 (Multiplication in \(\mathbb{F}_{2^8}\))

Multiply \(\mathtt{0x57}\) and \(\mathtt{0x83}\) in AES’s field.

\(\mathtt{0x57} = x^6 + x^4 + x^2 + x + 1\) and \(\mathtt{0x83} = x^7 + x + 1\).

Their product modulo \(p(x)\) gives \(\mathtt{0xC1}\).

This is implemented efficiently using the \(\mathtt{xtime}\) function (multiply by \(x\), i.e., left-shift and conditional XOR with \(\mathtt{0x1B}\)).

docs.title: 1.7 Summary and Security Reductions
docs.text:
The hardness assumptions from the previous sections form a hierarchy. Breaking a higher-level problem is no harder than breaking the assumption it reduces to.

Security reductions are a double-edged tool. They let you say “if you can break this protocol, you can break this hard problem,” which is reassuring. But they don’t say anything in the other direction: a protocol might be broken without solving the underlying hard problem, if the protocol design has a flaw. This is why proving security in a formal model matters — the reduction only covers the mathematical core, not implementation bugs, side channels, or protocol-level design errors.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1.1

Compute \(17^{-1} \bmod 31\) using the extended Euclidean algorithm. Verify your answer.

Exercise 1.2

Show that \(|\mathbb{Z}_{pq}^*| = (p-1)(q-1)\) for distinct primes \(p, q\).

Exercise 1.3

Using Fermat’s Little Theorem, compute \(2^{100} \bmod 13\).

Exercise 1.4

Let \(G = \mathbb{Z}_{23}^*\) with generator \(g = 5\). Alice’s public key is \(A = 5^a \bmod 23 = 8\) and Bob’s is \(B = 5^b \bmod 23 = 19\). Compute the shared DH secret \(g^{ab} \bmod 23\). (Hint: find \(a\) and \(b\) by trial — the small numbers make this feasible.)

Exercise 1.5

Grover’s algorithm attacks AES-128 achieving \(O(\sqrt{2^{128}}) = O(2^{64})\) operations. Compare this to the classical birthday bound for a hash function with 128-bit output. What does this imply for recommended hash output sizes in the quantum era?

Exercise 1.6 (Entropy Analysis)

A system uses 8-character passwords from a lowercase alphabet (26 letters). An attacker can test \(10^9\) passwords/second offline.

  1. Calculate the entropy of a uniformly random 8-character lowercase password.

  2. How long on average does exhaustive search take?

  3. What alphabet size or length would give \(\geq 80\) bits of entropy?

docs.title: Chapter 2: Symmetric Cryptography
docs.text: Symmetric cryptography uses the same key for both encryption and decryption. It’s orders of magnitude faster than public-key cryptography and forms the workhorse for bulk data encryption. This chapter covers block ciphers, stream ciphers, authenticated encryption, and the formal security definitions that make these claims precise.

docs.title: 2.1 Block Ciphers
docs.text:
Definition 2.1 (Block Cipher)

A block cipher with block size \(n\) and key size \(k\) is a family of permutations:

\[E: \{0,1\}^k \times \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^n\]

For each key \(K \in \{0,1\}^k\), \(E_K(\cdot)\) is a permutation on \(\{0,1\}^n\) with inverse \(D_K = E_K^{-1}\).

A block cipher is a keyed shuffling function: given the same key, the same input block always produces the same output block, and the mapping is invertible. The key selects one specific permutation from an astronomically large family of possible permutations. Security depends on the key-selected permutation being indistinguishable from a random permutation — an adversary who can’t see the key shouldn’t be able to tell the cipher apart from a random function with access to only a polynomial number of input-output pairs.

docs.title: 2.1.1 Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
docs.text:
AES (FIPS 197, 2001) operates on a \(4 \times 4\) matrix of bytes called the state, over \(\mathbb{F}_{2^8}\).

Parameters:

Variant Key Size Rounds AES-128 128 bits 10 AES-192 192 bits 12 AES-256 256 bits 14

Round structure (each of \(r-1\) full rounds):

  1. SubBytes: Apply S-box (a non-linear substitution in \(\mathbb{F}_{2^8}\)) to each byte independently.

  2. ShiftRows: Cyclically shift row \(i\) left by \(i\) positions.

  3. MixColumns: Multiply each column by a fixed \(4 \times 4\) matrix over \(\mathbb{F}_{2^8}\).

  4. AddRoundKey: XOR state with round key derived from key schedule.

The final round omits MixColumns.

Each of the four operations targets a different cryptographic requirement. SubBytes provides non-linearity: without it, AES would be a linear map over \(\mathbb{F}_2\), and an attacker could solve for the key with a handful of known plaintexts using linear algebra. ShiftRows ensures that bytes from the same column don’t stay together round after round, so a single modified input byte eventually affects all output bytes. MixColumns is the diffusion engine: each output byte depends on all four input bytes in its column, so any single-bit change propagates widely within two rounds (the “avalanche effect”). AddRoundKey binds everything to the secret key.

Figure 2.1. AES round function (MixColumns omitted in final round).

S-Box construction: Invert in \(\mathbb{F}_{2^8}\) (with \(0 \mapsto 0\)) then apply affine transformation. This provides:

  • Confusion: Non-linear; algebraic degree 7

  • Maximum nonlinearity; no fixed points or complement fixed points

The S-box nonlinearity is measured by how much it deviates from all linear Boolean functions. AES’s S-box achieves the maximum possible nonlinearity for an \(8 \times 8\) bijection, leaving no linear approximation with correlation significantly above \(1/2\), which is the property that blocks linear cryptanalysis. The fixed-point condition (no \(x\) where \(\mathrm{S}(x) = x\), and no \(x\) where \(\mathrm{S}(x) = \overline{x}\)) prevents weak keys that collapse certain cipher states.

docs.title: 2.1.2 AES Security
docs.text:
Best known attacks on full AES:

Attack Target Complexity Notes Biclique AES-128 \(2^{126.1}\) Marginal improvement over brute force Related-key AES-256 \(2^{99.5}\) Requires related keys — not realistic Side-channel All Low Timing, cache, power attacks Brute force AES-128 \(2^{128}\) Infeasible classically Grover AES-128 \(2^{64}\) Quantum; use AES-256 for quantum resistance

The related-key attack on AES-256 exploits weaknesses in the key schedule, not in the rounds themselves. In practice it’s irrelevant because no real protocol exposes related keys — the attacker would need to see ciphertexts encrypted under keys related by a known difference, which doesn’t happen in properly designed systems. Side-channel attacks are the real operational threat: a correctly implemented AES-256 in a leaky environment is weaker than a correctly implemented AES-128 on constant-time hardware.

AES Side-Channel Attacks

AES table-based implementations using T-tables are vulnerable to cache-timing attacks (Bernstein 2005). Use AES-NI hardware instructions or bit-sliced implementations for side-channel resistance.

docs.title: 2.1.3 Modes of Operation
docs.text:
A block cipher encrypts exactly one block. Modes extend it to arbitrary-length messages.

Mode Parallelizable IV Needed Auth ECB Yes (both) No No CBC Dec only Yes (random) No CTR Yes (both) Yes (nonce) No GCM Yes (both) Yes (nonce) Yes CCM Partial Yes (nonce) Yes SIV Yes Deterministic Yes

The mode of operation is often where implementations go wrong. The cipher itself might be perfect, but the wrong mode choice (ECB), a reused IV (CBC, CTR, GCM), or a missing MAC (CBC without authentication) converts a strong primitive into a broken system. In practice, the rule is simple: use GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 for nearly all new applications, and treat anything without built-in authentication as a footgun.

ECB Mode — Never Use

ECB encrypts each block independently with the same key. Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, leaking structure. The classic demonstration: encrypting a bitmap image in ECB mode still reveals the image’s outline.

CBC Mode:

\[\begin{align*} C_i &= E_K(P_i \oplus C_{i-1}), \quad C_0 = \mathrm{IV} \\ P_i &= D_K(C_i) \oplus C_{i-1} \end{align*}\]

The IV must be random and unpredictable; reusing it with the same key is catastrophic.

CBC’s chaining creates a critical asymmetry: encryption must run sequentially (each ciphertext block depends on the previous one), but decryption can run in parallel (you have all ciphertext blocks upfront). This is why CBC was popular for disk encryption before better modes existed — you could read any block without decrypting the whole disk. The IV predictability requirement bites HTTPS in the BEAST attack (2011): CBC in TLS 1.0 used the last ciphertext block of the previous record as the IV, making it predictable and enabling chosen-plaintext attacks against session cookies.

CTR Mode:

\[C_i = P_i \oplus E_K(\text{nonce} \| i)\]

Turns a block cipher into a stream cipher; the nonce-counter pair must never repeat.

CTR mode is elegant: the block cipher runs entirely on predictable counter values, so you can precompute the keystream before the plaintext arrives. This makes it ideal for latency-sensitive applications. The catch is that nonce-counter uniqueness is a strict requirement with no tolerance. If the same (key, nonce, counter) combination ever produces the same keystream block twice, any two plaintexts encrypted at those positions are XORed together and recoverable.

GCM (Galois/Counter Mode):

  • Encryption: CTR mode with starting counter 2

  • Authentication: GHASH (polynomial hash in \(\mathbb{F}_{2^{128}}\)) over ciphertext + AAD

  • Output: ciphertext + 128-bit authentication tag

  • Critical: Nonce must be unique per (key, nonce) pair; reuse reveals the keystream and GHASH key

GCM nonce reuse has catastrophic consequences beyond just exposing the keystream. Because GHASH uses a secret polynomial evaluation key \(H = E_K(0^{128})\), and because a nonce-reuse attack lets an attacker recover \(H\) from two (ciphertext, tag) pairs, the attacker can then forge valid authentication tags for arbitrary ciphertexts. This breaks both confidentiality and integrity simultaneously. For applications where nonce management is difficult (e.g., stateless servers, distributed systems), AES-GCM-SIV or AES-SIV provide misuse resistance at modest performance cost.

Example 2.1 (AES-GCM in Python)

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
import os

key = os.urandom(32)          # 256-bit key
nonce = os.urandom(12)        # 96-bit nonce (unique per key!)
aad = b"Associated data"      # Authenticated but not encrypted

aesgcm = AESGCM(key)

# Encrypt
plaintext = b"Secret message"
ciphertext = aesgcm.encrypt(nonce, plaintext, aad)
# ciphertext contains encrypted bytes + 16-byte authentication tag appended

# Decrypt (raises InvalidTag if authentication fails)
recovered = aesgcm.decrypt(nonce, ciphertext, aad)
assert recovered == plaintext

docs.title: 2.2 Stream Ciphers
docs.text:
Definition 2.2 (Stream Cipher)

A stream cipher generates a pseudorandom keystream from a key (and nonce), which is XORed with plaintext: \(C = P \oplus \text{KS}\).

Stream ciphers shine in environments where data arrives in a continuous stream, block boundaries are inconvenient, or latency is critical. A hardware sensor sending sensor readings byte-by-byte doesn’t naturally produce 16-byte blocks, and forcing it to buffer up to a block before encrypting introduces unacceptable latency. A well-designed stream cipher handles this naturally. The security burden shifts entirely to nonce uniqueness: the keystream must never repeat, so the nonce must change with each message.

ChaCha20-Poly1305 (RFC 8439):

  • ChaCha20: ARX (Add-Rotate-XOR) based; 20 rounds on \(4 \times 4\) matrix of 32-bit words

  • Poly1305: 128-bit MAC using polynomial evaluation over \(\mathbb{F}_{2^{130}-5}\)

  • Security: 256-bit key; 96-bit nonce; 128-bit tag

  • Advantage over AES-GCM: no hardware instruction dependency; constant time in software

  • Used in: TLS 1.3, SSH, WireGuard

ChaCha20 was designed by Bernstein as a response to RC4’s weaknesses and AES-GCM’s requirement for hardware support. On CPUs without AES-NI (including many ARM processors in mobile devices at the time), AES in software is slow and prone to timing side-channels; ChaCha20 is naturally constant-time because it uses only addition, rotation, and XOR — none of which branch on secret data or access lookup tables. Google adopted ChaCha20-Poly1305 in Chrome for HTTPS connections to mobile users, which is partly why it became a TLS 1.3 mandatory cipher.

Stream Cipher Key/Nonce Reuse

If two plaintexts \(P_1, P_2\) are encrypted with the same key and nonce:

\[C_1 \oplus C_2 = P_1 \oplus P_2\]

The XOR of ciphertexts is the XOR of plaintexts — both messages are compromised. This is the “two-time pad” failure. Nonces must never repeat.

docs.title: 2.3 Authenticated Encryption (AEAD)
docs.text:
Definition 2.3 (AEAD)

An Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data scheme provides both:

  1. Confidentiality: ciphertext reveals nothing about plaintext

  2. Integrity + Authenticity: any modification of ciphertext or AAD is detected

Interface: \(\mathsf{Enc}(K, N, M, A) \to C\) and \(\mathsf{Dec}(K, N, C, A) \to M\) or \(\perp\).

The “associated data” field is easy to overlook but critical in practice. Consider an encrypted database record where the record ID is stored in plaintext alongside the ciphertext — without authenticating the record ID, an attacker can swap the IDs and cause the server to decrypt record 7’s ciphertext while believing it’s record 3, potentially returning another user’s data. Binding the record ID into the AEAD’s AAD field ensures any such manipulation is detected and rejected.

Always Use AEAD

Never use unauthenticated encryption in practice. Unauthenticated ciphertexts are vulnerable to padding oracle attacks (CBC), bit-flipping attacks, and decryption oracle attacks. TLS 1.3 mandates AEAD; only AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are allowed.

The padding oracle attack deserves explicit attention because it has broken real systems. In CBC mode without a MAC, the server’s error response when decryption fails with a padding error leaks one bit of information per query: does the decrypted last block have valid PKCS#7 padding? An attacker who can observe this error can send crafted ciphertexts and determine the plaintext byte by byte, using roughly \(256\) queries per plaintext byte. The BEAST, POODLE, and Lucky13 attacks all exploit this pattern in different contexts. AEAD eliminates the vulnerability entirely because the authentication tag is checked before any decryption output is returned.

docs.title: 2.4 The Data Encryption Standard (DES) and Triple-DES
docs.text:
DES (1977): 64-bit block, 56-bit key, 16 rounds (Feistel network). Brute-forced in 22 hours by the EFF DES Cracker (1998). Do not use.

3DES (Triple-DES): \(C = E_{K_3}(D_{K_2}(E_{K_1}(P)))\) with 3 independent keys — effective security 112 bits (due to meet-in-the-middle). NIST deprecated 3DES in 2023; disallowed after 2024.

DES’s 56-bit key wasn’t an accident of mathematics — it was an engineering decision made under NSA influence that deliberately restricted the key space to what government decryption capabilities of the era could handle. The academic community complained at the time; by 1998 the EFF built the DES Cracker for $250,000 and proved the concern justified. 3DES was a stopgap: it re-uses DES hardware by applying it three times, but the meet-in-the-middle attack means you only get 112 bits of security from 168 bits of key material. Any new system using DES or 3DES should treat it as a bug, not a feature.

docs.title: 2.5 Pseudorandom Functions and Permutations
docs.text:
Definition 2.4 (PRF Security)

A function family \(F: \{0,1\}^k \times \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^m\) is a pseudorandom function (PRF) if no efficient adversary can distinguish \(F_K(\cdot)\) (for random \(K\)) from a truly random function.

Definition 2.5 (PRP Security)

A block cipher \(E_K: \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^n\) is a pseudorandom permutation (PRP) if it is computationally indistinguishable from a random permutation.

A secure PRP is also a secure PRF (PRP/PRF switching lemma: advantage difference \(\leq q^2/2^n\) for \(q\) queries).

The PRF/PRP distinction matters when analyzing modes of operation. CTR mode uses a block cipher as a PRF (it only calls the cipher in the forward direction, never the inverse), which means its security analysis can use the PRF assumption directly. The birthday bound in the switching lemma is the reason you need to re-key or change nonces well before reaching \(2^{n/2}\) blocks encrypted under one key: for AES with a 128-bit block, this limit is \(2^{64}\) blocks — about \(1.8 \times 10^{19}\) bytes, which sounds large, but high-throughput encrypted links can approach it faster than you’d expect.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 2.1

Encrypt the ASCII string "HELLO" (padded to 16 bytes) with AES-128 in ECB mode using key \(K = \texttt{0x00}^{16}\). Then encrypt with CBC using a random IV. Explain why ECB is insecure for structured data.

Exercise 2.2

Prove that GCM encryption is not secure if nonces are repeated: given two GCM ciphertexts \((C_1, T_1)\) and \((C_2, T_2)\) encrypted under the same key \(K\) and nonce \(N\), show how to recover the GHASH key \(H\).

Exercise 2.3

A developer encrypts a 32-byte message with AES-128-CBC without appending a MAC. An attacker intercepts and modifies the last 16 bytes of the ciphertext. Describe exactly what the decrypted plaintext looks like. How does AES-GCM prevent this?

Exercise 2.4

Compare ChaCha20-Poly1305 and AES-256-GCM on: (a) security level, (b) performance on systems without AES hardware instructions, (c) nonce misuse resistance, (d) suitability for TLS 1.3.

Exercise 2.5 (Security Proof Sketch)

Define IND-CPA security for a symmetric cipher. Prove that CTR mode instantiated with a PRF is IND-CPA secure, given that nonces are chosen randomly. What is the probability of nonce collision for \(q\) encryptions with 96-bit nonces?

docs.title: Chapter 3: Public-Key Cryptography
docs.text:
Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography uses mathematically linked key pairs: a public key for encryption or signature verification, and a private key for decryption or signing. It solves the key distribution problem that makes symmetric cryptography awkward at scale.

Before public-key cryptography, every pair of communicating parties needed to securely exchange a shared secret out-of-band — by courier, phone, or in person. For \(n\) parties, that’s \(O(n^2)\) pairwise secrets to manage. Public-key cryptography collapses this: each party publishes one public key, and anyone can now initiate a secure channel with them without any prior coordination. The tradeoff is speed — asymmetric operations are roughly 1000x slower than AES, which is why real protocols use public-key crypto only to bootstrap a symmetric session key, then switch to symmetric encryption for bulk data.

docs.title: 3.1.1 Key Generation and Core Operations
docs.text:
Definition 3.1 (RSA Key Generation)

  1. Choose large random primes \(p, q\) (each \(\sim k/2\) bits); set \(n = pq\).

  2. Compute \(\lambda(n) = \mathrm{lcm}(p-1, q-1)\) (Carmichael’s totient).

  3. Choose \(e\) with \(1 < e < \lambda(n)\) and \(\gcd(e, \lambda(n)) = 1\); typically \(e = 65537\).

  4. Compute \(d \equiv e^{-1} \pmod{\lambda(n)}\) via extended Euclidean algorithm.

  5. Public key: \((n, e)\). Private key: \((n, d)\) (with \(p, q\) for CRT optimization).

Encryption: \(c = m^e \bmod n\) Decryption: \(m = c^d \bmod n\)

The choice \(e = 65537 = 2^{16} + 1\) is near-universal in practice. It has only two set bits in binary, which minimizes the number of multiplications in the square-and-multiply exponentiation. More importantly, \(e = 3\) (the smallest valid choice) creates dangerous edge cases: for messages \(m < n^{1/3}\), the ciphertext \(c = m^3 \bmod n = m^3\) doesn’t even reduce modulo \(n\), leaking \(m\) by simply taking the cube root of \(c\) over the integers. \(e = 65537\) avoids all such small-exponent pathologies.

Theorem 3.1 (RSA Correctness)

If \(\gcd(m, n) = 1\) (true with overwhelming probability for random \(m\)):

\[(m^e)^d = m^{ed} \equiv m \pmod{n}\]

since \(ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\lambda(n)}\), so \(m^{ed} = m^{1 + k\lambda(n)} = m \cdot (m^{\lambda(n)})^k \equiv m \cdot 1 \equiv m\).

Example 3.1 (RSA with Small Numbers)

Let \(p = 11\), \(q = 13\), so \(n = 143\), \(\lambda(n) = \mathrm{lcm}(10, 12) = 60\).

Choose \(e = 7\) (since \(\gcd(7, 60) = 1\)). Then \(d = 7^{-1} \bmod 60 = 43\) (check: \(7 \times 43 = 301 = 5 \times 60 + 1\)).

Encrypt \(m = 9\): \(c = 9^7 \bmod 143 = 9\).

Decrypt: \(c^d = 9^{43} \bmod 143 = 9\). ✓

docs.title: 3.1.2 RSA Padding Schemes
docs.text:
Textbook RSA is Insecure

Unpadded RSA has multiple vulnerabilities: small message exponent attacks, multiplicative homomorphism (given \(c_1 = m_1^e\) and \(c_2 = m_2^e\), compute \(c_1 c_2 = (m_1 m_2)^e\)), and chosen-ciphertext attacks. Always use proper padding.

The multiplicative homomorphism of textbook RSA is a particularly sharp pitfall in practice. A TLS server that decrypts under RSA and returns different error messages for different failure modes is a decryption oracle. The Bleichenbacher 1998 attack exploits PKCS#1 v1.5 padding errors in exactly this way: the server reveals whether the decrypted plaintext starts with the two bytes 0x00 0x02, which is enough of a one-bit oracle to reconstruct the full plaintext after about \(10^6\) queries. The ROBOT attack in 2017 showed this vulnerability was still present in major TLS implementations, including some from F5 and Citrix, nearly two decades after it was first documented.

RSAES-OAEP (RFC 8017): For encryption.

\[\text{OAEP encode: } M \to \mathrm{EM} = (DB \oplus \mathrm{mask}_1 \| \mathrm{seed} \oplus \mathrm{mask}_2)\]

where masks are derived from a mask generation function (MGF1-SHA-256). OAEP is IND-CCA2 secure in the random oracle model.

RSASSA-PSS: For signatures. Probabilistic; provably secure; recommended over PKCS#1 v1.5.

PKCS#1 v1.5: Legacy; vulnerable to Bleichenbacher’s 1998 padding oracle attack (ROBOT attack, 2017 — still present in \(27\%\) of top-million domains). Avoid for new systems.

OAEP works by randomizing the message before the RSA operation using a hash-based mask. The randomization means identical messages produce different ciphertexts on each encryption (no determinism), which breaks the multiplicative structure that textbook RSA leaks. The MGF1 function serves as a random oracle in the security proof, which is why OAEP’s security only holds in the random oracle model — a limitation worth knowing but not usually a practical concern with SHA-256 as the underlying hash.

docs.title: 3.1.3 RSA Key Size Recommendations
docs.text:
Modulus Classical Security Quantum Security Status 1024 bits \(< 80\) bits Broken Deprecated 2048 bits 112 bits Broken Minimum; avoid for new deployments 3072 bits 128 bits Broken Acceptable to 2030 4096 bits 140 bits Broken Recommended now

RSA offers no quantum resistance. Shor’s algorithm factors \(n\) in polynomial time on a quantum computer, recovering \(p\) and \(q\) and thus the private key \(d\). No key size makes RSA quantum-safe — this is fundamental, not fixable by using larger keys. Organizations planning for long-term data confidentiality (data encrypted today that must remain secret past 2030) should begin transitioning to post-quantum algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) now. “Harvest now, decrypt later” attacks are a real threat: adversaries can store today’s RSA-encrypted traffic and decrypt it retroactively once quantum computers mature.

docs.title: 3.2 Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange
docs.text:
Definition 3.2 (Finite-Field DH (FFDH))

Let \(p\) be a prime, \(g\) a generator of \(\mathbb{Z}_p^*\). Alice and Bob exchange:

  1. Alice: \(a \leftarrow_\$ [2, p-2]\); send \(A = g^a \bmod p\).

  2. Bob: \(b \leftarrow_\$ [2, p-2]\); send \(B = g^b \bmod p\).

  3. Shared secret: \(S = A^b \bmod p = B^a \bmod p = g^{ab} \bmod p\).

DH solves a subtle but profound problem: two parties who have never met can establish a shared secret over a public channel, even with a passive eavesdropper recording every message. The insight is that the eavesdropper sees \(g^a\) and \(g^b\), but computing \(g^{ab}\) from those two values is the CDH problem — believed hard in properly chosen groups. Neither party ever transmits their secret exponent \(a\) or \(b\); they only transmit the one-way images.

DH Group Requirements

The DH group must be large enough to resist index calculus. NIST recommends:

  • RFC 3526 groups: Group 14 (2048-bit) minimum; Group 15/16 (3072/4096-bit) preferred.

  • RFC 7919 FFDHE groups: pre-standardized for TLS 1.3.

  • Avoid: groups \(< 2048\) bits, Oakley Group 1/2, non-standard custom groups.

The group choice matters beyond just the prime size. Using a custom non-standard group is dangerous because the group might have weak structure: a small order, a smooth order (whose factorization has many small prime factors), or a subgroup of known discrete logarithm. RFC 7919’s named groups were specifically chosen with large safe-prime orders to resist these attacks. Any implementation that allows configuring an arbitrary DH group should be treated as a security defect.

Logjam Attack (2015)

Researchers showed that 512-bit DH (export-grade) could be broken in hours using number field sieve precomputation. Many TLS servers were downgraded to 512-bit DH via FREAK-like negotiation. State-level adversaries could precompute logs for common 768/1024-bit groups used by millions of servers.

Defense: Disable DHE \(<\) 2048-bit; prefer ECDHE; use RFC 7919 named groups.

docs.title: 3.3.1 ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm)
docs.text:
Definition 3.3 (ECDSA)

Parameters: curve \(E\), generator \(G\) of prime order \(n\), hash function \(H\).

Key generation: \(d \leftarrow_\$ [1, n-1]\); \(Q = dG\) (public key).

Signing message \(m\):

  1. \(k \leftarrow_\$ [1, n-1]\) (ephemeral, random, unique per signature)

  2. \(R = kG\); \(r = R_x \bmod n\) (x-coordinate of \(R\))

  3. \(s = k^{-1}(H(m) + r \cdot d) \bmod n\)

  4. Signature: \((r, s)\)

Verification of \((r, s)\) on message \(m\):

  1. \(w = s^{-1} \bmod n\)

  2. \(u_1 = H(m) \cdot w \bmod n\); \(u_2 = r \cdot w \bmod n\)

  3. \((x, y) = u_1 G + u_2 Q\)

  4. Valid if \(x \equiv r \pmod{n}\)

The verification step works because expanding \(u_1 G + u_2 Q = H(m) w G + r w (dG) = w(H(m) + rd) G = (w \cdot ks) G = k G = R\). The signer picks a random \(k\), computes a “commitment” \(R = kG\), then reveals \(r = R_x\) (a one-way image of the commitment) and a response \(s\) that ties \(r\) to the message and private key. A verifier who knows the public key \(Q = dG\) can reconstruct \(R\) without knowing \(k\) or \(d\), because the math collapses correctly.

ECDSA Nonce Reuse — Catastrophic

If the ephemeral key \(k\) is reused for two signatures \((r, s_1)\) and \((r, s_2)\) on messages \(m_1, m_2\):

\[s_1 - s_2 = k^{-1}(H(m_1) - H(m_2)) \bmod n\]

From this, \(k\) can be recovered, and then the private key:

\[d = r^{-1}(s_1 k - H(m_1)) \bmod n\]

Real-world impact: Sony PlayStation 3 (2010) — static \(k = 1\) used for all firmware signatures, secret key extracted; Bitcoin wallets with weak RNG compromised; HTTPS servers with broken PRNG exposed private keys.

The PlayStation 3 break is a textbook example of catastrophic nonce failure. Sony used \(k = 1\) in their ECDSA implementation, which meant every firmware signature had the same value of \(r = G_x \bmod n\). Two signatures with the same \(r\) immediately reveals \(k = 1\) from the signature equation, and then \(d\) follows by simple arithmetic. The entire firmware signing key was recovered from just two signatures, and custom firmware could be signed as if it were official Sony software. This failure cost Sony control over their console security and was entirely avoidable.

docs.title: 3.3.2 EdDSA (Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm)
docs.text:
EdDSA (RFC 8032) addresses ECDSA’s nonce-sensitivity by deriving \(k\) deterministically:

\[k = H(b_{\text{prefix}} \| m) \bmod \ell\]

where \(b_{\text{prefix}}\) is part of the private key. Because \(k\) depends on both key and message, reuse is structurally impossible.

The deterministic nonce derivation is the key design win: signing the same message twice always produces the same signature, because \(k\) is determined by the combination of private key and message. There’s no external randomness to fail. EdDSA also doesn’t require an inverse modulo \(n\) during signing — the signature computation is a scalar multiplication and a few additions, which is simpler to implement correctly. The simpler implementation path means fewer opportunities for side-channel leakage through timing differences.

Ed25519 (Curve25519 + SHA-512):

  • \(\sim 128\)-bit security; 64-byte signatures; 32-byte public key

  • Constant-time operations: resistant to timing side-channels

  • \(\sim 70{,}000\) verifications/second on modern hardware

  • Used in: SSH (host keys), TLS 1.3, Tor, Signal, Age encryption

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ed25519 import Ed25519PrivateKey

# Key generation
private_key = Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()
public_key = private_key.public_key()

# Sign
message = b"This message is authenticated"
signature = private_key.sign(message)  # 64 bytes

# Verify (raises InvalidSignature on failure)
public_key.verify(signature, message)

# Serialize public key (32 bytes)
pub_bytes = public_key.public_bytes_raw()

docs.title: 3.3.3 X25519 (ECDH with Curve25519)
docs.text:
X25519 (RFC 7748) is the Diffie-Hellman function on Curve25519, using the Montgomery ladder for constant-time scalar multiplication:

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.x25519 import X25519PrivateKey

# Alice
alice_private = X25519PrivateKey.generate()
alice_public = alice_private.public_key()

# Bob
bob_private = X25519PrivateKey.generate()
bob_public = bob_private.public_key()

# Shared secret computation
alice_shared = alice_private.exchange(bob_public)  # 32 bytes
bob_shared = bob_private.exchange(alice_public)    # 32 bytes
assert alice_shared == bob_shared

# Derive actual key via HKDF (raw shared secret is NOT a key --- must be hashed)
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
derived_key = HKDF(
    algorithm=hashes.SHA256(),
    length=32,
    salt=None,
    info=b"handshake"
).derive(alice_shared)

The comment in the code about hashing the raw shared secret before use is not optional. The raw X25519 output is a group element, not uniformly random — it lives in a specific subgroup and has algebraic structure. Passing it through HKDF removes that structure and produces a uniformly distributed key. Skipping this step can leak information about the shared secret or produce keys with predictable bias.

docs.title: 3.4 ElGamal Encryption
docs.text:
Definition 3.4 (ElGamal)

Group \(G\) of prime order \(q\), generator \(g\). Secret key \(x\); public key \(h = g^x\).

Encrypt \(m \in G\): choose \(r \leftarrow_\$ [1, q-1]\); ciphertext \(= (g^r, m \cdot h^r)\).

Decrypt \((c_1, c_2)\): \(m = c_2 \cdot (c_1^x)^{-1} = c_2 \cdot h^{-r}\).

ElGamal encryption is semantically secure under the DDH assumption: an adversary who can’t distinguish \(g^{ab}\) from a random group element also can’t distinguish encryptions of different messages. The ciphertext \((g^r, m \cdot h^r)\) hides \(m\) because the masking value \(h^r = g^{xr}\) is computationally indistinguishable from random, which means \(m \cdot h^r\) reveals nothing about \(m\) to an observer who doesn’t know \(x\) or \(r\).

ElGamal on elliptic curves underlies ECIES (Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme), the EC analog used in many protocols.

docs.title: 3.5 RSA vs ECC Comparison
docs.text:
ECC provides equivalent security with much smaller keys, resulting in faster operations and smaller certificates. The table below maps security levels across algorithm families.

Security RSA/DH ECC AES SHA 80 bits 1024 bits 160 bits 80 bits 160 bits 112 bits 2048 bits 224 bits 112 bits 224 bits 128 bits 3072 bits 256 bits 128 bits 256 bits 192 bits 7680 bits 384 bits 192 bits 384 bits 256 bits 15360 bits 512 bits 256 bits 512 bits

The key size difference isn’t just about storage — it directly affects performance. Generating an RSA-3072 key pair is noticeably slower than generating an ECDSA P-256 key pair, and RSA signature verification at equivalent security levels is considerably slower than Ed25519 verification. On constrained devices (smart cards, IoT sensors, embedded controllers), this matters enormously: an Ed25519 verify might take milliseconds while RSA-3072 verify takes seconds. The size difference also affects TLS handshake latency: smaller certificates mean fewer packets, which matters on high-latency mobile connections.

docs.title: 3.6 Hybrid Encryption
docs.text:
Public-key encryption is orders of magnitude slower than symmetric encryption and can’t encrypt arbitrary-length messages efficiently. Hybrid encryption solves both:

  1. Generate random symmetric key \(K\) (e.g., 256-bit AES key).

  2. Encrypt \(K\) with recipient’s public key: \(C_K = \mathrm{RSAES\text{-}OAEP}(pk, K)\).

  3. Encrypt message with \(K\): \(C_M = \mathrm{AES\text{-}256\text{-}GCM}(K, M)\).

  4. Send \((C_K, C_M)\).

This is the basis of TLS, PGP, CMS (S/MIME), and virtually all asymmetric encryption in practice. Modern KEM+DEM (Key Encapsulation Mechanism + Data Encapsulation Mechanism) formalizes this construction.

The KEM/DEM split is more than organizational convenience. A KEM produces a key and an encapsulation; a DEM encrypts data under that key. Separating these two functions allows you to swap out the KEM independently of the DEM — exactly the kind of modularity needed for post-quantum migration. NIST’s ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is a post-quantum KEM designed to be a drop-in replacement for ECDH/RSA key encapsulation: swap the KEM, keep the AES-GCM DEM, and the system gains quantum resistance without redesigning the bulk encryption layer.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 3.1

Generate an RSA-2048 key pair in Python (using the cryptography library). Encrypt a 32-byte random message with OAEP-SHA256. Decrypt and verify. Time the operations.

Exercise 3.2

Explain the Bleichenbacher attack on PKCS#1 v1.5 RSA encryption. Why does the oracle (invalid padding \(\to\) error response) allow the attacker to decrypt any ciphertext?

Exercise 3.3 (ECDSA Nonce Recovery)

Suppose an ECDSA signer uses the same \(k\) for two messages with hashes \(h_1 = 10\) and \(h_2 = 20\), over a group of order \(n = 37\), yielding \(r = 13\), \(s_1 = 15\), \(s_2 = 25\). Recover \(k\) and the private key \(d\).

Exercise 3.4

Compare ECDSA and EdDSA: which is more resistant to implementation errors? Which provides stronger security guarantees? Why does EdDSA derive \(k\) deterministically?

Exercise 3.5

Implement a hybrid encryption scheme in Python: use X25519 for key agreement, HKDF-SHA256 for key derivation, and AES-256-GCM for symmetric encryption. Document each step.

Exercise 3.6

A certificate authority uses RSA-1024 as its signing key in a legacy system. A security team proposes migrating to (a) RSA-4096, (b) ECDSA P-256, (c) Ed25519. Compare these options on: security level, signature size, verification speed, and post-quantum considerations.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Cryptographic Hash Functions and MACs
docs.text: Hash functions appear in nearly every cryptographic protocol — digital signatures, message authentication, key derivation, commitment schemes, and data integrity checks all depend on them. This chapter covers the security properties they must satisfy, the main algorithm families, and the MAC constructions built on top of them.

docs.title: 4.1 Cryptographic Hash Functions
docs.text:
Definition 4.1 (Cryptographic Hash Function)

A hash function \(H: \{0,1\}^* \to \{0,1\}^n\) must satisfy:

  1. Preimage resistance: Given \(y\), hard to find \(x\) with \(H(x) = y\). (One-way)

  2. Second preimage resistance: Given \(x\), hard to find \(x' \neq x\) with \(H(x') = H(x)\).

  3. Collision resistance: Hard to find any \(x \neq x'\) with \(H(x) = H(x')\).

Collision resistance \(\Rightarrow\) second preimage resistance \(\Rightarrow\) preimage resistance (for fixed output length).

The three properties serve different protocol roles. Preimage resistance is what makes password hashing useful: you can store \(H(\text{password})\) without storing the password, and a database leak doesn’t immediately hand attackers the passwords. Second preimage resistance is what digital signatures rely on: if an attacker can find a different document with the same hash as the one you signed, they can forge your signature on their document. Collision resistance is the strongest property and is what certificate authorities need: if MD5 has collisions, two different certificate requests could hash to the same value, allowing a fraudulent certificate to carry a legitimate CA signature.

docs.title: SHA-256 (SHA-2)
docs.text:
SHA-256 uses the Merkle-Damgård construction with Davies-Meyer compression function:

Figure 4.1. Merkle-Damgård construction used by SHA-256. The message is padded, split into 512-bit blocks, and processed through compression function \(f\) iteratively.

SHA-256 constants: 8 initial hash values from fractional parts of square roots of the first 8 primes; 64 round constants from fractional parts of cube roots of the first 64 primes.

Round function: \(\Sigma_0, \Sigma_1\) (rotation-based), \(\text{Ch}\) (choice), \(\text{Maj}\) (majority) functions operating on 32-bit words.

The rotation-based operations in SHA-256 are designed to spread individual bit changes across the entire 256-bit state within a small number of rounds — the avalanche property. A single flipped input bit should, after a few rounds, have changed approximately half the output bits in an unpredictable pattern. The SHA-2 designers chose specific rotation amounts to maximize this diffusion based on algebraic and differential analysis of candidate designs. SHA-256 processes each 512-bit message block through 64 rounds before producing an intermediate hash value, ensuring any local correlation between input and output is destroyed.

docs.title: SHA-3 (Keccak)
docs.text:
SHA-3 uses the sponge construction — fundamentally different from Merkle-Damgård:

  • State: \(1600\)-bit permutation state (for SHA3-256)

  • Absorb: XOR message blocks into rate portion of state; apply Keccak-\(f[1600]\) permutation

  • Squeeze: Extract output from rate portion of state

  • Properties: Resistant to length-extension attacks (SHA-2 is vulnerable); SHAKE-128/256 provides variable-length output (XOF)

The sponge construction’s security argument is cleaner than Merkle-Damgård’s. If the inner permutation is modeled as a random permutation, the sponge is provably indistinguishable from a random oracle, with security bounded by the capacity (the hidden portion of the state). For SHA3-256, the state is 1600 bits split into 1088-bit rate and 512-bit capacity; the 512-bit capacity gives 256 bits of security against collision attacks. By contrast, Merkle-Damgård’s security relies on the compression function being collision resistant, which is a stronger and less elegant assumption.

SHA-3 wasn’t adopted because SHA-2 was broken — SHA-2 remains secure. NIST ran the SHA-3 competition (2007–2012) as insurance: if weaknesses were found in SHA-2’s Merkle-Damgård structure, the cryptographic community would already have a tested, analyzed alternative. Keccak won the competition. Having SHA-3 available has already proven valuable for protocols that need length-extension immunity or variable-length output (SHAKE variants), which SHA-2 can’t provide natively.

Algorithm Output Block Security Vulnerable to Extension MD5 128 bits 512 bits Broken Yes SHA-1 160 bits 512 bits Broken (2017) Yes SHA-256 256 bits 512 bits 128 bits Yes SHA-384 384 bits 1024 bits 192 bits No (truncated) SHA-512 512 bits 1024 bits 256 bits Yes SHA3-256 256 bits Sponge 128 bits No SHA3-512 512 bits Sponge 256 bits No BLAKE2b 512 bits 1024 bits 256 bits No (keyed)

docs.title: 4.1.2 The Birthday Attack
docs.text:
Theorem 4.1 (Birthday Bound)

In a group of \(k\) people, the probability that two share a birthday exceeds \(50\%\) when \(k \approx 1.17\sqrt{N}\) (where \(N\) is the number of possible birthdays). For hash functions with \(n\)-bit output, collisions are expected after approximately \(2^{n/2}\) evaluations.

The birthday attack works because you’re not looking for one specific collision — you’re looking for any collision among the hashes you’ve computed. With \(2^{n/2}\) hashes stored, there are roughly \(2^n/2\) pairs, and by the birthday bound the expected number of collisions among them is around one. This is a much weaker requirement than finding a preimage (which would take \(2^n\) evaluations), and it’s why a 128-bit hash provides only 64-bit collision resistance.

In practice, birthday attacks enable chosen-prefix collisions, which are more powerful than simple collisions. In a chosen-prefix collision, the attacker can pick two different meaningful prefixes \(P_1\) and \(P_2\), then find suffixes \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) such that \(H(P_1 \| S_1) = H(P_2 \| S_2)\). This is what made the 2008 MD5 rogue CA certificate attack practical: the attacker built two certificate requests with different legitimacy but the same hash, causing the CA’s signature on the legitimate one to also validate the fraudulent one.

Example 4.1 (Birthday Attack on MD5)

MD5 produces 128-bit output. A birthday attack requires approximately \(2^{64}\) hash evaluations, which is feasible with modern GPU clusters. The 2008 Chosen-Prefix Collision Attack required only \(2^{49}\) operations and was used to forge a rogue CA certificate.

SHAttered (2017): Google and CWI Amsterdam produced the first practical SHA-1 collision: two different PDF files with identical SHA-1 hash. The attack required \(2^{63.1}\) SHA-1 compressions. SHA-1 is now completely deprecated.

docs.title: 4.1.3 Length Extension Attacks
docs.text:
Length Extension Attack on SHA-256

For Merkle-Damgård hash functions (SHA-256, SHA-512):

If \(H(m)\) is known, an attacker can compute \(H(m \| \text{padding} \| m')\) for any \(m'\) without knowing \(m\).

Impact: APIs using \(\mathrm{HMAC} = H(k \| m)\) are vulnerable: the attacker extends a forged message.

Real-world: Flickr API (2009), many web APIs using improper MAC construction.

Defense: Use HMAC (which wraps the key in two hash computations) or SHA-3.

The length extension attack exploits the fact that the Merkle-Damgård final hash state is exactly the input you’d need to continue hashing. If you see \(H(m)\), you know the internal state of the hash function after processing \(m\) (plus padding), and you can resume hashing from there without knowing \(m\). This is why \(H(k \| m)\) as a MAC is broken: the attacker computes \(H(k \| m \| \text{padding} \| m')\) from just the hash output and their chosen \(m'\), without ever knowing \(k\). The attack is algebraically clean and requires zero cryptanalysis of the hash function itself.

docs.title: 4.2 Message Authentication Codes (MACs)
docs.text:
Definition 4.2 (MAC)

A MAC scheme \((\mathsf{Gen}, \text{Mac}, \text{Vrfy})\):

  • \(\mathsf{Gen}(1^\lambda) \to K\): generates key \(K\)

  • \(\text{Mac}(K, m) \to t\): produces tag \(t\) for message \(m\)

  • \(\text{Vrfy}(K, m, t) \to \{0,1\}\): verifies tag

Security: existential unforgeability under chosen-message attack (EU-CMA).

A MAC is a keyed hash: only parties with the shared key can produce valid tags. Unlike a digital signature, MAC verification is symmetric — the same key creates and verifies the tag, so MACs can’t provide non-repudiation (either party could have created the tag). For communication between two parties sharing a symmetric key (like TLS session parties), MACs are the right tool; for proving to a third party who created a message, digital signatures are needed.

docs.title: 4.2.1 HMAC
docs.text:
Definition 4.3 (HMAC Construction (RFC 2104))

\[\mathrm{HMAC}(K, m) = H\bigl((K' \oplus \texttt{opad}) \| H((K' \oplus \texttt{ipad}) \| m)\bigr)\]

where \(K'\) is \(K\) padded to block size, \(\texttt{opad} = \texttt{0x5c...5c}\), \(\texttt{ipad} = \texttt{0x36...36}\).

HMAC-SHA256 is PRF-secure under the assumption that the underlying compression function is a PRF. It’s immune to length-extension attacks.

The double-hash structure is specifically what kills length extension. The inner hash \(H(\text{ipad} \| K \| m)\) produces an intermediate value that an attacker can’t extend from, because to compute \(H(\text{opad} \| K \| \cdot)\) they’d need to know \(K\). Even if the inner hash had a length-extension vulnerability, the outer hash prevents it from being exploited. The ipad and opad constants aren’t arbitrary: they ensure the inner and outer keys are different (XOR difference is \(\texttt{0x6a...6a}\)), so an attacker can’t correlate the two hash evaluations.

import hmac
import hashlib
import os

key = os.urandom(32)      # 256-bit key
message = b"Authenticated message"

tag = hmac.new(key, message, hashlib.sha256).digest()  # 32-byte tag

# Verify (constant-time comparison to prevent timing oracle)
def verify_mac(key, message, tag):
    expected = hmac.new(key, message, hashlib.sha256).digest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, tag)  # Constant-time

assert verify_mac(key, message, tag)

Timing Oracle Attack on MAC Verification

A non-constant-time comparison (e.g., Python == or C strcmp) leaks the position of the first byte mismatch. An attacker can forge a valid MAC byte-by-byte with \(O(256n)\) queries (where \(n\) is MAC length in bytes). Always use hmac.compare_digest() or equivalent constant-time comparison.

The timing oracle attack on MAC verification is a subtle but real threat. A strcmp-style comparison returns immediately when it finds the first mismatching byte, so a comparison that takes slightly longer has more matching leading bytes. With enough measurements (to average out network jitter and clock noise), an attacker can determine the correct MAC one byte at a time: try all 256 values for byte 0, pick the one that takes longest, move to byte 1, and repeat. This is practical against local services with low timing noise. hmac.compare_digest() compares all bytes regardless of where the first mismatch is, returning in constant time.

docs.title: 4.2.2 CMAC (Cipher-Based MAC)
docs.text:
CMAC (NIST SP 800-38B) uses AES as a block cipher MAC:

  • Process message blocks through CBC-like mode with XOR tweaks \(L\), \(2L\)

  • Sub-key generation: \(L = E_K(0^n)\); \(K_1 = 2L\); \(K_2 = 4L\) (in \(\mathbb{F}_{2^n}\))

  • Tag = final CBC-MAC block XORed with appropriate sub-key

  • Used in: IPsec (RFC 4493), S/MIME, NIST protocols

docs.title: 4.2.3 Poly1305
docs.text:
Polynomial MAC used with ChaCha20:

\[\text{Poly1305}(r, s, m) = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{\lceil |m|/16 \rceil} m_i \cdot r^i + s\right) \bmod (2^{130} - 5)\]

Properties: \(r, s\) are 128-bit one-time keys; \(r\) is clamped to reduce bias; \(2^{130}-5\) is a pseudo-Mersenne prime for efficient arithmetic. Provided as ChaCha20-Poly1305 in TLS 1.3 (RFC 8439).

Poly1305 is a one-time MAC: the key pair \((r, s)\) must never be reused. In ChaCha20-Poly1305, the MAC key is derived from the ChaCha20 keystream so it’s automatically fresh with each nonce; this is why nonce reuse in ChaCha20-Poly1305 is catastrophic — it not only reuses the encryption keystream, it also reuses the MAC key, breaking authentication as well. The pseudo-Mersenne prime \(2^{130} - 5\) enables fast reduction on 64-bit hardware by exploiting the structure of the modulus in ways that a random prime wouldn’t support.

docs.title: 4.3 Key Derivation Functions (KDFs)
docs.text:
Definition 4.4 (Key Derivation Function)

A KDF derives one or more cryptographic keys from a source of keying material (IKM) and optional context/salt:

\[\text{KDF}(\text{IKM}, \text{salt}, \text{info}) \to (K_1, K_2, …)\]

KDFs serve a purpose distinct from hash functions: they turn potentially weak or structured keying material into strong, uniformly distributed keys. A Diffie-Hellman shared secret, for example, is a group element with algebraic structure — it’s not simply random bits. Passing it through HKDF removes the structure and produces output indistinguishable from random, regardless of the DH group’s specific structure. Similarly, a user’s password has low entropy and predictable patterns; a password-based KDF adds a work factor to slow brute-force attacks before producing the actual encryption key.

docs.title: 4.3.1 HKDF (RFC 5869)
docs.text:
Two-phase construction:

  1. Extract: \(\text{PRK} = \mathrm{HMAC}(\text{salt}, \text{IKM})\) — concentrate entropy

  2. Expand: \(K_i = \mathrm{HMAC}(\text{PRK}, K_{i-1} \| \text{info} \| i)\) — expand to needed length

HKDF is used in TLS 1.3’s key schedule, the Signal protocol, and WhatsApp E2EE.

The Extract-then-Expand structure handles two different problems separately. Extract takes potentially non-uniform input (a DH output, a password hash, a hardware random value) and produces a uniformly distributed pseudo-random key (PRK) of fixed size. Expand then stretches that PRK into however many key bytes the protocol needs, binding different keys to different info strings so the encryption key, the MAC key, and the IV are all cryptographically independent even though they came from the same PRK. Using the same info string for two different keys would be a subtle but serious mistake — they’d be derived identically.

docs.title: 4.3.2 Password-Based KDFs
docs.text:
Password-based KDFs intentionally incorporate significant computational cost (work factor) to slow brute-force attacks:

KDF Algorithm Memory Parallelism Use PBKDF2 HMAC-SHA Low No Legacy; TLS 1.2 PRF bcrypt Blowfish Fixed 4KB No Unix passwords scrypt SHA + block mix High (tunable) No Password hashing Argon2id Blake2 High (tunable) Yes NIST recommended

The memory-hard requirement in scrypt and Argon2 is specifically designed to defeat GPU and ASIC attacks. A modern GPU can hash billions of PBKDF2-SHA256 iterations per second, because each hash computation is independent and fits entirely in a GPU core’s registers and cache. Memory-hard functions require gigabytes of memory access with sequential read-write patterns that can’t be trivially parallelized across thousands of GPU cores — GPU memory bandwidth becomes the bottleneck, not arithmetic throughput. This levels the playing field between attackers with specialized hardware and defenders using commodity server hardware.

from argon2 import PasswordHasher

ph = PasswordHasher(
    time_cost=3,        # Number of iterations
    memory_cost=65536,  # 64 MB memory
    parallelism=4,      # Parallel threads
    hash_len=32,        # Output length
    salt_len=16         # Salt length
)

# Hash password (includes random salt automatically)
password = "correct-horse-battery-staple"
hash_value = ph.hash(password)
# e.g.: $argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$...

# Verify (raises VerifyMismatchError on failure)
ph.verify(hash_value, password)  # True

# Check if rehash needed (parameters changed)
if ph.check_needs_rehash(hash_value):
    hash_value = ph.hash(password)  # Re-hash with updated parameters

Password Storage Best Practices

  • Use Argon2id (NIST SP 800-63B recommends) with \(\geq 64\)MB memory

  • Never store plaintext passwords; never use MD5 or SHA alone

  • Always use random salt (\(\geq 16\) bytes, unique per password)

  • Server-side secret key (pepper): \(H(\text{pepper} \| \text{hash})\) — protects against DB leak

  • Have I Been Pwned API: check new passwords against known breach lists

Salting is non-negotiable for password hashing. Without a unique salt per password, an attacker who obtains the password database can precompute hashes for all common passwords once (a rainbow table), then look up every hash in the table simultaneously — attacking millions of accounts at the cost of one computation.
