With a unique random salt, precomputation doesn’t work: the attacker must hash each candidate password combined with each user’s salt separately, making the attack scale linearly with the number of users. The salt doesn’t need to be secret; it just needs to be unique.

docs.title: 4.4 Commitment Schemes
docs.text:
Definition 4.5 (Commitment Scheme)

A commitment scheme lets a prover commit to a value without revealing it, then open the commitment later:

  • \(\text{Commit}(m; r) \to c\): binding (cannot open to different value) and hiding (no info revealed)

  • \(\text{Open}(c, m, r)\): verifier checks \(c = \text{Commit}(m; r)\)

Simple hash commitment: \(c = H(r \| m)\) where \(r\) is a random 256-bit nonce. Hiding follows from \(H\)’s output revealing nothing about \(m\); binding follows from \(H\)’s collision resistance.

The random nonce \(r\) is what makes the commitment hiding. Without \(r\), an attacker could brute-force small message spaces: if the committed message is a price from $1 to $100, they just hash all 100 values and compare. With a 256-bit random nonce, the effective message space is \(2^{256}\) regardless of how small \(m\) is. This is why hash commitments always include randomness — they’re not just hashing the message, they’re hashing the message with a randomly chosen blinding factor.

Commitment schemes underlie auction protocols, coin flipping, zero-knowledge proofs, and blockchain applications.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 4.1

Compute SHA-256 of the empty string and of "abc" using Python. Verify against NIST test vectors.

Exercise 4.2

Implement a length-extension attack against \(H(K \| m)\) where \(H\) is SHA-256. Given the hash of K || "original" (assume \(|K| = 32\) bytes), compute the hash of K || "original" || padding || "appended" without knowing \(K\).

Exercise 4.3

Prove that HMAC is secure assuming the underlying hash function’s compression function is a PRF. Why does the double application of the hash prevent length extension?

Exercise 4.4

A web application stores passwords as \(\text{SHA-256}(\text{password})\) without salt. Explain: (a) why this is vulnerable to precomputation (rainbow tables), (b) why the lack of salt enables multi-target attacks, (c) how Argon2id with unique salt addresses both issues.

Exercise 4.5

Design a secure commit-reveal protocol for a two-party coin flip over the internet using hash commitments. Prove it is fair (neither party can bias the result after seeing the other’s commitment).

Exercise 4.6 (Argon2 Tuning)

You must select Argon2id parameters for a web login system. Your goals: (a) at most 500ms authentication time on server hardware, (b) resist GPU-based offline attack requiring \(> 2^{50}\) hash attempts. Discuss how you would tune time_cost, memory_cost, and parallelism.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Key Management and Public Key Infrastructure
docs.text: Cryptographic algorithms provide security only when keys are properly managed. Weak generation, improper storage, or absent rotation negates the strongest algorithms. This chapter covers the full key lifecycle, the PKI trust hierarchy, HSMs, secret sharing, and crypto-agility.

docs.title: 5.1 Key Management Lifecycle
docs.text:
Definition 5.1 (Key Management Lifecycle)

The cryptographic key lifecycle consists of stages:

  1. Generation: Create key using cryptographically secure random source

  2. Distribution: Securely deliver key to authorized parties

  3. Storage: Protect key at rest against unauthorized access

  4. Usage: Apply key for cryptographic operations

  5. Rotation: Replace key periodically or on compromise

  6. Revocation: Invalidate key before normal expiry if compromised

  7. Destruction: Securely delete key material (zeroization)

Every stage of the lifecycle is a potential failure point. Attackers don’t need to break AES-256 if they can steal the key from memory, predict it from a weak PRNG, or recover it from a disk because it was never properly zeroed. In practice, the most common key management failures are mundane: keys stored in environment variables committed to Git repos, hardcoded in application source, or written to log files during debugging. No amount of algorithm strength compensates for these operational mistakes.

docs.title: 5.1.1 Secure Key Generation
docs.text:
Keys must be generated from a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG):

import os
import secrets

# OS CSPRNG (reads /dev/urandom on Linux, CryptGenRandom on Windows)
aes_key = os.urandom(32)           # 256-bit AES key
hmac_key = os.urandom(32)          # 256-bit HMAC key

# secrets module (Python 3.6+): cryptographically secure
token = secrets.token_bytes(32)    # 256 random bits
hex_token = secrets.token_hex(32)  # 64-hex-char token
url_safe = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)

# WRONG: Do NOT use random module for cryptographic keys
import random
# bad_key = random.randbytes(32)   # Predictable! MT random is not secure

Entropy Sources

A CSPRNG is only as secure as its seed. Common failures:

  • Debian OpenSSL bug (2008): patch accidentally zeroed PID-based seed — only \(32{,}767\) possible keys for 1024-bit RSA

  • Android SecureRandom bug (2013): insufficient entropy at boot — Bitcoin wallet keys predictable

  • Virtual machines: entropy starvation at boot — wait for \(\texttt{/dev/random}\) to accumulate entropy

Modern Linux \(\texttt{getrandom()}\) syscall blocks until sufficient entropy; \(\texttt{/dev/urandom}\) does not block.

The Debian OpenSSL bug is worth studying in detail because it shows how a well-intentioned change can have catastrophic consequences. A developer trying to fix a Valgrind warning about reading uninitialized memory commented out two lines that contributed to the entropy pool. The result was that RSA keys generated on Debian-based systems for two years depended on only 15 bits of process ID. An attacker could enumerate all 32,767 possible keys and break any RSA, DSA, or ECDSA key generated on those systems. The fix required regenerating every affected key — a massive operational undertaking that many administrators delayed or skipped.

docs.title: 5.1.2 Envelope Encryption and Key Hierarchy
docs.text:
Definition 5.2 (Key Hierarchy)

A key hierarchy wraps lower-level keys with higher-level keys:

  • Root Key / Master Key: Top-level; never leaves HSM; used only to encrypt other keys

  • Key Encryption Key (KEK): Encrypts data encryption keys; rotated less frequently

  • Data Encryption Key (DEK): Used for bulk data encryption; rotated frequently

Figure 5.1. Key hierarchy. The root key never touches application servers; compromise of a DEK does not expose the KEK or Root Key.

The hierarchy exists to limit blast radius. If a single DEK is compromised — say, extracted from a running server’s memory — only the data encrypted under that specific DEK is exposed. The KEK and Root Key remain safe. When the compromise is detected, you can revoke and replace that DEK, re-encrypt the affected data under a new DEK, and the rest of the system keeps running. Without a hierarchy, a single compromised key could expose all encrypted data.

Example 5.1 (AWS KMS Envelope Encryption)

  1. Root key (Customer Master Key, CMK) stored in AWS KMS HSM — never exportable.

  2. Application calls \(\texttt{GenerateDataKey}(CMK)\) and receives plaintext DEK + encrypted DEK.

  3. Application encrypts data with plaintext DEK (in-memory); immediately discards plaintext DEK.

  4. Application stores data alongside encrypted DEK (ciphertext envelope).

  5. To decrypt: call \(\texttt{Decrypt}(CMK, \text{encrypted DEK})\) to get plaintext DEK, then decrypt data.

Key rotation: call \(\texttt{ReEncrypt}\) to re-wrap existing DEKs with new CMK — no re-encryption of data required.

docs.title: 5.2 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI)
docs.text:
Definition 5.3 (X.509 Certificate)

An X.509 certificate binds a public key to an identity, digitally signed by a Certificate Authority:

  • Subject: Identity (Common Name, Organization, Country, SANs)

  • Public Key: Subject’s public key (RSA/ECDSA/Ed25519)

  • Issuer: CA that signed this certificate

  • Validity: Not-Before and Not-After dates

  • Serial Number: Unique within issuing CA

  • Extensions: Subject Alternative Names, Key Usage, Basic Constraints

  • Signature: CA’s digital signature over all fields

X.509 certificates are the web’s identity infrastructure, but they’re frequently misunderstood. A certificate doesn’t prove that a website is trustworthy or legitimate — it proves only that a CA was convinced, at issuance time, that the subject controlled the listed domain names or had the listed identity. A phishing site can have a perfectly valid TLS certificate for its fake domain, which is why the browser padlock has always meant “encrypted connection,” not “safe site.” Domain Validated (DV) certificates in particular require only proof of domain control, which is easily automated and doesn’t verify the site’s purpose.

docs.title: 5.2.1 PKI Hierarchy
docs.text:
Figure 5.2. PKI hierarchy. Root CA private key kept offline; intermediates sign end-entity (leaf) certificates.

Why Offline Root CA?

The Root CA’s private key is the foundation of all trust. Compromising it invalidates every certificate in the hierarchy. Keeping the Root CA air-gapped means it’s only brought online for rare operations, such as signing a new intermediate CA certificate. Day-to-day issuance uses intermediate CAs; their compromise is contained.

“Offline” means literally offline: the Root CA HSM is stored in a physical vault, powered down, and brought out only for ceremonial key signings. Major public CAs document their Root CA ceremonies in detail, with notaries, external auditors, and on-camera key ceremonies. The entire process is designed around the assumption that the Root CA could be physically attacked or compromised, so its contact with networked systems is minimized to near-zero. When DigiNotar was compromised in 2011, an attacker who gained access to their online infrastructure was able to issue fraudulent certificates for Google, Yahoo, and others — the damage was possible precisely because the signing infrastructure had insufficient air-gap protection.

docs.title: 5.2.2 Certificate Validation — Chain of Trust
docs.text:
A browser validates a server certificate by:

  1. Parse server’s certificate chain (leaf + intermediates)

  2. Verify each certificate’s signature using issuer’s public key

  3. Verify each certificate’s validity period, key usage, basic constraints

  4. Verify root CA is in trusted root store (OS/browser maintained)

  5. Check Certificate Revocation: OCSP or CRL

  6. Verify hostname matches Subject/SANs (HTTPS: example.com)

Step 5 (revocation checking) is the weakest link in practice. Most browsers implement “soft fail” for OCSP: if the OCSP responder is unreachable (due to network issues, DoS, or CA outage), the browser proceeds anyway. This means an attacker who can block OCSP traffic effectively makes revocation invisible, turning revocation into a false sense of security rather than an actual control. Chrome moved to CRLite (a probabilistic bloom filter of revoked certificates distributed as browser updates) partly to address this reliability problem.

docs.title: 5.2.3 Certificate Revocation
docs.text:
Mechanism Description Limitation CRL (RFC 5280) Signed list of revoked serials Stale; large files OCSP (RFC 6960) Real-time per-cert status query Privacy leak; CA availability OCSP Stapling Server prefetches OCSP response Only current session CRLite / OCSP Must-Staple Compressed CRL in browser Limited adoption

OCSP stapling is a meaningful improvement over raw OCSP: the server fetches its own OCSP response and staples it to the TLS handshake, so clients don’t need to contact the CA. This eliminates the privacy leak (the CA learning which clients are visiting which sites), removes the CA as a reliability dependency, and prevents the soft-fail attack. OCSP Must-Staple (an X.509 extension that tells browsers to reject the certificate if no stapled response is present) would close the loop entirely, but adoption has been slow because it adds operational complexity for certificate operators.

docs.title: 5.2.4 Certificate Transparency (CT)
docs.text:
Definition 5.4 (Certificate Transparency (RFC 9162))

CT requires CAs to log every issued certificate to publicly auditable, append-only logs. Browsers require:

  • At least 2 Signed Certificate Timestamps (SCTs) from different CT logs

  • SCT embedded in certificate, TLS extension, or OCSP response

CT lets domain owners monitor for misissuance — rogue certificates for their domain.

CT logs use a Merkle hash tree structure to provide tamper evidence: appending a new certificate extends the tree, and the log operator must provide a consistency proof showing the new tree is a superset of the old one. Any retrospective deletion or modification of a logged certificate would require changing the tree root, which is publicly signed by the log operator. Multiple independent logs make it infeasible for even a colluding log operator and CA to silently remove evidence of misissuance — at least one log will have the record.

BGP Hijack to Obtain DV Certificate (2018)

An attacker hijacked BGP routes for an IP prefix, then passed ACME HTTP-01 domain validation for that IP range, obtaining a legitimate DV certificate for example.com. CT logs detected the misissuance within minutes. Certificate Transparency enables detection but not prevention.

Mitigations: DNSSEC + CAA records; multi-perspective validation (Let’s Encrypt validates from 4+ locations since 2020).

docs.title: 5.3 Hardware Security Modules (HSMs)
docs.text:
Definition 5.5 (HSM)

A Hardware Security Module is a tamper-resistant hardware device that:

  • Generates and stores cryptographic keys in hardware

  • Performs cryptographic operations internally (key never leaves HSM in plaintext)

  • Detects and responds to physical tampering (key zeroization)

  • Meets FIPS 140-3 or Common Criteria certification requirements

An HSM’s fundamental promise is that the private key never exists outside the HSM boundary in plaintext form. When you ask an HSM to sign data, it performs the computation internally and returns only the signature — the private key never leaves. This property is what makes HSMs valuable for CA signing keys and payment credentials: even a fully compromised operating system can’t extract the key, because the key only ever lives in the HSM’s own tamper-resistant storage. An attacker who compromises a server using an HSM can at most request signatures, not steal the key itself.

Use Case HSM Type Example Products PKI Root CA Network HSM / offline USB HSM Thales Luna, Entrust nShield TLS private keys Network HSM AWS CloudHSM, Google Cloud HSM Payment (PINs) PCI-HSM Thales payShield, Utimaco SecurityServer Code signing USB token Yubikey (FIPS), SafeNet eToken IoT key injection Manufacturing HSM nCipher nShield Connect

FIPS 140-3 Levels:

  1. Level 1: Software only; no physical protection

  2. Level 2: Tamper-evident labels; RBAC

  3. Level 3: Tamper-resistant; key zeroization on tamper detection

  4. Level 4: Complete physical protection; environmental attack response

Level 4 is genuinely impressive engineering. These devices monitor for unusual temperature, voltage, radiation, and physical pressure; detect epoxy-removal attempts; and respond by actively zeroizing all key material within microseconds of detecting an anomaly. An attacker who drills into a Level 4 HSM triggers key destruction before the drill reaches the secure element. In practice, most commercial deployments use Level 3, which provides strong physical protection at a reasonable cost; Level 4 is reserved for the most sensitive government and financial applications.

In practice, HSM operations add latency: a typical network HSM signing operation takes 1–5ms, compared to microseconds for an in-memory software operation. For TLS termination serving millions of connections per second, this latency matters. The standard architectural pattern is to store the TLS private key in the HSM but generate ephemeral session keys in software — the HSM only participates in the initial handshake, after which the session runs on symmetric keys in software. This preserves the key protection benefit while keeping bulk encryption throughput high.

docs.title: 5.4 Secret Sharing
docs.text:
Definition 5.6 (Shamir’s Secret Sharing)

A \((t, n)\) threshold scheme splits a secret \(S\) into \(n\) shares such that any \(t\) shares recover \(S\), but any \(t-1\) shares reveal nothing about \(S\).

Construction (over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) for prime \(p > S\)):

  1. Choose random polynomial \(f(x) = S + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + \cdots + a_{t-1} x^{t-1}\) over \(\mathbb{F}_p\)

  2. Shares: \((i, f(i))\) for \(i = 1, …, n\)

  3. Reconstruction: Lagrange interpolation on any \(t\) shares recovers \(f(0) = S\)

Shamir’s scheme provides information-theoretic security: even an unbounded adversary who has \(t-1\) shares learns nothing about \(S\). This is stronger than computational security and doesn’t depend on any hardness assumption. The reason is that for any value \(v\), there exists exactly one polynomial of degree \(t-1\) through the \(t-1\) known points that has \(f(0) = v\) — so all values of \(S\) are equally consistent with the observed shares, giving zero information to an adversary.

Example 5.2 (\((2, 3)\)-Threshold Secret Sharing)

Recover secret from shares with \(p = 17\).

Shares: \((1, 5)\), \((2, 3)\), \((3, 1)\). Use Lagrange interpolation on the first two:

\[f(x) = 5 \cdot \frac{x - 2}{1 - 2} + 3 \cdot \frac{x - 1}{2 - 1} = -5(x-2) + 3(x-1) = -2x + 7\]

Secret: \(f(0) = 7\).

Solution. Verify: \(f(1) = -2 + 7 = 5\) ✓, \(f(2) = -4 + 7 = 3\) ✓, \(f(3) = -6 + 7 = 1\) ✓.

Secret = \(7\).

Applications:

  • Root CA key protection: \((3, 5)\) — 3 of 5 key custodians required

  • HSM quorum for key recovery

  • Bitcoin BIP-39/SLIP-39 wallet seed backup

  • Secure multi-party computation (MPC) protocols

Real-world secret sharing deployments require careful operational procedures beyond the mathematics. Shares are typically printed on smart cards or written on paper and distributed to custodians in sealed envelopes. The custodians must be geographically distributed (so a single physical disaster can’t destroy quorum), belong to different organizational units (preventing insider collusion), and have clear documented procedures for convening a key ceremony. When Amazon, Google, or a major CA performs a root key ceremony, the share distribution and access controls are audited by external parties.

docs.title: 5.5 Key Rotation and Crypto-Agility
docs.text:
Definition 5.7 (Crypto-Agility)

A system is crypto-agile if cryptographic algorithms can be swapped without architectural changes — by configuration, negotiation, or API-level abstraction. This is essential for post-quantum migration.

Crypto-agility is the difference between a smooth post-quantum migration and an emergency rearchitecture project. Systems that hardcode algorithm choices into wire formats, database schemas, or key derivation logic can’t adapt without breaking changes. TLS demonstrates good agility: algorithm negotiation is built into the handshake, so transitioning from RSA to ECDSA to ML-DSA requires server and client updates but no protocol redesign. By contrast, systems that embed “SHA1WithRSA” literally in their certificate parsing code or that assume 128-byte signature buffers will need painful, risky rewrites to support ML-DSA’s larger signatures (2420 bytes for ML-DSA-44).

Key rotation best practices:

Key Type Rotation Frequency Rationale TLS certificate (public CA) 90 days Let’s Encrypt default; limits exposure TLS certificate (internal) 1 year Operational overhead vs. exposure SSH host key Every 1-2 years Or after suspected compromise DKIM signing key Quarterly Limits exposure window KMS data encryption key Annually AWS default auto-rotation API keys / tokens Per-session or 24h JWTs: short-lived; refresh tokens: rotate on use

Automated rotation is the only reliable rotation. Manual rotation processes get missed during vacations, org changes, or urgent incidents — the certificate that expired over Christmas weekend while the team was on holiday is a cliché because it happens constantly. Let’s Encrypt’s 90-day certificate lifetime was chosen specifically to force automation: manually renewing every 90 days is painful enough that operators build automation, and once automation exists, rotating more frequently is essentially free. Organizations using longer certificate lifetimes are often implicitly admitting that their renewal process is manual.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 5.1

Implement Shamir’s \((3, 5)\) secret sharing in Python. Generate shares for secret \(S = 42\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{97}\). Demonstrate reconstruction from any 3 shares. Show that 2 shares reveal nothing (compute the distribution of \(f(0)\) given only 2 shares).

Exercise 5.2

Inspect a TLS certificate from github.com using openssl s_client -connect github.com:443 or Python ssl module. Identify: issuer, subject, SANs, key type, validity period, CT SCTs, and OCSP URL.

Exercise 5.3

Explain why Certificate Transparency does not prevent the issuance of fraudulent certificates but does enable detection. Design a monitoring workflow for an organization to detect unauthorized certificates for their domains.

Exercise 5.4

An organization uses a 2048-bit RSA key for their Root CA, created in 2010. List all migration steps required to: (a) rekey to ECDSA P-384, (b) plan for post-quantum migration to ML-DSA, (c) maintain operational continuity during transition.

Exercise 5.5

Design a key management policy for a healthcare application storing encrypted PHI (Protected Health Information). Address: key types and hierarchy, storage location, rotation schedule, emergency recovery, and compliance with HIPAA Technical Safeguards.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Cryptographic Protocols and Security Proofs
docs.text:
Cryptographic protocols combine primitives to achieve security goals. This chapter introduces formal security definitions — games, reductions, and proofs — that transform intuitive claims like “this is secure” into precise, falsifiable statements.

The gap between “sounds secure” and “is provably secure” is where most real-world disasters live. WEP was designed by engineers who believed XOR-with-a-keystream was sufficient; RC4’s statistical biases and IV reuse made it catastrophically broken in practice. Formal definitions exist precisely to close that gap: by pinning down what an adversary is allowed to do and what “winning” means, we convert vague intuition into something a reduction argument can actually refute.

docs.title: 6.1 Security Definitions and Games
docs.text:
Definition 6.1 (IND-CPA Security)

A symmetric cipher \((\mathsf{Enc}, \mathsf{Dec})\) is IND-CPA (indistinguishable under chosen-plaintext attack) secure if for all PPT adversaries \(\mathcal{A}\):

\[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{ind\text{-}cpa}}_{\mathcal{A}} = \left|\Pr\left[\mathcal{A} \text{ wins}\right] - \frac{1}{2}\right| \leq \mathsf{negl}(\lambda)\]

where the game is:

  1. Challenger generates \(K \leftarrow_\$ \mathcal{K}\), bit \(b \leftarrow_\$ \{0,1\}\)

  2. \(\mathcal{A}\) may query encryption oracle \(\mathsf{Enc}_K(\cdot)\) polynomially many times

  3. \(\mathcal{A}\) submits challenge messages \(m_0, m_1\) with \(|m_0| = |m_1|\)

  4. Challenger returns \(c^* = \mathsf{Enc}_K(m_b)\)

  5. \(\mathcal{A}\) outputs \(b'\); wins if \(b' = b\)

The encryption oracle in step 2 is what separates IND-CPA from simple message privacy. Allowing an adversary to encrypt arbitrary plaintexts models real deployment: in TLS, an attacker who controls part of a web page can inject chosen content into HTTPS-encrypted requests (the BEAST and CRIME attacks exploited exactly this). A cipher that leaks anything about the plaintext — even a single bit — when the adversary can choose what else gets encrypted fails IND-CPA. This is why ECB mode fails immediately: encrypting the same block always yields the same ciphertext, so distinguishing \(m_0 = \texttt{AAAA}\) from \(m_1 = \texttt{BBBB}\) requires only one chosen-plaintext query.

Definition 6.2 (IND-CCA2 Security)

Extends IND-CPA by allowing decryption queries before and after the challenge (but not on \(c^*\) itself). CCA2 security is required for public-key encryption schemes.

The CCA2 oracle models an attacker who can cause a victim system to decrypt ciphertexts and observe the result — through error messages, timing differences, or padding oracle responses. RSA-PKCS#1v1.5 without additional integrity protection is famously CCA2-insecure: Bleichenbacher’s 1998 attack submitted millions of modified ciphertexts, used the “bad padding” error response as a decryption oracle, and recovered the full plaintext. OAEP padding was designed to resist exactly this class of attack by making every decryption failure indistinguishable from any other. The lesson is that IND-CPA security isn’t enough whenever the adversary can observe anything about failed decryptions — which is almost always true in practice.

docs.title: 6.1.1 Security Reductions
docs.text:
A security proof shows that breaking scheme \(B\) would imply breaking a hard problem \(A\):

Reductions are contrapositive arguments: if problem \(A\) is hard (no efficient algorithm exists), then scheme \(B\) must be secure (no efficient attack exists either), because an efficient attack on \(B\) would give an efficient solver for \(A\). The quality of a reduction matters enormously. A “tight” reduction loses no advantage: an adversary with advantage \(\epsilon\) against \(B\) translates directly to advantage \(\epsilon\) against \(A\). A “loose” reduction might lose a factor of \(q\) (the number of oracle queries), which forces larger parameter choices to compensate. Practical cryptographers care about tightness because it determines the concrete security level, not just the asymptotic one.

Example 6.1 (ElGamal is IND-CPA Secure under DDH)

Theorem: ElGamal encryption over a group where DDH holds is IND-CPA secure.

Proof sketch: Suppose \(\mathcal{A}\) breaks ElGamal IND-CPA with non-negligible advantage \(\epsilon\). Construct reduction \(\mathcal{R}\) that uses \(\mathcal{A}\) to distinguish \((g^a, g^b, g^{ab})\) from \((g^a, g^b, g^c)\) for random \(c\):

Given DDH challenge \((g^a, g^b, g^c)\): set \(pk = g^a\), simulate the IND-CPA game using \(g^b\) as the nonce, \(g^c\) as the mask. If \(c = ab\): ciphertext is valid ElGamal, so \(\mathcal{A}\) guesses correctly with probability \(1/2 + \epsilon\). If \(c\) is random: ciphertext looks like a random group element, so \(\mathcal{A}\) guesses uniformly. \(\mathcal{R}\)’s DDH advantage \(= \epsilon\), contradicting DDH hardness. \(\square\)

docs.title: 6.2 Formal Verification of Protocols
docs.text:
Manual analysis of cryptographic protocols fails in ways that are hard to anticipate. The Needham-Schroeder Public Key protocol was published in 1978 and widely taught as correct; Gavin Lowe found a man-in-the-middle attack in 1995 using an automated tool, seventeen years later. The attack is subtle: it requires an active attacker who is also a legitimate principal, and it exploits an identity confusion that no amount of informal reasoning had caught.

This is why formal verification tools exist. They don’t just check the cases humans think to check — they exhaustively explore the state space of all possible attacker behaviors and message orderings, making it impossible to overlook a clever interleaving.

docs.title: 6.2.1 ProVerif and Tamarin
docs.text:
ProVerif models protocols in an applied pi-calculus and automatically searches for traces that violate stated security properties. It handles unbounded sessions and an arbitrary number of protocol participants, so it catches attacks that only manifest after many runs. The tool works by translating the protocol into Horn clauses and running a resolution procedure; if the resolution terminates without finding a violating trace, secrecy or authentication is proved. ProVerif was used to formally verify the Signal Protocol, TLS 1.3, and portions of WireGuard.

Tamarin uses a different model: multiset rewriting rules with a built-in adversary who can intercept, drop, and forge messages on the Dolev-Yao network model. Security properties are expressed in a fragment of linear temporal logic. Where ProVerif resolves automatically, Tamarin sometimes requires manual guidance via lemma annotations, but it handles stateful protocols and complex key derivation hierarchies more naturally. The TLS 1.3 draft was analyzed with Tamarin; the tool uncovered that certain resumption modes had weaker forward secrecy than the core handshake.

What both tools catch that manual analysis misses: reflection attacks (where a prover’s own message is replayed back to it), type confusion (where a nonce intended as a session ID is accepted as an authenticator), and parallel session attacks (where interleaving two simultaneous runs creates a state the protocol designer never considered). The Needham-Schroeder attack is a parallel session attack. Manual analysts naturally reason about a single session; tools reason about all sessions simultaneously.

The limitation of symbolic verification is the Dolev-Yao abstraction: messages are treated as terms, not bit strings. The model assumes encryption is perfect and that XOR and modular arithmetic behave ideally. Computational soundness results (Backes-Pfitzmann-Waidner, Cortier-Warinschi) partially bridge this gap, but symbolic verification can miss attacks that exploit algebraic structure — such as the malleability attacks on CBC mode that symbolic models treat as impossible.

docs.title: 6.3 Zero-Knowledge Proofs
docs.text:
Definition 6.3 (Zero-Knowledge Proof)

An interactive proof \((P, V)\) for language \(L\) is zero-knowledge if it satisfies:

  1. Completeness: If \(x \in L\), honest \(P\) convinces \(V\) with high probability

  2. Soundness: If \(x \notin L\), no cheating \(P^*\) convinces \(V\) except with negligible probability

  3. Zero-Knowledge: \(V\) learns nothing beyond \(x \in L\): \(\exists\) simulator \(S\) such that \(\{(P, V)(x)\} \approx S(x)\)

The simulator argument is the precise meaning of “learns nothing.” If a simulator who doesn’t know the witness can produce transcripts that are computationally indistinguishable from real ones, then the verifier can’t extract the witness from the transcript — because anything in the transcript could have been generated without the witness. This is what distinguishes zero-knowledge from merely “not revealing the witness directly”: even statistical correlations that don’t directly expose the witness are forbidden.

docs.title: 6.3.1 Schnorr Protocol (Sigma Protocol)
docs.text:
Proves knowledge of discrete logarithm \(x\) such that \(h = g^x\) in group \(G\):

Prover (knows \(x\)) Verifier (knows \(g, h\)) \(r \leftarrow_\$ \mathbb{Z}_q\); \(R = g^r\) \(\xrightarrow{R}\) \(\xleftarrow{c}\) \(c \leftarrow_\$ \mathbb{Z}_q\) \(s = r + cx \bmod q\) \(\xrightarrow{s}\) Check: \(g^s = R \cdot h^c\)?

Soundness: Given two transcripts \((R, c, s)\) and \((R, c', s')\) with \(c \neq c'\):

\[g^{s-s'} = h^{c-c'} \Rightarrow x = (s-s')(c-c')^{-1} \bmod q\]

The extractor recovers witness \(x\) — proving knowledge.

The randomness of \(r\) is load-bearing. If a prover reuses \(r\) across two challenges \(c\) and \(c'\), the equation above lets anyone compute the secret \(x\) from the two responses. This is how Sony’s PlayStation 3 ECDSA key was extracted in 2010: the firmware signing used a static nonce instead of a fresh random \(r\). The attacker observed two signatures over different messages with the same \(r\) value, then solved the resulting pair of equations. A correct Schnorr implementation must use a fresh, uniformly random \(r\) for every proof.

Fiat-Shamir Transform: Replace the verifier’s random challenge with a hash of the commitment: \(c = H(g, h, R)\). This converts the Sigma protocol to a non-interactive zero-knowledge (NIZK) proof. Used in Schnorr signatures, STARK proofs, and many ZKP systems.

The Fiat-Shamir transform is secure in the random oracle model, where \(H\) behaves as a truly random function. In the standard model, it can fail against adversaries who program the hash function. In practice, the hash function must include all public parameters and the full commitment — omitting any component creates a selective-forgery attack. Early implementations of ECDSA in embedded devices sometimes hashed only the message, omitting the curve parameters, enabling cross-curve forgeries.

docs.title: 6.3.2 Modern ZKP Systems
docs.text:
System Type Proof Size Verify Time Trusted Setup Groth16 zk-SNARK \(\sim 200\) bytes \(\sim 1\) ms Yes (per circuit) PLONK zk-SNARK \(\sim 400\) bytes \(\sim 5\) ms Universal setup STARKs ZK-STARK \(\sim 100\) KB \(\sim 100\) ms No Bulletproofs NIZK \(\sim 700\) bytes \(\sim 1\) sec No

Applications: blockchain privacy (Zcash uses zk-SNARKs; Monero uses Bulletproofs), identity verification, regulatory compliance without data disclosure, secure voting.

The trusted setup in Groth16 is a significant practical concern. The ceremony generates a structured reference string (SRS) from secret randomness; if any participant in the ceremony retains their secret contribution, they can forge proofs for any statement. Zcash’s “Powers of Tau” ceremony involved thousands of contributors precisely to make it computationally implausible that all of them colluded. PLONK’s universal setup mitigates this somewhat: one ceremony covers all circuits of bounded size, rather than requiring a new ceremony per circuit. STARKs eliminate the trusted setup entirely by replacing polynomial commitments with hash-based cryptography — at the cost of much larger proofs.

docs.title: 6.4 Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC)
docs.text:
Definition 6.4 (MPC)

Multiple parties \(P_1, …, P_n\) each hold private input \(x_i\). They jointly compute \(f(x_1, …, x_n)\) such that each party learns only the output — not others’ inputs.

Yao’s Garbled Circuits: Two-party protocol where one party garbles (encrypts each gate) and the other evaluates. Enables arbitrary function computation. Used in secure auctions and private set intersection.

SPDZ Protocol: Multi-party protocol with preprocessing; allows \(n\) parties with security against active adversaries corrupting \(< n/2\) parties. Used in financial computation and healthcare data analysis.

Threshold Signatures (MPC-based): Rather than secret sharing a private key (Shamir), ECDSA signing is performed as MPC — the key is never assembled in one place. Used by Fireblocks, crypto custodians, and multi-sig wallets.

The correctness of MPC security proofs depends heavily on the corruption model. The semi-honest model assumes corrupted parties follow the protocol but try to learn information from their views; the malicious model assumes corrupted parties can deviate arbitrarily. Protocols secure against malicious adversaries require additional mechanisms — zero-knowledge proofs, MACs, or authenticated secret sharing — and are substantially more expensive. Most deployed MPC systems make an explicit choice between these models, and that choice should match the threat model: semi-honest security is appropriate when the parties are trusted organizations but privacy must be provable; malicious security is required when any party could be adversarial.

docs.title: 6.5 Oblivious RAM (ORAM)
docs.text:
Definition 6.5 (ORAM)

Oblivious RAM lets a client access a remote database such that the server learns nothing about which locations are accessed — only that accesses occurred.

Standard RAM reveals access patterns. If a cloud server knows you repeatedly access record id=42 before a stock trade, it can infer your trading strategy.

Construction (trivial): Fetch the entire database on each access — \(O(N)\) bandwidth. Efficient constructions (PathORAM, Ring ORAM) achieve \(O(\log N)\) bandwidth overhead.

PathORAM works by mapping each data block to a random leaf in a binary tree and storing encrypted blocks along every root-to-leaf path. Every access follows the same procedure: read the entire path (hiding which block you want), retrieve the target block, and write the path back with the block re-randomized to a new leaf. The \(O(\log N)\) cost comes from the path length. The key insight is that re-randomizing positions on every access prevents the server from correlating accesses even if it observes every read and write. In practice, ORAM carries a 20–100\(\times\) bandwidth overhead compared to direct access, which limits its use to latency-tolerant or highly privacy-sensitive applications such as secure enclaves and encrypted search.

docs.title: 6.6.1 TLS 1.3 Handshake (Forward Reference)
docs.text:
Client Server \(\xrightarrow{\text{ClientHello: key\_share}(g^a)}\) \(b \leftarrow_\$ \mathbb{Z}_q\); compute \(g^{ab}\); derive keys \(\xleftarrow{\text{ServerHello: key\_share}(g^b), \text{Certificate, Finished}}\) Client derives keys from \(g^{ab}\); verifies cert \(\xrightarrow{\text{Finished}}\)

Key schedule (TLS 1.3): Uses HKDF with \(\text{early secret} \to \text{handshake secret} \to \text{master secret} \to \text{application keys}\). Full forward secrecy: session keys derived from ephemeral \(g^{ab}\), so compromise of the long-term server key does not reveal past session keys.

TLS 1.3 eliminated every cipher suite that didn’t provide forward secrecy — RSA key exchange, static DH, and all the export-grade ciphers that fueled FREAK and Logjam. The only handshake modes that survive are (EC)DHE and PSK-with-DHE. This was a deliberate, breaking change from TLS 1.2: any server that still advertises RSA key exchange is running 1.2 or earlier.

0-RTT Security Considerations. TLS 1.3 introduced 0-RTT resumption, which lets a client send application data in the first flight without waiting for the server. This works because both sides retain a resumption master secret from the previous session. The security trade-off is significant: 0-RTT data has no forward secrecy (if the resumption secret is later compromised, the data is exposed) and it is not replay-protected. The TLS specification explicitly forbids non-idempotent operations over 0-RTT; HTTP GET requests are acceptable candidates, but POST requests that create orders or transfer funds are not. Servers that enable 0-RTT without enforcing idempotency create a replay window that attackers can exploit: intercepting the 0-RTT data and retransmitting it to a different server instance (or to the same server after the anti-replay state expires) causes the operation to execute twice. Mitigations include single-use session tickets and replay caches, but these impose state costs that undermine the performance argument for 0-RTT in large-scale deployments.

docs.title: 6.7 Signal Protocol (Double Ratchet)
docs.text:
The Signal Protocol (used by Signal, WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, iMessage) provides:

  • Forward secrecy: Compromise of current key does not reveal past messages

  • Break-in recovery (Post-Compromise Security): Recover security after compromise

  • Asynchronous setup: Pre-keys enable communication when recipient is offline

X3DH (Extended Triple Diffie-Hellman): Initial key agreement using identity keys + signed pre-keys + one-time pre-keys.

The X3DH design is careful about what each key type protects. The one-time pre-key (OPK) provides the strongest forward secrecy for the initial message: once it’s consumed, no future compromise can reveal the initial shared secret. But pre-keys must be uploaded to the server in batches before a conversation starts; if the server runs out of OPKs for a recipient, the protocol falls back to the signed pre-key (SPK) alone, which is slightly weaker. Signal’s server doesn’t learn anything about which pre-keys get used for which conversations, but it does know when an OPK is consumed, which creates a timing correlation. The cryptographic design acknowledges this and treats it as an acceptable metadata leak.

Double Ratchet:

  1. Diffie-Hellman ratchet: Each message in a new session derives new root and chain keys via DH step; provides break-in recovery

  2. Symmetric ratchet: Within a session, derives per-message keys via KDF chain; provides forward secrecy

The Double Ratchet achieves both forward secrecy and post-compromise security simultaneously through the interplay of its two ratchets, and understanding why requires seeing them as complementary mechanisms rather than redundant ones. The symmetric ratchet alone can provide forward secrecy: each message derives a fresh key by feeding the previous chain key through a KDF, so deleting used keys means past messages can’t be decrypted even with the current chain key. But symmetric ratcheting offers no recovery after compromise — if an attacker captures the current chain key, they can compute all future message keys by running the KDF forward. The DH ratchet fixes this: every time a new DH public key appears in an incoming message, both sides perform a fresh DH exchange and inject the result into the root KDF, producing new chain keys that the attacker’s captured chain key can’t predict. This is break-in recovery: the window of compromise is bounded by the DH ratchet step, which happens at least once per direction of conversation. An adversary who compromises a device during a conversation can read messages sent before the next DH ratchet step, but loses access after both sides rotate their DH ephemeral keys — which happens automatically on the next round-trip.

Out-of-order message handling is an important edge case. The symmetric ratchet is sequential: keys are derived in order and deleted after use. If message 5 arrives before message 4, the receiver must compute and cache the key for message 4 (by running the KDF one extra step) without being able to delete it yet. Signal caps the number of skipped message keys it caches to limit the damage if a device is compromised while holding future keys.

docs.title: 6.8 Noise Protocol Framework
docs.text:
The Noise Protocol Framework is a systematic toolkit for building handshake protocols from a small set of composable patterns. Rather than inventing a new protocol for every application (with the attendant risk of subtle errors), developers select a Noise handshake pattern that matches their authentication requirements and get a protocol with a formal security analysis essentially for free.

A Noise handshake pattern describes a sequence of message flows, each consisting of DH operations and key derivations. The pattern XX handles mutual authentication when neither party knows the other’s static key in advance: both sides transmit their static public keys during the handshake, encrypted under the evolving handshake state. The pattern IK handles the case where the initiator already knows the responder’s static key (as in Signal’s X3DH setup), enabling one fewer round-trip. The pattern NX handles one-sided authentication, analogous to a web server presenting a certificate to an unauthenticated client.

The framework’s key insight is that all of these patterns share the same underlying machinery: a chained hash state that accumulates every sent and received byte, a running symmetric key derived by mixing in each DH output, and AEAD encryption for payload confidentiality and integrity. The security properties — which parties authenticate to which, when forward secrecy begins, what an adversary who compromises a key learns about past sessions — follow mechanically from the pattern structure, and the Noise specification proves these properties for each named pattern.

Noise sees practical deployment in WireGuard, which uses the IKpsk2 pattern (IK with a pre-shared symmetric key as an additional layer of authentication). The tight codebase and formal foundation are two reasons WireGuard’s security properties are substantially easier to audit than IKEv2’s. Lightning Network BOLT 8 also uses Noise (XK pattern) for encrypted peer-to-peer channels. A common implementation pitfall is failing to include all public keys in the handshake hash: omitting a static or ephemeral key from the “mixed” transcript allows key substitution attacks where an attacker replaces the key with their own, breaking authentication without breaking the AEAD integrity.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 6.1

Prove that a one-time pad (OTP) is IND-CPA secure. Then show it is not IND-CCA2 secure by constructing a decryption oracle attack.

Exercise 6.2

Implement the Schnorr identification protocol in Python over \(\mathbb{Z}_p^*\) for a 256-bit prime \(p\). Demonstrate both the interactive version and the Fiat-Shamir non-interactive version.

Exercise 6.3

In the context of TLS 1.3: (a) Explain why TLS 1.3 provides forward secrecy while TLS 1.2 with RSA key exchange does not. (b) What does “0-RTT” (zero round-trip time) resumption achieve and what security trade-off does it make?

Exercise 6.4 (Signal Protocol)

Explain the Double Ratchet algorithm: (a) What does the DH ratchet provide that the symmetric ratchet alone cannot? (b) Why does each new conversation require a new ephemeral DH key? (c) How does the protocol handle message loss (messages arriving out of order)?

Exercise 6.5

Describe a practical application of zero-knowledge proofs in identity verification: a user proves they are over 18 without revealing their birthdate. Sketch the ZKP construction using Schnorr-based techniques.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Quantum Cryptography and Post-Quantum Migration
docs.text:
Quantum computers threaten the mathematical foundations of RSA, ECC, and Diffie-Hellman. This chapter covers the specific quantum algorithms responsible, the NIST post-quantum standards published in 2024, and practical migration strategies.

The threat is asymmetric: quantum computers don’t break all cryptography, just the cryptography whose security rests on factoring or discrete logarithm problems. Symmetric ciphers and hash functions are weakened but not broken. Understanding this distinction is essential for scoping the migration effort — organizations that replace AES-256 with a lattice-based cipher have misread the threat model, while those that ignore the RSA and ECDH in their TLS certificates have underreacted.

docs.title: 7.1.1 Shor’s Algorithm
docs.text:
Theorem 7.1 (Shor’s Algorithm, 1994)

A quantum computer can factor an \(n\)-bit integer in \(O(n^3)\) quantum gate operations and compute discrete logarithms in \(O(n^3)\) operations. Both run in polynomial time, breaking RSA, DH, ECDH, ECDSA, and DSA.

Shor’s algorithm works by reducing factoring to period-finding, then solving period-finding with a quantum Fourier transform. The period-finding step runs exponentially faster on a quantum computer than on a classical one because quantum superposition lets the circuit evaluate the function at all inputs simultaneously. This isn’t magic parallelism — measurement collapses the superposition, so the trick is designing the interference pattern so that the period (which divides into the factored answer) has high probability when measured. The algorithm requires a fault-tolerant quantum computer with roughly \(4{,}000\) logical qubits and millions of physical qubits to break RSA-2048; no such machine exists today, but the trajectory of error-correction research makes it a credible 10–15 year prospect.

Algorithm Broken by Shor Recommended Replacement RSA-2048 Yes ML-KEM / ML-DSA ECDH (all curves) Yes ML-KEM (key exchange) ECDSA / Ed25519 Yes ML-DSA / SLH-DSA AES-128 No (Grover: \(2^{64}\)) AES-256 (sufficient) AES-256 No (Grover: \(2^{128}\)) Unchanged SHA-256 No (Grover: \(2^{128}\)) SHA-384 / SHA3-256

docs.title: 7.1.2 Grover’s Algorithm
docs.text:
Theorem 7.2 (Grover’s Algorithm, 1996)

A quantum computer can search an unstructured database of \(N\) items in \(O(\sqrt{N})\) quantum operations, vs. \(O(N)\) classically.

Impact on symmetric cryptography:

  • AES-128: brute force in \(O(2^{64})\) — double key length to AES-256

  • SHA-256: preimage resistance \(O(2^{128})\) — use SHA-256 or larger

  • HMAC: key length determines security — use HMAC with 256-bit keys

Grover’s algorithm is often described as “halving the bit security” of symmetric primitives, which is accurate but sometimes misunderstood. It doesn’t break AES-256 — \(2^{128}\) quantum oracle queries is still astronomically large. The practical implication is simply that any symmetric key or hash output that previously provided 128-bit classical security now provides 64-bit quantum security, which is too weak. AES-256 and SHA-256 already have the right key lengths for a post-quantum world; AES-128 and SHA-1 do not. No algorithm changes are required for symmetric cryptography, only parameter upgrades.

docs.title: 7.1.3 Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL)
docs.text:
HNDL Attack

Nation-state adversaries are recording encrypted traffic now, intending to decrypt it once cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQC) become available.

Timeline: Most estimates place CRQC at 5–15 years. Data with long secrecy requirements (state secrets, medical records, financial data) must be protected by PQC today.

Evidence: CISA, NSA, and NIST have confirmed this threat. NSA CNSA 2.0 (2022) mandates PQC transition for national security systems.

The HNDL threat is concrete, not theoretical. Traffic collection at internet exchange points and undersea cable landing stations is well within the capability of major intelligence agencies, and large-scale encrypted data archiving is operationally simple compared to the actual decryption problem. The implication for data classification is uncomfortable: any TLS session key negotiated with ECDH today is potentially stored somewhere and will be decryptable in a decade. This means the window for protecting sensitive data that must remain confidential for ten or more years has already closed for classical key exchange. Organizations with genuinely long-lived confidentiality requirements — law firms, healthcare systems, government contractors — should already be deploying hybrid PQC key exchange in their TLS stacks.

docs.title: 7.2.1 ML-KEM: FIPS 203 (Key Encapsulation)
docs.text:
Based on CRYSTALS-Kyber, Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) problem:

Definition 7.1 (Learning With Errors (LWE))

Given many samples \((A_i, b_i)\) where \(A_i \leftarrow_\$ \mathbb{Z}_q^n\) and \(b_i = A_i^T s + e_i\) for secret \(s\) and small error \(e_i\), find \(s\). This is believed hard even for quantum computers.

The noise term \(e_i\) is what makes LWE hard. Without noise, solving the system is straightforward Gaussian elimination over \(\mathbb{Z}_q\). With small noise, the equations don’t have exact solutions and the best known classical or quantum algorithms require exponential time in \(n\). The “module” variant operates over polynomial rings rather than raw integer vectors, which allows more efficient key and ciphertext sizes while preserving the hardness reduction. The practical implication of LWE-based cryptography is that key sizes are much larger than classical schemes: ML-KEM-768 public keys are 1,184 bytes versus 32 bytes for X25519, which matters for constrained devices and protocol designs that assume short keys.

ML-KEM key encapsulation:

  1. KeyGen: Generate polynomial ring matrices \((A, s, e)\); public key \(pk = (A, As + e)\)

  2. Encaps:\((pk) \to (K, c)\): Encrypt random shared secret using public key

  3. Decaps:\((sk, c) \to K\): Recover shared secret using secret key

Parameter Set Security Public Key Ciphertext ML-KEM-512 128 bits (NIST Level 1) 800 bytes 768 bytes ML-KEM-768 192 bits (NIST Level 3) 1184 bytes 1088 bytes ML-KEM-1024 256 bits (NIST Level 5) 1568 bytes 1568 bytes 
import oqs

# Key Encapsulation with ML-KEM-768
kem_alg = 'ML-KEM-768'

with oqs.KeyEncapsulation(kem_alg) as recipient:
    public_key = recipient.generate_keypair()

    # Sender encapsulates shared secret
    with oqs.KeyEncapsulation(kem_alg) as sender:
        ciphertext, shared_secret_sender = sender.encap_secret(public_key)

    # Recipient decapsulates
    shared_secret_recipient = recipient.decap_secret(ciphertext)

assert shared_secret_sender == shared_secret_recipient
print(f"Shared secret: {shared_secret_sender.hex()}")  # 32 bytes

docs.title: 7.2.2 ML-DSA: FIPS 204 (Digital Signatures)
docs.text:
Based on CRYSTALS-Dilithium, MLWE + MSIS (Module Short Integer Solution):

import oqs

sig_alg = 'ML-DSA-65'  # 192-bit security

with oqs.Signature(sig_alg) as signer:
    public_key = signer.generate_keypair()
    message = b"Document requiring PQC signature"
    signature = signer.sign(message)      # ~3293 bytes for ML-DSA-65

with oqs.Signature(sig_alg) as verifier:
    is_valid = verifier.verify(message, signature, public_key)
    print(f"Signature valid: {is_valid}")  # True

Signature size comparison:

Algorithm Signature Size Security Level ECDSA P-256 64 bytes 128 bits (broken by quantum) Ed25519 64 bytes 128 bits (broken by quantum) RSA-2048 PSS 256 bytes 112 bits (broken by quantum) ML-DSA-44 2420 bytes 128 bits (quantum resistant) ML-DSA-65 3293 bytes 192 bits (quantum resistant) SLH-DSA-128s 7856 bytes 128 bits (hash-based)

docs.title: 7.2.3 SLH-DSA: FIPS 205 (Hash-Based Signatures)
docs.text:
Definition 7.2 (SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+))

SLH-DSA builds signatures from hash functions only — no algebraic structure. Security relies solely on hash function properties (preimage resistance, collision resistance).

Construction: Hypertree of Merkle trees + FORS (Forest of Random Subsets). Stateless — no need to track used keys (unlike XMSS, LMS).

The natural use case is Root CA signatures and firmware signing where the strongest possible conservatism is warranted, since security depends only on the hash function, not on unproven lattice assumptions. If lattice cryptography turns out to have an unexpected weakness (as happened with multivariate schemes that NIST removed from consideration), SLH-DSA signatures remain valid because their security reduces solely to hash function collision resistance. The trade-off is size: a 7,856-byte signature is impractical for high-frequency signing (TLS certificates, code signing at scale) but acceptable for long-lived root CA certificates that are rarely re-signed. Organizations planning their PQC migration should plan to use ML-DSA for most signature applications and reserve SLH-DSA for the highest-value, lowest-frequency signatures.

docs.title: 7.3 Hybrid Cryptography for Migration
docs.text:
During the transition period, hybrid schemes combine classical and post-quantum components. If either component holds, the combined secret holds. This is the right default posture for most organizations right now: it provides immediate protection against HNDL attacks (because an attacker who archives traffic today can’t use a future quantum computer to recover the PQC component) while preserving protection against a hypothetical break in the lattice assumption (because the classical ECDH component still holds). Hybrid deployment doesn’t require abandoning existing PKI — it adds an additional key share to the TLS handshake alongside the existing ECDH share, which is backward compatible in TLS 1.3’s key share extension.

Definition 7.3 (Hybrid Key Exchange)

Combine classical (X25519) and PQC (ML-KEM-768) key shares:

\[\text{SharedSecret} = \mathrm{HKDF}\left(\mathrm{X25519\_shared} \| \mathrm{MLKEM\_shared}\right)\]

Security holds if either the classical or PQC component is secure.

Protocol Hybrid Group Status TLS 1.3 X25519 + ML-KEM-768 Chrome 124+, Firefox (experimental) SSH curve25519 + ML-KEM-768 OpenSSH 9.9+ IKEv2 (IPsec) ECDH + ML-KEM RFC draft; limited support

docs.title: 7.4 Quantum Key Distribution (QKD)
docs.text:
Definition 7.4 (BB84 Protocol)

The quantum channel sends qubits in one of four states: \(\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle, |+\rangle, |-\rangle\}\) (rectilinear and diagonal bases). Eavesdropping disturbs the quantum state (no-cloning theorem) and is therefore detectable.

The shared key is derived from matching-basis measurements; an error rate above threshold causes the protocol to abort.

QKD Limitation Notes Distance: \(\sim 100\) km without repeater Quantum repeaters in research Requires dedicated fiber or free-space link No internet-scale deployment Expensive: \(>\$100\)K per link Not cost-effective for most organizations Authentication still needed Requires classical authenticated channel

Consensus: The NIST PQC standards are the practical path forward; QKD is niche (government point-to-point links).

QKD advocates point out that its security is information-theoretic rather than computational: no amount of computing power breaks BB84 because the eavesdropping detection is based on quantum mechanics, not hardness assumptions. This is true in principle. The practical objection is that the authentication layer required to run QKD still uses classical cryptography, so QKD’s theoretical purity is already compromised. More fundamentally, the distance and infrastructure constraints mean QKD will never scale to the internet: protecting a single 500-km link requires a chain of trusted repeater nodes, each of which is a classical attack surface. PQC, by contrast, runs over existing infrastructure with a software update.

docs.title: 7.5 Migration Strategy
docs.text:
1. Inventory: Discover all RSA/ECC usage (certificates, code signing, VPN, SSH)

  2. Prioritize: Long-lived data first (HNDL risk); then authentication; then ephemeral

  3. Hybrid deployment: Add ML-KEM alongside ECDH in TLS/SSH now (double protection)

  4. Crypto agility: Refactor to algorithm-negotiation architecture

  5. HSM updates: Firmware updates for ML-KEM/ML-DSA support

  6. Certificate re-issuance: Plan for ML-DSA certificates as CA support grows

  7. Timeline: NIST/NSA mandate: classical algorithm retirement by 2030–2035

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 7.1

Using the oqs Python library, implement a complete hybrid TLS-like key exchange: X25519 + ML-KEM-768. Derive a 256-bit session key using HKDF from the combined shared secrets.

Exercise 7.2

An organization stores encrypted medical records using RSA-2048 key wrapping. Estimate how many years of data are at risk from HNDL attacks if a CRQC emerges in 10 years. What is the immediate remediation?

Exercise 7.3

Compare the bandwidth impact of migrating TLS certificates from ECDSA P-256 to ML-DSA-65: calculate the increase in certificate size, the impact on TLS handshake size, and the latency overhead for a mobile user on a 50 Mbps connection.

Exercise 7.4

Explain why AES-256 is considered quantum-safe while RSA-2048 is not. Specifically, why does Grover’s algorithm require \(2^{128}\) queries to break AES-256 but Shor’s algorithm can break RSA-2048 efficiently?

Exercise 7.5 (NSA CNSA 2.0 Compliance)

The NSA CNSA 2.0 Suite requires PQC for all National Security Systems by 2030. List the specific algorithm transitions required for: (a) key agreement in classified VPNs, (b) software signing for weapons systems, (c) encrypted storage in classified networks. Map each to FIPS standards.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Network Security Fundamentals
docs.text:
Network security protects data in transit and the infrastructure that carries it. Understanding TCP/IP, routing, and network architecture is prerequisite to deploying effective defenses. This chapter builds that foundation before the deeper dives into firewalls, IDS/IPS, and protocol-specific security.

The original designers of TCP/IP optimized for resilience and interoperability, not security. The assumption was a cooperative network of trusted hosts; authentication and integrity were intentionally left to higher layers. Forty years later, the internet runs on the same core protocols, and their original design assumptions are the source of most network-layer attacks. Understanding why a protocol is vulnerable is more useful than memorizing the attack name: it lets you generalize across protocol generations and anticipate where new vulnerabilities will emerge.

docs.title: 8.1 Network Attack Surface
docs.text:
The TCP/IP stack presents attack surfaces at every layer:

Layer Protocol Threat Defense Physical Ethernet Wiretapping, jamming Fiber, physical security Link ARP, STP ARP spoofing, VLAN hopping DAI, port security Network IP, ICMP IP spoofing, routing attacks BCP38, RPKI Transport TCP, UDP SYN flood, session hijack SYN cookies, TLS Application HTTP, DNS Injection, spoofing Input validation, DNSSEC

docs.title: 8.1.1 TCP Three-Way Handshake and Attacks
docs.text:
SYN Flood DoS

The attacker sends many SYN packets with spoofed source IPs. The server allocates half-open connections, filling the backlog queue, and legitimate connections are rejected.

Defense: SYN cookies (encode state in ISN; no memory allocation until SYN-ACK acknowledged); rate limiting; SYN proxy (firewall).

SYN cookies are elegant precisely because they make the server stateless for the connection establishment phase. The server encodes the full TCP state (initial sequence number, window size, timestamp) into the SYN-ACK sequence number using a cryptographic hash of the four-tuple (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port) plus a secret. When the ACK arrives, the server recomputes the cookie and verifies it without having stored anything. The cost is that TCP options negotiated in the SYN (like SACK and window scaling) can’t be remembered, which degrades throughput for legitimate connections established during an attack. SYN cookies aren’t free — they trade memory exhaustion for a slight throughput penalty, which is almost always the right trade.

TCP Session Hijacking

If the attacker can predict TCP sequence numbers, they can inject packets into an existing session. Network-level MITM enables eavesdropping.

Defense: TLS (encrypts and authenticates all data); random ISN generation; OS-level RST protection.

Early TCP implementations used predictable ISN generation (often a counter that incremented by a fixed amount every second), which made blind sequence number prediction trivial. Kevin Mitnick exploited this in the 1994 attack against Shimomura: by predicting the server’s sequence numbers, he injected an RSH command without needing to intercept any traffic. Modern operating systems use cryptographically random ISN generation, but the lesson generalizes: any protocol field that an attacker can predict and that the receiver trusts for authentication is a potential injection vector.

docs.title: 8.2 Firewalls
docs.text:
Definition 8.1 (Firewall)

A firewall enforces an access control policy between network zones by filtering traffic based on defined rules.

Firewall rules are processed top-to-bottom (or in priority order), and the first matching rule wins. This means rule ordering is a security property, not just a performance property. A rule that allows traffic before a deny rule reaches the deny rule first, negating it. Auditing firewall rule bases is partly an exercise in reading them in order and identifying shadowed rules (rules that can never be reached because an earlier rule matches all their traffic) and over-permissive rules that were added for a specific use case but never narrowed.

docs.title: 8.2.1 Packet Filter (Stateless)
docs.text:
Examines each packet independently against a rule table:

# Default deny all incoming
iptables -P INPUT DROP
iptables -P FORWARD DROP
iptables -P OUTPUT ACCEPT

# Allow established/related connections
iptables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# Allow SSH from management network only
iptables -A INPUT -s 10.0.0.0/24 -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT

# Allow HTTP/HTTPS from anywhere
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp -m multiport --dports 80,443 -j ACCEPT

# Allow loopback
iptables -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT

# Log and reject everything else
iptables -A INPUT -j LOG --log-prefix "DROP: "
iptables -A INPUT -j DROP

docs.title: 8.2.2 Stateful Inspection
docs.text:
Tracks connection state (NEW, ESTABLISHED, RELATED, INVALID). Only responses to outbound connections are allowed. Unsolicited inbound traffic is blocked even from otherwise-allowed ports.

Stateful firewalls track the connection table in memory, which creates a resource exhaustion attack: an attacker who sends many SYN packets (never completing the three-way handshake) fills the state table, preventing the firewall from tracking new legitimate connections. This is why stateful firewalls should sit behind rate-limiting and anti-spoofing mechanisms, not before them. The RELATED state is also a source of subtle vulnerabilities: FTP active mode uses a control connection on port 21 and a data connection on a dynamically chosen port, and the firewall must parse the FTP control channel to know which data port to allow. Application-layer protocol parsers in stateful firewalls can themselves contain vulnerabilities, as demonstrated by the numerous CVEs in connection tracking modules over the years.

docs.title: 8.2.3 Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW)
docs.text:
NGFW adds application-layer inspection:

  • Application ID: Identify application regardless of port (e.g., SSH tunneled over HTTPS)

  • User ID: Tie policies to user identities (AD integration)

  • Content inspection: Decrypt TLS, inspect for malware, IPS

  • URL filtering: Categorize and block web content

  • Threat prevention: Integrated IPS + anti-malware

  • Products: Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet FortiGate, Check Point, Cisco FTD

docs.title: 8.3.1 IPsec
docs.text:
IPsec operates at Layer 3, providing transparent encryption for all IP traffic:

Mode Scope Use Case Transport Protects payload only; IP header in clear Host-to-host Tunnel Encapsulates entire IP packet in new IP Site-to-site, remote access

IKEv2 (RFC 7296) — key exchange:

  1. IKE_SA_INIT: Propose crypto algorithms; DH exchange; nonce exchange

  2. IKE_AUTH: Authenticate peers (certificate or PSK); establish first Child SA

  3. CREATE_CHILD_SA: Additional SAs; rekeying

IKEv2 supports a wide range of cipher suites through its SA proposal negotiation, which is both a strength and a liability. The Logjam attack (2015) exploited the ability to downgrade DH key exchange to 512-bit export-grade groups, which a state-level adversary could precompute. IKEv2 deployments that allow weak DH groups (group 1: 768-bit MODP, group 2: 1024-bit MODP) should remove them explicitly. RFC 8247 mandates a minimum of 2048-bit MODP or ECDH with P-256. Dead Peer Detection (DPD) is another practical configuration consideration: without DPD, a crashed remote peer leaves a phantom SA consuming firewall state until the rekeying timer expires, sometimes hours later.

docs.title: 8.3.2 WireGuard
docs.text:
Modern VPN protocol using:

  • Crypto: Curve25519 (DH), ChaCha20-Poly1305 (AEAD), BLAKE2s (hash), SipHash (hashtable), HKDF (key derivation)

  • Noise Protocol Framework: Formal handshake

  • Code size: \(\sim 4,000\) lines (vs OpenVPN \(\sim 100,000\); IPsec much more)

WireGuard’s opinionated crypto selection — no cipher negotiation, no algorithm agility — is a deliberate security choice. IPsec’s negotiation phase has been the source of numerous downgrade attacks; WireGuard eliminates the attack surface by removing the negotiation entirely. If a future cryptographic break affects ChaCha20 or Curve25519, WireGuard would need a protocol version bump rather than a configuration change, which is a steeper migration but a much smaller attack surface in the meantime. The protocol’s “silent rejection” of packets from unknown peers (no response, no error message) also prevents fingerprinting: a scanner can’t distinguish a WireGuard endpoint from a closed UDP port.

WireGuard has a notable privacy property: it doesn’t track which peers are “online” in the traditional sense. Peers don’t send keepalive packets unless PersistentKeepalive is configured, so an inactive peer generates no traffic. However, WireGuard does associate each peer with a static public key, which means the server sees a persistent identifier for each device. This is appropriate for site-to-site VPNs but worth considering for user-privacy contexts where device tracking is a concern.

# Server /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf
[Interface]
PrivateKey = <server_private_key>
Address = 10.0.0.1/24
ListenPort = 51820

# Allow traffic through (NAT for internet access)
PostUp   = iptables -A FORWARD -i wg0 -j ACCEPT; \
           iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE
PostDown = iptables -D FORWARD -i wg0 -j ACCEPT; \
           iptables -t nat -D POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE

[Peer]
PublicKey = <client_public_key>
AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.2/32  # Which client IPs are allowed from this peer

docs.title: 8.4 Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Definition 8.2 (Network Segmentation)

Dividing a network into zones with controlled access between them limits lateral movement after compromise.

Segmentation’s value is containment: when an attacker compromises one system, they face additional authentication and access control barriers before reaching more valuable targets. Without segmentation, a compromised developer workstation can reach production database servers directly, because “all internal traffic is trusted.” With segmentation, the same compromised workstation can only reach the systems that workstation’s role legitimately requires — the developer doesn’t need to connect directly to production databases, so the firewall between the developer VLAN and the production VLAN blocks that traffic.

DMZ: Public-facing services (web, email, DNS); accessible from internet but isolated from internal. Internal: Corporate users, workstations; no direct internet access. Restricted: Servers with sensitive data (PCI, PHI, source code); strict access control. Management: Out-of-band; only jump server access; no user applications.

docs.title: 8.4.1 Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA)
docs.text:
Zero Trust is a response to the failure of the perimeter model. When an organization’s data lives in SaaS applications, employees work from home networks and coffee shops, and adversaries routinely compromise VPN credentials, the concept of a trusted inside and an untrusted outside stops being useful. ZTNA replaces implicit network-location-based trust with explicit identity-and-posture-based access decisions for every request.

Zero Trust Principles

NIST SP 800-207 seven tenets:

  1. All data sources and services are resources

  2. All communication is secured regardless of network location

  3. Access to individual resources is granted per-session

  4. Access determined by dynamic policy (identity + device + behavior)

  5. Monitor and measure integrity of all owned assets

  6. Authentication and authorization strictly enforced before access

  7. Collect data to improve security posture

The practical implementation of Zero Trust requires solving three distinct problems. Identity verification (who is this user?) is solved by strong MFA and identity providers like Okta or Azure AD. Device posture assessment (is this device healthy?) requires an MDM or EDR agent that attests to patch level, disk encryption status, and the presence of endpoint security software before granting access. Least-privilege access (what should this identity on this device be able to reach?) requires moving beyond VPN-style “access to the network” to application-level access policies — a contractor’s laptop gets access to the specific project management tool they need, not a route to the entire corporate subnet. Micro-segmentation enforces least-privilege at the network level by creating per-application trust zones rather than per-VLAN trust zones, which is what traditional segmentation provides.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 8.1

Design iptables rules for a web server hosting HTTP/HTTPS, with SSH access restricted to a management subnet 192.168.100.0/24, and all other traffic blocked. Include rate limiting for HTTP.

Exercise 8.2

Compare IPsec tunnel mode and WireGuard for a remote access VPN on: key management, performance, crypto agility, and post-quantum readiness. Which do you recommend and why?

Exercise 8.3

A SYN flood attack sends 1 million SYN packets per second. A server without SYN cookies can hold 1024 half-open connections for 30 seconds each. Calculate: (a) how many legitimate new connections are blocked, (b) how SYN cookies eliminate this bottleneck.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Firewalls, IDS, and IPS
docs.text:
Intrusion detection and prevention systems (IDS/IPS) monitor network traffic and host activity to detect and respond to attacks in real time. This chapter covers deployment architectures, detection methods, rule syntax, and the SIEM and SOC infrastructure that ties everything together.

No firewall policy is perfect, and no ruleset anticipates every attacker technique. IDS and IPS exist because network defenders accept this reality: some traffic will reach the interior of a network, and the question is how fast the team detects and responds to it. The distinction between detection and prevention sounds like a product-marketing choice, but it reflects a genuine engineering trade-off about where to accept false positives in the detection pipeline.

docs.title: 9.1 IDS vs IPS Architecture
docs.text:
Definition 9.1 (IDS/IPS)

  • IDS (Intrusion Detection System): Monitors traffic, generates alerts, but does not block. Passive mode; inline or out-of-band (span/tap).

  • IPS (Intrusion Prevention System): Inline deployment; can block, drop, or reset traffic in real time. Adds latency but can prevent attacks.

docs.title: 9.1.1 Deployment Topology Decisions
docs.text:
The IDS-vs-IPS choice isn’t made once for an entire network; it’s made per segment, per traffic class, and per tolerance for both false positives and latency.

An out-of-band IDS deployment (tap or SPAN port) has zero impact on production traffic flow. If the IDS crashes or falls behind on packet processing, no legitimate traffic is dropped. This makes it the right choice for high-throughput links where availability is paramount — a 100 Gbps backbone that carries SLA-protected traffic simply can’t tolerate the risk of a software bug in the detection engine dropping packets. The trade-off is that the IDS can only alert, not block: by the time the analyst sees the alert and acts, the attack payload has already reached the destination. For fast-moving attacks like exploit delivery, a detection-only posture often means the attacker has already won by the time the team responds.

An inline IPS deployment interposes the detection engine in the traffic path, which means both blocking and additional latency. Typical software-based IPS engines add 1–5 ms per packet for full signature inspection; hardware-accelerated appliances (FPGA-based inspection in Palo Alto and Check Point gear) keep this below 100 µs at line rate. The latency cost matters enormously for trading systems and real-time industrial control networks, and it’s negligible for most enterprise web traffic. The failure mode also differs: a failing inline IPS either fails open (all traffic passes, losing blocking capability) or fails closed (all traffic drops, causing an outage). Fail-open is nearly universal in enterprise deployments because a security outage is less damaging than a production outage, but this means the IPS protection disappears exactly when the device is under stress — which is often when an attack is in progress.

A mature enterprise network typically deploys both: out-of-band IDS for high-throughput internal backbone links (detection only, comprehensive logging), inline IPS at internet ingress and egress (blocking known-bad signatures), and host-based IDS (HIDS) on critical servers (file integrity monitoring, process execution logging). The layers compensate for each other’s blind spots. Network IDS misses encrypted traffic and host-level activity; HIDS misses lateral movement between hosts; inline IPS at the perimeter misses attacker-controlled systems inside the network.

Network TAP vs. SPAN port: Both deliver a copy of traffic to an out-of-band sensor, but they differ in reliability. A TAP (test access point) is a passive optical or electrical device that physically splits the signal; it copies traffic even during switch CPU saturation and can’t drop packets. A SPAN port is a switch software feature that mirrors traffic, but during high load the switch prioritizes forwarding over SPAN copying — under a DDoS, the SPAN port may deliver 20% of the traffic the IDS expects to see. For forensic-quality capture, hardware TAPs are mandatory; for operational detection, SPAN is usually adequate.

docs.title: 9.2 Detection Methods
docs.text:
Method How Pros Cons Signature-based Match known attack patterns Low false positives Misses zero-days Anomaly-based Deviate from statistical baseline Detects unknowns High false positive rate Behavioral Patterns of behavior over time Detects APT Complex tuning Heuristic Rule-based logic beyond signatures Flexible Can be evaded

Signature-based detection is fast and precise because signatures encode specific, known-bad patterns: a byte sequence in a packet payload, a JA3 TLS fingerprint, or a particular combination of HTTP headers. The false positive rate is low when signatures are well-written, which is why signature-based engines work well in high-volume environments where every false positive requires analyst time. The fundamental weakness is coverage: a signature can only match attacks the signature writer has already seen. Zero-day exploits, novel malware families, and living-off-the-land attacks that use legitimate system tools don’t trigger signatures.

Anomaly detection inverts the problem: build a statistical model of normal behavior and alert on deviations. This theoretically catches anything sufficiently unusual, including attacks that have never been seen before. The operational problem is that enterprise networks are not stationary: baseline traffic changes with business hours, software deployments, marketing campaigns, and seasonal load. An anomaly system tuned during a quiet period will flood analysts with alerts after a software release that changes network patterns. The false positive rate in production environments without careful continuous tuning is typically high enough to cause alert fatigue, which is arguably worse than missing detections because it teaches analysts to ignore the SIEM.

docs.title: 9.3 Snort/Suricata Rule Syntax
docs.text:
# Detect Cobalt Strike default Certificate (JA3 hash)
alert tls any any -> any any ( \
  msg:"Cobalt Strike JA3 Fingerprint"; \
  ja3.hash; content:"a0e9f5d64349fb13191bc781f81f42e1"; \
  sid:1000001; rev:1; )

# Detect SQL injection attempt in HTTP URI
alert http any any -> $HTTP_SERVERS any ( \
  msg:"SQL Injection Attempt"; \
  flow:established,to_server; \
  http.uri; content:"union+select"; nocase; \
  sid:1000002; rev:1; )

# Detect PowerShell download cradle
alert http any any -> any any ( \
  msg:"PowerShell Download Cradle"; \
  flow:established,to_server; \
  http.user_agent; content:"PowerShell"; \
  sid:1000003; rev:1; )

# Detect C2 beacon (periodic connection to same host)
alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any ( \
  msg:"Potential C2 Beacon"; \
  flow:established,to_server; \
  detection_filter:track by_src, count 10, seconds 60; \
  threshold:type both, track by_src, count 10, seconds 60; \
  sid:1000004; rev:1; )

Definition 9.2 (Snort/Suricata Rule Format)

action proto src_ip src_port -> dst_ip dst_port (options)
