  • action: alert, drop, pass, reject

  • proto: tcp, udp, icmp, http, tls, dns

  • options: msg, content, pcre, sid, rev, flow, threshold

The JA3 fingerprint rule in the example above catches the default Cobalt Strike certificate fingerprint without inspecting the encrypted TLS payload — JA3 is computed from the unencrypted ClientHello fields (TLS version, cipher suites, extensions, elliptic curves, and curve point formats). This is an important technique: TLS encryption hides application data, but metadata in the handshake is always visible. Sophisticated red teams randomize their JA3 fingerprints to evade such rules, so production rulesets should also examine certificate subject fields, server certificate validity periods, and connection timing patterns rather than relying on a single fingerprint.

The C2 beacon rule uses a detection_filter to avoid alerting on normal outbound connections: it only fires after ten connections to the same destination within sixty seconds from the same source. This catches the periodic callback behavior of most C2 frameworks (Cobalt Strike default beacon interval is 60 seconds) while tolerating normal bursty outbound web traffic. Tuning these thresholds requires understanding the baseline: a development machine constantly pulling from a package registry might trigger this rule legitimately.

docs.title: 9.3.1 YARA Rules for Threat Hunting
docs.text:
While Suricata and Snort operate on network traffic in real time, YARA operates on files, memory dumps, and disk images — making it the primary tool for malware identification and threat hunting across endpoints and storage.

Definition 9.3 (YARA Rule)

A YARA rule describes a pattern (strings, byte sequences, regular expressions) combined with a boolean condition. The scanner matches the rule against a file or memory region and returns whether the condition is satisfied.

rule CobaltStrike_Beacon_PE
{
    meta:
        author      = "SOC Team"
        description = "Detects Cobalt Strike Beacon in PE files"
        severity    = "high"
        mitre       = "T1059.003"

    strings:
        // Default Cobalt Strike named pipes
        $pipe1 = "\\\\.\\pipe\\msagent_" wide ascii
        $pipe2 = "\\\\.\\pipe\\status_"  wide ascii

        // Beacon configuration watermark (XOR-encoded header)
        $cfg_magic = { 00 01 00 01 00 02 }

        // Common reflective loader export
        $refl = "ReflectiveLoader" ascii

        // Sleep obfuscation artifact
        $sleep_mask = "sleep_mask" ascii

    condition:
        uint16(0) == 0x5A4D          // MZ header (PE file)
        and filesize < 10MB
        and (
            $refl
            or 2 of ($pipe1, $pipe2, $cfg_magic)
            or ($sleep_mask and $cfg_magic)
        )
}

The meta section is purely documentary — YARA ignores it during matching, but analysts rely on it for triage. Including MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs and a severity rating lets automated platforms route matches to the right response playbook without requiring an analyst to look up context. The strings section defines named patterns; hex byte sequences (enclosed in braces) match raw bytes and are endian-aware, making them useful for catching magic numbers and binary structures that text patterns would miss. The condition block is where the logic lives: the uint16(0) == 0x5A4D check reads the first two bytes of the file and confirms this is a PE (Windows executable), which avoids scanning through every file type looking for strings that could appear coincidentally in text. Restricting to filesize < 10MB cuts down scan time; Cobalt Strike beacons are almost always under 1 MB.

YARA rules should express the minimum sufficient condition, not try to be maximally specific. A rule that matches only exact byte sequences will miss repacked or recompiled malware; a rule that matches only generic PE headers will have an unacceptable false positive rate. The art is in identifying indicators that are stable across malware variants (build artifacts, protocol structures, naming conventions chosen by the malware author) rather than indicators that change every compilation (hashes, specific addresses).

For live threat hunting, YARA integrates with EDR platforms (CrowdStrike Falcon, Carbon Black, SentinelOne), memory forensics tools (Volatility), and SIEM pipelines. A common workflow is to write a YARA rule from a malware sample discovered in an incident, then retrospectively scan endpoint memory dumps and quarantined files across the fleet to determine whether the same threat touched other systems — a lateral movement check that can run in hours across thousands of endpoints.

docs.title: 9.4 SIEM — Security Information and Event Management
docs.text:
Definition 9.4 (SIEM)

A SIEM aggregates, correlates, and analyzes log data from across the environment to detect security incidents and support investigation.

Core SIEM functions:

  1. Log collection: Syslog, Windows Event Forwarding, Beats agents, API

  2. Normalization: Parse heterogeneous log formats to common schema

  3. Correlation: Apply detection rules across multiple sources and time windows

  4. Alerting: Generate incidents on rule matches; enrich with threat intel

  5. Investigation: Search interface; timeline visualization; case management

-- Detect PowerShell with encoded command (ATT&CK T1059.001)
index=windows source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4688
  NewProcessName="*powershell.exe*"
  CommandLine="*-enc*" OR CommandLine="*-EncodedCommand*"
| stats count by Computer, Account, CommandLine
| where count > 0
| sort -count

-- Detect impossible travel (login from two different countries within 1 hour)
index=auth
| iplocation src_ip
| stats values(Country) as Countries, values(src_ip) as IPs by user, span(time,1h)
| where mvcount(Countries) > 1

docs.title: 9.4.1 Correlation Logic and Alert Fatigue Mitigation
docs.text:
Correlation is what separates a SIEM from a log aggregator. A single failed SSH login is noise; a hundred failed SSH logins from the same IP across fifty different accounts in five minutes is a credential-stuffing attack. A single administrative tool execution is normal; the same tool executed by a service account outside business hours on a system it has never touched is anomalous. Correlation rules combine signals from multiple log sources and time windows to produce higher-confidence detections.

Writing effective correlation rules requires understanding both the attack technique and the baseline. The MITRE ATT&CK framework maps techniques to the log sources and event IDs that surface them: T1003.001 (LSASS memory dumping) generates Event ID 4656 (object access) on LSASS, as well as Sysmon Event 10 (process access); correlating both provides higher confidence than either alone. A rule that fires on Event ID 4656 alone generates enormous volume from legitimate processes; combining it with a GrantedAccess mask of 0x1410 (the mask used by Mimikatz) narrows the signal substantially.

Alert fatigue is the primary operational failure mode of SIEM deployments. When analysts receive more alerts than they can investigate, triage quality degrades: alerts get marked “false positive” without investigation because it’s faster, real incidents get dismissed because they look like the thousandth identical noisy alert, and eventually the SIEM becomes a compliance checkbox rather than a detection platform. Mitigating alert fatigue requires active effort:

  • Threshold tuning: After every false positive, adjust the rule threshold or add exclusion filters. Keep a log of adjustments to track drift.

  • Risk scoring: Weight alerts by asset criticality (a Domain Controller login alert is more urgent than the same alert on a developer workstation), threat intel enrichment (does the IP appear in a blocklist?), and behavioral context (has this account done this before?).

  • Alert suppression: Suppress repeated alerts for the same source/destination pair within a time window once an incident ticket is open. The analyst is already working it.

  • Correlation before alerting: Fire an alert only when multiple low-confidence signals combine, rather than alerting on each individually. A single outbound connection to a rare domain is noise; the same host also running whoami.exe and net user /domain within ten minutes is an alert.

docs.title: 9.4.2 Machine Learning-Based Detection
docs.text:
Rule-based detection fails against novel attacks that don’t match known patterns. ML-based detection addresses this by learning what normal looks like and flagging deviations — the same goal as anomaly detection, but with models sophisticated enough to handle the high dimensionality of network and endpoint telemetry.

Isolation Forests are a practical algorithm for anomaly detection in network flow data. The core idea is intuitive: anomalous points are “easier to isolate” than normal points. The algorithm builds an ensemble of random binary trees by repeatedly selecting a random feature and a random split value. An anomalous data point (unusual source port, unusual byte volume, unusual timing) gets isolated in a short path because its feature values are far from the normal cluster; a normal data point requires many splits because it’s surrounded by similar points. The anomaly score is the average path length across all trees, normalized to a 0–1 scale.

An isolation forest applied to network flows might use features such as: bytes per second, packet inter-arrival time, ratio of inbound to outbound bytes, number of unique destination ports per source per hour, and time-of-day. A host that suddenly starts exfiltrating data via DNS (unusually high bytes per DNS query, unusually high query volume) will have feature values outside the normal distribution and receives a high anomaly score. Unlike a threshold rule, the forest adapts automatically as baseline behavior shifts over time through periodic retraining.

The operational challenge is not the algorithm — isolation forests are fast to train and score — but the feedback loop. ML models generate scored events, not categorized alerts. The security team must choose a score threshold that converts scores into alerts, and that threshold must balance false positive rate (too low: every batch job triggers an alert) against false negative rate (too high: real attacks are missed). Without analyst feedback on which high-scored events are real threats, the model can’t improve. Effective ML-based detection in a SOC requires a labeled dataset of confirmed incidents, a feedback pipeline from analyst verdicts back to the model, and ongoing tuning as attacker techniques evolve.

docs.title: 9.5 SOC Architecture
docs.text:
Definition 9.5 (Security Operations Center (SOC))

A SOC is the centralized function responsible for continuous security monitoring, detection, analysis, and response.

SOC Tiers:

  1. Tier 1 — Triage: Monitor SIEM alerts; initial categorization; escalate to Tier 2

  2. Tier 2 — Analysis: Deep investigation; threat hunting; escalate incidents

  3. Tier 3 — Response/Threat Intel: Malware reverse engineering; advanced threat hunting; adversary attribution

Key SOC Metrics:

Metric Definition Target MTTD Mean time to detect \(< 24\) hours MTTR Mean time to respond \(< 4\) hours MTTC Mean time to contain \(< 8\) hours Alert-to-Incident ratio Alerts resulting in real incidents Improve signal/noise

docs.title: 9.5.1 Threat Hunting Workflow
docs.text:
Reactive alert-driven SOC operations catch attacks that trigger rules. Threat hunting is the complementary proactive practice: analysts hypothesize that a threat actor is already present in the environment and go looking for evidence, regardless of whether any alert fired. The assumption is that sophisticated adversaries know how to avoid triggering standard detection rules, so waiting for an alert is insufficient.

A structured threat hunting workflow follows four stages:

1. Hypothesis generation. A good hypothesis is specific enough to be testable. “Adversaries are present” is not testable. “A threat actor using Living Off the Land techniques is using wmic.exe to run remote commands for lateral movement (ATT&CK T1047)” is testable: it specifies the tool, the technique, and the log sources that would capture it (Windows Event 4688 process creation logs, Sysmon Event 1). Hypotheses come from threat intelligence reports (“this threat actor is known to use technique X against organizations in our sector”), recently published CVEs in software the organization runs, purple team exercises, and anomalous data patterns that don’t quite rise to alert thresholds.

2. Data collection and querying. The analyst queries the SIEM or a dedicated data lake for evidence of the hypothesized activity. For the wmic.exe example, this means searching for process creation events where the parent process is wmic.exe, restricting to service accounts or privileged users (lateral movement typically uses elevated accounts), and looking for activity on hosts where that account has never previously run wmic.exe. The hunt uses a broader query than a detection rule would: the goal is to find needles even if there’s a lot of hay, so initial queries intentionally produce more results than an automated rule can handle.

3. Investigation and triage. The analyst works through the results, distinguishing legitimate administrative use from suspicious activity. This requires context: is this system a jump server where wmic.exe queries are normal? Is the account a legitimate IT administrator? Does the timing align with a change window? The output of this stage is either “this is benign, update our exclusion list” or “this is suspicious, open an incident.”

4. Operationalization. Every confirmed true positive from a hunt should become a detection rule or a refinement of an existing rule, so the next occurrence alerts automatically. Every false positive should become an exclusion or a threshold adjustment. The hunt improves the detection stack even when it finds nothing, because the analyst learns which queries are noisy and why. Without this feedback loop, hunts remain labor-intensive one-off exercises instead of building institutional detection capability.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 9.1

Write a Suricata rule to detect DNS requests for domains longer than 50 characters (potential DNS tunneling/DGA). Include a threshold to reduce false positives.

Exercise 9.2

A SOC receives 10,000 alerts per day but has capacity to investigate 100. Design a prioritization framework incorporating: asset criticality, threat intelligence, alert source, and MITRE ATT&CK technique stage.

Exercise 9.3

Compare signature-based IDS and anomaly-based IDS: which has the higher false positive rate? Which detects zero-day attacks? Design a deployment architecture combining both approaches.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Network Protocol Security
docs.text:
This chapter examines security mechanisms built into foundational Internet protocols. We analyze where the original protocol designers made security trade-offs, how attackers exploit those gaps, and how modern extensions restore the integrity and confidentiality properties that were missing from early designs.

The pattern repeats across protocols: DNS, BGP, ARP, and NDP were all designed before adversarial internet-scale deployment was a realistic concern. Each was later retrofitted with authentication extensions (DNSSEC, RPKI, DAI, SEND) that preserve backward compatibility at the cost of complexity. Understanding the original vulnerability and the retrofit’s limitations prepares practitioners to reason about which deployments actually close the attack surface versus which create a false sense of security.

docs.title: 10.1 DNSSEC: Authenticating the Domain Name System
docs.text:
The Domain Name System was designed in the early 1980s with no authentication whatsoever. A resolver that receives a DNS response cannot distinguish a legitimate answer from a forged one injected by an on-path attacker—a vulnerability exploited in the Kaminsky attack of 2008, which could poison a caching resolver in under a minute.

The Kaminsky attack works because DNS uses 16-bit transaction IDs (TXID) and UDP source port randomization as the only anti-spoofing mechanism. An attacker who can send forged responses faster than the legitimate nameserver can race to answer the resolver’s query. With a 16-bit TXID and a fixed source port, there are only 65,535 possible values: a fast attacker floods the resolver with all 65,535 forged responses, betting one will arrive and match the TXID before the legitimate answer. Kaminsky’s insight was that an attacker could cause the resolver to make many queries in rapid succession by querying random subdomains (each generates a new TXID), giving thousands of shots at the race without waiting for cache TTLs to expire. Modern resolvers use both source port randomization (extending the space to \(65535 \times 65535 \approx 2^{32}\)) and 0x20 encoding (randomizing the case of query letters, since DNS is case-insensitive for resolution but case-preserving in the response, so a forged response must match the exact capitalization the resolver used). Even so, a 32-bit entropy space is vulnerable to off-path spoofing attacks from fast networks. DNSSEC is the only complete fix.

DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions, RFC 4033–4035) retrofits public-key signatures onto DNS. Every zone operator generates a key pair; the public key is published as a DNSKEY record, and every resource record set (RRset) is signed, producing an RRSIG record.

docs.title: 10.1.1 ZSK/KSK Split and the Chain of Trust
docs.text:
DNSSEC Key Hierarchy

KSK (Key Signing Key) Long-lived, high-value key. Used only to sign the DNSKEY RRset. Typically 2048-bit RSA or P-256 ECDSA. ZSK (Zone Signing Key) Shorter-lived key used to sign all other RRsets. Rolling ZSKs every 30–90 days limits exposure. DS record A hash of the child zone’s KSK, published by the parent zone, forming the chain of trust up to the root.

The root zone’s KSK is the Trust Anchor. ICANN maintains an offline ceremony to sign the root KSK; the 2010 and 2018 key rollovers were broadcast publicly. A validator begins at a locally configured trust anchor (often the root), walks the DS chain downward, and verifies each RRSIG with the corresponding DNSKEY.

The 2018 root KSK rollover highlighted an operational risk in DNSSEC: about 25 million resolvers worldwide had their trust anchor configured to the old KSK only and had not fetched the new one via RFC 5011 automatic rollover. Had ICANN not delayed the rollover, those resolvers would have started returning SERVFAIL for all DNSSEC-signed domains globally. A trust anchor is a hard dependency — if the validator’s configured trust anchor doesn’t match the current signed key at the root, everything under that zone appears forged. Operators who deploy DNSSEC validation must implement automated trust anchor updates and monitor for rollover events.

DNSSEC also doesn’t protect the last mile between the recursive resolver and the client application. A validating recursive resolver at 8.8.8.8 performs full DNSSEC validation, but if your application sends its DNS query over plain UDP to the resolver, an attacker on your local network can still inject a forged response before it arrives. DNS-over-TLS or DNS-over-HTTPS between the client and the validating resolver closes this gap.

Figure 10.1. DNSSEC chain of trust from root to resource record.

docs.title: 10.1.2 NSEC3 Authenticated Denial of Existence
docs.text: When a queried name does not exist, DNSSEC must prove that fact without leaking the full zone contents. NSEC records expose the sorted list of all names; NSEC3 (RFC 5155) uses salted SHA-1 hashes of owner names to prevent zone enumeration while still allowing authenticated denial.

docs.title: 10.1.3 Key Rollover
docs.text: RFC 7583 defines the recommended ZSK pre-publish rollover: (1) publish new ZSK in DNSKEY RRset; (2) wait one TTL for caches to pick it up; (3) switch all signing to new ZSK; (4) wait one TTL; (5) remove old ZSK. KSK rollover additionally requires updating the DS record at the parent.

docs.title: 10.2 DNS Privacy: DoH, DoT, and ODoH
docs.text:
Plain DNS leaks query contents to every hop between the client and resolver. Three standards address this:

Table 10.1. DNS Privacy Protocol Comparison Protocol Port RFC Notes DNS-over-TLS (DoT) 853 TCP RFC 7858 Easy to block; resolver sees client IP DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) 443 TCP RFC 8484 Blends with web traffic; resolver sees IP Oblivious DoH (ODoH) 443 TCP RFC 9230 Proxy decouples IP from query content DNS-over-QUIC (DoQ) 853 UDP RFC 9250 Low latency; nascent deployment

ODoH introduces an Oblivious Proxy between client and target resolver. The client encrypts the DNS query for the target using HPKE; the proxy cannot read the query; the target cannot see the client IP. Combined with DNSSEC, ODoH provides both confidentiality and integrity.

The threat model for DNS privacy protocols differs from DNSSEC’s. DNSSEC protects the content of DNS answers against forgery. DoT, DoH, and ODoH protect the confidentiality of DNS queries against eavesdroppers. These are orthogonal: you can have forged answers delivered confidentially (DoH without DNSSEC) or authentic answers delivered in plaintext (DNSSEC without DoT/DoH). A complete DNS security posture requires both. DoH also has an important operational impact: because it uses port 443 and looks like HTTPS traffic, enterprise firewalls can’t easily block it without also blocking legitimate web traffic, which means employees can bypass corporate DNS filtering using a hard-coded DoH resolver. Enterprise deployments therefore typically deploy canary DNS domains or TLS inspection to detect DoH usage that bypasses the corporate resolver.

docs.title: 10.3 BGP Security and RPKI
docs.text:
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) was designed in 1989 with no authentication. Any autonomous system (AS) can announce any IP prefix, enabling prefix hijacking and route leaks.

Pakistan Telecom BGP Hijack, 2008

On 24 February 2008, Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) announced a more-specific 208.65.153.0/24 prefix that covered YouTube’s 208.65.152.0/22. The announcement propagated globally within minutes, black-holing YouTube traffic for approximately 2 hours. No cryptographic authentication was required to make the announcement.

RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure, RFC 6480) binds IP address blocks to their legitimate holder via X.509 certificates rooted at the five Regional Internet Registries (RIRs). An operator creates a Route Origin Authorization (ROA):

Route Origin Authorization:
  AS:        64496
  Prefix:    192.0.2.0/24
  Max-Length: 24
  Not Before: 2024-01-01
  Not After:  2025-01-01

Routers running an RPKI-to-Router (RTR) daemon obtain validated prefix-origin pairs and can set route preference: Valid, Invalid, or NotFound. BGPsec (RFC 8205) adds per-hop AS-path signatures but has seen limited deployment due to performance cost.

docs.title: 10.3.1 What RPKI Validates and What It Doesn’t
docs.text:
RPKI with ROAs validates one thing precisely: that the AS announcing a prefix is authorized to originate it. It does not validate the AS path — the list of intermediate autonomous systems through which the announcement traveled. An attacker can take a legitimate ROA-valid origin announcement and prepend their own AS to the path (a route leak), and RPKI won’t flag it. They can also announce a more-specific prefix that overlaps with a ROA-covered block; if the ROA’s max-length field permits the more-specific announcement, RPKI marks it valid even though it causes traffic to divert.

The max-length field is a common misconfiguration. Operators sometimes set it too permissively (e.g., max-length: 32 for a /24 allocation), which means any more-specific prefix up to a /32 from that AS is RPKI-valid. An attacker who hijacks a host route inside that block gets a “Valid” RPKI result because the origin AS matches and the prefix length is within bounds. Correct ROA hygiene requires max-length to equal the actual prefix length of all announced prefixes, with separate ROAs for each aggregate and more-specific announcement that legitimately originates.

Even with perfect ROA coverage, RPKI enforcement is uneven. Routers that receive an “Invalid” route can drop it (route origin validation in strict mode), prefer valid routes, or ignore the status entirely. As of 2024, roughly 50% of IPv4 prefixes have ROAs but enforcement by receiving ASes is far less consistent. A route marked Invalid by one AS’s RPKI validator may still be accepted by an AS that hasn’t enabled validation. BGPsec would close the AS-path gap but requires all ASes along a path to sign their announcements, and a single non-participating AS breaks the chain — which is why BGPsec deployment remains near zero despite years of standardization effort.

docs.title: 10.4 ARP Spoofing and Dynamic ARP Inspection
docs.text:
ARP has no authentication. An attacker on the same Layer-2 segment can send gratuitous ARP replies, poisoning the ARP cache of victims and enabling man-in-the-middle attacks. ARP caches accept unsolicited replies — a host can send a gratuitous ARP (a reply with no corresponding request) and every device on the segment that receives it will update its cache. Tools like arpspoof and ettercap automate this: the attacker sends gratuitous ARPs claiming the gateway IP maps to the attacker’s MAC, then sends the same for the victim, positioning themselves between all gateway-bound traffic. Because ARP operates below the transport layer, TLS provides no protection against the man-in-the-middle position itself — but TLS certificate verification prevents the attacker from decrypting intercepted HTTPS traffic (assuming the victim doesn’t click through a certificate warning).

Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) is a Cisco IOS feature that validates ARP packets against the DHCP snooping binding table (IP \(\leftrightarrow\) MAC \(\leftrightarrow\) port):

! Enable DHCP snooping globally
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10,20

! Mark uplinks and server ports as trusted
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip dhcp snooping trust
 ip arp inspection trust

! Enable DAI per VLAN
ip arp inspection vlan 10,20

! Rate-limit ARP on untrusted ports
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 ip arp inspection limit rate 100

Packets with MAC-to-IP bindings not found in the snooping table are dropped and the port may be error-disabled.

docs.title: 10.5 IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Security
docs.text: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) replaces ARP and adds router discovery, but inherits the same lack of authentication. Key threats include rogue Router Advertisements (RAs) that redirect all traffic through an attacker.

docs.title: 10.5.1 RA Guard (RFC 6105)
docs.text: Switches inspect incoming ICMPv6 packets and drop RA messages received on ports configured as host-facing. Only uplink ports designated as router-facing are permitted to forward RAs.

docs.title: 10.5.2 SEND (RFC 3971)
docs.text: Secure Neighbor Discovery uses Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA): the lower 64 bits of an IPv6 address are derived from the node’s public key via SHA-1. Every NDP message is signed with the corresponding private key, preventing spoofing. Deployment is rare due to high computational overhead.

docs.title: 10.5.3 Privacy Extensions (RFC 8981)
docs.text: Nodes generate temporary, randomized interface identifiers for outbound connections, renewed periodically (default: 24 h preferred, 48 h valid). The stable address derived from EUI-64 or stable-opaque (RFC 7217) is used for inbound services.

docs.title: 10.6 WPA3-Personal: SAE/Dragonfly Key Exchange
docs.text:
WPA2-Personal used the 4-way handshake with a Pre-Shared Key (PSK) that is vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks if the handshake is captured. WPA3-Personal replaces PSK with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE), also known as Dragonfly (RFC 7664).

SAE Handshake Steps

  1. Both parties independently derive a Password Element (PE)—a point on an elliptic curve—from the password and their MAC addresses, using a deterministic hunting-and-pecking or hash-to-curve algorithm.

  2. Each party generates a random scalar \(r\) and element \(E\), then sends a Commit message: \((scalar, element) = (r + mask \bmod q,\; -(mask \cdot PE))\).

  3. After receiving the peer’s Commit, each derives the shared secret \(K = (r_{self} + mask_{self})(r_{peer} \cdot PE + E_{peer})\).

  4. A Confirm message (HMAC of the transcript) proves knowledge of \(K\) without revealing it.

SAE provides forward secrecy: capturing the exchange does not allow offline password guessing because no verifier of the password is transmitted. WPA3 also mandates PMF (Protected Management Frames, 802.11w) to prevent deauthentication attacks.

WPA2’s vulnerability to offline dictionary attacks was severe in practice. An attacker who captures the 4-way handshake (which airodump-ng and a deauthentication frame make trivially easy to collect) can test billions of password candidates offline using GPU-accelerated tools like hashcat. For an 8-character password from the printable ASCII alphabet, the full keyspace is about \(95^8 \approx 6 \times 10^{15}\); a modern GPU cluster running at \(10^{11}\) tests per second searches it in under a day. SAE eliminates this attack entirely: every SAE exchange produces a unique shared secret derived from the ephemeral randomness, so captured SAE transcripts contain no offline-testable verifier. The only way to test a password guess is to attempt a new SAE handshake, which the access point rate-limits and can lock out after repeated failures.

A known limitation of SAE is the Dragonblood vulnerability family (2019): timing and cache side-channel attacks against the hunting-and-pecking algorithm allowed offline password recovery from observed handshake timing. The fix was to replace hunting-and-pecking with a hash-to-curve algorithm that runs in constant time; updated implementations (WPA3 R2) are immune, but older devices that received no firmware update remain vulnerable.

docs.title: 10.7 ICMP Security Policy
docs.text: Table 10.2. Recommended ICMP Filtering Policy Type Name Direction Action 0 Echo Reply In Allow (if stateful) 3 Destination Unreachable In Allow (needed for PMTUD) 8 Echo Request In Allow (selective) / Drop 11 Time Exceeded In Allow (traceroute) 3/4 Fragmentation Needed In Allow (PMTUD critical) 5 Redirect In Drop (potential attack) 17 Address Mask Request Both Drop (obsolete)

docs.title: 10.8 Protocol Security Deployment Status
docs.text: Table 10.3. Protocol Security Extension Deployment Status (2024) Protocol Mechanism Deployment DNS DNSSEC \(\sim\)35% of TLDs fully signed; patchy recursive validation DNS DoT / DoH Growing; major resolvers (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8) support both BGP RPKI \(\sim\)50% of IPv4 prefixes have ROAs; enforcement varies BGP BGPsec Experimental only IPv6 SEND Minimal; academic Wi-Fi WPA3 Mandatory for Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) certification Email DNSSEC+DANE \(<\)5% of mail servers

docs.title: 10.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 10.1

A DNSSEC validator receives an RRSIG with a signature expiry timestamp in the past. The resolver’s system clock is accurate. Describe what the validator should do and explain the security consequence of accepting expired signatures.

Exercise 10.2

You are the network administrator for AS64497. You discover that a neighboring AS is announcing a more-specific prefix that overlaps with your legitimate 203.0.113.0/24 allocation. Describe two immediate technical actions and one long-term structural remedy.

Exercise 10.3

A penetration tester on a wired LAN segment captures an ARP exchange and observes that the victim’s ARP cache now maps the gateway IP to the attacker’s MAC. List the prerequisites for this attack, three artifacts a forensic analyst could find to prove it occurred, and the exact DAI configuration needed to prevent it.

Exercise 10.4

Compare the forward secrecy properties of WPA2-Personal (4-way handshake with PSK) and WPA3-Personal (SAE). Assume an attacker recorded 1,000 WPA2-Personal handshakes and 1,000 WPA3-Personal SAE exchanges using a password-length-8 dictionary. How many offline operations does each scenario require, and why?

docs.title: Chapter 11: Web Application Security Fundamentals
docs.text: Web applications are the dominant attack surface for external threats. This chapter surveys the most critical vulnerability classes, their underlying causes, and proven mitigations. All code examples reflect patterns observed in bug bounty programmes and penetration tests.

docs.title: 11.1 OWASP Top 10 (2021) Overview
docs.text: Table 11.1. OWASP Top 10 2021 ID Category Representative CWEs A01 Broken Access Control CWE-200, 201, 284 A02 Cryptographic Failures CWE-259, 327, 331 A03 Injection CWE-89, 77, 79 A04 Insecure Design CWE-209, 256, 501 A05 Security Misconfiguration CWE-16, 611 A06 Vulnerable Components CWE-1035, 937 A07 Auth & Session Failures CWE-287, 384 A08 Software & Data Integrity CWE-494, 829 A09 Security Logging Failures CWE-117, 778 A10 SSRF CWE-918

docs.title: 11.2 SQL Injection
docs.text:
SQL injection remains one of the most impactful vulnerability classes. When user-supplied input is concatenated into a SQL query, an attacker can alter the query’s logic, extract arbitrary data, or in some configurations execute OS commands. The root cause is a failure to separate data from code: the database parser can’t distinguish between the SQL the developer intended and the SQL the attacker smuggled in through the input.

A subtler variant called second-order injection trips up developers who correctly escape input on the way in but then re-use that stored data in a subsequent query without re-escaping. An attacker registers a username of admin’--, which is stored safely. Later, a password-reset routine reads the username from the database—trusting it as “already sanitised”—and drops it directly into a new query. The stored payload fires at that second use. This is why the fix must be parameterised queries everywhere, not just at the input boundary.

ORMs (Object-Relational Mappers like SQLAlchemy, Django ORM, or Hibernate) give a false sense of security if developers drop into raw SQL for complex queries. Calling session.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name=’name’") inside Django is just as dangerous as doing it in raw Python—the ORM doesn’t magically sanitise strings you interpolate yourself. The safe path is always to use the ORM’s parameterised query helpers (filter(), raw() with bound parameters) rather than string formatting.

docs.title: 11.2.1 Detection and Manual Testing
docs.text:
A single quote ’ is the canonical probe. A syntax error response indicates potential injection. Boolean-based detection uses pairs such as:

  • ’ OR ’1’=’1 (always true)

  • ’ OR ’1’=’2 (always false)

If the two responses differ in content or size, SQL injection is likely.

docs.title: 11.2.2 Blind SQL Injection
docs.text:
When the application doesn’t return query results, attackers use time-based or boolean-based blind techniques:

-- If the first character of the database name is 'a', sleep 5 seconds
' AND IF(SUBSTRING(database(),1,1)='a', SLEEP(5), 0) -- -

-- Extract version character by character (boolean)
' AND (SELECT SUBSTRING(@@version,1,1))='5' -- -

# Basic detection and dump
sqlmap -u "https://target.example/item?id=1" --dbs

# Dump a specific table, tamper script for WAF evasion
sqlmap -u "https://target.example/item?id=1" \
       -D shopdb -T users --dump \
       --tamper=space2comment,between \
       --level=5 --risk=3

docs.title: 11.2.3 Prepared Statements in Python
docs.text:
import psycopg2

def get_user(username: str) -> dict | None:
    conn = psycopg2.connect(dsn="dbname=shop")
    cur  = conn.cursor()
    # NEVER do: cur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='{username}'")
    cur.execute(
        "SELECT id, email, role FROM users WHERE username =
        (username,)          # <-- tuple prevents injection
    )
    row = cur.fetchone()
    cur.close()
    conn.close()
    return {"id": row[0], "email": row[1], "role": row[2]} if row else None

docs.title: 11.3 Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
docs.text: XSS lets an attacker execute JavaScript in a victim’s browser, leading to session hijacking, credential theft, or malware delivery. All three XSS variants share the same root cause—unescaped user-controlled data ends up being interpreted as code—but they differ sharply in how they’re delivered, who they affect, and how hard they are to detect.

docs.title: 11.3.1 Reflected XSS
docs.text: The payload is embedded in a URL parameter and reflected immediately in the response. Example: https://example.com/search?q=<script>... Reflected XSS requires the victim to click a crafted link, so the attacker must combine it with phishing or URL shorteners to get delivery. The impact is limited to users who click that specific link, which makes it easier to contain but also harder to detect—the payload never touches the server’s database, so log-based detection often misses it. Real-world examples include the 2014 eBay XSS campaign where crafted auction listing URLs redirected buyers to phishing sites, and a 2011 Twitter worm that triggered XSS via malformed onmouseover attributes in tweets.

docs.title: 11.3.2 Stored XSS
docs.text: The payload is persisted (in a database, log viewer, or similar store) and served to every visitor. This is the highest-impact category because it requires no victim interaction beyond a normal page visit. A single injected payload can silently compromise every user who views the affected page—account takeover at scale. The 2005 Samy worm on MySpace is the canonical example: a stored XSS payload added the attacker as a friend and reproduced itself to each visitor’s profile, infecting over a million accounts in 20 hours. Log viewers and admin dashboards are particularly dangerous targets because stored XSS there directly attacks privileged sessions.

docs.title: 11.3.3 DOM-based XSS
docs.text:
The payload never reaches the server; it’s written into the DOM via unsafe sinks (innerHTML, document.write, eval) reading from attacker-controlled sources (location.hash, postMessage). Because the server only ever sees a benign URL or POST body, server-side scanners and WAFs are blind to DOM XSS entirely. The entire exploit lives in JavaScript. Single-page applications built with Angular, React, or Vue are common targets because their heavy reliance on client-side routing and dynamic content creation multiplies the number of potential sinks. Bypassing DOM XSS requires auditing client-side JavaScript directly, not just HTTP responses.

// VULNERABLE: attacker controls location.hash
document.getElementById('out').innerHTML = location.hash.slice(1);

// FIXED: use textContent; never innerHTML for untrusted data
document.getElementById('out').textContent = location.hash.slice(1);

docs.title: 11.3.4 Content Security Policy
docs.text:
Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'none';
  script-src  'self' 'nonce-{RANDOM_PER_REQUEST}';
  style-src   'self';
  img-src     'self' data:;
  connect-src 'self' https://api.example.com;
  frame-ancestors 'none';
  base-uri    'none';
  form-action 'self';

A nonce-based CSP invalidates all inline scripts that don’t carry the server-generated nonce, eliminating most XSS impact even when injection is present.

The nonce must be a fresh cryptographically random value (minimum 128 bits) generated per request—not per session or per deployment. If you reuse nonces, an attacker who can observe any prior response can replay the nonce value. Each script tag the server generates gets the matching nonce="..." attribute; any injected script the attacker inserts lacks it and the browser refuses to execute it.

Hashes are the alternative: instead of a nonce, you compute SHA-256( script_content), base64-encode it, and include ’sha256- <hash>’ in the CSP header. Hashes work for truly static inline scripts where the content doesn’t change per request. They don’t work well for scripts that embed per-request data (like a CSRF token embedded in JavaScript), which is why nonces are generally more practical for dynamic applications.

unsafe-inline completely defeats the inline-script protection that is the entire point of having a CSP. Adding it to script-src—often done as a quick fix when a script suddenly stops working—means an attacker’s injected <script> tag executes just as before. Any CSP containing unsafe-inline in script-src provides virtually no XSS protection; a scanner reporting “CSP present” on such a policy is giving a misleading green tick. Similarly, unsafe-eval must be absent; it re-enables eval(), setTimeout with a string argument, and new Function(), all common XSS escalation paths.

docs.title: 11.4 Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
docs.text: CSRF forces an authenticated user’s browser to submit a state-changing request to a target site by exploiting the browser’s automatic inclusion of session cookies. The attacker doesn’t need to read the response—they just need the side effect of the request to happen (transferring funds, changing an email address, adding an admin account). That asymmetry is what makes CSRF powerful: the same-origin policy prevents the attacker from reading cross-origin responses, but it doesn’t prevent cross-origin form submissions or image requests from being sent.

docs.title: 11.4.1 Synchronizer Token Pattern
docs.text:
The server generates a cryptographically random token per session, embeds it in forms, and validates it on submission. Tokens must be bound to the session:

import secrets, hashlib

def generate_csrf_token(session_id: str) -> str:
    secret = app.config["SECRET_KEY"].encode()
    return hashlib.sha256(secret + session_id.encode()).hexdigest()

docs.title: 11.4.2 SameSite Cookie Attribute
docs.text:
SameSite=Strict prevents cookies from being sent on any cross-site request. SameSite=Lax (the modern browser default) permits GET navigation but blocks cross-site POSTs—sufficient to defend most CSRF scenarios.

SameSite=None opts the cookie back in to cross-site delivery and must be paired with Secure or browsers reject it. Developers reach for it when they need cookies sent in embedded iframes or cross-origin API calls from a browser. Any endpoint that receives a SameSite=None session cookie remains fully exposed to CSRF, so those endpoints still need CSRF tokens or the double-submit pattern. OAuth callbacks and payment redirect flows are common cases where SameSite=None is genuinely required, and they’re also the flows that attackers target specifically because developers often forget to add CSRF protection back in once SameSite stops providing it. Don’t treat SameSite as a complete CSRF defence—treat it as a useful defence-in-depth layer that happens to be free.

docs.title: 11.4.3 Double-Submit Cookie Pattern
docs.text: An alternative for stateless APIs: the server sets a random cookie; JavaScript reads it and sends it in a custom header (e.g., X-CSRF-Token). The server checks that header and cookie match. A cross-site attacker can’t read the cookie (SOP prevents it), so can’t replicate the header value.

docs.title: 11.5 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
docs.text:
SSRF causes the server to make HTTP requests to attacker-specified URLs, providing access to internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, and RFC 1918 address space. The server is the unwitting proxy: it has privileged network access that the attacker lacks directly, and SSRF turns that access into a weapon. Features that commonly introduce SSRF include webhook configuration (“enter a URL we’ll POST events to”), URL-based image imports, PDF generators that fetch remote CSS or images, and any “preview this link” functionality.

Cloud Metadata Abuse via SSRF

AWS EC2 instance metadata is available at http://169.254.169.254/latest/ meta-data/. An SSRF against this endpoint can retrieve IAM role credentials:

GET http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
    iam/security-credentials/webapp-role

The response contains AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and Token, giving the attacker full access to any AWS API the role permits. IMDSv2 (requiring a PUT request to obtain a session token first) mitigates this—but only if IMDSv1 is disabled.

SSRF bypass techniques: DNS rebinding, http://[::1]/, http://0.0.0.0/, decimal IP http://2130706433/ (=127.0.0.1), URL redirect chains, IPv6 scope IDs.

Defense: allowlist outbound hosts; resolve the hostname server-side and validate the resolved IP against a blocklist of private/link-local/loopback ranges before connecting; use a dedicated egress proxy.

docs.title: 11.6 XML External Entity Injection (XXE)
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [
  <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">
]>
<data><user>&xxe;</user></data>

Blind OOB XXE uses an external DTD hosted on an attacker server to exfiltrate file contents via DNS or HTTP:

<!DOCTYPE foo [
  <!ENTITY


]>

XXE vulnerabilities also appear inside SVG images, DOCX/XLSX containers (ZIP archives containing XML), and SAML assertions.

Mitigation: disable external entity processing in the XML parser. In Python lxml: use XMLParser(resolve_entities=False). In Java: set FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING and disable LOAD_EXTERNAL_DTD.

docs.title: 11.7 Path Traversal and Command Injection
docs.text:
# VULNERABLE
@app.route('/download')
def download():
    filename = request.args.get('file')
    return open(f'/var/app/files/{filename}', 'rb').read()

# Payload: /download?file=../../etc/shadow

# FIXED: resolve and validate against allowed base directory
import os, pathlib
BASE = pathlib.Path('/var/app/files').resolve()

@app.route('/download')
def download():
    filename = request.args.get('file', '')
    path = (BASE / filename).resolve()
    if not str(path).startswith(str(BASE)):
        abort(400)
    return open(path, 'rb').read()

Command injection occurs when user input is interpolated into shell commands. Always use subprocess with a list (no shell=True):

import subprocess
# NEVER: subprocess.run(f"ping {host}", shell=True)
result = subprocess.run(
    ["ping", "-c", "4", host],   # host is passed as argument, not shell-expanded
    capture_output=True, timeout=10
)

docs.title: 11.8 HTTP Security Headers
docs.text: Table 11.2. Essential HTTP Security Response Headers Header Recommended Value / Purpose Strict-Transport-Security max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload — forces HTTPS for 2 years X-Frame-Options DENY — prevents clickjacking (legacy; prefer CSP frame-ancestors) X-Content-Type-Options nosniff — prevents MIME-type confusion Content-Security-Policy See §11.3.4 above; use nonce-based policy Permissions-Policy camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=() — restricts APIs Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin — limits referrer leakage Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy same-origin — isolates browsing context for Spectre Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy same-origin — prevents cross-origin reads

docs.title: 11.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 11.1

The following Python Flask route is used for a product search feature. Identify every security vulnerability, explain the impact of each, and rewrite the route securely.

@app.route('/search')
def search():
    q = request.args.get('q')
    sql = "SELECT name,price FROM products WHERE name LIKE '
    results = db.execute(sql).fetchall()
    return f"<html><body>Results for {q}: {results}</body></html>"

Exercise 11.2

A web application accepts SVG image uploads and renders them in an <img> tag. Construct a proof-of-concept payload that would exfiltrate the contents of /etc/hostname to an out-of-band HTTP server, and describe two mitigations the developer should implement.

Exercise 11.3

Explain why SameSite=Lax alone is insufficient CSRF protection for an application that uses GET requests to perform state-changing actions (e.g., /admin/delete?id=5). What additional controls are required?

Exercise 11.4

You find a URL parameter redirect=https:// example.com/ dashboard that the server fetches before returning a 302. Describe a methodology for testing whether this is an SSRF vulnerability, including five payloads you would try and the evidence that would confirm the finding.

Exercise 11.5

A web security scanner reports a missing Content-Security-Policy header. The developer responds that they use output encoding everywhere and there is no XSS risk, so CSP is unnecessary. Write a 200-word technical response either supporting or refuting this claim, citing specific attack scenarios that CSP would or would not prevent.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Authentication, Authorization, and Access Control
docs.text: Modern security systems rest on three pillars: verifying who a user is, determining what they’re allowed to do, and recording what they did. This chapter examines each pillar along with the protocols and attacks surrounding them.

docs.title: 12.1 The AAA Framework
docs.text:
Definition 12.1 (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting)

Authentication (AuthN) verifies the identity of a principal. Authorization (AuthZ) determines which resources and actions an authenticated principal may access. Accounting (Audit) records principal actions for forensic analysis and compliance.

Authentication factors fall into three categories:

Factor Type Examples Something you know Knowledge Password, PIN, security question Something you have Possession Hardware token, smart card, phone Something you are Inherence Fingerprint, face, retina, voice

docs.title: 12.2.1 Password Hashing: bcrypt and Argon2
docs.text:
Storing plaintext or MD5/SHA-1 passwords is a serious vulnerability. Modern systems use adaptive password hashing algorithms that are deliberately slow and memory-hard.

Definition 12.2 (Adaptive Password Hash)

An adaptive password hash function incorporates a cost factor that can be increased as hardware becomes faster, keeping brute-force attacks economically infeasible. It also incorporates a random salt to prevent precomputation (rainbow table) attacks.

Algorithm Memory-Hard Parallelism NIST Recommended MD5 (legacy) No Yes No bcrypt No No Acceptable scrypt Yes Limited Acceptable Argon2id Yes Configurable ✓

NIST SP 800-63B Password Guidance

NIST SP 800-63B (2024 revision) recommends: minimum 8-character passwords (64+ preferred); no mandatory periodic rotation unless compromise is suspected; check against breached-password lists (Have I Been Pwned corpus); no complexity rules that produce predictable substitutions (e.g., P@ssw0rd); allow all printable ASCII and Unicode characters.

docs.title: 12.2.2 Credential Stuffing
docs.text:
Credential Stuffing

Attackers use leaked username/password pairs from one breach to attack other services, exploiting password reuse. Defences include: breach monitoring (HaveIBeenPwned API), rate limiting, CAPTCHA, device fingerprinting, and multi-factor authentication.

docs.title: 12.3.1 TOTP: Time-Based One-Time Passwords
docs.text:
RFC 6238 defines TOTP as an extension of HOTP (RFC 4226) that uses the current Unix time rather than a counter. The shared secret and time window produce a short-lived code. The 30-second window exists to tolerate clock drift between the user’s device and the server—in practice most implementations also accept codes from the adjacent windows (valid_window=1) to handle users who generate a code just as the window expires. That tolerance creates a 60-second replay window, which is why servers should record the last accepted code and reject it if presented again within the same window.

\[\begin{align*} T &= \left\lfloor \frac{\text{Unix time}}{30} \right\rfloor \\ \text{HOTP}(K, T) &= \text{Truncate}\!\left(\text{HMAC-SHA1}(K, T)\right) \bmod 10^6 \end{align*}\] 
import pyotp
import time

# Provision: share base32 secret with user (shown in QR code)
secret = 'JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP'
totp = pyotp.TOTP(secret)

# Generate current code (valid for 30-second window)
current_code = totp.now()
print(f"Current OTP: {current_code}")

# Verify a user-supplied code (allows 1 window drift)
user_input = input("Enter OTP: ")
valid = totp.verify(user_input, valid_window=1)
print(f"Valid: {valid}")

# Provisioning URI for QR code generation
uri = totp.provisioning_uri(name='alice@example.com',
                            issuer_name='MyApp')
print(uri)

docs.title: 12.3.2 FIDO2 and WebAuthn
docs.text:
FIDO2 consists of the W3C WebAuthn API and the FIDO CTAP2 protocol. Credentials are public-key pairs where the private key never leaves the authenticator. Authentication proves possession of the private key via a challenge-response signature.

WebAuthn Advantages

WebAuthn credentials are origin-bound: the relying party ID is cryptographically bound to the credential, making phishing attacks that use lookalike domains ineffective. Passkeys extend WebAuthn by syncing credentials across devices via cloud keychain.

TOTP codes are fundamentally phishable: nothing stops a real-time phishing proxy from relaying the victim’s code to the legitimate site before it expires. Attacker-in-the-middle toolkits like Evilginx2 do exactly this, harvesting both the session cookie and the TOTP code in one automated flow. FIDO2/WebAuthn is the only widely deployed MFA mechanism that is phishing-resistant by design—the origin binding means a credential registered at bank.example simply can’t be used at bank-secure.attacker.example.

SIM-swapping is the other dominant attack on TOTP and SMS-based MFA. An attacker calls the victim’s mobile carrier, impersonates the victim (often with data from previous breaches or social engineering), and convinces the carrier to port the number to a new SIM the attacker controls. From that point the attacker receives all SMS codes and TOTP is not involved at all. High-profile SIM-swap attacks have hit Twitter’s internal tooling (2020), cryptocurrency exchange accounts, and even journalists. FIDO2 hardware tokens are immune to SIM-swapping because they don’t involve telephony. For TOTP, the only mitigations are carrier-level port freeze requests and pushing users toward hardware tokens instead of authenticator apps.

docs.title: 12.4.1 OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow
docs.text: OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) delegates authorization—not authentication—to an Authorization Server. The Authorization Code flow is the recommended pattern for confidential clients. The word “authorization” is load-bearing here: OAuth tells you what a user has granted permission to do, not who that user is. Using an access token to determine identity is a common mistake that leads to account takeover when tokens are issued to multiple clients—OIDC’s ID token is the correct mechanism for identity assertions.

docs.title: 12.4.2 PKCE: Proof Key for Code Exchange
docs.text:
PKCE (RFC 7636) prevents authorization code interception attacks in public clients (mobile apps, SPAs). The client generates a code_verifier (random 43–128 chars), computes code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA-256(code_verifier)), and sends the challenge in the authorization request. The token endpoint then verifies the verifier.

The intuition behind PKCE is straightforward: an attacker who intercepts the authorization code (via a malicious app registered on the same custom URI scheme, or via a compromised redirect URI) can’t exchange it for a token without also knowing the code_verifier that was generated in the same session on the legitimate device. The verifier never travels in the redirect, so intercepting the redirect is useless. PKCE was originally designed for public clients that can’t hold a client secret securely, but RFC 9700 recommends it for all clients including confidential server-side apps. Even when a client secret exists, PKCE adds a second factor specific to that authorization request, preventing code injection attacks where an attacker tricks the server into accepting a stolen code mid-flow.

Implicit Flow Deprecated

The OAuth 2.0 Implicit flow (response_type=token) is deprecated per RFC 9700. Access tokens in URL fragments are exposed in browser history and referrer headers. All new deployments must use Authorization Code with PKCE.

The implicit flow’s fundamental flaw isn’t just history and referrer leakage—it’s that access tokens appear in URLs, which means they end up in server access logs, browser history sync, and any browser extension that can read URLs. These tokens have no code verifier binding, so anyone who captures the token from any of those sources gets full access. The flow was designed for browser-based apps that couldn’t do a back-channel token request in the pre-CORS era; that constraint no longer exists, removing the only rationale for its use.

docs.title: 12.4.3 OpenID Connect and JWT Structure
docs.text:
OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds an ID token (a signed JWT) on top of OAuth 2.0, enabling authentication. A JWT has three Base64URL-encoded parts separated by dots:

\[\underbrace{\texttt{eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9}}_{\text{Header}} \texttt{.} \underbrace{\texttt{eyJzdWIiOiJ1c2VyMTIzIn0}}_{\text{Payload (claims)}} \texttt{.} \underbrace{\texttt{<signature>}}_{\text{Signature}}\]

Standard OIDC claims include sub (subject), iss (issuer), aud (audience), exp (expiry), iat (issued-at), and nonce.

docs.title: 12.5 JWT Attacks
docs.text:
Algorithm Confusion: alg=none and RS256 \(\to\) HS256

alg=none: Some libraries accept JWTs with "alg":"none" and no signature, treating them as valid. Defence: reject tokens where alg is not in an explicit allowlist.

RS256 \(\to\) HS256: If the server uses the RSA public key as the HMAC secret when alg=HS256 is supplied, an attacker can forge tokens using the (public) key. Defence: pin the expected algorithm server-side; never derive the verification key from the token header.

The RS256\(\to\)HS256 confusion attack deserves more detail because it surprises even experienced developers. In RS256, the server signs with an RSA private key and verifies with the public key—and the public key is, by definition, public. A vulnerable JWT library selects the verification algorithm from the token’s own alg header. An attacker changes that header to HS256, then signs the token with the server’s RSA public key (which the attacker has). When the vulnerable library verifies, it reads alg=HS256 and computes HMAC-SHA256(token, publicKey), which matches exactly—so verification succeeds. The attacker has produced a token claiming any identity they want. The fix is one line: algorithms=[’RS256’] passed to the decode call. Never let the token header dictate which algorithm you use; that field is attacker-controlled.

The alg:none attack exploits a misguided feature in early JWT specifications that allowed unsigned tokens for internal messaging. Some libraries implemented it as a valid algorithm value, meaning a token with "alg":"none" and an empty signature field passes “verification.” Real-world exploits of both attacks appeared in Auth0’s legacy sdk, the python-jose library, and numerous custom JWT implementations. Check your library’s changelog for CVEs mentioning “algorithm confusion” before trusting it in production.

kid Injection

The JWT kid (key ID) header parameter may be used to look up a key in a database. If unsanitised, an attacker can inject SQL: "kid":"’ UNION SELECT ’attacker_key’ --". Defence: validate kid against a strict allowlist; use parameterised queries.

docs.title: 12.6 SAML and XML Attacks
docs.text:
Definition 12.3 (SAML Assertion)

Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) 2.0 uses XML documents called assertions signed by an Identity Provider (IdP) to convey authentication and attribute statements to a Service Provider (SP).

XML Signature Wrapping (XSW)

XSW attacks exploit the gap between which element is signed and which is processed. An attacker duplicates the signed element, injects a malicious clone elsewhere in the XML tree, and tricks the SP into processing the unsigned clone while the signature validates over the legitimate copy. Mitigation: validate that the signed element is the one actually consumed; use strict XML canonicalisation.

docs.title: 12.7 Access Control Models
docs.text:
Definition 12.4 (RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC)

Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): permissions assigned to roles; users assigned to roles. Simple and auditable but coarse-grained. Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC): policies evaluate subject, resource, and environment attributes. Expressive but complex. Relationship-Based Access Control (ReBAC): access determined by graph relationships between users and objects (e.g., Google Zanzibar, “user X owns document Y”).

docs.title: 12.7.1 Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Definition 12.5 (Privilege Escalation)

Vertical privilege escalation: a lower-privileged user gains higher-privileged capabilities (e.g., a regular user becomes an admin). Horizontal privilege escalation: a user accesses resources belonging to another user of the same privilege level (also called IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference).

docs.title: 12.8 Broken Access Control and IDOR
docs.text:
Broken Access Control is the OWASP Top 10 #1 vulnerability (2021–2025). A classic form is IDOR:

from flask import Flask, request, jsonify, g

app = Flask(__name__)

# VULNERABLE: no ownership check
@app.route('/api/invoice/<int:invoice_id>')
def get_invoice_bad(invoice_id):
    invoice = db.query('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ?',
                       invoice_id)
    return jsonify(invoice)   # Any user can fetch any invoice!

# SECURE: verify authenticated user owns the resource
@app.route('/api/invoice/<int:invoice_id>')
def get_invoice_good(invoice_id):
    user_id = g.current_user['id']
    invoice = db.query(
        'SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?',
        invoice_id, user_id)
    if not invoice:
        return jsonify({'error': 'Not found'}), 404
    return jsonify(invoice)

docs.title: 12.9 Session Management
docs.text:
Secure Cookie Attributes

  • HttpOnly — prevents JavaScript access; mitigates XSS-based session theft.

  • Secure — cookie transmitted only over HTTPS.

  • SameSite=Strict — cookie not sent on cross-site requests; prevents CSRF.

  • __Host- prefix — cookie scoped to the exact host, no subdomains.

Session Fixation

An attacker sets a known session ID on the victim’s browser (e.g., via URL parameter or cross-subdomain cookie), then waits for the victim to authenticate. The server elevates the fixed session, giving the attacker an authenticated session. Defence: regenerate the session ID on every privilege change, including login.

Session fixation and session hijacking are often confused but differ in when the attacker acquires the session token. In hijacking, the attacker steals a session that is already authenticated—typically via XSS, network sniffing on HTTP, or a predictable session ID. In fixation, the attacker plants a known session ID before authentication; they don’t need to steal anything because they already know the value. The defence for hijacking is making tokens hard to steal (HttpOnly, Secure, short lifetime, binding to IP or User-Agent). The defence for fixation is simpler and more reliable: always issue a brand-new session ID the moment the authentication state changes. Flask’s session.regenerate(), Django’s request.session.cycle_key(), and Spring Security’s sessionFixation().newSession() all do this. Most modern frameworks do it automatically, but custom session implementations frequently forget it.

Session hijacking remains relevant even with HttpOnly cookies because XSS can make authenticated requests in the context of the victim’s session without needing to read the cookie. Attackers exfiltrate data or perform actions—they don’t need the token string itself. This is why XSS mitigation (CSP, output encoding) and session security are complementary layers, not alternatives.

docs.title: 12.10 Zero Trust Identity
docs.text:
Definition 12.6 (Zero Trust)

Zero Trust (NIST SP 800-207) assumes no implicit trust based on network location. Every access request is evaluated against identity, device posture, and context continuously, not just at login. The principle: “never trust, always verify.”

Key Zero Trust controls include continuous risk scoring, device health attestation (via TPM or MDM), just-in-time privilege, and microsegmentation of workloads.

docs.title: 12.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 12.1

Implement a Python TOTP provisioning and verification service. Your implementation must: (a) generate a random base32 secret and return a QR-code URI; (b) verify a supplied 6-digit code with a \(\pm 1\) window tolerance; (c) enforce rate limiting so that no more than 5 verification attempts are allowed per 30-second window. Explain how the time window tolerance creates a replay window and how to minimise it.

Exercise 12.2

Analyse the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow threat model. For each of the following adversary capabilities, state whether the flow is vulnerable with and without PKCE, and explain the mechanism of attack or defence: (a) attacker can intercept the redirect URI on a mobile device; (b) attacker controls a malicious app registered on the same custom URI scheme; (c) attacker can read the victim’s browser history.

Exercise 12.3

A web application exposes GET /api/ users/ {id}/ documents. An authenticated user with ID 42 discovers they can access documents for user ID 43 by modifying the path. (a) Classify this vulnerability. (b) Write a Flask route that correctly prevents this. (c) Describe how automated IDOR scanning tools detect such endpoints.

Exercise 12.4

Explain the JWT RS256\(\to\)HS256 algorithm confusion attack in detail. Include: (a) the attacker’s step-by-step procedure to forge a token; (b) why the server accepts the forged token in the vulnerable case; (c) two distinct code-level defences a JWT library should implement.

Exercise 12.5

A security engineer wants to enforce MFA for all administrative actions but allow password-only for read operations. Design an ABAC policy schema (as JSON or pseudocode) that expresses this requirement. Your schema should include subject attributes, resource attributes, and environment attributes (e.g., mfa_verified, action, resource_sensitivity).

Exercise 12.6

Describe the XML Signature Wrapping attack against a SAML Service Provider. Draw a simplified XML tree before and after the attack, indicating which element is signed and which element the vulnerable SP processes. Propose a concrete mitigation at the XML parsing layer.

docs.title: Chapter 13: API Security
docs.text: Application Programming Interfaces are the connective tissue of modern software. REST, GraphQL, and gRPC APIs expose business logic and data to web clients, mobile apps, and partner integrations—making them a primary attack surface. This chapter surveys the OWASP API Security Top 10, examines SSRF in depth, and covers API design patterns that reduce risk.

docs.title: 13.1.1 Authentication and Authorization
docs.text:
APIs authenticate callers using one of several credential types:

Credential Type Transport Notes API Key Header / query param Simple; no expiry by default Bearer Token (JWT) Authorization header Stateless; must verify signature OAuth 2.0 Access Token Authorization header Scoped; short-lived Mutual TLS (mTLS) TLS handshake Strong; client cert required HMAC Signature Custom header Request integrity + auth

docs.title: 13.1.2 Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Rate limiting defends against brute-force, enumeration, and denial-of-service attacks. Common strategies include fixed-window, sliding-window, and token-bucket algorithms. Apply limits per user, per IP, and per endpoint.

Understanding the algorithm differences matters for choosing the right one. The token bucket algorithm maintains a conceptual bucket that fills with tokens at a fixed rate (e.g., 10 tokens per second) up to a maximum capacity. Each request consumes one token. If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected. The key property is that it allows bursts up to the bucket capacity while enforcing an average rate over time—a client can spend their whole bucket in a fraction of a second, which is useful for interactive applications that need occasional high-speed access but shouldn’t be able to sustain it. Implementations need only track two values per client: current token count and last refill timestamp.

The leaky bucket (or leaky bucket as a queue) enforces a strictly constant output rate regardless of input bursts. Incoming requests queue up, and the queue drains at a fixed rate. Excess requests that would overflow the queue are dropped. Leaky bucket smooths traffic completely, which suits network bandwidth shaping but can feel punishing for API users who expect to handle short bursts. For most REST APIs, token bucket is the better choice because it allows the burst headroom that legitimate clients need during page loads or batch operations.

The sliding window algorithm is a middle ground: it tracks requests across a rolling time window rather than a fixed one. Fixed windows have a well-known boundary attack where a client sends half their limit at the end of one window and half at the start of the next, doubling their effective rate at the boundary. Sliding windows close that gap. HTTP headers like X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and X-RateLimit-Reset should always accompany rate limit responses so clients can backoff gracefully rather than hammering the server until they hit a 429.

docs.title: 13.2 OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023)
docs.text:
Definition 13.1 (OWASP API Security Top 10)

The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023 edition) catalogues the most critical API vulnerabilities observed in production systems. Each entry describes a class of flaw, its exploitability, and recommended controls.

ID Name Description API1 Broken Object Level Auth (BOLA) Accessing objects owned by other users API2 Broken Authentication Weak credentials, missing MFA API3 Broken Object Property Level Auth Exposing/updating sensitive fields API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption Missing rate limits; DoS API5 Broken Function Level Auth (BFLA) Accessing admin functions as user API6 Unrestricted Business Flows Bypassing workflow logic API7 Server Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Fetching internal resources via API API8 Security Misconfiguration Open CORS, verbose errors, debug on API9 Improper Inventory Management Forgotten / shadow APIs API10 Unsafe Consumption of Third-Party APIs Trusting external API output unsafely

docs.title: 13.2.1 BOLA (API1) and Mass Assignment (API3)
docs.text:
from flask import Flask, jsonify, g

app = Flask(__name__)

# VULNERABLE: BOLA - no ownership check
@app.route('/api/orders/<int:order_id>', methods=['GET'])
def get_order_vulnerable(order_id):
    order = db.find_order(order_id)        # Any user can fetch!
    return jsonify(order)

# SECURE: enforce object-level authorization
@app.route('/api/orders/<int:order_id>', methods=['GET'])
def get_order_secure(order_id):
    order = db.find_order(order_id)
    if order is None or order['user_id'] != g.current_user['id']:
        return jsonify({'error': 'Not found'}), 404
    return jsonify(order)

# VULNERABLE: Mass Assignment - client sets 'is_admin'
@app.route('/api/users/me', methods=['PUT'])
def update_user_vulnerable():
    data = request.get_json()
    db.update_user(g.current_user['id'], **data)  # Dangerous!
    return jsonify({'status': 'updated'})

# SECURE: allowlist updatable fields
UPDATABLE_FIELDS = {'display_name', 'email', 'bio'}

@app.route('/api/users/me', methods=['PUT'])
def update_user_secure():
    data = request.get_json()
    safe = {k: v for k, v in data.items() if k in UPDATABLE_FIELDS}
    db.update_user(g.current_user['id'], **safe)
    return jsonify({'status': 'updated'})

docs.title: 13.3 GraphQL Security
docs.text:
GraphQL’s flexibility introduces security challenges not present in REST APIs. Where REST exposes a fixed set of endpoints with defined shapes, GraphQL lets clients compose arbitrary queries, which shifts the surface area in ways that catch developers off-guard.

GraphQL Introspection Disclosure

GraphQL introspection allows clients to query the full schema. In production, introspection should be disabled or restricted to authenticated users—it reveals all types, fields, and mutations to an attacker doing reconnaissance.

Introspection abuse is frequently the first step of a GraphQL attack, not the attack itself. An attacker issues an introspection query to get the full schema, then examines it for hidden or undocumented mutations (like updateUserRole), fields marked as admin-only in comments but not actually guarded by authorization checks, and relationships between types that suggest BOLA opportunities. Tools like graphql-voyager and InQL visualise and scan GraphQL schemas automatically. Disabling introspection makes reconnaissance harder but doesn’t fix authorization holes—a determined attacker will fuzz field names from common conventions anyway. So disable introspection and fix authorization; don’t treat them as alternatives.

GraphQL DoS via Deep Nesting

GraphQL allows recursive queries. An attacker submits a deeply nested query that causes exponential resolver calls: { user { friends { friends { friends {...} } } } }. Defences: enforce maximum query depth (e.g., 10 levels), maximum query complexity, and query timeout.

Depth limiting alone isn’t sufficient because a query can be wide instead of deep: requesting a hundred top-level fields or a list of a million items via first: 1000000 both cause server-side exhaustion without deep nesting. A proper defence assigns a cost score to each field and list argument—a field costs 1, and a paginated list multiplies the field cost by the requested page size—and rejects queries whose total complexity exceeds a threshold before any resolvers run. The graphql-cost-analysis and graphql-query-complexity libraries implement this pattern. Aliases are another GraphQL feature that multiplies work: alias1: expensiveField, alias2: expensiveField, ... evaluates the same expensive resolver many times under different names, potentially bypassing naive per-field rate limits.

docs.title: 13.4 REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC Security Comparison
docs.text: Property REST GraphQL gRPC Auth mechanism JWT / OAuth2 / API key JWT / OAuth2 mTLS / OAuth2 Input validation Schema (OpenAPI) Schema + custom rules Protobuf types BOLA risk High (path params) High (resolver args) Medium Introspection OpenAPI optional Enabled by default Reflection optional DoS via query complexity Low High (nested queries) Medium (streaming) Transport HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 HTTP/2 only Rate limiting Standard Per-query complexity Per-RPC or streaming Error verbosity Configurable Errors in JSON body gRPC status codes

docs.title: 13.5 API Gateway Security
docs.text:
Definition 13.2 (API Gateway)

An API gateway is a reverse proxy that centralises cross-cutting concerns: authentication, rate limiting, TLS termination, request logging, and routing. Examples include AWS API Gateway, Kong, Apigee, and Nginx.

The gateway enforces: IP allowlisting, JWT signature validation (delegating to the IDP), request size limits, and per-client rate limits. Backend services trust only requests arriving via the gateway and verify the forwarded identity claim.

docs.title: 13.6 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
docs.text:
Definition 13.3 (SSRF)

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) occurs when an attacker can cause the server to issue HTTP requests to an attacker-controlled destination. The server’s network position gives access to internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, and localhost ports inaccessible to the attacker directly.

docs.title: 13.6.1 AWS IMDSv1 Exploitation
docs.text:
SSRF to AWS Instance Metadata

The AWS EC2 Instance Metadata Service (IMDSv1) is accessible at 169.254.169.254. An SSRF vulnerability lets an attacker steal IAM credentials:

# Attacker-controlled payload --- server fetches this URL
curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
# Returns: role name, then:
curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/MyRole
# Returns: AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, Token (valid ~6 hours)

Mitigations: enforce IMDSv2 (token-required PUT before GET); block 169.254.0.0/16 in egress firewall; use instance profiles only when needed.

docs.title: 13.6.2 SSRF Filter Bypasses
docs.text:
Naive SSRF filters block strings like 169.254.169.254 but can be bypassed:

Bypass Technique Example Decimal IP http://2852039166/ Octal IP http://0251.0376.0251.0376/ IPv6 loopback http://[::1]/ IPv6 mapped http://[::ffff:169.254.169.254]/ DNS rebinding Resolve to public IP; rotate to internal URL redirect https://trusted.example/?url=http://internal/

Defence: use an allowlist of permitted egress destinations; resolve and validate the IP after DNS resolution; reject private RFC 1918 and link-local ranges.

DNS rebinding is the most dangerous SSRF filter bypass and the one most commonly missed. The attack works in two phases. First, the attacker’s domain resolves to a legitimate public IP (to pass the server’s allowlist or IP blocklist check). The server fetches the URL, the DNS response is cached, and everything looks fine. Second, after a very short TTL expires, the attacker’s DNS server rotates the same domain to resolve to 127.0.0.1 or an internal IP. When the server makes a follow-up request—or even on retry after a redirect—the hostname now resolves to the internal address. Naive SSRF defences that check the hostname at request construction time are vulnerable; the correct fix is to resolve the hostname to an IP, check that IP against the blocklist, then make the connection to that specific IP rather than re-resolving the hostname.

Cloud metadata endpoints deserve special mention because the consequences of reaching them are so severe. AWS IMDSv2 requires a PUT request with a custom header to obtain a session token before the metadata service will respond—a pure GET-based SSRF can’t satisfy this requirement. GCP metadata at http://metadata.google.internal/ is protected by a required Metadata-Flavor: Google header. Azure IMDS at http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance requires Metadata: true. Critically, these required headers must be set by the attacker through the SSRF vector, which means SSRF via a simple URL fetch (image fetcher, PDF generator, webhook tester) can only reach the older, unprotected IMDSv1 endpoints. IMDSv1 must be explicitly disabled—it’s off by default on new AWS accounts, but many existing deployments still have it enabled from before that change.

docs.title: 13.7 API Key Management and HMAC Signing
13.7.1 API Key Best Practices
docs.text:
API Key Hygiene

  • Scope keys to minimum required permissions (least privilege).

  • Store keys in a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault), never in source code or environment variables of shared systems.

  • Rotate keys automatically on a defined schedule and immediately on suspected exposure.

  • Log every API key usage with timestamp and source IP.

docs.title: 13.7.2 HMAC Request Signing
docs.text:
AWS Signature Version 4 style signing authenticates every request, preventing replay attacks via a request timestamp and verifying request integrity.

import hmac, hashlib, datetime

def sign_request(method, path, body, secret_key, access_key):
    timestamp = datetime.datetime.utcnow().strftime('
    date_stamp = timestamp[:8]

    # Canonical request
    payload_hash = hashlib.sha256(body.encode()).hexdigest()
    canonical = f"{method}\n{path}\n\n" \
                f"host:api.example.com\nx-amz-date:{timestamp}\n\n" \
