                f"host;x-amz-date\n{payload_hash}"

    # String to sign
    string_to_sign = (f"AWS4-HMAC-SHA256\n{timestamp}\n"
                      f"{date_stamp}/us-east-1/execute-api/aws4_request\n"
                      + hashlib.sha256(canonical.encode()).hexdigest())

    # Derived signing key
    def hmac_sha256(key, data):
        return hmac.new(key, data.encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest()

    signing_key = hmac_sha256(
        hmac_sha256(
            hmac_sha256(
                hmac_sha256(f"AWS4{secret_key}".encode(), date_stamp),
                'us-east-1'),
            'execute-api'),
        'aws4_request')

    signature = hmac.new(signing_key,
                         string_to_sign.encode(),
                         hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return timestamp, signature

docs.title: 13.8 Python FastAPI: JWT Bearer Authentication
docs.text:
from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer, HTTPAuthorizationCredentials
import jwt   # PyJWT

app = FastAPI()
bearer_scheme = HTTPBearer()
PUBLIC_KEY = open('rsa_public.pem').read()
ALGORITHM = 'RS256'          # Pin algorithm --- never read from token

def get_current_user(
    creds: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(bearer_scheme)
):
    token = creds.credentials
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token, PUBLIC_KEY,
                             algorithms=[ALGORITHM],
                             audience='my-api')
    except jwt.ExpiredSignatureError:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail='Token expired')
    except jwt.InvalidTokenError as e:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail=str(e))
    return payload

@app.get('/api/profile')
def read_profile(user = Depends(get_current_user)):
    return {'sub': user['sub'], 'email': user.get('email')}

docs.title: 13.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 13.1

Design a rate limiting strategy for a public REST API that serves both anonymous users and authenticated users. Specify: (a) the rate limit tiers (requests per minute) for each user class; (b) how you identify anonymous users fairly without exposing fingerprinting privacy risks; (c) how the API communicates rate-limit status to clients (HTTP headers); (d) the algorithm (token bucket vs sliding window) and your justification.

Exercise 13.2

A developer presents the following API endpoint for code review: GET /api/admin/users?role=admin. The endpoint requires a JWT but does not check the user’s role. Identify which OWASP API Security category applies, explain the impact, and rewrite the endpoint handler in Python (Flask or FastAPI) to fix the vulnerability.

Exercise 13.3

Explain the SSRF attack chain from initial vulnerability to IAM credential theft on AWS. For each step, state the attacker’s action and the server’s response. Then describe three independent controls that would break the chain at different points.

Exercise 13.4

A GraphQL API exposes a Post type with a comments field, which itself has a replies field, which has a comments field, and so on. Write the most destructive query an attacker could submit. Calculate the number of resolver invocations for depth \(d\) if each node has \(n\) children. Propose a query complexity scoring formula and a safe maximum complexity threshold.

Exercise 13.5

Review the HMAC signing code in Section 13. (a) What attack does the timestamp prevent? (b) What is the recommended clock skew tolerance? (c) If the x-amz-date header is omitted from the signed headers, what new attack becomes possible? (d) How does AWS SigV4 protect against a path traversal attack via the canonical request?

docs.title: Chapter 14: Side-Channel Attacks
docs.text: A cryptographic algorithm may be mathematically sound yet leak its secrets through physical observables: execution time, power consumption, electromagnetic radiation, acoustic noise, or cache behaviour. These side channels bypass formal security proofs, which assume a black-box adversary with access only to inputs and outputs. This chapter surveys the principal side-channel categories and their countermeasures.

docs.title: 14.1 Side-Channel Attack Taxonomy
docs.text:
Definition 14.1 (Side-Channel Attack)

A side-channel attack exploits information leaked by the physical implementation of a cryptographic system rather than weaknesses in the underlying algorithm. The leaked information is called the side channel.

Category Observable Examples Timing Execution time Kocher RSA, cache hit/miss Power (SPA) Single power trace RSA square-and-multiply Power (DPA) Statistical analysis of many traces AES S-box correlation Electromagnetic EM field emitted by chip TEMPEST, EM-DPA Cache Cache state / timing Flush+Reload, Spectre Acoustic Sound from capacitors, coils RSA acoustic attack Fault Injection Induced computational errors Voltage glitch, laser

docs.title: 14.2 Timing Attacks
docs.text:
Theorem 14.1 (Kocher Timing Attack (1996))

Paul Kocher demonstrated that RSA private key bits can be recovered by measuring the time taken to perform modular exponentiation for chosen ciphertexts. Even nanosecond-level timing differences, measured over many trials, reveal whether a “square-and-multiply” step includes the multiply (bit = 1) or not (bit = 0).

The attack works because standard binary exponentiation has a data-dependent branch: \(m^d \bmod n\) processes each bit of \(d\), squaring for every bit and multiplying only when the bit is 1. That timing difference is measurable.

In a TLS context, timing attacks on the server’s private-key operations are particularly dangerous because an attacker can trigger thousands of handshakes from the internet without any privileged access. The ROBOT attack (2018) revived Bleichenbacher’s original 1998 timing oracle against RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 padding in TLS, affecting implementations in F5, Cisco, Citrix, and others. The attacker sends crafted TLS ClientKeyExchange messages and measures response timing (or error type) to determine whether the padding was valid. Given enough queries, the attacker decrypts the premaster secret from previously recorded TLS sessions. The lesson is that even a timing difference measured over a network—with jitter, retransmissions, and variable server load—can be exploited at scale.

Constant-time comparisons matter not just for HMAC verification but wherever secret data influences a conditional. Password hashing functions deliberately produce fixed-time output for exactly this reason, but developers often then compare the resulting hash strings with == and undo that protection. Even len() checks before a constant-time comparison can leak information: returning early because “the token has the wrong length” reveals how long the expected token is. The correct approach is to always run hmac.compare_digest() on the full outputs, accepting that a wrong-length input will simply not match.

docs.title: 14.2.1 Variable-Time String Comparison
docs.text:
A common programming error: comparing secret values (tokens, MACs) with ordinary equality operators, which short-circuit on the first mismatched byte.

import hmac
import time

secret_token = b'supersecret_api_token_abc123'

# VULNERABLE: early exit on first differing byte
def verify_token_bad(user_token: bytes) -> bool:
    return user_token == secret_token   # Variable-time!

# SECURE: constant-time comparison --- no early exit
def verify_token_good(user_token: bytes) -> bool:
    # hmac.compare_digest is guaranteed constant-time in CPython
    return hmac.compare_digest(user_token, secret_token)

# Demonstration of timing oracle (conceptual)
def measure_compare(guess: bytes) -> float:
    start = time.perf_counter_ns()
    verify_token_bad(guess)
    return time.perf_counter_ns() - start

# An attacker can enumerate byte-by-byte using timing measurements

Always Use Constant-Time Comparison

In Python use hmac.compare_digest(). In C use CRYPTO_memcmp() (OpenSSL) or timingsafe_bcmp() (BSD). Never use memcmp() or string equality for secret comparison.

docs.title: 14.3.1 Simple Power Analysis (SPA)
docs.text:
SPA examines a single power trace to extract secret information. In RSA with binary exponentiation, the trace shows a distinct pattern for each “square” and “square-and-multiply” pair, directly revealing key bits.

The distinction between SPA and DPA is not just about how many traces you need—it reflects a fundamentally different threat model. SPA requires that the secret-dependent operations produce a visually distinguishable signal in a single trace. This is realistic when the operations are coarse-grained and have very different power profiles: a modular multiply takes far longer and consumes more power than a mere square, so RSA key bits are directly readable. SPA countermeasures focus on making all code paths consume identical power and take identical time regardless of the secret—so-called regular implementations.

DPA is far more powerful because it extracts secrets statistically, using many traces to average out noise. An implementation that adds random jitter, randomises memory access patterns, or uses balanced logic gates can defeat SPA entirely yet still be vulnerable to DPA—the attacker simply collects more traces and averages out the randomness. Defeating DPA requires masking: the intermediate values that correlate with the key are XOR-masked with a fresh random value every computation, so the raw power value at any moment is uncorrelated with the key byte. First-order DPA requires only one unmasked value in a trace; first-order masking defeats this by ensuring every intermediate result is always the XOR of the real value with an independent random mask. Second-order DPA then targets the combination of two such masked values—the mask and the masked result—by using a second-order statistical analysis, which is why high-security implementations use higher-order masking schemes.

docs.title: 14.3.2 Differential Power Analysis (DPA)
docs.text:
To understand DPA, start with the physical intuition: CMOS circuits draw more current when they switch more bits. This leads to a workable model of power consumption.

Definition 14.2 (Hamming Weight Power Model)

The Hamming weight model assumes that the instantaneous power consumption of a CMOS gate is proportional to the number of 1-bits in the value being processed:

\[P_{\text{measured}} \approx \alpha \cdot \mathrm{HW}(v) + P_{\text{noise}}\]

where \(\mathrm{HW}(v) = \sum_{i} v_i\) is the Hamming weight of intermediate value \(v\) and \(\alpha\) is a device-dependent constant.

DPA, introduced by Kocher, Jaffe, and Jun (1999), uses statistical analysis of many power traces to overcome measurement noise. Given the model above, the attack proceeds as follows.

docs.title: 14.3.3 DPA Attack Steps Against AES
docs.text:
1. Collect traces: encrypt \(N\) known plaintexts \(p_1, …, p_N\); record power trace \(T_i(t)\) for each.

  2. Choose intermediate value: select a one-byte AES S-box output \(v_{k}(p_i) = \mathrm{SBox}(p_i[b] \oplus k[b])\) for byte \(b\) and key guess \(k\).

  3. Hypothetical power: compute \(H_{k,i} = \mathrm{HW}(v_{k}(p_i))\) for all \(N\) traces and all 256 key guesses \(k \in \{0,…,255\}\).

  4. Correlate: compute Pearson correlation \(\rho_k(t)\) between \(\{H_{k,i}\}_{i=1}^N\) and \(\{T_i(t)\}_{i=1}^N\) for each time sample \(t\).

  5. Identify key: the key guess \(k^*\) that maximises \(\max_t |\rho_k(t)|\) is the correct key byte.

docs.title: 14.3.4 Correlation Power Analysis (CPA)
docs.text: CPA is a refinement of DPA that uses Pearson’s linear correlation coefficient rather than a difference-of-means statistic, achieving better key recovery with fewer traces—typically hundreds rather than thousands for AES-128.

docs.title: 14.4.1 Flush+Reload
docs.text: Flush+Reload exploits shared memory (e.g., shared libraries) between attacker and victim. The attacker flushes a cache line using clflush, waits for the victim to execute, then times a reload. A fast reload indicates the victim accessed that address.

docs.title: 14.4.2 Spectre (CVE-2017-5753)
docs.text:
Spectre: Branch Predictor Poisoning

Spectre mistrains the CPU’s branch predictor to speculatively execute code that accesses out-of-bounds memory. Although the out-of-bounds access is architecturally squashed, the cache state it creates is observable via a timing side channel.

  1. Attacker mistrains branch predictor to predict “branch taken.”

  2. Victim runs code with bounds check: if (x < array_len) val = array[x];.

  3. CPU speculatively executes with attacker-controlled \(x\) beyond array_len.

  4. Speculative load brings secret[i] into cache via side_channel[val * 512].

  5. Branch resolves as not-taken; results discarded, but cache state persists.

  6. Attacker measures timing of side_channel[0..255 * 512] to recover val.

docs.title: 14.4.3 Meltdown (CVE-2017-5754)
docs.text:
Meltdown exploits out-of-order execution to read kernel memory from user space before the CPU enforces privilege checks. It’s mitigated by Kernel Page-Table Isolation (KPTI), which maps kernel memory out of the user-space page table.

The microarchitectural mechanism behind Spectre is worth understanding in detail because it explains why software mitigations are so difficult. Modern CPUs use a branch predictor to guess which way a conditional branch will go before the condition has been evaluated. The CPU then speculatively executes instructions along the predicted path while the actual evaluation completes in parallel. If the prediction was correct, the speculative results commit and execution continues with no delay. If the prediction was wrong, the results are discarded—but crucially, any microarchitectural side effects (such as cache line loads) are not reversed. Spectre variant 1 mistrains this predictor deliberately: by repeatedly executing the victim’s bounds-checked code with values that make the branch predictably take the “in-bounds” path, the attacker conditions the predictor. Then the attacker supplies an out-of-bounds index. The predictor speculatively takes the “in-bounds” path and loads secret memory before the bounds check fails. The secret value ends up encoding itself in the cache state, where the attacker reads it via a Flush+Reload timing channel.

The reason Spectre is so hard to fully mitigate is that it exploits a fundamental performance optimisation. KPTI (which mitigates Meltdown) doesn’t help for Spectre because the out-of-bounds access happens within a single privilege domain. Compiler mitigations insert lfence barriers that serialise instruction execution, preventing speculative execution from crossing the barrier—but every such barrier has a measurable performance cost, and inserting them conservatively enough to be safe while not throttling performance is an ongoing engineering problem. Retpoline replaces indirect branches with a construct that prevents speculative execution of attacker-chosen target addresses, which closes Spectre variant 2 (branch target injection) but not variant 1.

docs.title: 14.5 TEMPEST and Electromagnetic Attacks
docs.text:
Definition 14.3 (TEMPEST / Van Eck Phreaking)

TEMPEST is the US government codename for standards governing compromising electromagnetic emanations. Van Eck phreaking (1985) demonstrated that CRT monitor signals could be reconstructed from their electromagnetic emissions at distance. Modern variants target LCD data cables, keyboards, and cryptographic chips.

EMSEC (Emission Security) standards (NATO SDIP-27, NIST SP 800-53 PE-19) define shielding requirements and inspection zones (Zones 0–2) based on threat distance.

docs.title: 14.6 Fault Injection
docs.text:
Definition 14.4 (Fault Injection)

Fault injection deliberately induces transient hardware faults—via voltage glitching, clock glitching, or focused laser pulses—to corrupt computations. Targets include: secure boot signature verification (skip check), AES key schedule (differential fault analysis), and PIN verification (force accept).

docs.title: 14.6.1 Rowhammer DRAM Attacks
docs.text:
Rowhammer

DRAM cells in adjacent rows electrically interfere. Repeatedly accessing (“hammering”) two aggressor rows causes bit flips in the victim row between them. Demonstrated attacks flip page table entries (PTEs) to escalate privileges. Mitigations: ECC memory, Target Row Refresh (TRR), LPDDR4X mitigations, and kernel-level access throttling.

docs.title: 14.7 Countermeasures
docs.text: Attack Countermeasure Mechanism Timing (software) Constant-time algorithms No data-dependent branches or memory accesses SPA / DPA Masking XOR intermediate values with random mask \(r\); unmask at output DPA (RSA) RSA blinding Compute \((r^e \cdot m)^d \bmod n\), divide by \(r\) Cache attacks Cache partitioning / flush Flush cache between security domains Spectre Retpoline / LFENCE Prevent speculative indirect branches Fault injection Redundant computation Compute twice; compare; abort on mismatch Rowhammer ECC DRAM Error-correcting codes detect/correct single-bit flips TEMPEST Shielding / distance Faraday cage; TEMPEST-certified hardware

docs.title: 14.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 14.1

Describe a complete DPA attack against the first round of AES-128 encryption. (a) State the intermediate value you target and why byte 0 of the AES S-box is a good choice. (b) Write pseudocode for the correlation step. (c) How many power traces are typically required for a successful attack against an unprotected hardware implementation? (d) How does first-order masking raise the number of required traces?

Exercise 14.2

The following Python function compares a user-supplied HMAC against a stored HMAC:

def check_mac(user_mac, expected_mac):
    return user_mac == expected_mac

(a) Explain the timing oracle this creates. (b) Describe how an attacker with 10,000 queries can recover the expected MAC byte-by-byte. (c) What is the correct fix? (d) Under what conditions does the fix fail to be constant-time at the CPU instruction level?

Exercise 14.3

Explain the Spectre variant 1 attack (bounds-check bypass). (a) Draw the speculative execution flow, marking which instructions execute architecturally and which execute only speculatively. (b) Explain how the cache state encodes the secret value. (c) Describe the Flush+Reload method used to decode the cache state. (d) Why does inserting lfence after the bounds check mitigate the attack?

Exercise 14.4

A secure boot implementation checks a firmware image signature before loading it. An attacker applies a brief voltage glitch during the signature verification routine, causing the comparison to return “equal” regardless of the actual signature. (a) What class of attack is this? (b) Propose three independent hardware countermeasures a chip designer could implement. (c) How does a redundant-execution countermeasure defend against a single glitch but fail against two precisely timed glitches?

Exercise 14.5

Rowhammer bit flips have been used to escalate privileges on Linux systems. (a) Explain the memory layout that makes a page-table entry (PTE) flip useful. (b) How does ECC DRAM mitigate single-bit Rowhammer flips? (c) Why is ECC insufficient against a double-sided Rowhammer attack that induces multiple flips? (d) List two OS-level mitigations that do not require specialised hardware.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Hardware Tamper Protection
docs.text: Physical access to a device has long been considered equivalent to full compromise. Hardware security engineering challenges this assumption by making tampering detectable, difficult, or physically impossible. This chapter covers the spectrum of hardware-rooted trust mechanisms, from Trusted Execution Environments to Physical Unclonable Functions and Hardware Security Modules.

docs.title: 15.1 Trusted Execution Environments
docs.text:
Definition 15.1 (Trusted Execution Environment (TEE))

A Trusted Execution Environment is an isolated execution context provided by processor hardware that protects code and data confidentiality and integrity from the rich operating system, hypervisor, and other applications running on the same processor. The TEE maintains a trust boundary enforced in hardware.

docs.title: 15.1.1 ARM TrustZone
docs.text:
ARM TrustZone partitions the processor into two worlds: the Secure World (TEE) and the Normal World (Rich OS). A hardware bit in each bus transaction determines which world can access a given memory region. The Secure Monitor Call (SMC) instruction is the only crossing point, arbitrated by a Secure Monitor running at EL3.

FIDO2 authenticators and mobile payment credentials are commonly stored in the TEE, where even a compromised Android or iOS kernel can’t extract the private keys. TEE-resident code is called a Trusted Application (TA).

docs.title: 15.2 Trusted Platform Module (TPM 2.0)
docs.text:
Definition 15.2 (TPM 2.0)

A Trusted Platform Module (ISO/IEC 11889) is a secure cryptoprocessor providing hardware-rooted trust services: key generation, secure key storage, attestation, sealing, and random number generation. TPM 2.0 (2014) is the current standard; it supports algorithm agility (RSA, ECC, AES, SHA-2/3).

docs.title: 15.2.1 TPM Key Hierarchy
docs.text: Key Full Name Purpose EK Endorsement Key Unique per TPM; used for attestation; non-migratable SRK Storage Root Key Root of the key storage hierarchy; never leaves TPM AIK Attestation Identity Key Pseudonymous key used in remote attestation Sealing Key (derived) Encrypts data bound to a specific PCR state

docs.title: 15.2.2 Platform Configuration Registers and Sealing
docs.text:
PCRs (Platform Configuration Registers) store cumulative SHA-256 hash digests of firmware, bootloader, and OS components measured at boot time. Each PCR extends as:

\[\text{PCR}[i] \leftarrow \text{SHA-256}\!\left(\text{PCR}[i] \,\|\, \text{new\_measurement}\right)\]

The extend operation is one-way and append-only: you can add measurements but you can’t remove or replace them, and you can’t reach a given PCR state without having extended with exactly the right sequence of measurements. A PCR starts at all-zeros; extending with measurement \(m_1\) gives \(\text{SHA-256}(\mathbf{0}^{256} \| m_1)\); extending again with \(m_2\) gives \(\text{SHA-256}(\text{PCR} \| m_2)\). Reordering measurements or substituting any component produces a completely different final PCR value. This means a TPM PCR is really a commitment to the entire sequence of software that ran during boot—not just a set of components.

Sealing binds a secret (e.g., a disk encryption key) to a specific PCR state. The TPM will only unseal it if the current PCR values match the values at seal time, so the secret is unavailable if the boot chain has been tampered with.

Remote attestation extends sealing to a verifier that doesn’t share the device. The flow works as follows: the verifier sends the TPM a fresh random nonce. The TPM constructs a quote—a signed structure containing the current PCR values and the nonce—signed with an Attestation Identity Key (AIK). The AIK’s certificate chains to the TPM’s Endorsement Key (EK), which is burned into the chip by the manufacturer and certified by the TCG Certificate Authority. The verifier checks: that the EK certificate is genuine (device is a real TPM), that the AIK certificate is properly bound to the EK (key is on that real TPM), that the nonce matches (freshness, preventing replay), and that the PCR values correspond to a known-good boot policy. If all checks pass, the verifier can be confident that the attesting machine ran exactly the software stack it claims. This is the mechanism underlying cloud confidential computing attestation in Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, and ARM CCA.

Example 15.1 (BitLocker TPM Sealing)

Windows BitLocker seals the Volume Master Key to TPM PCRs 0, 2, 4, 7, and 11 (covering firmware, option ROMs, bootloader, Secure Boot policy, and BitLocker access control). Any firmware update or boot-path change causes PCR mismatch, preventing unseal until the user authenticates with a recovery key.

docs.title: 15.3 Secure Boot Chain
docs.text:
UEFI Secure Boot uses a key database (db) of trusted certificates and a deny list (dbx) of revoked hashes/certificates. The Platform Key (PK) is the root of trust held by the OEM; the Key Exchange Key (KEK) lets OS vendors update db and dbx. On Linux, Microsoft signs the shim bootloader; shim verifies GRUB using a Machine Owner Key (MOK) stored in NVRAM.

When a user disables UEFI Secure Boot in the firmware settings, the entire chain of trust from that point forward collapses. The UEFI firmware will load any bootloader regardless of its signature, which means an attacker with brief physical access can boot a live USB containing a modified kernel or a rootkit installer. With a rootkit in place before the legitimate OS boots, any subsequent software-based integrity checks are meaningless—the rootkit controls the environment those checks run in. This is why enterprise device management policies (Microsoft Intune, Jamf, Google BeyondCorp) report Secure Boot status as a health signal and deny network access to machines with it disabled. The TPM’s PCR 7 specifically records the Secure Boot policy state, so attestation-based network access control can detect if Secure Boot was disabled even after the machine was re-enabled.

Shim exists because of a practical key management problem. Microsoft’s KEK controls updates to the UEFI db, and most consumer and enterprise hardware ships with Microsoft’s certificate in db as the only trusted signing authority. Linux distributions can’t independently add their own certificates to every OEM’s key database. The solution is a small Microsoft-signed stub bootloader—shim—that serves as a trust extension point. Shim carries a compiled-in certificate (the distribution’s own key), verifies the GRUB2 binary against it, and then hands off. The Machine Owner Key (MOK) mechanism lets administrators add their own keys to shim’s trusted list without going through Microsoft. This is essential for custom or unsigned kernels, driver modules signed by local keys, or custom hardware. The tradeoff is that shim is a single point of trust: compromising the shim binary or the signing key that Microsoft uses to sign it would break the entire Linux Secure Boot chain, which is why the 2020 BootHole vulnerability (CVE-2020-10713), a buffer overflow in GRUB2’s config parser, required a coordinated dbx update across essentially every UEFI system in existence.

docs.title: 15.4 Physical Unclonable Functions
docs.text:
Definition 15.3 (Physical Unclonable Function (PUF))

A PUF exploits unavoidable manufacturing process variations to produce a unique and unpredictable response for each challenge. The response is reproducible on the same device but infeasible to clone or predict from device specifications alone. Formally, a PUF is a function \(f: \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^m\) implemented in uncontrollable physical variation.

docs.title: 15.4.1 SRAM PUF
docs.text: SRAM cells power up to a “preferred” state (0 or 1) determined by transistor mismatch. Reading SRAM immediately after power-on yields a unique bitstring—the SRAM PUF fingerprint. Across power cycles on the same chip the fingerprint is stable (with a small error rate corrected by fuzzy extractors), and no two chips produce the same fingerprint.

docs.title: 15.4.2 Arbiter PUF
docs.text: A race condition between two signal paths with nominally identical length, caused by manufacturing variation in gate delays, determines a 1-bit response for each challenge (path selection input). Chaining \(n\) stages produces \(2^n\) challenge-response pairs.

docs.title: 15.4.3 Challenge-Response Pair Enrollment and Aging
docs.text:
PUF deployment requires an enrollment phase during manufacturing. The device is placed in a controlled environment, and a large set of challenges is applied to the PUF. The corresponding responses are measured, and the (challenge, response) pairs—called CRPs—are stored securely in a server-side database. In the field, authentication works by the server sending a challenge the device has never seen (to prevent replay) and comparing the device’s response to the stored CRP. Strong PUFs like the arbiter PUF can have exponentially many CRPs, making exhaustive CRP theft impractical. Weak PUFs like SRAM PUFs have a fixed-size fingerprint used for key generation rather than per-challenge authentication.

Aging is the adversary of PUF reliability. Semiconductor transistors degrade over time via Hot Carrier Injection (HCI) and Bias Temperature Instability (BTI), which cause the threshold voltages of transistors to drift. An SRAM cell that powered up to “1” at manufacturing might drift toward “0” after years of use, causing bit flips in the PUF fingerprint. The error rate of a freshly manufactured device is typically 1–5%; after 10 years in the field at elevated temperatures, it can rise substantially. Fuzzy extractors handle this by applying an error-correcting code (ECC) during enrollment: the enrollment process identifies which bits are “noisy” (unreliable across multiple measurements) and constructs helper data that allows the ECC decoder to correct the expected bit flip errors on subsequent readings without revealing the underlying secret. The helper data is safe to store in non-volatile memory—it leaks nothing about the PUF response because it was designed so that the corrected output is information- theoretically independent of the helper data. However, if aging pushes the error rate above the ECC correction capacity, key reconstruction fails, which can lock the device out of its own secrets. This is why PUF-based systems are designed with comfortable margins between the expected aging-induced error rate and the ECC correction capacity, and why accelerated aging tests during qualification are essential.

docs.title: 15.4.4 Use Cases
docs.text:
• Device fingerprinting: authenticate a specific chip without pre-provisioned keys.

  • Key generation: derive a cryptographic key from the PUF response at runtime; the key is never stored, only reconstructed on demand.

  • Anti-cloning: prove a hardware device is the genuine article.

docs.title: 15.5 Hardware Security Modules
docs.text:
Definition 15.4 (Hardware Security Module (HSM))

An HSM is a dedicated cryptographic device providing key management, key storage, and cryptographic operations within a tamper-resistant hardware boundary. HSMs are evaluated against FIPS 140-3 (2023) or Common Criteria.

FIPS 140-3 Level Security Requirements Level 1 Software-only; no physical requirements; approved algorithms only Level 2 Tamper-evident seals; role-based authentication Level 3 Tamper-response: zeroize keys on intrusion; identity-based auth Level 4 Complete physical protection; detect environmental attacks (voltage, temp)

Commercial HSM examples: Thales Luna Network HSM (Level 3), AWS CloudHSM (Level 3), YubiHSM 2 (Level 3, compact USB form factor). When an HSM detects tampering it zeroizes all stored keys, making the device useless to an attacker even after physical extraction.

docs.title: 15.6 Anti-Tamper Techniques
docs.text:
Hardware Anti-Tamper Mechanisms

  • Epoxy potting: security-critical circuitry is encased in opaque epoxy; removal destroys the component.

  • Mesh wires: a fine conductive grid covers the chip die; cutting the mesh to reach internals breaks continuity, triggering zeroisation.

  • Active shields: top-layer conductors on a chip carry random bit patterns; any attempt to probe underlying layers shorts the shield and is detected.

  • Voltage/temperature monitors: circuits that trigger key erasure if supply voltage or die temperature exceeds safe bounds (targeting glitch attacks).

docs.title: 15.7 Cold Boot Attacks
docs.text:
Cold Boot Attack

DRAM retains data for seconds to minutes after power is removed, especially when cooled with compressed air or liquid nitrogen (which extends retention to minutes or hours). An attacker reboots a locked or sleeping computer and boots from USB, dumping RAM. Encryption keys found in memory compromise full-disk encryption.

Defence: require a TPM+PIN or TPM+USB key so that the VMK (Volume Master Key) is never held in plaintext RAM; use memory encryption (AMD SME); configure BIOS to disable USB boot; enable pre-boot authentication that clears the key from RAM on lock.

docs.title: 15.8 Memory Encryption
docs.text:
Definition 15.5 (AMD SME and SEV)

AMD Secure Memory Encryption (SME) encrypts all DRAM using a 128-bit AES key stored in the CPU, making cold-boot attacks impractical. AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) extends this by providing per-VM encryption keys, so a compromised hypervisor can’t read guest VM memory.

Intel Total Memory Encryption (TME) provides analogous DRAM encryption from the CPU memory controller, transparent to software.

docs.title: 15.9 JTAG Security
docs.text:
JTAG (IEEE 1149.1) debug ports provide direct access to processor registers, memory, and peripheral state. In production devices, JTAG must be disabled:

  • Permanently disable via fuse programming (one-time programmable bits).

  • Use secure debug: JTAG access requires cryptographic authentication (a challenge-response protocol with a device-unique key), enabling authorised field debugging without opening an attack surface on unmodified devices.

docs.title: 15.10 Hardware Security Mechanisms Comparison
docs.text: Property TEE TPM HSM PUF Key storage Yes (volatile) Yes (NV) Yes (NV, zeroize) No (derived) Physical tamper resist Moderate Moderate High (FIPS 140-3 L3+) Inherent Remote attestation Yes (proprietary) Yes (standard) Limited Yes (CRP) Crypto performance High Low Very high N/A Standard GlobalPlatform ISO/IEC 11889 FIPS 140-3 / CC No formal std Clonability Possible (soft copy) No (EK bound) No No (by design) FIPS validated No Yes (2.0) Yes (Level 1–4) No

docs.title: 15.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 15.1

Design a remote attestation flow using TPM 2.0 for a cloud virtual machine. Your design must: (a) specify which PCRs are measured and what they cover (firmware, bootloader, kernel, initrd); (b) describe how the Attestation Identity Key (AIK) proves the attestation came from a genuine TPM without revealing the device’s Endorsement Key; (c) explain how a verifier (attestation service) validates the PCR quote; (d) identify what an attacker can and cannot do if they compromise the hypervisor but not the guest TEE.

Exercise 15.2

Compare HSM and TEE for the following key storage scenarios, justifying your recommendation in each case: (a) signing keys for a certificate authority issuing millions of TLS certificates per day; (b) FIDO2 private keys on a smartphone; (c) payment terminal PIN encryption keys subject to PCI HSM requirements; (d) a secrets manager for a Kubernetes cluster running on bare metal.

Exercise 15.3

A laptop uses BitLocker with TPM-only mode (no PIN). An attacker steals the laptop while it is in sleep (S3) mode. (a) Describe the cold boot attack procedure. (b) Explain why TPM-only mode (without PIN) does not protect against this attack. (c) How does enabling the BitLocker pre-boot PIN improve security? (d) How does AMD SME change the attacker’s capabilities if enabled?

Exercise 15.4

Explain how an SRAM PUF can be used to derive a symmetric encryption key without ever storing the key in non-volatile memory. Your answer should address: (a) the role of a fuzzy extractor in handling the PUF’s unstable bits; (b) how helper data (stored in NVM) enables key reconstruction without revealing the key; (c) the security consequence of an attacker obtaining the helper data; (d) why identical manufacturing processes (e.g., two chips from the same mask) still produce different PUF responses.

Exercise 15.5

An IoT firmware update server signs firmware images with an RSA-2048 private key. The matching public key is burned into the device’s secure boot key database. An attacker gains access to the signing server and extracts the private key. (a) What is the immediate impact? (b) Describe the revocation mechanism available via UEFI Secure Boot’s dbx. (c) Explain why revocation via hash is more granular than revocation via certificate, and when each is preferable. (d) Propose a key ceremony procedure that limits the exposure window if the signing key is compromised.

docs.title: Chapter 16: Transport Layer Security
docs.text: Transport Layer Security is the cryptographic protocol underpinning secure communication on the Internet: HTTPS, SMTPS, IMAPS, FTPS, and hundreds of application protocols rely on it. TLS has evolved through a sequence of versions, each addressing newly discovered weaknesses. This chapter traces that evolution, dissects the TLS 1.3 handshake, catalogues historical attacks, and covers operational topics including certificate management, fingerprinting, and mutual TLS.

docs.title: 16.1 Protocol History
docs.text:
Version Year Status SSL 2.0 1995 Broken; prohibited (RFC 6176) SSL 3.0 1996 Broken (POODLE); prohibited (RFC 7568) TLS 1.0 1999 Deprecated (RFC 8996, 2021) TLS 1.1 2006 Deprecated (RFC 8996, 2021) TLS 1.2 2008 Supported; requires careful configuration TLS 1.3 2018 Recommended; PFS-only; reduced attack surface

Disable TLS 1.0/1.1 and SSL 3.0

RFC 8996 (March 2021) formally deprecates TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1. Major browsers removed support in 2020. Any server still offering these versions fails PCI DSS and HIPAA compliance baselines. Use the ssl_protocols directive in Nginx or SSLProtocol in Apache to restrict to TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.

docs.title: 16.2 TLS 1.3 Handshake
docs.text: TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) reduces the handshake to one round trip (1-RTT), eliminates the RSA key-exchange step, and makes all cipher suites forward-secret.

docs.title: 16.2.1 0-RTT Early Data
docs.text:
TLS 1.3 supports 0-RTT resumption: the client sends application data in the first flight using a Pre-Shared Key (PSK) derived from a previous session. This improves latency but reintroduces replay vulnerability.

0-RTT Replay Risk

0-RTT early data has no replay protection. An attacker who records the initial flight can replay it to any server accepting that ticket. Applications must treat 0-RTT requests as idempotent and safe (e.g., HTTP GET, not POST). Servers should enforce anti-replay via a server-side cache of used ticket nonces.

docs.title: 1-RTT vs. 0-RTT: The Latency–Security Tradeoff
docs.text:
The 1-RTT handshake is TLS 1.3’s default. The client sends a ClientHello with its key share; the server replies with its own key share plus an encrypted Certificate and Finished; the client sends its Finished. Only after that exchange can the client send application data. That one round trip is the latency cost of a fresh, fully forward-secret connection.

0-RTT flips this tradeoff. On a resumed session, the client derives an early traffic secret from the PSK and sends encrypted application data in the very first flight — alongside the ClientHello itself. The server can begin processing the request before the handshake completes. For a transatlantic connection with 80 ms RTT, this saves 80–160 ms per connection, which matters for high-frequency API calls or page loads on mobile networks.

The security cost is real and specific. 0-RTT data has no forward secrecy: the early traffic secret derives entirely from the PSK ticket, so if the server’s ticket encryption key is ever exposed, all recorded 0-RTT data for that key period becomes decryptable. More critically, 0-RTT data is replayable. There is no ephemeral nonce shared before the first flight, so nothing prevents an on-path attacker from replaying the captured flight to a different server instance. RFC 8446 requires servers to accept only idempotent requests as early data — HTTP GET and HEAD are the canonical examples. HTTP POST, PUT, DELETE, and any state-mutating operation must never be sent as 0-RTT. Nginx exposes this through the ssl_early_data on directive combined with a check of the $ssl_early_data variable so that back-ends can reject non-idempotent early data with a 425 Too Early response.

docs.title: Session Ticket Key Rotation
docs.text:
TLS 1.3 session resumption relies on session tickets: opaque blobs the server issues at the end of a handshake, encrypted with a server-side symmetric key. The client presents this ticket on reconnection; the server decrypts it to recover the resumption PSK and the session context without consulting an external session cache. This is stateless from the server’s perspective, which makes it attractive for load-balanced deployments where any backend can resume any session — as long as all backends share the ticket encryption key.

That shared key is a high-value secret. If it leaks, every session ticket ever encrypted with it can be decrypted, and all 0-RTT data protected only by those tickets loses its confidentiality. The defensive control is regular key rotation. A practical approach maintains two keys at all times: the current encryption key and the previous decryption-only key (to honour tickets issued just before rotation). A 24-hour rotation cycle balances operational overhead against exposure window. Nginx exposes this through ssl_session_ticket_key pointing to a key file; rotating the file and triggering a reload propagates the new key to workers without dropping connections. AWS ALB and Cloudflare rotate ticket keys internally on short cycles; self-managed servers need explicit rotation automation. The key material must never appear in configuration management databases in plaintext — it belongs in a secrets manager with audit logging on every read.

docs.title: 16.2.2 TLS 1.3 Cipher Suites
docs.text: TLS 1.3 eliminates all cipher suites with RSA key exchange, static DH, CBC mode, RC4, 3DES, and MD5/SHA-1. Only five cipher suites are defined:

docs.title: Why TLS 1.3 Removed Entire Algorithm Families
docs.text:
The removals in TLS 1.3 are not arbitrary: each reflects a class of attack that proved impossible to patch within TLS 1.2’s cipher suite model.

RSA Key Exchange.

In TLS 1.2 and earlier, one common mode had the client generate a random pre-master secret, encrypt it under the server’s RSA public key, and send it in a ClientKeyExchange message. The session key derived entirely from that secret. If the server’s long-term RSA private key was ever compromised — whether through a breach today or through a recording of traffic today and a quantum computer tomorrow — an attacker could decrypt every past session retroactively. This violates forward secrecy by design. TLS 1.3 mandates ephemeral Diffie-Hellman: the key agreement uses fresh key pairs generated for each handshake and discarded immediately after. Past sessions cannot be decrypted even with the server’s private key in hand.

Export Cipher Suites and FREAK.

During the 1990s, US export regulations restricted the strength of cryptographic software sold internationally to 40-bit symmetric keys and 512-bit RSA keys. Web servers kept these “export” cipher suites in their code for two decades after the regulations expired. The FREAK attack (2015, CVE-2015-0204) showed that a man-in-the-middle could downgrade a TLS 1.2 handshake to an export-grade RSA key exchange, factor the 512-bit RSA key in roughly 7 hours on Amazon EC2 for $100, and then decrypt or tamper with the session. TLS 1.3 has no export suites; they cannot be negotiated at all.

MD5 and SHA-1: the SLOTH Attack.

The SLOTH attack (Security Losses from Obsolete and Truncated Transcript Hashes, 2016) exploited collision vulnerabilities in MD5 and SHA-1 to mount transcript collision attacks against TLS handshake authentication. Because TLS 1.2 allowed MD5 and SHA-1 in signature algorithms, an attacker who could find hash collisions could forge server identity in some configurations. TLS 1.3 requires SHA-256 or stronger for all signatures and the HKDF-based key schedule; MD5 and SHA-1 are not referenced anywhere in RFC 8446.

CBC Mode.

CBC mode in TLS suffered from a sequence of padding oracle attacks (POODLE, Lucky13, BEAST) that required increasingly complex mitigations. Rather than continuing to patch CBC, TLS 1.3 mandates AEAD-only cipher suites (GCM, CCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305), which provide authenticated encryption in a single pass with no padding scheme to attack.

Cipher Suite Components TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 AES-128-GCM, HKDF-SHA256 TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 AES-256-GCM, HKDF-SHA384 TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 ChaCha20-Poly1305, HKDF-SHA256 TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256 AES-128-CCM, HKDF-SHA256 TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256 AES-128-CCM-8, HKDF-SHA256

docs.title: 16.3 Certificate Validation
docs.text:
Definition 16.1 (Chain of Trust)

A TLS certificate is validated by building a chain of trust from the end-entity certificate to a Root CA trusted by the client’s trust store. Each certificate in the chain is signed by the one above it; the Root CA self-signs. The chain is: Root CA \(\to\) Intermediate CA \(\to\) End-Entity certificate.

docs.title: 16.3.1 Revocation: OCSP and CRL
docs.text:
CRL (Certificate Revocation List): a signed list of revoked serial numbers published by the CA. Drawbacks: large size, stale data, privacy leakage (the CA sees which sites a client validates).

OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol): the client queries the CA’s OCSP responder in real time. More current than CRL but adds latency and a privacy concern.

OCSP Stapling: the server obtains and caches a signed OCSP response, stapling it to the TLS handshake. This eliminates client round trips and CA privacy leakage.

docs.title: 16.3.2 Certificate Transparency
docs.text:
Definition 16.2 (Certificate Transparency (CT))

RFC 9162 requires that every publicly trusted certificate be logged to an append-only, auditable CT log before browsers accept it. Domain owners can monitor CT logs to detect mis-issued certificates. As of 2024, Chrome requires at least two SCTs (Signed Certificate Timestamps) from distinct CT logs for all publicly trusted certificates.

docs.title: 16.4 Historical TLS Attacks
docs.text: Attack CVE / Year Mechanism Mitigation BEAST CVE-2011-3389 CBC IV predictable in TLS 1.0 TLS 1.2; RC4 (later: 1/n split) CRIME CVE-2012-4929 Compress+secret \(\to\) length oracle Disable TLS compression BREACH CVE-2013-3587 HTTP gzip + secret \(\to\) length oracle Per-request masking POODLE CVE-2014-3566 SSLv3 CBC padding oracle Disable SSLv3; TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV FREAK CVE-2015-0204 Downgrade to 512-bit RSA export Remove export cipher suites Logjam CVE-2015-4000 Downgrade to 512-bit DH Min 2048-bit DH; prefer ECDHE DROWN CVE-2016-0800 SSLv2 oracle decrypts TLS RSA Disable SSLv2; no shared keys ROBOT CVE-2017-13099 Bleichenbacher RSA PKCS#1 Constant-time RSA; prefer ECDHE RC4 bias CVE-2013-2566 RC4 keystream biases \(\to\) plaintext Remove all RC4 suites

docs.title: 16.5 Perfect Forward Secrecy
docs.text:
Definition 16.3 (Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS))

A key exchange protocol provides Perfect Forward Secrecy if compromise of the server’s long-term private key does not expose the session keys of past sessions. PFS is achieved by ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE) or ephemeral ECDH (ECDHE) key exchange, where the ephemeral key pair is discarded after the handshake.

Theorem 16.1 (Why RSA Key Exchange Lacks PFS)

In static RSA key exchange (removed in TLS 1.3), the client encrypts the pre-master secret with the server’s RSA public key. If the server’s RSA private key is later compromised, an attacker who recorded the TLS sessions can decrypt all past sessions retroactively. Ephemeral ECDH prevents this: even with the server private key, past ephemeral key halves are gone.

docs.title: 16.6 TLS Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Definition 16.4 (JA3 Fingerprint)

JA3 (Salesforce, 2017) fingerprints TLS clients by hashing a subset of ClientHello fields: TLS version, cipher suites, extensions, elliptic curves, and elliptic curve point formats. The result is an MD5 hash, often stable across client versions and useful in IDS rules.

JA3 is used to detect malware and C2 frameworks: Cobalt Strike beacons have well-known JA3 hashes (e.g., 72a589da586844d7f0818ce684948eea) that can trigger IDS alerts. JA3S fingerprints the ServerHello, allowing detection of specific server software. Attackers evade detection by randomising extension order or using JA3 bypass libraries.

docs.title: 16.7 Certificate Pinning
docs.text:
Definition 16.5 (Certificate Pinning)

Certificate pinning (or public key pinning) instructs a client to accept only a specific certificate or public key for a given domain, rejecting connections even if a different certificate is issued by a trusted CA. This mitigates CA compromise and mis-issuance attacks.

HPKP Deprecated

HTTP Public Key Pinning (HPKP) was deprecated and removed from browsers (2018–2019) because a single misconfiguration permanently locks users out of the site. Prefer application-layer pinning (in mobile SDKs) or Expect-CT headers that report mis-issuance without hard-failing.

docs.title: Modern Alternatives: Expect-CT and CT Monitoring
docs.text:
HPKP’s failure mode was catastrophic: a site owner who lost the pinned private key, or who pinned the wrong key, could lock all users out with no recovery path. Browsers pulled support rather than maintain a mechanism that routinely bricked high-traffic sites.

The recommended replacement is a monitoring-based model rather than a hard-fail model. The Expect-CT HTTP response header instructed browsers to enforce Certificate Transparency logging for the domain and to report violations to a specified endpoint. A browser receiving a certificate that lacked valid SCTs (Signed Certificate Timestamps) from two distinct CT logs would either report the violation or enforce it, depending on the enforce directive. Expect-CT has itself been deprecated as of 2021 because Chrome now requires CT compliance universally — every certificate issued by a publicly trusted CA must appear in at least two CT logs before Chrome accepts it, making a per-site header redundant.

What remains practical is active CT log monitoring. Tools such as certspotter (SSLMate) and Facebook’s ct-monitor watch every certificate logged to CT that matches your domain. When a CA mis-issues a certificate for your domain — whether through a compromised CA, a social-engineering attack on a domain validation process, or a simple operator error — you receive an alert within minutes of the certificate being logged, long before an attacker can deploy it. This is a stronger security control than HPKP because it detects the mis-issuance rather than merely blocking a specific key, and it carries no operational risk.

Mobile applications still pin certificates, but do so in code rather than via HTTP headers. The common approaches are: (1) bundling the expected server certificate’s SHA-256 hash of the Subject Public Key Info (SPKI) in the app binary, (2) pinning the intermediate CA’s SPKI hash for more operational flexibility, or (3) using the platform’s network security configuration mechanism (network_security_config.xml on Android, App Transport Security on iOS) to express pin hashes declaratively. The critical operational rule is to pin at least two keys — the active one and a backup stored offline — so that a certificate rotation can proceed without pushing an emergency app update. iOS and Android both support a backup pin in their pin set APIs.

docs.title: 16.8 TLS Downgrade Attacks
docs.text:
Protocol downgrade attacks trick a TLS implementation into negotiating a weaker protocol version or cipher suite than both parties actually support, exposing the session to attacks that the stronger version would have prevented. The attacks described here represent a progression from opportunistic to deliberate exploitation and shaped every major version of TLS.

BEAST (2011, CVE-2011-3389).

TLS 1.0 used the last ciphertext block of one record as the IV for the next, making the IV predictable. BEAST (Browser Exploit Against SSL/TLS) exploited this with a chosen-plaintext attack via a MITM injecting JavaScript into HTTP traffic. With enough crafted requests, an attacker could recover cookie bytes one at a time. Mitigations included the 1/n-1 split record trick and, ultimately, the industry’s move to TLS 1.2 with GCM.

POODLE (2014, CVE-2014-3566).

POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) targeted SSLv3’s CBC padding scheme, which specified only that the last byte must equal the padding length and left all preceding padding bytes undefined. A MITM who could inject 256 crafted requests could recover one byte of plaintext. The practical attack against HTTPS required 256 requests per byte, feasible against a session cookie. The root fix was disabling SSLv3 entirely. Any server still responding to SSLv3 ClientHello messages is vulnerable today.

DROWN (2016, CVE-2016-0800).

DROWN (Decrypting RSA with Obsolete and Weakened eNcryption) was a cross-protocol attack. If a server shared its RSA private key between a TLS endpoint and an SSLv2 endpoint — or if any server using the same key supported SSLv2 — an attacker could exploit the SSLv2 export-grade RSA decryption oracle to decrypt TLS RSA-key-exchange sessions. Roughly one third of HTTPS servers were vulnerable at disclosure. The fix: disable SSLv2 on every server that shares an RSA key with a TLS service, or avoid RSA key exchange entirely (TLS 1.3 does this by design).

FREAK (2015, CVE-2015-0204).

A MITM could modify the ClientHello to advertise only export-grade RSA cipher suites, triggering the server to use a 512-bit RSA key for key exchange. The attacker factored the 512-bit key and decrypted the session. The fix was removing export cipher suites from both client and server implementations.

Logjam (2015, CVE-2015-4000).

Similar to FREAK but targeting Diffie-Hellman. A MITM downgraded the DH group to 512-bit export-grade DHE. The NSA’s ability to pre-compute discrete logs for specific 1024-bit groups (used by a large fraction of HTTPS, SSH, and VPN servers) was also highlighted. Mitigations: minimum 2048-bit DH groups; prefer ECDHE.

TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV.

RFC 7507 defines the Signalling Cipher Suite Value TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV (0x56 00). A client that retries a connection at a lower protocol version after a failed handshake must include this sentinel value in its cipher suite list. A server that supports a higher version than the one negotiated recognises the sentinel and responds with an inappropriate_fallback alert, aborting the connection. This prevents an active attacker from causing a version downgrade by injecting TCP resets to make the client retry at a lower version. TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV is a defence-in-depth measure — it works only if both client and server support it, and TLS 1.3’s removal of old versions is the more complete fix.

docs.title: 16.9 Mutual TLS (mTLS)
docs.text:
Definition 16.6 (Mutual TLS)

In standard TLS, only the server presents a certificate. In mutual TLS (mTLS), both client and server present certificates, enabling bidirectional authentication. This is used in service mesh architectures (Istio, Linkerd), zero trust networking, and API authentication where strong client identity is required.

In a service mesh, each workload (pod) is issued a short-lived SPIFFE SVID (X.509 certificate) by the mesh control plane. mTLS is enforced transparently by Envoy sidecars without application code changes, providing workload identity and encryption at zero additional development cost.

docs.title: How mTLS Works in Practice
docs.text:
In a standard TLS handshake the server sends its certificate during the Certificate message; the client verifies it and the handshake proceeds without the server ever learning which client it is talking to (beyond the IP address). In mTLS, after the server sends its certificate, it also sends a CertificateRequest message asking the client to present a certificate. The client replies with its own Certificate message and a CertificateVerify message containing a signature over the handshake transcript made with the client’s private key. The server verifies both the certificate chain (it must chain to a CA the server trusts) and the signature (it proves key possession). Authentication is now mutual: each side has cryptographic evidence of the other’s identity.

The operational challenge is certificate issuance and rotation at scale. A service mesh like Istio solves this with a dedicated certificate authority (Citadel / istiod) that issues SPIFFE SVIDs — X.509 certificates with a spiffe:// URI SAN identifying the workload (e.g., spiffe://cluster.local/ns/payments/sa/checkout-service). SVIDs have short lifetimes, typically 24 hours, and rotate automatically. The Envoy sidecar proxies handle the TLS negotiation so that application pods write ordinary unencrypted traffic to localhost; encryption is transparent.

docs.title: Client Certificate Revocation in mTLS
docs.text:
When a service account or client certificate is compromised, revocation must be fast. The two standard mechanisms are:

  • CRL (Certificate Revocation List): the CA periodically publishes a signed list of revoked serial numbers at a URL embedded in the certificate’s CRL Distribution Point extension. The server fetches and caches this list. CRL’s weakness in mTLS is staleness: a CRL issued daily still allows a revoked certificate to authenticate for up to 24 hours after compromise is discovered.

  • OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol): the server queries the CA’s OCSP responder in real time for each client certificate. This gives immediate revocation status but adds latency to the TLS handshake and creates a dependency on the CA’s availability. OCSP Must-Staple, where the client is required to include a fresh OCSP response stapled to its certificate, reduces CA load but requires client-side support.

In high-velocity service mesh environments, short-lived certificates are a better answer than either CRL or OCSP. If SVIDs expire every 24 hours and a compromised credential is discovered within hours, the attacker’s window closes without any revocation infrastructure at all. The CA simply stops issuing new certificates for the compromised identity; existing ones expire on their own schedule. This is why Istio defaults to 24-hour SVID lifetimes and why zero-trust architectures favour short-lived credentials over long-lived certificates with revocation.

docs.title: mTLS in Zero Trust Network Access
docs.text: Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) frameworks — BeyondCorp, Cloudflare Access, Zscaler Private Access — rely on mTLS to assert device and user identity at every connection rather than trusting network location. A corporate laptop carries a device certificate issued by the organisation’s device CA (often via MDM enrollment). When a user opens a browser to an internal application, the ZTNA proxy performs mTLS with the device certificate as the client credential, checks the user’s identity token, evaluates policy (device posture, user group, time of day), and either proxies the connection or denies it. No VPN tunnel is needed because trust is computed per-request rather than per-session at the network perimeter.

docs.title: 16.10 TLS Inspection
docs.text:
Corporate TLS inspection proxies (Zscaler, BlueCoat, Forcepoint) perform a man-in-the-middle by re-signing server certificates with a corporate CA trusted by managed endpoints. This enables DLP (Data Loss Prevention) scanning and malware detection but:

  • breaks certificate pinning in applications;

  • introduces an additional TLS session that may use weaker configuration;

  • the proxy sees all decrypted plaintext, creating a high-value target.

docs.title: 16.11 OpenSSL Commands and Python TLS
docs.text:
# Check certificate chain and expiry
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com \
    -showcerts < /dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates

# Test supported TLS versions (expect TLS 1.3 or 1.2 only)
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1   # Should fail
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_1 # Should fail
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_2 # May succeed
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_3 # Should succeed

# Inspect cipher suites offered by server
nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 example.com

# OCSP stapling check
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -status < /dev/null 2>/dev/null \
    | grep -A 10 'OCSP Response'

import ssl
import socket
import datetime

def check_tls(hostname: str, port: int = 443) -> dict:
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
    # Enforce minimum TLS 1.2; prefer 1.3
    ctx.minimum_version = ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_2
    # Certificate verification is ON by default (do not disable!)
    # ctx.check_hostname = False  # NEVER do this in production
    # ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE  # NEVER do this in production

    with socket.create_connection((hostname, port), timeout=5) as sock:
        with ctx.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=hostname) as tls_sock:
            cert = tls_sock.getpeercert()
            cipher = tls_sock.cipher()
            version = tls_sock.version()

    # Parse expiry
    not_after = datetime.datetime.strptime(
        cert['notAfter'], '
    days_left = (not_after - datetime.datetime.utcnow()).days

    return {
        'hostname': hostname,
        'tls_version': version,
        'cipher': cipher[0],
        'cert_expiry': not_after.isoformat(),
        'days_remaining': days_left,
        'subject': dict(x[0] for x in cert['subject']),
        'issuer': dict(x[0] for x in cert['issuer']),
    }

if __name__ == '__main__':
    import json
    result = check_tls('example.com')
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

docs.title: 16.12 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 16.1

For each historical TLS attack listed in the table (BEAST, CRIME, POODLE, FREAK, Logjam, DROWN, ROBOT), state: (a) whether it affects TLS 1.2 with a modern configuration (ECDHE cipher suites only, no export ciphers, no compression); (b) whether it affects TLS 1.3; (c) one configuration check or OpenSSL command an administrator can run to verify the server is not vulnerable. Present your answers in a table.

Exercise 16.2

Implement a Python script that connects to a given HTTPS server and reports: (a) the TLS version negotiated; (b) the cipher suite; (c) whether the cipher suite provides PFS (check for DHE or ECDHE in the name); (d) the certificate’s Subject Alternative Names and days until expiry; (e) a pass/fail assessment for each check. Your script should exit with a non-zero status code if any check fails.

Exercise 16.3

A mobile application pins the server’s leaf certificate. Six months later, the certificate is renewed with a new key pair. (a) What happens to the app at the moment the new certificate is deployed? (b) How should the application have implemented pinning to avoid this failure? (c) Compare three pinning strategies (leaf cert, intermediate CA public key, root CA) in terms of resilience to certificate renewal vs resilience to CA compromise. (d) How does Certificate Transparency provide a monitoring-only alternative to hard pinning?

Exercise 16.4

Your security team wants to deploy TLS inspection on all outbound HTTPS traffic. (a) List three security capabilities that TLS inspection enables. (b) List three security or privacy risks that TLS inspection introduces. (c) How does the inspection proxy present a valid certificate to the client browser? (d) A developer argues that TLS inspection breaks certificate pinning in their app. Propose a technical solution that satisfies both the security team and the developer.

Exercise 16.5

A network defender captures a TLS ClientHello and computes JA3 fingerprint 72a589da586844d7f0818ce684948eea. (a) What information in the ClientHello is hashed to produce a JA3 fingerprint? (b) How can an attacker evade JA3-based detection while still connecting to the same C2 server? (c) What additional TLS metadata (beyond JA3) would strengthen the detection rule? (d) Explain JA3S and how correlating JA3 with JA3S narrows down the specific malware family.

Exercise 16.6

In a zero trust service mesh using mTLS: (a) Explain how SPIFFE/SPIRE issues workload identity certificates. (b) How does the mesh enforce that service A may call service B but not service C, using only mTLS and no application-layer tokens? (c) What is the certificate lifetime best practice for workload SVIDs and why? (d) If the control plane (Istio Pilot) is compromised, what is the worst-case blast radius, and how does certificate rotation limit the impact?

docs.title: Chapter 17: SSH Security
docs.text: Secure Shell is the backbone of remote server administration, replacing insecure predecessors such as Telnet and rsh. Despite its ubiquity, SSH is frequently misconfigured, letting attackers pivot across infrastructure, establish covert tunnels, or harvest credentials. This chapter dissects the SSH-2 protocol, examines every authentication method, and builds hardened server configurations from the ground up.

docs.title: 17.1 SSH-2 Protocol Architecture
docs.text:
SSH-2 supersedes the insecure SSH-1 (which suffered from a CRC32 manipulation vulnerability) and is mandated by RFC 4251–4254. The protocol is organised into three layered sub-protocols.

Definition 17.1 (SSH Protocol Layers)

SSH-2 is composed of three logically separate layers that operate over TCP port 22:

  1. Transport Layer (RFC 4253) – Handles key exchange, server authentication, encryption, and integrity protection. Provides a binary packet protocol with negotiated algorithms.

  2. User Authentication Layer (RFC 4252) – Authenticates the client to the server using methods such as publickey, password, and keyboard-interactive.

  3. Connection Layer (RFC 4254) – Multiplexes the authenticated session into logical channels: interactive shells, exec commands, port-forwarding, and X11 forwarding.

The SSH handshake proceeds in five steps: (1) version exchange, (2) algorithm negotiation (SSH_MSG_KEXINIT), (3) key exchange producing a shared secret, (4) server host key verification, and (5) service request to begin authentication.

docs.title: 17.2 Key Exchange
docs.text:
Key exchange establishes a shared session key without transmitting it over the network. The negotiated KEX algorithm appears in the KexAlgorithms field of sshd_config.

Definition 17.2 (Diffie-Hellman Group 14 SHA-256)

diffie-hellman-group14-sha256 uses a 2048-bit MODP group (RFC 3526, Group 14). The shared secret is hashed with SHA-256 to derive symmetric keys. Acceptable for compatibility but inferior to elliptic-curve methods.

Definition 17.3 (curve25519-sha256)

curve25519-sha256 (RFC 8731) performs an ECDH key exchange on Curve25519. It provides 128 bits of security, is resistant to implementation timing attacks, and is the recommended default for modern deployments.

Recommended KEX Algorithms (2024+)

Prefer in order:

  1. curve25519-sha256 – Curve25519 ECDH, fastest and most secure

  2. sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com – Post-quantum hybrid (CRYSTALS-Kyber + Curve25519)

  3. diffie-hellman-group16-sha512 – 4096-bit DH, fallback

Avoid: diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 (Logjam-vulnerable 768-bit), diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1.

docs.title: 17.2.1 The Terrapin Attack (CVE-2023-48795)
docs.text:
Disclosed in December 2023 by Bäumer, Brinkmann, and Schwenk, Terrapin is a prefix truncation attack on the SSH binary packet protocol. It targets specific cipher mode combinations — specifically chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com and any cipher in -etm@openssh.com (Encrypt-then-MAC) mode for CBC ciphers — that were, at the time of disclosure, the strongest algorithm choices available and widely recommended.

The attack works because the SSH binary packet protocol initialises the sequence number to zero at the start of each direction independently and increments it per packet, but the sequence number is not itself cryptographically bound during the initial handshake phase before keys are derived. An active MITM positioned between client and server can inject or delete a controlled number of messages during the unencrypted handshake prologue (the version string exchange and KEXINIT messages) without the other party detecting the manipulation. After rekeying, the sequence numbers on each side are off by the number of injected or deleted messages. This offset breaks the synchronisation that AEAD nonces depend on for ChaCha20-Poly1305 and undermines the integrity guarantee of EtM MACs.

In practice the most serious consequence is the ability to downgrade the client’s offered host key algorithms or extension negotiation results. For example, an attacker could suppress the ext-info-c extension that enables RSA-SHA2 algorithm negotiation, forcing a fall-back to weaker RSA-SHA1 signatures for host key verification without either side raising an error.

Fix: Strict KEX Extension.

OpenSSH 9.6 (released December 2023 alongside the disclosure) introduced the kex-strict-c-v00@openssh.com and kex-strict-s-v00@openssh.com extension negotiation flags. When both client and server advertise strict KEX, the protocol resets the sequence number to zero immediately after the first key exchange completes and cryptographically binds the handshake transcript so that any injected or deleted message causes a MAC verification failure. Strict KEX is backward compatible: if either side does not advertise it, the session falls back to the old behaviour. Upgrading both client and server to OpenSSH 9.6 or later is the complete fix; patching only one side provides partial protection. Distributions that cannot upgrade immediately should remove chacha20-poly1305 and EtM cipher modes from sshd_config as a temporary workaround, though this degrades security in other respects.

docs.title: 17.3 Host Key Verification
docs.text:
The server presents a host key to authenticate itself to the client, preventing man-in-the-middle attacks. Clients record host keys in  /.ssh/known_hosts.

Definition 17.4 (Trust on First Use (TOFU))

TOFU is the default SSH policy: on first connection the client displays the host key fingerprint and stores it in known_hosts. Subsequent connections verify the fingerprint matches. This provides no protection on the first connection, where a MITM could substitute a rogue key.

TOFU is Not Authentication

TOFU defers the trust decision to a moment when users rarely verify fingerprints. Attackers performing ARP spoofing or DNS poisoning at initial connection time can establish a persistent MITM. For production infrastructure, use SSH certificate authorities or DNSSEC-signed SSHFP records instead.

Strict host checking prevents silent acceptance of changed keys:

# ~/.ssh/config
Host *
    StrictHostKeyChecking yes
    HashKnownHosts yes

docs.title: 17.4.1 Password Authentication
docs.text: Password authentication transmits the password encrypted inside the SSH tunnel. It’s vulnerable to brute force, credential stuffing, and phishing. Disable it on all public-facing servers.

docs.title: 17.4.2 Public Key Authentication
docs.text:
The client proves possession of a private key corresponding to a public key listed in  /.ssh/authorized_keys. The server sends a challenge; the client signs it with the private key.

Recommended Key Types

  • Ed25519 – 256-bit EdDSA on Curve25519; fast, compact, and resistant to weak RNG attacks. Preferred.

  • ECDSA (P-256/P-384) – Acceptable; avoid P-521 for compatibility.

  • RSA-4096 – Legacy interoperability only; prefer Ed25519.

  • DSA – Broken; do not use.

# Generate key pair
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice@workstation" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

# Deploy public key to server
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub user@server.example.com

# Verify authorized_keys entry
cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
# ssh-ed25519 AAAA... alice@workstation

docs.title: 17.4.3 SSH Certificate-Based Authentication
docs.text:
SSH certificates extend public key authentication with a CA model, eliminating TOFU for both host and user authentication.

Definition 17.5 (SSH Certificate Authority)

An SSH CA is an ordinary key pair (typically Ed25519) whose public key is distributed via configuration. The CA signs user or host public keys, embedding validity period, principals, and extensions into a certificate. Clients and servers trust certificates signed by a configured CA, removing the need to distribute individual public keys.

# Generate CA key (keep private key offline or in HSM)
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f /etc/ssh/ca_user_key -C "UserCA"
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f /etc/ssh/ca_host_key -C "HostCA"

# Sign a user public key: valid 8h, for principal "alice"
ssh-keygen -s /etc/ssh/ca_user_key \
           -I "alice@laptop-2024" \
           -n alice \
           -V +8h \
           ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
# Produces: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-cert.pub

# Sign a host public key: valid 52 weeks
ssh-keygen -s /etc/ssh/ca_host_key \
           -I "web01.example.com" \
           -h \
           -V +52w \
           /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub

# sshd_config: trust the host CA (eliminates TOFU)
# TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/ca_user_key.pub
# HostCertificate /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key-cert.pub

docs.title: Why SSH CAs Beat authorized_keys at Scale
docs.text:
Managing authorized_keys across hundreds of servers is painful. Adding a new engineer requires touching every server they need access to. Revoking access when someone leaves requires the same sweep, and a single missed server leaves a live credential. SSH certificate authorities solve both problems by inverting the trust model.

Instead of distributing individual public keys to servers, you distribute a single CA public key to every server’s TrustedUserCAKeys file. When the server receives a connection, it checks whether the client’s certificate is signed by a trusted CA and whether the requested login name matches one of the certificate’s principals — the list of Unix usernames the certificate is valid for (e.g., -n alice,deploy). No per-user entry is needed anywhere on the server.

Revocation is equally clean. Revoking the CA key invalidates every certificate it ever signed — a nuclear option for a security incident where the CA private key is compromised. For individual certificate revocation (e.g., a specific user’s certificate was stolen), OpenSSH supports a RevokedKeys file or a key revocation list (KRL) via ssh-keygen -k that servers consult before accepting a certificate.

Short-lived certificates and JIT access.

The most secure pattern issues certificates that are valid for the duration of a work session — 8 to 12 hours — and requires re-authentication through the CA each day. Tools like Hashicorp Vault SSH Secrets Engine, Netflix BLESS, and Teleport automate this: a user authenticates to the CA backend (with MFA), receives a signed certificate scoped to the production principals they need, uses it for the day, and has no persistent credential afterward. The server needs no revocation check: if the certificate is expired, it’s rejected. This eliminates the standing-access problem that makes long-lived SSH keys attractive to attackers doing lateral movement.

docs.title: 17.5 Key Exchange Diagram
docs.text: Figure 17.1. Simplified SSH-2 handshake: version exchange, algorithm negotiation, key exchange, and authentication.

docs.title: 17.6 Hardening sshd_config
docs.text:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config  -- hardened template

Protocol 2
Port 22  # Consider non-standard port + port-knock for obscurity

# Host keys: Ed25519 only
 HostKey /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key

# KEX / Cipher / MAC allowlists
KexAlgorithms curve25519-sha256,sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com
Ciphers chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com,aes256-gcm@openssh.com
MACs hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com

# Authentication
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
AuthorizedKeysFile .ssh/authorized_keys
ChallengeResponseAuthentication no
UsePAM yes
MaxAuthTries 3
LoginGraceTime 30

# Restrict access
AllowUsers alice bob deploy
AllowGroups sshusers

# Session hardening
ClientAliveInterval 300
ClientAliveCountMax 2
TCPKeepAlive no

# Feature restrictions
X11Forwarding no
AllowTcpForwarding no      # Set to "local" if tunnels needed
AllowAgentForwarding no
PermitTunnel no
Banner /etc/ssh/banner.txt # Legal warning banner

docs.title: Directive-by-Directive Rationale
docs.text:
The directives in the hardened template are not cargo-culted defaults — each closes a specific attack vector. The following explains what each one does and why it matters.

PermitRootLogin no.

Remote root login combines the highest-privilege account with a predictable username, making it a primary brute-force target. Disabling it forces attackers to first compromise an unprivileged account and then escalate locally, adding a detection opportunity. On systems that require root access, a jump via sudo from a named account preserves the audit trail; remote root would leave only the source IP in logs with no user attribution.

PasswordAuthentication no.

Password authentication is vulnerable to brute force, credential stuffing from breached databases, and phishing. Disabling it forces public key authentication, which requires physical possession of the private key (and its passphrase, if set). This single directive eliminates the entire class of automated scanning attacks that probe SSH on TCP/22 — scanners immediately drop connections to servers that refuse password auth because there is nothing left to guess.

AllowUsers and AllowGroups.

Without an explicit allowlist, any local account can attempt SSH login. System accounts created by packages (e.g., www-data, mysql, nobody) shouldn’t have SSH access. AllowUsers alice bob deploy creates an explicit whitelist; any other account gets an “Access denied” at authentication regardless of key. On larger systems, AllowGroups sshusers is easier to maintain: add users to the group rather than editing sshd_config each time.

MaxAuthTries 3.

Limits authentication attempts per connection. After 3 failures the connection is closed. This rate-limits brute-force attacks without requiring external tooling, though fail2ban should still run as a complementary layer that blocks source IPs after repeated reconnects.

LoginGraceTime 30.

Closes unauthenticated connections that haven’t completed login within 30 seconds. Without this, an attacker can leave thousands of half-open connections, contributing to resource exhaustion. The default is 120 seconds — far too long for any legitimate use case.

ClientAlive Interval and ClientAlive CountMax.

Setting ClientAlive­Interval 300 sends a keepalive probe over the encrypted channel every 300 seconds. ClientAlive­CountMax 2 drops the connection after 2 missed probes — effectively a 10-minute idle timeout. Together they terminate abandoned sessions that might otherwise persist indefinitely and remain accessible if an attacker reuses the terminal window. Setting TCPKeepAlive no disables the less secure TCP-level keepalive (which operates below the encrypted channel and is spoofable) in favour of the application-level SSH mechanism.

AllowAgentForwarding no.

On a bastion or general-purpose server, forwarding the SSH agent socket means any root-level process on that server can impersonate the connecting user to any host that trusts their key. This is not theoretical: SSH_AUTH_SOCK is visible in /proc/$pid/environ for processes running as root. Disable globally and enable only for specific, explicitly trusted bastions in the client-side  /.ssh/config when ProxyJump is not viable.

Banner /etc/ssh/banner.txt.

A pre-login legal warning is required by compliance frameworks (PCI DSS, HIPAA) and strengthens prosecutions under computer fraud statutes.
