Modern malware families use varied communication protocols to blend into normal network traffic and avoid signature-based detection. Understanding each protocol’s fingerprint and detection approach is a core skill for network defenders.

HTTP/S beaconing with jitter.

The most common C2 pattern is periodic HTTP or HTTPS requests to the C2 server (“beaconing”). The malware agent sleeps for a configured interval (often 60 seconds), wakes up, sends a check-in request (often a POST to a path like /gate.php or a fake favicon request) containing encoded victim data, receives tasking, sleeps again. The predictable periodicity creates a detectable signal: network flow records show regular connections to the same host at near-fixed intervals.

To defeat period-based detection, sophisticated C2 frameworks (Cobalt Strike, Brute Ratel C4) add jitter — a random variation applied to the sleep interval. With 30% jitter on a 60-second beacon, each sleep is between 42 and 78 seconds. The average is still 60 seconds, but no individual interval is predictable. Detection shifts from looking for fixed intervals to looking for statistical regularity: a host that makes exactly one outbound HTTPS request per minute (on average) to the same IP over many hours is almost certainly beaconing even with jitter. Tools like RITA (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics) perform beacon analysis by computing inter-connection timing statistics across NetFlow records.

Malleable C2 profiles (Cobalt Strike’s configuration system) go further, allowing the C2 traffic to mimic specific legitimate applications — replicating Amazon S3 request headers, Google Analytics parameters, or Microsoft Teams API calls. JA3 fingerprinting partially defeats this by fingerprinting the TLS ClientHello, but malleable profiles can randomise ClientHello parameters to defeat JA3.

DNS tunneling.

DNS tunneling encodes data in DNS query names and TXT or A record responses, exploiting the fact that most firewalls permit DNS traffic. Data is base64-encoded and split across subdomain labels: aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ.c2.attacker.com carries the data aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ (base64 for “hello world”) to the attacker’s authoritative DNS server. The attacker’s server decodes the query, executes the command, and returns the response encoded in the TXT record value. Tools like iodine and dnscat2 implement full bidirectional tunnels over DNS.

Detection indicators for DNS tunneling include: (1) unusually long query names (legitimate DNS queries average 30–40 bytes; tunneled queries often exceed 100 bytes); (2) high frequency of queries to a single authoritative server; (3) high NX-domain ratio (failed lookups from timing issues or encoding errors); (4) queries with high entropy in subdomain labels (base64 has higher entropy than human-readable subdomains); (5) TXT record responses that are unusually long or high-entropy. Network-level detection tools like Zeek with the dns-tunneling package and commercial NDR platforms flag these patterns automatically.

Domain Generation Algorithms in depth.

DGAs seed a pseudo-random number generator with a deterministic value — commonly the current date, a hardcoded constant, or data fetched from a public website (e.g., the current Bitcoin block hash, which serves as a shared seed that both malware and attacker compute independently). The PRNG produces a sequence of domain names, often 1,000 to 50,000 per day. The malware iterates through the list, attempting to resolve each domain. The attacker pre-registers a small subset (perhaps 10–20) and points them at the C2 infrastructure. Even if defenders blocklist today’s active C2 domains, the malware moves to tomorrow’s generated list.

DGA detection approaches: (1) machine learning classifiers trained on character n-grams and length distributions (DGA domains look random; legitimate domains have English words or brand names); (2) DNS NX-domain monitoring — a host querying dozens of NXDOMAIN responses per minute before a successful resolution is likely iterating a DGA list; (3) DGA reverse-engineering — if analysts extract the seed algorithm from a sample through static or dynamic analysis, they can pre-compute the entire domain list, register sinkhole domains for all of them, and observe all victim check-ins. The Cisco Umbrella security team has published seed algorithms for dozens of DGA families.

docs.title: 20.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 20.1

Write a YARA rule to detect ransomware samples that exhibit the following characteristics: (a) a valid PE header, (b) shadow copy deletion via vssadmin or wmic, (c) references to common file extensions targeted by ransomware (e.g., .docx, .xlsx, .pdf), and (d) network connectivity imports (wininet.dll or ws2_32.dll). Test your rule against a benign executable to verify there are no false positives.

Exercise 20.2

Describe how a PowerShell-based fileless malware attack evades traditional file-based antivirus detection. What artefacts, if any, does such an attack leave on disk, in the registry, and in memory? List three detection controls that specifically target fileless malware, explaining the technical basis for each.

Exercise 20.3

A malware sample is observed making DNS queries at regular 5-minute intervals to domains with the pattern [8-character-random].c2domain.com. Identify this behaviour pattern and explain the DGA mechanism. Describe how you would: (a) confirm it is a DGA using static analysis, (b) predict future C2 domains if the seed algorithm is discovered, and (c) deploy network-level detection for this C2 pattern without knowing the specific domains in advance.

docs.title: Chapter 21: Reverse Engineering
docs.text:
Reverse engineering (RE) is the process of recovering design, architecture, and implementation details from a compiled binary when source code is unavailable. It underpins malware analysis, vulnerability research, CTF competitions, interoperability work, and software auditing. This chapter covers the foundational skills: assembly comprehension, tool selection, anti-analysis bypass, deobfuscation, and cryptographic identification.

The progression in this chapter follows the natural workflow of a practising analyst—starting with static techniques, moving to dynamic debugging, then tackling the anti-analysis obstacles that real-world samples erect along the way.

docs.title: 21.1 Assembly and Calling Conventions
docs.text:
Definition 21.1 (x86-64 System V AMD64 ABI (Linux))

On 64-bit Linux, function arguments are passed in registers in order: RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9. Additional arguments are pushed on the stack right-to-left. The return value is in RAX (or RAX:RDX for 128-bit). Caller-saved registers: RAX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, R8--R11. Callee-saved: RBX, RBP, R12--R15.

Definition 21.2 (Microsoft x64 Calling Convention (Windows))

Windows 64-bit passes the first four arguments in RCX, RDX, R8, R9; remaining arguments go on the stack. The callee must allocate a 32-byte “shadow space” above the return address for the four register arguments. RAX carries the return value. Callee-saved: RBX, RBP, RDI, RSI, R12--R15.

Example 21.1 (Function Prologue and Epilogue)

; Function prologue (standard frame setup)
push    rbp              ; save caller's base pointer
mov     rbp, rsp         ; establish new stack frame
sub     rsp, 0x40        ; allocate 64 bytes of local storage
; ... function body ...

; Function epilogue (frame teardown)
mov     rsp, rbp         ; restore stack pointer
pop     rbp              ; restore caller's base pointer
ret                      ; pop return address, jump to caller

; Leaf function (no local variables, no calls): omits frame setup
; Common in highly optimised or obfuscated code

docs.title: 21.2 Disassembly vs. Decompilation
docs.text:
Definition 21.3 (Disassembly)

Disassembly converts machine code bytes into human-readable assembly mnemonics. It operates at the instruction level and is always possible for any binary. Linear-sweep disassembly (objdump) decodes bytes sequentially; recursive-descent disassembly (IDA, Ghidra) follows control flow and handles indirect jumps more accurately.

Definition 21.4 (Decompilation)

Decompilation reconstructs high-level language constructs (C pseudocode) from disassembly by inferring variable types, data structures, loops, and function signatures. Output quality depends on compiler optimisation level and obfuscation. IDA Pro’s Hex-Rays decompiler and Ghidra’s built-in decompiler are the two most capable tools.

docs.title: 21.2.1 IDA Pro vs. Ghidra vs. Binary Ninja
docs.text:
Choosing a disassembler shapes your entire workflow, so it is worth understanding the trade-offs before committing to one.

IDA Pro remains the industry benchmark. Its processor module library covers obscure embedded architectures (AVR, MIPS microcontrollers, obscure DSPs) that the others lack, and its autoanalysis heuristics—FLIRT signature matching, stack variable naming, struct propagation—are the most mature. The Hex-Rays decompiler plug-in produces the cleanest pseudo-C output for x86-64 and ARM64 and supports interactive type-editing that propagates across the database. The downside is cost: a floating IDA Pro licence with Hex-Rays runs tens of thousands of dollars per seat, which puts it out of reach for individuals and small teams.

Ghidra, released by the NSA in 2019, closed most of that gap for free. Its built-in decompiler handles most common architectures well, and the collaborative server mode—a feature IDA lacks natively—lets a team share an analysis database in real time, which is invaluable for large firmware images. The extension API (Java and Python) is well-documented, and community plugins now cover everything from YARA scanning to Golang symbol recovery. The main practical complaint is the Java runtime: startup is slower than IDA’s, and the GUI can feel sluggish on large binaries.

Binary Ninja occupies a middle ground. Its API is the most developer-friendly of the three—a clean Python/Rust API with a headless mode that makes it easy to write analysis scripts that run in CI without a GUI. It introduces a multi-level intermediate language (LLIL, MLIL, HLIL) that progressively lifts machine code toward high-level constructs, giving scripted analyses stable representations to work against. It’s the tool of choice when you need to automate triage over hundreds of firmware samples rather than deeply analyse a single binary.

All three produce decompiled pseudo-C output, support YARA-based search, and can import type information from PDB or DWARF. For most practitioners the realistic choice is Ghidra for daily use supplemented by a trial or team IDA licence for cases where Hex-Rays quality matters.

Table 21.1. Reverse engineering tool comparison Tool Platform Cost Decompiler Strengths IDA Pro Win/Lin/Mac Commercial Hex-Rays (extra) Industry standard; scripting; FLIRT Ghidra All Free (NSA) Built-in Open-source; team collab; plugins Binary Ninja Win/Lin/Mac Commercial Built-in Modern API; headless mode; MLIL Hopper Mac/Linux Commercial Built-in Lightweight; good for macOS/iOS Radare2 All Free r2dec/rz-ghidra CLI; scriptable; CTF-friendly x64dbg Windows Free No (debugger) Best Windows debugger; plugin-rich

docs.title: 21.3 Static Analysis Techniques
docs.text:
Static Analysis Workflow

  1. Import analysis: identify DLLs and API calls; network functions (WSAConnect, InternetOpenA) indicate C2; crypto functions (CryptEncrypt) indicate payload encryption.

  2. String references: locate plaintext IoCs (URLs, registry keys, mutex names, error messages).

  3. Cross-references (XREFs): find all callers of a function or all references to a string/global variable.

  4. Control flow graph (CFG): visualise conditional branches and loops to understand decision logic.

  5. Function signatures: use FLIRT (IDA) or Ghidra’s Function ID to auto-name statically linked library code.

Static analysis is the starting point for any sample. It costs nothing—no sandbox, no network access, no risk of detonating a live payload—and often reveals the majority of what you need to know before a single instruction executes.

docs.title: 21.3.1 Binary Diffing
docs.text:
When a vendor ships a security patch, the fixed binary is often public before most operators have deployed it. BinDiff (Google) and Diaphora (an open-source alternative that runs inside IDA and Ghidra) compare two binary versions function-by-function, scoring structural similarity using isomorphic subgraph matching on the control flow graph. Functions that changed between the pre-patch and post-patch builds surface immediately—the changed function is almost always where the vulnerability lived.

The workflow is straightforward: open both binaries in IDA, export the .i64 database files, then run BinDiff to produce a ranked similarity report. Functions scoring below around 0.8 similarity warrant close inspection. Diffing against a build that includes public debug symbols (PDB files or split DWARF) has a secondary benefit: BinDiff matches named functions from the debug build against the stripped release binary, letting you propagate names like handle_request or parse_header across without manually identifying each one. This dramatically reduces the time spent on standard library routines—once memcpy or sprintf is named, you can skip those call sites and focus on application logic.

Diaphora extends BinDiff’s approach with heuristics such as cyclomatic complexity matching, prime hash comparison of basic-block mnemonics, and pseudo-code diffing. It exports results as an SQLite database, which makes scripted querying straightforward. For CTF patch-diffing challenges, Diaphora’s SAME_MD_INDEX category (identical basic-block hash sequences) lets you skip unmodified functions entirely.

docs.title: 21.4 Dynamic Analysis with Debuggers
docs.text:
Where static analysis answers what is in the binary, dynamic analysis answers how it behaves. A debugger lets you pause execution at any instruction, inspect register state and memory, and patch values on the fly.

# Install GEF (GDB Enhanced Features)
pip3 install gef
echo "source /path/to/gef.py" >> ~/.gdbinit

# Attach to running process
gdb -p $(pgrep malware_sample)

# Set breakpoint at function entry by name or address
(gdb) break *0x401337
(gdb) break malloc

# Run and examine state at breakpoint
(gdb) run
(gdb) info registers          # show all registers
(gdb) x/20wx $rsp             # hex dump 20 words from stack pointer
(gdb) x/s $rdi                # print string at RDI (first argument)

# Step through code
(gdb) ni    # next instruction (step over calls)
(gdb) si    # step into calls
(gdb) finish # run until return from current function

# GEF: enhanced heap and memory views
(gdb) heap chunks             # display heap allocations
(gdb) pattern create 200      # generate cyclic pattern for offset finding

docs.title: 21.5 Anti-Analysis Techniques
docs.text: Most production malware includes some form of anti-analysis. The analyst’s job is to recognise these obstacles and bypass them without spending more time than the sample is worth.

docs.title: 21.5.1 Anti-Disassembly
docs.text:
Definition 21.5 (Opaque Predicates)

Opaque predicates are conditional branches whose outcome is always known to the author (always-true or always-false) but appears data-dependent to a static analyser. The false branch is filled with junk bytes that cause disassemblers to misinterpret subsequent legitimate code. A typical example: cmp eax, eax; jz legitimate_code with garbage bytes between the jz and legitimate_code.

docs.title: 21.5.2 Anti-Debugging
docs.text:
#include <windows.h>

// Technique 1: IsDebuggerPresent API check
BOOL check_debugger_api(void) {
    return IsDebuggerPresent();  // returns TRUE if debugger attached
}

// Technique 2: PEB.BeingDebugged flag (same as above, lower level)
BOOL check_peb(void) {
    // Reads PEB!BeingDebugged at offset 0x2 (x64: gs:[0x60]+2)
    BOOL dbg;
    __asm__ (
        "movq
        "movzbl 0x2(
        : "=r"(dbg) : : "rax"
    );
    return dbg;
}

// Technique 3: Timing check (RDTSC delta)
BOOL check_timing(void) {
    unsigned long long t1, t2;
    __asm__ volatile ("rdtsc" : "=A"(t1));
    // ... perform some work ...
    __asm__ volatile ("rdtsc" : "=A"(t2));
    return (t2 - t1) > 1000000ULL;  // threshold exceeded -> debugger
}

/* -------------------------------------------------------
   BYPASS: In x64dbg, set software breakpoint at the
   IsDebuggerPresent call, then:
   Option A: after call returns, manually set RAX = 0
   Option B: NOP out the conditional jump that follows:
             JNZ 0x401234  ->  NOP NOP (0x90 0x90)
   Option C: Use ScyllaHide plugin (hides debugger
             from all common detection methods)
   ------------------------------------------------------- */

docs.title: Deeper Anti-Debugging Techniques and Bypasses
docs.text:
The IsDebuggerPresent() API call is just the surface of a much larger catalogue. Experienced malware authors layer multiple checks so that disabling one leaves others intact.

The NtGlobalFlag check reads a DWORD at offset 0xBC from the Process Environment Block (PEB). Under a debugger, Windows sets flags 0x70 (heap tail checking, free checking, and parameter checking), whereas a non-debugged process has this field set to zero. Reading it with inline assembly is a single instruction and adds no import entry that a scanner would flag.

Timing checks exploit the fact that a debugger introduces measurable latency. The RDTSC instruction reads the processor’s timestamp counter, which increments billions of times per second. Malware calls RDTSC twice around a trivial code block, subtracts the values, and treats a delta above a threshold as evidence of single-stepping. On a modern CPU without a debugger, a handful of instructions completes in under 100 cycles; a human single-stepping in x64dbg takes millions.

Exception-based detection places a deliberate INT3 (opcode 0xCC) in the code stream. Under normal execution, the CPU raises an exception that the application’s own vectored exception handler catches and handles—execution continues normally. If a debugger is attached, it intercepts the INT3 first and pauses execution, which the exception handler detects because the exception never arrived.

Bypassing these requires more than NOPing a single check:

  • Hardware breakpoints (DR0–DR3 registers) do not modify the code stream, so they avoid INT3-based detection and do not affect timing checks the way software breakpoints do.

  • ScyllaHide is an x64dbg plugin that patches the TEB, PEB, and relevant kernel structures to hide the debugger from IsDebuggerPresent, NtGlobalFlag, NtQueryInformationProcess, heap flags, and several other common check points simultaneously. It also spoofs the RDTSC delta to a plausible non-debugged value.

  • For samples that check their own code bytes for 0xCC (software breakpoint bytes), hardware breakpoints combined with ScyllaHide cover the typical attack surface.

docs.title: 21.5.3 Anti-VM Detection
docs.text:
// Check for VMware registry key
BOOL check_vmware_registry(void) {
    HKEY hKey;
    return RegOpenKeyExA(HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE,
        "SOFTWARE\\VMware, Inc.\\VMware Tools",
        0, KEY_READ, &hKey) == ERROR_SUCCESS;
}

// Check CPUID hypervisor bit (bit 31 of ECX with leaf 1)
BOOL check_hypervisor_bit(void) {
    unsigned int ecx = 0;
    __asm__ ("cpuid" : "=c"(ecx) : "a"(1) : "ebx", "edx");
    return (ecx >> 31) & 1;  // hypervisor present bit
}
/* Bypass: patch conditional jump; or run on bare metal;
   or use al-khaser sandbox detection bypass tools */

docs.title: 21.6 Symbolic Execution with angr
docs.text:
Static analysis tells you what code exists; dynamic debugging tells you what one execution path does. Symbolic execution explores all feasible execution paths simultaneously by treating program inputs as symbolic variables rather than concrete values. At each conditional branch, the engine forks into two states—one where the condition is true, one where it is false—and a constraint solver (typically Z3) accumulates the path conditions that must hold for each state to be reachable.

angr is the dominant Python-based symbolic execution framework for binary analysis. Its Project object loads an ELF, PE, or raw binary; a SimulationManager then drives exploration across states.

import angr, claripy

# Load a 64-bit ELF (disable auto-loading of shared libs for speed)
project = angr.Project('./crackme', auto_load_libs=False)

# Create a symbolic stdin: 16 symbolic bytes labelled 'flag'
flag_chars = [claripy.BVS(f'flag_{i}', 8) for i in range(16)]
flag       = claripy.Concat(*flag_chars)

# Constrain to printable ASCII (optional, reduces search space)
state = project.factory.entry_state(stdin=angr.SimFile(
    name='stdin', content=flag, size=16))
for ch in flag_chars:
    state.solver.add(ch >= 0x20, ch <= 0x7e)

simgr = project.factory.simulation_manager(state)

# explore(find=...) halts states that reach the target address
# explore(avoid=...) prunes states that reach the failure path
simgr.explore(find=0x401234, avoid=[0x401500, 0x401600])

if simgr.found:
    winning_state = simgr.found[0]
    # Evaluate the symbolic stdin to get the concrete solution
    solution = winning_state.solver.eval(flag, cast_to=bytes)
    print(f"[+] Solution: {solution}")

The explore API drives the simulation manager until at least one state reaches the find address (success) while pruning any state that steps into an avoid address (failure path, e.g., a “Wrong password!” print). In a CTF crackme, this pattern typically solves the challenge in seconds—the solver produces the exact byte sequence that satisfies every branch condition on the path to the success print.

docs.title: 21.6.1 State Explosion and Veritesting
docs.text:
The fundamental weakness of symbolic execution is path explosion: a loop that iterates \(n\) times with a branch inside doubles the state count on each iteration, producing \(2^{n}\) states. A simple 32-iteration loop generates over four billion states, which exhausts both time and memory.

Veritesting (Avgerinos et al., 2014) mitigates this by automatically merging paths that reconverge after a conditional block. Instead of maintaining separate states for both branches of an if/else, Veritesting encodes the branch outcome as a conditional expression in the single merged state’s constraint set, then splits again only when paths truly diverge into irreconcilable control flow. angr implements Veritesting via the veritesting=True option on the simulation manager.

Other practical mitigations include under-constrained symbolic execution—running a single function in isolation with unconstrained inputs—and concolic execution (SAGE, DART), which runs concrete inputs through the binary while simultaneously tracking symbolic constraints, using coverage gaps to generate new concrete test cases. For large real-world binaries, these hybrid approaches are often more productive than pure symbolic exploration.

docs.title: 21.7 Unpacking: Finding the OEP
docs.text:
Definition 21.6 (Original Entry Point (OEP))

Packers encrypt or compress the original executable and add a stub that decompresses/decrypts the payload at runtime before transferring control to the OEP. Finding the OEP is the key step in unpacking:

  1. Load packed binary in x64dbg; note entry point (packer stub).

  2. Set hardware breakpoint on memory write to .text section (will trigger during decompression).

  3. Allow packer to run until decompression completes.

  4. At OEP, the code resembles a normal function prologue.

  5. Dump process memory and fix import table with Scylla plugin.

docs.title: 21.7.1 Packer Analysis and Import Reconstruction
docs.text:
Understanding the packer is as important as finding the OEP. Every packed binary follows the same high-level pattern: a stub runs first, it decompresses or decrypts the original code into a new memory region, then it transfers control to the OEP. What varies is the complexity of the stub.

UPX is trivially unpacked—the command upx -d target.exe restores the original binary in seconds. UPX is so well-known that antivirus products flag it immediately; any sample using UPX is usually the outer layer of a multi-stage dropper, not the final payload.

Custom packers require manual analysis. The tell-tale signs at load time are: the binary has few or no readable imports (often only LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress), the PE sections have names like .mpress, .pack, or randomised strings, and the entry point sits in a section marked with execute, read, and write permissions—unusual for legitimate code because writable executable memory is a red flag. The stub uses VirtualAlloc to allocate the unpacked region, writes the decompressed PE into it, then patches its own import table by calling GetProcAddress for each imported function before jumping to the OEP.

The unpacking workflow in x64dbg proceeds as follows. After attaching, set a hardware breakpoint (ba w4) on the beginning of the .text section—this fires when the stub writes the decompressed code. Allow execution to continue; the breakpoint will trigger mid-decompression. Step through until the decompression loop finishes and the stub performs a long jump (jmp eax or push eax; ret) into the freshly written region—that target address is the OEP.

Import reconstruction is the final step. The unpacked image in memory has a valid code section but a broken or empty import table, because the original Import Address Table (IAT) was stripped. The Scylla plugin for x64dbg handles this automatically: point it at the OEP, click “IAT Autosearch”, and it walks the code looking for indirect calls through a table of function pointers, then resolves each pointer back to the originating DLL export. “Dump” writes the unpacked PE to disk and “Fix Dump” patches the import table into the new file, producing a fully functional reconstructed binary that IDA or Ghidra can analyse without the packer stub overhead.

Recognising the decompression algorithm helps predict what to expect. LZ-family (LZMA, aPLib) produce expanding output; AES-CBC decryption produces equal-size output with a 16-byte-aligned ciphertext block. Entropy scanning (detect-it-easy, PEiD) gives a quick fingerprint before you invest time in manual analysis.

docs.title: 21.8 Deobfuscation: XOR Decoding
docs.text:
XOR encoding is the most common obfuscation primitive in malware. It’s fast to implement, trivially reversible, and works on any payload. Frequency analysis cracks single-byte and short repeating keys in seconds.

import sys

def find_xor_key(data: bytes, key_length: int) -> bytes:
    """
    Recover repeating XOR key using frequency analysis.
    Assumes the plaintext is ASCII with high frequency of 0x00 / spaces.
    """
    key = bytearray(key_length)
    for i in range(key_length):
        # Collect every key_length-th byte
        chunk = bytes(data[j] for j in range(i, len(data), key_length))
        # Most frequent byte XOR'd with 0x00 gives the key byte
        freq = max(range(256), key=lambda b: chunk.count(bytes([b])))
        key[i] = freq  # assuming plaintext 0x00 most common (or use ' ')
    return bytes(key)

def xor_decode(data: bytes, key: bytes) -> bytes:
    return bytes(b ^ key[i

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with open(sys.argv[1], "rb") as f:
        payload = f.read()

    # Try known key lengths (1-16 bytes)
    for klen in range(1, 17):
        key = find_xor_key(payload, klen)
        decoded = xor_decode(payload, key)
        printable = sum(32 <= b < 127 for b in decoded)
        score = printable / len(decoded)
        if score > 0.80:
            print(f"Key length {klen}: key={key.hex()} score={score:.2
            with open(f"decoded_{klen}.bin", "wb") as out:
                out.write(decoded)

docs.title: 21.9 Recognising Crypto in Binaries
docs.text:
Cryptographic algorithms leave distinctive fingerprints: lookup tables, characteristic constants, and arithmetic patterns. Knowing these lets an analyst quickly identify what a binary is encrypting, and with what.

Definition 21.7 (AES S-Box Constant)

AES is identified in binaries by the presence of its S-box lookup table, which begins with the bytes 0x63, 0x7C, 0x77, 0x7B, 0xF2, 0x6B, 0x6F, 0xC5, 0x30, 0x01. Search for this byte sequence in IDA/Ghidra to locate the AES implementation; surrounding code reveals the key schedule and modes in use.

Definition 21.8 (RSA Identification)

RSA is commonly identified by the public exponent 65537 (0x10001) as an immediate value or embedded constant, and by large modular exponentiation loops. The Montgomery multiplication algorithm and Barrett reduction are characteristic code patterns. High-entropy 256- or 512-byte buffers adjacent to these constants are likely RSA key material.

docs.title: 21.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 21.1

A binary sample passes control to a function containing the following assembly sequence before performing sensitive operations:

call IsDebuggerPresent
test eax, eax
jnz  0x401500    ; jumps to exit() if debugger detected
; ... sensitive payload code at 0x4014A0 ...

Identify the anti-debugging technique being used. Describe three distinct methods to bypass this check in x64dbg without modifying the sample on disk. What is the difference between a software breakpoint and a hardware breakpoint, and why might a hardware breakpoint evade the timing-based variant of this check?

Exercise 21.2

A malware sample contains an encrypted payload. Static analysis reveals a loop that XORs each byte of a 512-byte buffer with a cycling key, reading key bytes from a 4-byte array at 0x403010. Write a Python script that takes the encrypted buffer (extracted as a binary file) and automatically determines the most likely 4-byte XOR key using frequency analysis, then decodes and writes the plaintext payload. What assumptions does your frequency analysis rely on?

Exercise 21.3

Describe the process of finding the Original Entry Point (OEP) of a UPX-packed PE binary using x64dbg. Include: the initial state when the packed binary loads, the specific technique used to identify when decompression is complete, the characteristic assembly instructions that identify the OEP in a MSVC-compiled binary, and the steps required to dump and reconstruct a working import table using the Scylla plugin.

docs.title: Chapter 22: Digital Forensics
docs.text:
Digital forensics is the science of recovering, preserving, and analysing digital evidence in a manner that withstands legal scrutiny. This chapter covers the foundational principles, disk and file system analysis, memory forensics, network forensics, and the emerging challenges of mobile and cloud environments—concluding with anti-forensics techniques that analysts must recognise.

The chapter follows the natural order of an investigation: evidence collection and preservation first, examination and analysis second, reporting last. Each phase has distinct technical and legal requirements, and skipping steps in the early phases can make later analytical work inadmissible.

docs.title: 22.1 Forensics Principles
docs.text:
Definition 22.1 (Locard’s Exchange Principle)

Every contact leaves a trace. In digital forensics, every action taken by an attacker on a system leaves artefacts: modified timestamps, log entries, registry keys, memory allocations, or network packets. The analyst’s task is to identify and interpret these traces. The analyst’s own examination also modifies the system (accessing files updates atime, for instance), which must be minimised and documented.

Definition 22.2 (Chain of Custody)

Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken record of who collected, handled, transferred, and stored digital evidence. Each transfer must be recorded with time, date, personnel, and hashes of the evidence at each stage. Gaps or inconsistencies in the chain may render evidence inadmissible in court.

Forensic Acquisition Principles

  • Write blockers: Hardware (Tableau, WiebeTech) or software write blockers prevent any writes to the evidence disk during acquisition, ensuring original evidence integrity.

  • Forensic copy: A bit-for-bit copy of the entire storage device, including slack space, deleted files, and unallocated space. Common tools: dd, FTK Imager, dcfldd.

  • Hash verification: MD5 or SHA-256 hash computed on the original device and on the forensic copy; they must match. This hash is documented in the case log.

# Block-level acquisition with dd (attach write-blocked drive as /dev/sdb)
dd if=/dev/sdb of=/evidence/case001_disk.img bs=512 conv=noerror,sync \
   status=progress

# Verify acquisition integrity
sha256sum /dev/sdb > /evidence/case001_original.sha256
sha256sum /evidence/case001_disk.img | diff - /evidence/case001_original.sha256

# dcfldd: dd with hashing and split output
dcfldd if=/dev/sdb of=/evidence/case001.img \
        hash=sha256 hashlog=/evidence/case001_hash.log \
        bs=4096 conv=noerror,sync sizeprobe=if

# Mount forensic image read-only for analysis
losetup -r /dev/loop0 /evidence/case001.img
mount -o ro,noatime,offset=1048576 /dev/loop0 /mnt/evidence

docs.title: 22.2.1 Write Blockers and Evidence Integrity
docs.text:
A write blocker sits between the examiner’s workstation and the suspect storage device, intercepting any write commands the OS might issue and returning a “write protected” response while allowing read commands through unaltered. This is not merely a precaution—it’s a legal requirement in most jurisdictions. If a write reaches the suspect drive (even something as innocuous as a filesystem journal update triggered by mounting), the chain of custody breaks and defence counsel can argue the evidence was tampered with.

Hardware write blockers are the gold standard. The Tableau TX1 and WiebeTech Forensic UltraDock are the two most widely used in professional labs. They connect via USB, eSATA, or PCIe to the suspect drive and expose a read-only interface to the forensic workstation. Because they operate at the hardware level, they block writes regardless of what the host OS does—mounting the drive, autorunning, or issuing TRIM commands all fail silently.

Software write blockers are acceptable when hardware blockers are unavailable. On Linux, hdparm -r 1 /dev/sdb sets the read-only flag for the block device, and mounting with mount -o ro,noatime ensures no access-time updates. On Windows, the registry key HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\ Control\StorageDevicePolicies with WriteProtect=1 achieves a similar effect. The risk with software write blockers is that a misconfigured OS—or one that ignores the flag during hot-plug—can still issue writes before the protection activates.

Hash verification closes the chain of custody loop. Compute an MD5 and SHA-256 of the original device (sha256sum /dev/sdb) before acquisition and record the values in the case log. After imaging, hash the image file and compare. A match proves bit-for-bit fidelity; any mismatch, no matter how small, invalidates the copy. Best practice is to hash both before and after every transfer (e.g., when moving the image from the acquisition laptop to the analysis server), so that any alteration—intentional or accidental—is detectable at the exact transfer where it occurred.

Definition 22.3 (NTFS Key Metadata Files)

NTFS maintains several system files critical for forensic analysis:

  • $MFT – Master File Table: one record per file/directory; contains timestamps (Created, Modified, Accessed, MFT-Modified – the “MACE” times), permissions, and data attribute offsets.

  • $LOGFILE – Transactional log for NTFS metadata operations; useful for recovering recently deleted file names.

  • $UsnJrnl:$J – Update Sequence Number journal: records file/directory create, rename, delete, and attribute change events with timestamps; persists across reboots.

  • $Bitmap – Records which clusters are allocated (in use) vs. unallocated (available for carving).

docs.title: 22.2.2 File Carving
docs.text:
Definition 22.4 (File Carving)

File carving reconstructs files from unallocated disk space using file format magic bytes (file signatures), without relying on file system metadata (which may be deleted or overwritten). Carving works even when the $MFT entry for a file has been reused.

Table 22.1. Common file signature magic bytes for carving File Type Extension Header (hex) Footer (hex) JPEG image .jpg FF D8 FF FF D9 PNG image .png 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A 49 45 4E 44 AE 42 60 82 PDF document .pdf 25 50 44 46 (%PDF) 25 25 45 4F 46 ZIP archive .zip 50 4B 03 04 50 4B 05 06 Windows PE .exe 4D 5A (MZ) N/A SQLite DB .db 53 51 4C 69 74 65 20 33 N/A OLE2 (Office) .doc D0 CF 11 E0 A1 B1 1A E1 N/A 
# Scalpel: configure /etc/scalpel/scalpel.conf to enable file types
# then run against disk image
scalpel -c /etc/scalpel/scalpel.conf \
        -o /evidence/carved/ \
        /evidence/case001.img

# PhotoRec: interactive; carves 480+ file types; ignores file system
photorec /evidence/case001.img

# Foremost: classic carver; specify types
foremost -t jpg,pdf,zip -i /evidence/case001.img -o /evidence/foremost/

docs.title: File Carving Challenges and Fragmented Recovery
docs.text:
Carving contiguous files is straightforward—the header and footer are both present in adjacent sectors and the tool simply extracts the bytes between them. The hard cases are fragmented files. When a large file was written to a nearly-full volume, the filesystem allocator scattered its clusters across multiple non-adjacent regions. After deletion, the cluster chain stored in the MFT entry is gone, so a carver has no map of which sectors belong together. Most tools handle this by using the maximum expected file size from the configuration file to limit how far they search for a footer after a header match. Set the limit too low and you truncate large files; set it too high and fragmented data from other files gets spliced in, producing corrupt output.

Foremost and Scalpel use static header/footer pairs from configuration files, which you can customise. JPEG carving is reliable because FF D8 FF is distinctive and FF D9 is a clean footer. ZIP-family formats (DOCX, XLSX, APK, JAR) present a harder problem: the central directory is at the end of the archive, not the beginning, and fragmentation between the local file headers and the central directory breaks most simple carvers.

PhotoRec takes a different approach: it understands the internal structure of over 480 file formats and uses this knowledge to validate carved candidates. For example, after finding a JPEG header it parses the JFIF/EXIF structure to determine the true file length, then extracts exactly that many bytes rather than searching for the footer. This format-aware approach produces fewer false positives and handles many fragmentation cases that header/footer carvers miss.

For a practical investigation, always run at least two carvers—their false positive and false negative rates differ by format. Use MD5 deduplication (md5deep -r) on the output directories to avoid re-examining identical files carved under different names. When time allows, bulk_extractor complements file carving by scanning for structured data (email addresses, credit card numbers, URLs, Base64 blobs) without attempting full file reconstruction.

docs.title: 22.3 Timeline Analysis
docs.text:
Definition 22.5 (Super-Timeline)

A super-timeline aggregates timestamps from all available sources on a system into a single chronological record, enabling reconstruction of the attacker’s activity sequence. Sources include: $MFT MACE times, $UsnJrnl, Windows Event Logs, Registry LastWrite times, prefetch files, browser history, LNK files, and shellbags.

# Create Plaso storage file from disk image
log2timeline.py --storage-file /evidence/case001.plaso \
                /evidence/case001.img

# Filter and export to CSV (sorted by time)
psort.py -o l2tcsv \
         -w /evidence/timeline.csv \
         /evidence/case001.plaso \
         "date > '2024-01-14 00:00:00' AND date < '2024-01-16 00:00:00'"

# Quick grep for suspicious events
grep -i "powershell\|mimikatz\|vssadmin\|net user" /evidence/timeline.csv | \
     sort -t',' -k1,1 | head -50

docs.title: 22.3.1 Log Correlation for Incident Reconstruction
docs.text:
A super-timeline built solely from disk artefacts gives you filesystem activity; layering event log and network data transforms it from a list of file timestamps into a narrative of what actually happened. The key is correlating artefacts across sources around the same timestamp windows.

Windows Event Log is the richest single source on Windows endpoints. Critical event IDs for incident reconstruction:

  • 4624 — Successful logon: records logon type (2 = interactive, 3 = network, 10 = remote interactive/RDP), source IP for type 3/10, and the authenticating account.

  • 4625 — Failed logon: correlate a cluster of 4625 events followed by 4624 to identify credential stuffing or brute force.

  • 4688 — Process creation (requires audit policy enablement): records parent PID, full command line, and creating user. The command line field reveals powershell -enc ... or wscript.exe suspicious.vbs immediately.

  • 4697 — Service installed: attackers commonly install malicious services for persistence; this event captures service name, binary path, and start type.

  • 4698 / 4702 — Scheduled task created/modified: a common persistence mechanism; the task XML embedded in the event contains the command that will execute.

  • 7045 — System event log: new service installed (similar to 4697 but logged to the System channel).

Web server access logs contribute HTTP method, URI, response code, and source IP. Correlating a suspicious POST to /wp-admin/upload.php (web server log) with an outbound connection to an unknown IP (firewall log) five minutes later (Zeek conn.log) and a new PowerShell process (Event ID 4688) five minutes after that is the pattern that confirms web shell deployment and first-stage command execution.

Plaso (log2timeline) ingests all of these sources—Windows Event Logs (.evtx), IIS/Apache logs, Windows Registry, LNK files, prefetch, Zeek logs, and many others—and merges them into a single .plaso storage file sorted by timestamp. psort.py then queries and exports slices to CSV or JSON for SIEM ingestion or manual review.

# Ingest disk image plus separately collected event logs
log2timeline.py --storage-file case.plaso \
                --parsers winevtx,prefetch,lnk,recycler,mft \
                /evidence/case001.img

# Add network logs from Zeek
log2timeline.py --storage-file case.plaso \
                --parsers zeek \
                /evidence/zeek_logs/

# Export 48-hour window around suspected compromise
psort.py -o l2tcsv -w /evidence/timeline_48h.csv case.plaso \
         "date > '2024-03-10 06:00:00' AND date < '2024-03-12 06:00:00'"

# Search the timeline for persistence indicators
grep -iE "4697|4698|schtasks|reg add|startup" /evidence/timeline_48h.csv | \
     sort -t',' -k1,1

When building the incident narrative, work backwards from a known bad event (e.g., ransomware encryption start visible in the USN journal) and trace each causal predecessor. The 4688 process creation before the encryption reveals the ransomware binary path; the 4624 logon before that reveals how the attacker authenticated; the firewall log before the logon reveals the source IP. This backward chaining through a correlated timeline is the core analytical technique.

docs.title: 22.4 Memory Forensics
docs.text:
Definition 22.6 (Memory Forensics)

Memory forensics analyses a snapshot (dump) of a system’s RAM to recover running processes, network connections, loaded modules, decrypted payloads, and credentials that exist only in volatile memory. Evidence in memory is lost on power-off, making timely acquisition essential.

# Acquisition on Windows (requires admin)
winpmem_mini_x64.exe /evidence/memory.dmp

# Acquisition on Linux (LiME kernel module)
insmod lime-5.15.0.ko "path=/evidence/memory.dmp format=lime"

# Volatility 3: list running processes
python3 vol.py -f /evidence/memory.dmp windows.pslist

# Show command-line arguments for each process
python3 vol.py -f /evidence/memory.dmp windows.cmdline

# Active network connections (like netstat on live system)
python3 vol.py -f /evidence/memory.dmp windows.netscan

# Find injected/suspicious memory regions (VAD with RWX permissions)
python3 vol.py -f /evidence/memory.dmp windows.malfind \
               --dump --output-dir /evidence/malfind_dumps/

# Extract NTLM hashes from LSASS
python3 vol.py -f /evidence/memory.dmp windows.hashdump

# Search for strings in all memory regions
python3 vol.py -f /evidence/memory.dmp windows.strings \
               --string-file /tools/interesting_strings.txt

windows.malfind Interpretation

windows.malfind identifies memory regions that are: (1) PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE or similar executable+writable permissions (uncommon in legitimate code), and (2) not backed by a file on disk (anonymous allocations). False positives: JIT-compiled code (.NET, JavaScript engines). True positives: shellcode, reflective DLL injections, unpacked malware stages. Always dump and analyse the flagged regions.

docs.title: 22.4.1 Process Injection Artefacts in Memory
docs.text:
Process injection is the technique attackers use to run malicious code inside a legitimate process, borrowing that process’s trust level and network identity. Recognising the artefacts each injection technique leaves in a memory dump is a core memory forensics skill.

Process hollowing (also called RunPE) creates a target process—often svchost.exe or explorer.exe—in a suspended state, unmaps its original image from memory, writes a malicious PE in its place, and resumes execution. The tell-tale artefact is a mismatch between the PE header in memory and the PE header of the file on disk: the in-memory image at the process base address has a different ImageBase, section names, or magic bytes than the legitimate executable. The Volatility plugin hollowfind compares the in-memory PE header against the on-disk file to detect this.

Classic DLL injection (via CreateRemoteThread + LoadLibrary) is detected by inspecting the target process’s module list for DLLs that don’t belong there. windows.dlllist enumerates the InLoadOrderModuleList from the PEB; any DLL whose path points to a temp directory, AppData, or a non-standard location is suspicious. Cross-referencing against a known-good baseline eliminates the vast majority of legitimate DLLs quickly.

Reflective DLL injection is harder to detect because the injected DLL maps itself into memory using a custom loader routine rather than the Windows loader, so it never appears in the PEB module list. The artefacts are: a memory region with RWX permissions whose content parses as a valid PE header (the “MZ” magic bytes at the start of the region), but with no corresponding module list entry or backing file path. windows.malfind catches most reflective injections by flagging anonymous RWX allocations with PE headers.

Process Doppelganging and Transacted Hollowing are newer variants that abuse Windows NTFS transactions (TxF) to write the malicious PE into a transacted file, map it, then roll back the transaction—leaving no file on disk but a fully mapped image in memory. These defeat on-disk scanning entirely and require memory-only indicators.

Practical Volatility workflow for injection detection:

# Detect RWX anonymous memory with MZ headers (malfind)
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.malfind --dump \
               --output-dir /evidence/malfind_dumps/

# Check each flagged PID's module list for rogue DLLs
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.dlllist --pid 1234

# Hollowfind: compares in-memory PE vs on-disk PE
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.hollowfind

# cmdline: show command-line of every process (injected processes
# sometimes have no argv or an implausible path)
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.cmdline

# For DLL injection: look for LoadLibrary thread start addresses
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.handles --pid 1234

When malfind dumps a region to a file, run file and strings against the dump. A PE header at offset 0 confirms injected code; strings containing C2 addresses, mutex names, or known malware markers give immediate indicators of compromise without waiting for sandbox execution.

docs.title: 22.5 Network Forensics
docs.text:
# Extract HTTP objects from pcap
tshark -r capture.pcap --export-objects http,/evidence/http_objects/

# List all DNS queries and responses
tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "dns" -T fields \
       -e frame.time -e ip.src -e dns.qry.name -e dns.a

# Extract TLS SNI (server names, even without decryption)
tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "tls.handshake.type == 1" \
       -T fields -e ip.dst -e tls.handshake.extensions_server_name

# Follow TCP stream (reassemble payload)
tshark -r capture.pcap -q -z follow,tcp,ascii,0

# Zeek: generate structured logs from pcap
zeek -r capture.pcap local
# Produces: conn.log, dns.log, http.log, ssl.log, files.log, etc.

# Analyse Zeek logs: find high-byte connections (potential exfiltration)
zeek-cut id.orig_h id.resp_h id.resp_p orig_bytes resp_bytes \
         duration < conn.log | sort -k5 -rn | head -20

docs.title: 22.5.1 PCAP Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
A packet capture is the closest thing to ground truth in network forensics: it records every byte that crossed the wire. The analyst’s challenge is extracting meaning from potentially gigabytes of raw data.

Wireshark display filters are the first triage tool. Unlike capture filters (which drop packets at collection time), display filters let you show or hide packets from a full capture without discarding anything. Useful patterns:

  • http.request.method == "POST" — shows only HTTP POST requests; immediately surfaces form submissions, file uploads, and API calls that carry data.

  • tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0 — SYN-only packets; each represents a new outbound connection attempt; scanning activity produces hundreds in rapid succession.

  • dns.qry.name contains "dga" — adapts to look for domain-generation-algorithm patterns or known bad domains.

  • tls.handshake.extensions_server_name — filters to TLS ClientHello packets; the SNI field reveals the intended destination hostname even though the TLS payload is encrypted.

Following TCP streams reconstructs the full application-layer conversation from a sequence of packets. In Wireshark, right-click any packet in the target stream and choose “Follow \(\to\) TCP Stream”. The reconstructed session appears in a scrollable window, with client data in red and server data in blue. This is the fastest way to read an HTTP exchange, FTP transfer, or any cleartext protocol without filtering packet by packet.

tshark is the command-line equivalent and is invaluable for automated processing:

# Extract HTTP host headers from all requests
tshark -r capture.pcap -T fields \
       -e frame.time -e ip.src -e http.host -e http.request.uri \
       -Y "http.request" > /evidence/http_requests.txt

# List unique DNS queries and their resolved IPs
tshark -r capture.pcap -T fields \
       -e dns.qry.name -e dns.a \
       -Y "dns.flags.response == 1" | sort -u

# Find all SYN packets to non-standard ports (potential C2)
tshark -r capture.pcap -T fields \
       -e ip.dst -e tcp.dstport \
       -Y "tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0 && \
           tcp.dstport != 80 && tcp.dstport != 443" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

# Export all HTTP objects (files transferred)
tshark -r capture.pcap --export-objects http,/evidence/http_objects/

Zeek (formerly Bro) processes pcap files or live traffic and generates structured log files for each protocol layer. The conn.log is particularly useful—it contains one row per completed TCP/UDP connection with source and destination IP, port, duration, and byte counts in each direction. Sorting conn.log by resp_bytes descending immediately highlights large data transfers; sorting by connection count per destination IP reveals beaconing behaviour (a constant, low-volume connection repeating every N seconds is a classic C2 heartbeat). The http.log, dns.log, ssl.log, and files.log similarly provide a concise, queryable summary of each protocol without requiring packet-level inspection.

For large captures, NetworkMiner passively reconstructs transferred files and credentials, while Rita (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics) runs statistical analysis on Zeek logs to score hosts for long-connection, beaconing, and DNS-tunnelling behaviour automatically.

docs.title: 22.6 Browser Forensics
docs.text:
import sqlite3, shutil, os

CHROME_PROFILE = os.path.expanduser(
    "~/.config/google-chrome/Default/")

# Chrome must be closed to read History (lock check)
def get_chrome_history(profile_path):
    db_path = os.path.join(profile_path, "History")
    tmp = shutil.copy2(db_path, "/tmp/chrome_history_copy")
    conn = sqlite3.connect(tmp)
    cur  = conn.cursor()
    cur.execute("""
        SELECT datetime(last_visit_time/1000000-11644473600,'unixepoch'),
               url, title, visit_count
        FROM   urls
        ORDER  BY last_visit_time DESC
        LIMIT  100
    """)
    for row in cur.fetchall():
        print(row)
    conn.close()

get_chrome_history(CHROME_PROFILE)

# Other forensically relevant Chrome SQLite DBs:
# Cookies    -> domain, name, value, expiry
# Login Data -> origin_url, username_value (password: DPAPI encrypted)
# Downloads  -> current_path, tab_url, total_bytes, received_bytes

docs.title: 22.7 Mobile Forensics
docs.text:
Definition 22.7 (iOS Forensic Acquisition Levels)

  • iCloud backup extraction: No device access needed; limited to iCloud backup contents; may not include all app data. Tools: Elcomsoft Phone Breaker.

  • Logical acquisition: Via iTunes/Finder backup; captures app data, messages, photos; requires an unlocked device or PIN.

  • Advanced logical / GrayKey: Exploits iOS vulnerabilities to bypass passcode and extract the file system; availability varies by iOS version.

  • Chip-off / JTAG: Physical access to NAND; rarely used for iOS due to hardware encryption making raw NAND useless without the key.

Definition 22.8 (Android Forensic Acquisition)

Android acquisition depends on encryption state and ADB access:

  • ADB backup: adb backup -all -apk -shared; limited on Android 12+ due to backup restrictions.

  • ADB pull: For rooted devices; adb pull /data/data/ extracts app databases.

  • FBE (File-Based Encryption): Android 7+ encrypts per-user with a key derived from PIN; data is inaccessible without the PIN.

  • Commercial tools: Cellebrite UFED, Magnet AXIOM support broader acquisition via exploits and vendor assistance.

docs.title: 22.8 Cloud Forensics
docs.text:
# List CloudTrail events for a specific user in a time window
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
    --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=Username,AttributeValue=compromised-user \
    --start-time "2024-01-15T00:00:00Z" \
    --end-time   "2024-01-16T00:00:00Z" \
    --query "Events[*].[EventTime,EventName,CloudTrailEvent]" \
    --output table

# Download and parse CloudTrail logs from S3
aws s3 cp s3://my-cloudtrail-bucket/AWSLogs/ /evidence/cloudtrail/ --recursive

# Parse with jq: find all IAM key creation events
cat /evidence/cloudtrail/*.json | \
    jq '.Records[] | select(.eventName == "CreateAccessKey") |
        {time: .eventTime, actor: .userIdentity.arn,
         target: .responseElements.accessKey.userName}'

# Athena query for GuardDuty findings correlated with CloudTrail
# (requires Athena table set up for CloudTrail logs)

docs.title: 22.9 Anti-Forensics
docs.text:
Definition 22.9 (Timestomping)

Timestomping modifies file system timestamps (MACE: Modified, Accessed, Created, MFT-Entry-Modified) to make malicious files appear older than they are or to match surrounding legitimate files. On NTFS, there are two sets of timestamps: \(STANDARD_INFORMATION</code> (manipulable by user-space tools) and <code>\)FILE_NAME (only modifiable from kernel mode, not by standard timestomping tools). Comparing these two sets reveals timestomping.

Common Anti-Forensics Techniques

  • Secure deletion: Tools like shred (Linux) or Eraser (Windows) overwrite file data before deletion. On SSDs, TRIM complicates recovery; on RAID or journalled filesystems, fragments may survive. The Gutmann 35-pass method is excessive for modern media; DoD 5220.22-M (3 passes) is sufficient.

  • Log deletion / manipulation: Attackers clear Windows Event Logs (wevtutil cl Security) or remove /var/log/auth.log entries. Centralised log shipping (SIEM) defeats this when logs were already forwarded.

  • Encrypted containers: VeraCrypt hidden volumes contain two encrypted volumes with different passwords; the outer volume is plausible deniability cover. Without the correct password, a hidden volume is cryptographically indistinguishable from random data.

  • Steganography: Hiding data within innocuous files (images, audio); steghide, OpenStego. Detected by statistical analysis (chi-square test, RS analysis).

docs.title: 22.12 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 22.1

You respond to an incident on a live Windows server believed to be running ransomware. Describe the memory forensics process from acquisition through analysis: (a) which memory acquisition tool would you use and why, (b) list the Volatility 3 plugins you would run and what each reveals, (c) explain how windows.malfind works technically and what its output means, and (d) describe how you would extract and analyse a flagged memory region to confirm malicious injection.

Exercise 22.2

A hard disk seized from a suspect has been imaged with dd. Explain the chain of custody procedures that must be followed from physical seizure through to presentation of evidence in court. What is the purpose of computing hash values at multiple stages, and what does a hash mismatch at any point mean for the evidential value of the data? How does write-blocking protect the admissibility of evidence?

Exercise 22.3

During a mobile forensics examination, an investigator discovers that the suspect’s Android device uses Android 13 with File-Based Encryption (FBE) and the screen lock is set to a 6-digit PIN. The device was seized in an unlocked state. Describe: (a) what data is accessible while the device remains unlocked (before/after first unlock vs. direct boot states), (b) the risk of the device locking during transport and how to mitigate it, (c) which commercial tools support acquisition from Android 13, and (d) what artefacts browser and application databases would reveal about the suspect’s activities.

docs.title: Chapter 23: Vulnerability Research and Fuzzing
docs.text: Vulnerability research is the systematic practice of discovering, analysing, and responsibly disclosing security weaknesses in software, hardware, and protocols. It underpins every other area of offensive and defensive security: without a solid understanding of how vulnerabilities arise, defenders cannot build effective mitigations and attackers cannot be studied empirically.

docs.title: 23.1 The Vulnerability Lifecycle
docs.text:
A vulnerability does not spring into existence at the moment it is discovered; it already exists in deployed systems, waiting. The vulnerability lifecycle describes the stages from initial discovery through remediation.

Definition 23.1 (Vulnerability Lifecycle)

The vulnerability lifecycle comprises the following stages:

  1. Discovery – A researcher, attacker, or automated tool identifies a potential weakness in a target.

  2. Analysis – The weakness is confirmed to be exploitable; root cause, impact, and affected versions are determined.

  3. Proof-of-Concept (PoC) – A minimal, demonstrable exploit is constructed to validate exploitability.

  4. Disclosure – The vulnerability is reported to the vendor (and/or the public) according to the chosen disclosure policy.

  5. Patch Development – The vendor engineers and tests a fix.

  6. CVE Assignment – MITRE assigns a CVE identifier; NIST NVD publishes the CVSSv3.1 score.

  7. Patch Deployment – Operators apply the patch; the patch gap (time between release and deployment) is a prime attack window.

docs.title: 23.1.1 Disclosure Policies
docs.text:
Three disclosure philosophies compete in practice:

Responsible (Coordinated) Disclosure The researcher notifies the vendor privately and allows a fixed embargo period (typically 90 days, as established by Google Project Zero) before public release. This balances vendor time-to-fix against the public’s right to know. Full Disclosure Details and PoC are released immediately without prior vendor notification. Proponents argue it maximises pressure to patch; opponents note it gives no remediation window. Bug Bounty Programs Vendors offer monetary rewards for responsible disclosure via platforms such as HackerOne and Bugcrowd. Researchers receive compensation while the vendor retains control over timing.

Zero-Day Markets

Vulnerabilities for which no patch exists (zero-days) are traded on grey and black markets. Government agencies (NSA, GCHQ) and brokers (Zerodium) pay millions of dollars for high-quality exploits, creating incentive structures that compete with responsible disclosure.

docs.title: 23.1.2 Bug Bounty Programs in Depth
docs.text:
Bug bounty programs have matured from informal arrangements into a structured industry worth hundreds of millions of dollars annually. Understanding how they work matters whether you’re submitting reports or running a programme.

Private vs. public programmes. Most vendors launch private first, inviting a curated set of researchers under NDA while the programme is still maturing. Private programmes give the vendor time to fix high-severity findings before a public announcement; researchers get access to a less-competed target. Once the triage backlog stabilises, the programme goes public and any researcher can submit. Apple Security Research Device Programme and Meta’s bug bounty are examples of well-run private-to-public transitions.

Bounty tiers. Payouts correlate with severity and impact, but the ranges vary enormously:

Severity Typical Range Example Critical (RCE, auth bypass) $10,000–$1,000,000+ Apple pays $1M for zero-click kernel RCE High (privilege escalation, data breach) $5,000–$50,000 Google $30k for Android PE Medium (stored XSS, SSRF) $1,000–$10,000 Bug-specific Low (self-XSS, info disclosure) $150–$1,000 Volume submissions

Scope documents define what is and isn’t permitted. In-scope sections list the specific domains, IP ranges, or application features the vendor wants tested. Out-of-scope sections prohibit actions like social engineering employees, physical access, DoS attacks, and testing third-party infrastructure. Exceeding scope—even accidentally—can result in legal action regardless of the bug bounty’s existence.

Disclosure timelines. The 90-day standard established by Google Project Zero (introduced in 2014) has become industry-accepted: if the vendor hasn’t produced a patch within 90 calendar days, the researcher publishes. Some vendors negotiate extensions for particularly complex fixes; others don’t engage at all. CERT/CC and other coordination bodies can act as intermediaries when a vendor is unresponsive, escalating toward public disclosure to create pressure.

The distinction between responsible disclosure, coordinated vulnerability disclosure (the ISO/IEC 29147 standard term), and full disclosure matters legally. Coordinated disclosure includes the vendor in the process from the start and allows them a reasonable remediation window. Full disclosure bypasses this, which in some jurisdictions can expose the researcher to liability even if the vulnerability is real. Researchers should read the programme’s legal safe-harbour clause carefully—most major platforms (HackerOne, Bugcrowd) include boilerplate that grants legal protection for good-faith testing within scope.

docs.title: 23.2 CVE and CVSSv3.1 Scoring
docs.text:
The Common Vulnerability Scoring System v3.1 (CVSSv3.1) provides a standardised numerical score (0.0–10.0) capturing both the technical characteristics of a vulnerability and its contextual severity.

Definition 23.2 (CVSSv3.1 Base Metrics)

The base score is derived from eight metrics grouped into two areas:

  • Exploitability: Attack Vector (AV), Attack Complexity (AC), Privileges Required (PR), User Interaction (UI).

  • Impact: Scope (S), Confidentiality (C), Integrity (I), Availability (A).

Each metric takes a set of discrete values; the resulting formula produces a score mapped to None / Low / Medium / High / Critical.

docs.title: 23.2.1 Log4Shell: A Worked CVSSv3.1 Example
docs.text:
CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) affected Apache Log4j 2.x and allowed unauthenticated remote code execution via a crafted JNDI lookup string in any logged value.

CVE-2021-44228 CVSSv3.1 Vector

CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H

AV:N Attack Vector = Network (exploitable remotely) AC:L Attack Complexity = Low (no special conditions) PR:N Privileges Required = None UI:N User Interaction = None S:C Scope = Changed (impact extends beyond vulnerable component) C:H Confidentiality = High I:H Integrity = High A:H Availability = High

Base Score: 10.0 Critical

docs.title: 23.2.2 CVSS v4.0 and EPSS
docs.text:
CVSS v4.0, released by FIRST in November 2023, addresses several criticisms of v3.1 that practitioners had raised over the preceding six years.

The most significant structural change is the replacement of the Temporal metric group with a Threat metric group containing a single metric: Exploit Maturity (values: Unreported, Proof-of-Concept, Attacked). This aligns the metric with observable threat intelligence—if active exploitation in the wild is confirmed, Exploit Maturity is set to Attacked, raising the effective score. The old Temporal metrics (Exploitability, Remediation Level, Report Confidence) mapped poorly to real-world data sources, so most organisations left them at defaults, rendering Temporal scores meaningless.

CVSS v4.0 also adds a Supplemental metric group that provides additional context without affecting the numeric score:

  • Safety: whether exploitation could cause physical harm to people (relevant for ICS/SCADA and medical devices).

  • Automatable: whether the exploitation steps can be fully automated (wormable vulnerabilities score Yes).

  • Recovery: whether the system returns to its pre-exploit state automatically, manually, or not at all.

  • Value Density: whether a single exploit delivers diffuse or concentrated impact (a cloud hypervisor vulnerability has high value density; a single-user desktop vulnerability has low).

The Scope Changed ambiguity—where v3.1’s S:C was interpreted inconsistently across vendors—is resolved in v4.0 by explicitly modelling the Subsequent System (downstream components affected by exploitation) separately from the Vulnerable System (the component containing the bug). This produces cleaner, more consistent scoring across CVEs.

EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System), maintained by FIRST, is increasingly used alongside CVSS for prioritisation. While CVSS measures severity—how bad exploitation would be—EPSS measures likelihood: the probability that a given CVE will be actively exploited in the wild within 30 days of its publication. EPSS is a machine-learning model trained on real exploitation data (Shadowserver, GreyNoise, and other threat intel feeds) and updated daily.

In practice, the combination of CVSS and EPSS is more actionable than either alone. A CVE-2024-1234 might score 9.8 on CVSS (Critical severity) but have an EPSS score of 0.002 (0.2% exploitation probability), meaning the severity is high but attackers aren’t actually using it. CVE-2024-5678 might score 7.5 (High severity) but have an EPSS of 0.61 (61% exploitation probability), meaning it’s actively weaponised. Any rational patching prioritisation should address the second CVE first. Organisations integrating EPSS into their vulnerability management workflows have reported measurably improved mean time to remediation for actively exploited CVEs.

docs.title: 23.3 Fuzzing
docs.text:
Fuzzing (fuzz testing) supplies malformed, unexpected, or semi-random inputs to a target program and monitors for crashes, hangs, or other anomalous behaviour. It remains one of the most productive bug-finding techniques per engineering hour.

Definition 23.3 (Dumb vs. Coverage-Guided Fuzzing)

Dumb Fuzzing Inputs are generated or mutated without feedback from the target. Simple and fast to set up; poor at reaching deep code paths. Coverage-Guided Fuzzing The fuzzer instruments the target to measure code coverage (edge/branch coverage). Inputs that discover new coverage are retained in the corpus and mutated further. Examples: AFL++, LibFuzzer, honggfuzz.

docs.title: 23.3.1 AFL++ Workflow
docs.text:
AFL++ (American Fuzzy Lop++) is the de facto standard for binary and source-level coverage-guided fuzzing.

# Compile target with AFL++ instrumentation
CC=afl-clang-fast CXX=afl-clang-fast++ ./configure && make

# Run fuzzer: corpus in, findings out, target reads from @@
afl-fuzz -i corpus/ -o findings/ -- ./target @@

# Parallel fuzzing: one main, N secondary instances
afl-fuzz -M main  -i corpus/ -o findings/ -- ./target @@
afl-fuzz -S sec01 -i corpus/ -o findings/ -- ./target @@

# Triage crashes
afl-triage -i findings/default/crashes/ -- ./target @@

AFL++ output includes: total execs/sec, coverage (edges found), number of crashes, and number of hangs. A healthy campaign shows steadily increasing edge count; a plateau suggests corpus exhaustion or a hard-to-reach code path.

docs.title: 23.3.2 Coverage-Guided Fuzzing Internals
docs.text:
AFL++ instruments the target at compile time by inserting a short callback at every basic block edge—the transition between each pair of consecutive basic blocks in the control flow graph. At runtime, this callback XORs the current block’s ID with the previous block’s ID and increments a counter in a 64 KB shared memory bitmap that both the fuzzer process and the target process map. After each test case execution, the fuzzer inspects the bitmap: if any counter changed that wasn’t set in previous runs, the input discovered new coverage and is added to the corpus. Inputs that exercise no new edges are discarded.

This feedback loop is what makes AFL++ dramatically more effective than dumb fuzzing. A dumb fuzzer that flips random bits can run for days without reaching a deeply nested error-handling path that requires the first four bytes of input to spell PNG\x89. A coverage-guided fuzzer discovers the magic byte check on the first run that happens to get the header right, adds that input to the corpus, and from then on only mutates inputs that already pass the check—converging on deep paths orders of magnitude faster.

The QEMU mode (afl-fuzz -Q) instruments binaries at the basic block level without source code, using QEMU’s dynamic translation layer. Coverage is coarser than source instrumentation but still dramatically outperforms dumb fuzzing on closed-source targets.

Grammar-based fuzzing takes a different approach for protocols with strict structure. Tools like Boofuzz and Peach (now open-sourced as Peach Community) model the protocol message format as a tree of typed fields—integers, strings, arrays—and mutate each field independently while keeping the surrounding structure valid enough for the target to parse. This reaches code paths that random mutation never would, because a randomly mutated TLS ClientHello is almost always rejected at the record-layer length check before any interesting parsing happens. Grammar-based fuzzing trades breadth of coverage for depth in specific protocol paths; combining it with AFL++ (using grammar-generated seeds as the initial corpus) gives both.

docs.title: 23.3.3 Mutation Strategies and Corpus Management
docs.text:
AFL++ employs bitflip, byte arithmetic, havoc (random), and splice mutations. Effective corpus management involves:

  • Minimising the initial seed corpus (afl-cmin) to remove redundant seeds.

  • Minimising individual crashing inputs (afl-tmin) for analysis.

  • Periodically harvesting crash inputs as new seeds.

docs.title: 23.3.4 Sanitizers
docs.text:
Sanitizers are compiler-inserted runtime checks that surface bugs that would otherwise be silent:

Sanitizer Flag Detects AddressSanitizer (ASan) -fsanitize=address Buffer overflows, UAF, heap-buffer-overflow UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan) -fsanitize=undefined Integer overflow, null-ptr deref MemorySanitizer (MSan) -fsanitize=memory Uninitialised memory reads ThreadSanitizer (TSan) -fsanitize=thread Data races

Always fuzz with ASan+UBSan enabled; this dramatically increases bug yield.

Figure 23.1. Coverage-guided fuzzing feedback loop

docs.title: 23.4 Binary Analysis: Symbolic Execution
docs.text:
Definition 23.4 (Symbolic Execution)

Symbolic execution explores program paths by treating inputs as symbolic variables rather than concrete values. A constraint solver (typically Z3) determines which concrete inputs satisfy path conditions.

Tools include angr (Python), KLEE (LLVM IR), and Triton (dynamic symbolic execution).

import angr

project = angr.Project('./crackme', auto_load_libs=False)
state    = project.factory.entry_state()
simgr    = project.factory.simulation_manager(state)

# Explore: reach 0x401234, avoid 0x401500 (bad path)
simgr.explore(find=0x401234, avoid=0x401500)

if simgr.found:
    solution = simgr.found[0]
    print(solution.posix.dumps(0))   # stdin that reaches target

docs.title: 23.4.1 Path Explosion Problem
docs.text:
The fundamental limitation of symbolic execution is path explosion: the number of distinct paths through a program grows exponentially with loops and branches. Mitigation strategies include:

  • Veritesting – automatically merge feasible paths.

  • Under-constrained execution – analyse functions in isolation.

  • Concolic execution – combine concrete and symbolic execution (SAGE, DART).

  • State merging – merge states with phi-nodes.

docs.title: 23.5 Static Analysis
docs.text:
Static analysis examines source or binary code without execution, finding defects at scale.

CodeQL GitHub’s semantic code analysis framework. Queries are written in a Datalog-like language; pre-built queries detect injection, path traversal, and unsafe deserialization. Semgrep Pattern-matching rules targeting AST nodes; fast enough for CI/CD integration; extensive community rule registry. Coverity / SonarQube Commercial and open-source tools with extensive interprocedural analysis; report taint flows and null-pointer paths. 
semgrep --config "p/c" \
        --pattern 'printf($X)' \
        --pattern-not 'printf("...", ...)' \
        ./src/

False positive management is the main operational challenge: high FP rates cause alert fatigue. Techniques include: tuning rule severity, suppression comments, and ML-based ranking.

docs.title: 23.5.1 CodeQL: Semantic Code Analysis
docs.text:
CodeQL (originally developed by Semmle, now maintained by GitHub/Microsoft) operates at a level above pattern matching. Rather than matching tokens or AST nodes in isolation, CodeQL extracts the entire program into a relational database of facts—every variable, expression, call site, data flow edge, and control flow edge becomes a queryable row. Queries are written in QL, a Datalog-like language that abstracts over AST nodes and lets you express end-to-end dataflow paths from source to sink.

The canonical SQL injection query in QL looks for any call to a database execute method where an argument is reachable via taint tracking from a user-controlled source. In pseudocode terms:

-- Sources: HTTP request parameters, headers, body fields
isSource(node) :- node is a RemoteFlowSource

-- Sinks: any argument to Statement.execute() or executeQuery()
isSink(node) :- exists MethodAccess call where
    call.getMethod().hasName("execute") and
    node.asExpr() = call.getAnArgument()

-- Report all taint paths from source to sink
select sink, source, sink, "SQL injection from this source"
where TaintTracking::hasFlowPath(source, sink)

This query doesn’t just flag individual expressions—it reports the complete dataflow path from the HTTP parameter through every intermediate assignment and method call until it reaches the SQL statement, making triage far faster than with line-level findings. The @kind path-problem annotation causes the GitHub code scanning interface to render the full path as an expandable call chain, so a developer sees exactly how untrusted data flows from request.getParameter("id") into stmt.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=" + id).

CodeQL integrates into GitHub Actions via codeql -action: add uses: github/ codeql-action/ analyze@v3 to your CI workflow and every pull request gets a security scan with results posted as code review comments. The --query-suite parameter selects the query pack; for a Java project, java-security-extended covers injection, XSS, SSRF, deserialization, and several other high-value bug classes. Because results are tied to specific source locations and display taint paths, developers can understand exactly what needs to change rather than guessing from a generic warning.

docs.title: 23.6.1 Protocol Fuzzing with Boofuzz
docs.text:
Boofuzz is a Python framework for network protocol fuzzing. It models protocol state machines and fuzzes each field systematically.

from boofuzz import *

session = Session(target=Target(
    connection=TCPSocketConnection("192.168.1.1", 21)))

s_initialize("USER")
s_string("USER", fuzzable=False)
s_delim(" ")
s_string("admin", name="username")   # fuzzed field
s_static("\r\n")

session.connect(s_get("USER"))
session.fuzz()

docs.title: 23.6.2 Patch Diffing
docs.text: When a vendor releases a silent patch, BinDiff or Diaphora can compare pre- and post-patch binaries to pinpoint changed functions. A security researcher can then reverse-engineer the changed function to understand the underlying vulnerability before most defenders have deployed the patch — the patch gap window.

docs.title: 23.7 Bug Classes
docs.text: Bug Class Description Buffer Overflow (BOF) Write beyond allocated buffer; corrupts adjacent memory Use-After-Free (UAF) Dereference pointer after memory is freed; object reuse leads to type confusion Double Free Free the same pointer twice; corrupts allocator metadata Type Confusion Object accessed via pointer of wrong type (common in JIT engines) Integer Overflow/Underflow Arithmetic wraps around; length checks bypassed Format String printf(user_input) allows stack read/write via %x/%n TOCTOU Race Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use; file path changes between check and use Logic Bug Incorrect program logic leads to unintended behaviour (e.g., auth bypass) Injection SQL/command/LDAP injection via unsanitised input

docs.title: 23.7.1 Heap Exploitation Primitives
docs.text:
Modern heap exploitation targets the glibc malloc (ptmalloc2) implementation:

tcache Poisoning The tcache (thread-local cache) stores freed chunks in singly-linked lists. If an attacker can overwrite a tcache fd pointer (via UAF or overflow), subsequent malloc() calls return an attacker-controlled address. Heap Spray Allocate many objects of a specific size to increase the probability that a dangling pointer refers to attacker-controlled data. Use-After-Free Concept Free an object; trigger reallocation of the same memory region by another object; access the original pointer to interact with the new object’s data.

docs.title: 23.8 Exploit Mitigations
docs.text:
