Mitigation Description ASLR Randomises base addresses of stack, heap, and libraries PIE Position-Independent Executable; randomises code segment base NX/DEP No-Execute / Data Execution Prevention; marks data pages non-executable Stack Canary Random value placed before return address; checked on function return RELRO (Full) Marks GOT read-only after dynamic linking; prevents GOT overwrites Control Flow Integrity (CFI) Restricts indirect call/jump targets to valid function entries SafeStack Separates sensitive stack data (return addresses) from general stack

Mitigation Layering

No single mitigation is sufficient. ASLR without PIE leaks the code segment base. NX without ASLR enables ret2libc with known addresses. Full RELRO + PIE + Stack Canary + ASLR + CFI creates a substantially hardened target, though information leaks and logic bugs can still bypass layered defences.

docs.title: 23.9 Fuzzing Tools Comparison
docs.text: Tool Instrumentation Target Type Notable Feature AFL++ Source (LTO) / QEMU / Frida Binary + source Diversified mutation strategies LibFuzzer Clang source (SanitizerCoverage) Source-level library In-process; fastest exec/s honggfuzz Source / HW perf counters Binary + source Multi-arch; hardware coverage Boofuzz None (black-box) Network protocols State-machine modelling syzkaller Kernel kcov Linux/BSD kernels Syscall grammar-aware

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 23.1

Calculate the CVSSv3.1 base score for a local privilege escalation vulnerability that requires low-privilege access, has low attack complexity, requires no user interaction, and achieves high Confidentiality and Integrity impact but no Availability impact, with Scope Unchanged. Use the NVD calculator to verify.

Exercise 23.2

Design a fuzzing campaign for a network-facing PDF parser library. Specify: (a) initial corpus collection strategy, (b) build flags (compiler and sanitizers), (c) AFL++ invocation including parallel instances, (d) crash triage workflow, and (e) criteria for stopping the campaign.

Exercise 23.3

Explain the path explosion problem in symbolic execution. Give a concrete example of a loop structure that causes state space explosion. Describe two mitigation strategies and their respective trade-offs in terms of completeness and performance.

Exercise 23.4

A vendor silently fixes a memory corruption bug in a widely deployed network daemon by incrementing a bounds-check constant from 1023 to 1024. Describe the patch diffing methodology an attacker might use to (a) identify the changed function, (b) determine the root cause, and (c) develop a proof-of-concept before most operators have patched. What policies could the vendor adopt to reduce the patch gap?

docs.title: Chapter 24: Exploit Development Fundamentals
docs.text:
Exploit development is the discipline of converting a confirmed vulnerability into a controlled, reliable program flow deviation. This chapter covers the technical foundations of memory corruption exploitation, the tools used by security researchers, and the mitigations that defenders deploy. All content is presented for educational and defensive purposes; no working shellcode is included.

Legal and Ethical Scope

Exploit development skills must only be applied to systems for which you have explicit written permission. Unauthorised exploitation is a criminal offence in virtually all jurisdictions (e.g., the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act in the USA, the Computer Misuse Act in the UK).

docs.title: 24.1 Process Memory Layout
docs.text:
Understanding how a process is laid out in virtual memory is the foundation of all memory-corruption exploitation.

Figure 24.1. Linux x86-64 virtual address space layout (simplified)

The stack grows downward; each function call pushes a stack frame containing saved registers, local variables, and the return address. The return address is the prime target in classical stack buffer overflow exploitation.

docs.title: 24.2 Stack Buffer Overflow
docs.text:
Definition 24.1 (Stack Buffer Overflow)

A stack buffer overflow occurs when data written into a fixed-size stack buffer exceeds the buffer’s allocated length, overwriting adjacent stack memory including, ultimately, the saved return address.

When the vulnerable function returns, the CPU loads the attacker-controlled return address into RIP and execution transfers there.

docs.title: 24.2.1 Finding the Offset
docs.text:
The pwntools library provides cyclic patterns for offset discovery:

from pwn import *

# Generate a 200-byte De Bruijn cyclic pattern
pattern = cyclic(200)
print(pattern)
# Send pattern to the binary, observe crash value in RIP

# After crash, find the offset
crashed_rip_value = 0x6161616261616161   # from debugger
offset = cyclic_find(crashed_rip_value)
print(f"[*] Offset to RIP: {offset} bytes")

docs.title: 24.2.2 Classic Exploitation Flow (Conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Determine the exact number of bytes to the saved return address (the offset).

  2. If NX is disabled, place a payload (e.g., shellcode) on the stack and redirect execution to it.

  3. If NX is enabled (the common case), use ret2libc: redirect execution to an existing library function such as system().

from pwn import *

# Attach to the local process (for research/CTF purposes)
elf  = ELF('./vuln')
libc = ELF('/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6')
p    = process('./vuln')

# Assume we have already leaked a libc address (see Section 24.4)
libc.address = leaked_base

offset   = 72                        # bytes to saved return address
pop_rdi  = p64(0x0000000000401234)   # ROP gadget: pop rdi; ret
ret_gadget = p64(0x000000000040101a) # stack-alignment gadget
system   = p64(libc.sym['system'])
bin_sh   = p64(next(libc.search(b'/bin/sh')))

# Payload: padding | pop_rdi | "/bin/sh" addr | ret (align) | system()
payload  = b'A' * offset
payload += pop_rdi
payload += bin_sh
payload += ret_gadget
payload += system

p.sendline(payload)
p.interactive()
# Note: this template illustrates structure only; real exploitation
# requires a working binary and explicit authorisation.

docs.title: 24.2.3 Heap Exploitation Fundamentals
docs.text:
The heap is the other major memory corruption target. Understanding glibc’s allocator internals—ptmalloc2—is essential for exploiting use-after-free and heap overflow bugs.

Every heap allocation in glibc is wrapped in a chunk whose header immediately precedes the user data. A free chunk contains two additional pointer fields overlaid on what was user data:

Field Offset (64-bit) Purpose prev_size chunk - 16 Size of previous chunk (if free) size chunk - 8 Size of this chunk; low 3 bits are flags fd chunk + 0 (Free only) Forward pointer to next free chunk bk chunk + 8 (Free only) Back pointer to previous free chunk

The classic unlink exploit (glibc pre-2.3.4) abused the doubly-linked free list: writing attacker-controlled fd and bk pointers into a free chunk header, then triggering a coalesce operation, caused glibc’s unlink macro to write an arbitrary value to an arbitrary address. Modern glibc adds safe-unlink checks that verify fd->bk == chunk and bk->fd == chunk before unlinking, defeating this primitive unless both pointers are controlled simultaneously.

Safe-linking (glibc 2.32+) adds an additional mitigation for tcache and fastbin free lists. The fd pointer of a freed chunk is no longer stored in plaintext but is mangled as:

\[\texttt{fd}_{\text{stored}} = \texttt{fd}_{\text{real}} \oplus (\texttt{chunk\_addr} \gg 12)\]

This means an attacker who can write to the fd field but doesn’t know the chunk’s own address cannot directly forge a valid pointer, because the XOR key depends on the chunk address. An information leak that reveals a heap address is now a prerequisite for tcache poisoning on glibc 2.32+.

Use-after-free (UAF) is the most productive heap exploit primitive on modern targets. The pattern:

  1. Allocate object A of size \(n\); acquire a pointer p.

  2. Free object A; p is now a dangling pointer.

  3. Allocate object B of the same size \(n\) (the allocator reuses the same region for B).

  4. Write attacker-controlled data into B via a separate reference.

  5. Dereference p—which now points into B—treating B’s data as A’s type (type confusion).

When object A is a C++ object containing a virtual function table (vtable) pointer, overwriting the vtable pointer in step 4 redirects the next virtual dispatch through p to an attacker-controlled function. This is the mechanism behind the majority of browser renderer exploits: the V8/SpiderMonkey JIT heap is full of objects with vtable pointers and the JavaScript engine creates and destroys objects at attacker-visible rates.

docs.title: 24.3 Return-Oriented Programming (ROP)
docs.text:
Definition 24.2 (Return-Oriented Programming)

ROP chains together short instruction sequences ending in ret (gadgets) that already exist in the binary or its libraries. Because these instructions reside in executable memory, NX/DEP is bypassed.

docs.title: 24.3.1 Finding Gadgets
docs.text:
ROPgadget --binary ./vuln --rop --depth 5

# Useful output examples:
# 0x0000000000401234 : pop rdi ; ret
# 0x000000000040101a : ret
# 0x0000000000401236 : pop rsi ; pop r15 ; ret

# Search for a specific gadget
ROPgadget --binary ./vuln --string "pop rdi"

A typical 64-bit ret2libc ROP chain for calling system("/bin/sh") is:

\[\underbrace{\texttt{pop rdi; ret}}_{\text{load 1st arg}} \;|\; \underbrace{\texttt{addr("/bin/sh")}}_{\text{argument}} \;|\; \underbrace{\texttt{ret}}_{\text{stack align}} \;|\; \underbrace{\texttt{system()}}_{\text{call target}}\]

docs.title: 24.3.2 ret2libc and ret2plt
docs.text:
ret2libc is the canonical NX bypass: instead of injecting shellcode on the stack, you redirect the return address into an existing library function—most commonly system("/bin/sh") in libc. The ROP chain loads the string address into RDI (the first argument register on x86-64 System V ABI) using a pop rdi; ret gadget, then returns into system().

The obstacle is ASLR: libc’s base address is randomised each time the process loads. You need a leak gadget—a read primitive that reveals a runtime libc address—before you can compute system()’s address. A format string %p read, a GOT entry printed via a vulnerable puts call, or an out-of-bounds read all work as leak primitives. Once you have any libc address, subtract its offset from the libc symbol table to get the base, then add the system offset:

from pwn import *

libc = ELF('/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6')

# Assume we leaked the address of puts() at runtime
leaked_puts = 0x7f3a4b2c1d40        # from info-leak exploit step

# The offset of puts in this libc version
puts_offset = libc.sym['puts']       # e.g. 0x80970

libc_base   = leaked_puts - puts_offset
system_addr = libc_base + libc.sym['system']
bin_sh_addr = libc_base + next(libc.search(b'/bin/sh'))

print(f"libc base:  {libc_base:#x}")
print(f"system():   {system_addr:#x}")
print(f"/bin/sh:    {bin_sh_addr:#x}")
# Note: libc version must match exactly; ldd ./vuln shows which version

ret2plt is a related technique that doesn’t require an explicit libc leak. The Procedure Linkage Table (PLT) contains stubs for every dynamically linked function; calling the PLT stub for a function triggers the dynamic linker to resolve the real address if it hasn’t been called yet, or jumps directly to the cached address in the GOT if it has. An attacker can call puts@plt with the GOT address of puts as the argument; puts will print the raw 8-byte GOT entry (the runtime libc address of puts), converting a call primitive into a leak without a pre-existing read gadget. This is the standard two-stage ret2plt + ret2libc pattern for 64-bit CTF binaries:

  1. Stage 1: Overflow, use ROP to call puts@plt(got["puts"]), read the printed bytes, compute libc base.

  2. Stage 2: Return to main or vuln() to get a second overflow opportunity; this time use the known libc base to call system("/bin/sh").

docs.title: 24.4 Format String Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Definition 24.3 (Format String Vulnerability)

A format string vulnerability arises when user-controlled input is passed directly as the format argument to printf or similar functions.

/* VULNERABLE: user controls the format string */
printf(user_input);

/* SAFE: user input is a data argument, not the format */
printf("

Format specifiers the attacker exploits:

  • %x / %p — read values off the stack (leak addresses for ASLR bypass).

  • %n — write the number of bytes printed so far to the pointed-to integer; achieves arbitrary write.

  • %k$x — direct parameter access: read the \(k\)-th argument (stack offset \(k\)).

docs.title: 24.4.1 The %n Write Primitive
docs.text:
The %n format specifier writes the count of bytes printed so far into the integer pointed to by the corresponding argument. Combined with a width specifier that pads output to a specific count, an attacker can write an arbitrary value to an arbitrary address. The format string "%100c%7$n" prints 100 characters of padding and then writes the value 100 into the memory location stored at stack argument position 7—if the attacker has placed a target address at that stack position (by controlling the format string buffer’s placement relative to the stack frame), this is a one-byte write to a chosen address.

Writing a full 8-byte pointer requires multiple %n writes, each targeting successive bytes of the destination address. The format string exploit is therefore verbose but extremely powerful: given a format string vulnerability and a stack layout that places attacker-controlled data in the argument list, an attacker can overwrite any writable memory location—GOT entries, the saved return address, or function pointers in global data.

The musl libc implementation deliberately omits %n support entirely. Any call to printf with a %n specifier on a musl-linked binary returns an error immediately, closing this attack surface. The glibc team added a __USE_FORTIFY_LEVEL check at level 1 that rejects %n in format strings that come from writable memory (i.e., not a string literal), catching the most common exploit pattern while preserving compatibility for legitimate uses of %n in hardcoded format strings.

docs.title: 24.5 ASLR Bypass Techniques
docs.text: Technique Description Information Leak Format string, heap pointer print, or out-of-bounds read leaks a runtime address; base is computed by subtracting known offset Partial Overwrite Overwrite only the low bytes of a pointer (page offset unchanged); avoids randomised high bytes Brute Force On 32-bit systems ASLR has only \(\approx 2^{16}\) effective positions; repeated attempts succeed quickly Heap Spray Fill heap with payload; statistically target the fixed-offset region

docs.title: 24.6 Heap Exploitation Overview
docs.text: tcache Poisoning (glibc \(\geq\) 2.26) Overwrite the fd pointer of a freed tcache chunk (e.g., via a UAF write) with a target address. Two subsequent malloc() calls return the target address, giving an arbitrary write primitive. Fastbin Dup Free the same fastbin chunk twice (double-free) to introduce it into the free list twice; the next two allocations of that size return the same address, enabling overlapping allocation. House of Force (legacy) Overwrite the wilderness (top) chunk size to an enormous value; subsequent malloc() can return nearly any address. Mitigated in modern glibc by top-chunk sanity checks.

docs.title: 24.6.1 Heap Spray Technique
docs.text:
Heap spray trades precision for probability. Rather than targeting a specific allocation at a specific address, the attacker allocates a very large number of objects—often tens of thousands—each containing a NOP sled followed by the payload (shellcode or a fake object). The sled means that any execution pointer landing anywhere within the sprayed region slides forward into the payload without crashing.

The technique is effective against use-after-free and type confusion bugs where the bug gives control over a pointer but not precise control over where that pointer lands. After spraying, the heap layout is highly predictable: most of the virtual address space in the 0x10000000–0x80000000 range will contain attacker data, so even a partially-controlled pointer has a high probability of landing in the spray.

Modern browser exploits use JavaScript to drive heap spray. The JavaScript engine allocates strings, ArrayBuffers, or typed arrays on behalf of the script; a few thousand allocations of 64 KB or 256 KB objects can saturate the relevant heap region in under a second. The typical spray loop in a browser exploit proof-of-concept looks like:

# Conceptual heap spray in JavaScript (pseudocode)
# Allocate N large ArrayBuffers each containing a NOP sled + fake vtable
spray = []
for i in range(0, 10000):
    buf = new ArrayBuffer(65536)
    view = new Uint32Array(buf)
    # Fill with 0x90909090 (NOP sled equivalent) then fake object data
    view.fill(0x90909090)
    view[view.length - 4] = fake_vtable_ptr
    spray.append(buf)
# Now trigger UAF/type confusion; pointer likely lands in spray

Browser vendors have deployed several countermeasures. Isolated Heap allocates certain sensitive objects (DOM nodes, JavaScript objects) in separate heap regions so that a UAF in one region can’t be exploited by spraying the other. MemGC (deferred garbage collection timing randomisation in older IE) and Page Heap (allocate each object on its own page with a guard page immediately after) increase the cost of reliable spraying. V8’s Pointer Compression (V8 8.0+) reduces all heap pointers to 32-bit offsets within a 4 GB cage, which limits the spray’s effective target range and makes pointer forgery harder. Despite these mitigations, heap spray remains relevant when combined with a second information leak that reveals the current spray base address.

docs.title: 24.7 CTF Pwn Methodology
docs.text:
A structured methodology for binary exploitation challenges:

checksec --file=./vuln
# Example output:
# RELRO:    Full RELRO
# STACK CANARY: Canary found
# NX:       NX enabled
# PIE:      PIE enabled
# RPATH:    No RPATH
# RUNPATH:  No RUNPATH

CTF Pwn Workflow

  1. Reconnaissance: checksec, file, strings; determine architecture, protections, and interesting strings.

  2. Bug Identification: Static analysis (Ghidra/IDA) or source review; classify bug (BOF, UAF, format string, etc.).

  3. Offset Finding: Cyclic pattern + GDB/pwndbg.

  4. Leak: Find an info-leak primitive to defeat ASLR/PIE.

  5. ROP Chain: Enumerate gadgets; build chain to call target function.

  6. Trigger: Send payload; verify control flow redirection.

  7. Stabilise: Handle stdout buffering; switch to interactive.

docs.title: 24.8 Browser Exploitation Concepts
docs.text:
Modern browser exploitation operates at multiple privilege levels:

Renderer Process (sandboxed) Exploits in the JavaScript engine (V8/SpiderMonkey) via type confusion or JIT spraying achieve arbitrary read/write within the renderer sandbox. Sandbox Escape A second vulnerability in the browser process or OS IPC mechanism is required to escape the renderer sandbox. JIT Spraying Massage the JIT compiler into emitting attacker-controlled constants as executable code; useful when ASLR makes direct targeting infeasible.

docs.title: 24.9 Kernel Exploitation Concepts
docs.text:
Kernel exploitation aims to elevate a process to root by exploiting bugs in OS kernel code.

/*
 * Illustrative only -- demonstrates the CONCEPT of committing
 * a root credential structure.  This is not functional code.
 */
// commit_creds(prepare_kernel_cred(0))
// prepare_kernel_cred(0) allocates a credential struct for uid=0
// commit_creds() installs it as the calling process's credentials
//
// Actual addresses must be resolved from /proc/kallsyms or leak.
// SMEP prevents user-space code running in kernel context.
// SMAP prevents kernel from dereferencing user-space pointers.
// ret2usr is obsolete on modern kernels with SMEP+SMAP enabled.

Kernel mitigations and their significance:

Mitigation Effect SMEP (Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention) CPU refuses to execute user-space pages in kernel mode SMAP (Supervisor Mode Access Prevention) CPU refuses to read/write user-space pages in kernel mode KASLR Randomises kernel base address KPTI (Page Table Isolation) Separates user/kernel page tables; mitigates Meltdown CFI (kernel) Restricts indirect call targets in kernel code paths

docs.title: 24.9.1 Kernel Mitigation Details and Bypass Chains
docs.text:
SMEP is enforced by bit 20 of the CR4 control register. When SMEP is set, any attempt by the kernel (CPL 0) to fetch an instruction from a page marked user-accessible (U/S bit set in the page table entry) triggers an immediate general protection fault. The historic ret2usr technique— which placed shellcode in user space and redirected kernel execution there via a corrupted kernel pointer—is entirely defeated by SMEP on all Intel CPUs since Ivy Bridge (2012) and AMD CPUs since Excavator (2015).

Defeating SMEP requires a kernel-space ROP chain before reaching user-space code. The typical chain:

  1. Find a gadget in the kernel .text segment (mapped executable, kernel-owned, not user-accessible) that overwrites CR4 bit 20 with zero (mov cr4, rdi; ret with RDI = 0x6f0), disabling SMEP.

  2. With SMEP disabled, redirect RIP to user-space shellcode that calls commit_creds( prepare_kernel_cred(0)) via addresses leaked from /proc/kallsyms.

SMAP (bit 21 of CR4) extends this: it prevents the kernel from even reading user-space memory without first executing the clac instruction to clear the AC flag, and stac to restore it. This blocks kernel code that dereferences user-supplied pointers without explicit copy_from_user calls. A SMAP bypass therefore requires disabling both SMAP and SMEP via CR4 manipulation.

KPTI (Kernel Page Table Isolation), merged into Linux 4.15 in response to Meltdown (CVE-2017-5754), maintains two separate page table sets per core: a user-mode page table that maps only the minimal kernel text required for system call entry, and a kernel-mode page table with full kernel mappings. Switching between them on every system call entry/exit flushes the TLB (expensive) but prevents the kernel’s virtual address space from being visible to Meltdown-style speculative reads from user space. KPTI also breaks some kernel ASLR bypass techniques that relied on reading kernel addresses from the user-visible vsyscall or vDSO pages.

Modern kernel exploit chains on a fully patched kernel therefore require: (1) an information leak to defeat KASLR, (2) a write primitive (UAF or overflow in a kernel allocation path), (3) kernel ROP to disable SMEP/SMAP via CR4 overwrite, and (4) privilege escalation via credential structure manipulation. Each step has gotten harder as the kernel team has added pointer authentication (PAC on ARM64), stack canaries in the kernel itself, and CFI restricting indirect call targets.

docs.title: 24.10 Exploit Mitigations Summary
docs.text: Mitigation Bypassed By Residual Risk ASLR Info-leak, partial overwrite, brute force (32-bit) Low on 64-bit with no leak PIE Info-leak of code pointer Low alone; key combined with ASLR NX/DEP ROP / ret2libc Moderate; ROP ubiquitous Stack Canary Format-string leak, overwrites that skip canary Moderate Full RELRO GOT overwrite impossible; heap/stack alternatives Low for GOT attacks CFI (clang) Limited to valid call targets; ROP within targets Medium

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 24.1

A 64-bit binary has NX enabled, ASLR enabled, PIE disabled, no stack canary, and no RELRO. The binary contains a format string vulnerability that leaks stack values. Describe step-by-step how you would: (a) leak the return address of main using %p format specifiers, (b) compute the offset from the leaked value to system(), and (c) construct a ROP chain to call system(). You do not need to write working code.

Exercise 24.2

Explain the difference between the fastbin dup and tcache poisoning heap exploitation techniques. Why did the introduction of tcache in glibc 2.26 initially make exploitation easier rather than harder? What mitigations have since been added to tcache?

Exercise 24.3

A binary is compiled with full protections: Full RELRO, stack canary, NX, PIE. You discover a stack-based buffer overflow. Enumerate the information leaks you must obtain before building a payload, and explain what each leak provides. Discuss why a single overflow is often insufficient and why researchers look for additional primitives.

Exercise 24.4

Using checksec output showing NX: enabled, PIE: enabled, and RELRO: Full, explain what each protection does and identify the remaining attack surface. How does PIE interact with ASLR at the OS level on Linux?

docs.title: Chapter 25: Security Architecture and Design
docs.text:
Security architecture translates abstract security requirements into concrete, implementable system designs. A well-designed architecture reduces the attack surface, limits the blast radius of any single compromise, and provides the visibility needed for detection and response.

This chapter moves from theoretical frameworks through practical controls and into the compliance requirements that often drive real procurement and design decisions.

docs.title: 25.1 Security Architecture Frameworks
docs.text:
• SABSA (Sherwood Applied Business Security Architecture) — A risk-driven, business-aligned framework with six layers: Contextual, Conceptual, Logical, Physical, Component, and Operational. Each layer answers the questions Who, What, Where, When, Why, and How for security.

  • TOGAF with Security Overlay — The Open Group Architecture Framework provides a generic enterprise architecture methodology; the Security Architecture domain extends it with threat and risk analysis at each ADM phase.

  • O-ESA (Open Enterprise Security Architecture) — An open standard from The Open Group focused on the logical and physical security architecture components: security services, security domains, and trust relationships.

docs.title: 25.2 Defence in Depth
docs.text:
Definition 25.1 (Defence in Depth)

Defence in depth is a layered security strategy in which multiple independent security controls protect an asset. The failure of any single control does not result in a complete compromise.

Figure 25.1. Defence in depth: concentric security layers

Each layer is implemented with different control types and technologies:

  • Physical: Fences, guards, badge readers, CCTV.

  • Network: Firewall, IDS/IPS, VPN, network segmentation.

  • Host: EDR, patch management, host-based firewall, disk encryption.

  • Application: Input validation, WAF, SAST/DAST, secure SDLC.

  • Data: Encryption at rest and in transit, DLP, access control lists.

docs.title: 25.3 Zero Trust Architecture
docs.text:
Definition 25.2 (Zero Trust Architecture)

Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), defined in NIST SP 800-207, treats every network location as potentially hostile. Access decisions are made dynamically based on identity, device posture, and contextual signals rather than network perimeter location.

docs.title: 25.3.1 NIST SP 800-207 Seven Tenets
docs.text:
1. All data sources and computing services are considered resources.

  2. All communication is secured regardless of network location.

  3. Access to resources is granted on a per-session basis.

  4. Resource access is determined by dynamic policy.

  5. The enterprise monitors and measures the integrity of all owned assets.

  6. All resource authentication and authorisation are dynamic and strictly enforced before access is granted.

  7. The enterprise collects information about the state of assets, network infrastructure, and communications to improve its security posture.

docs.title: 25.3.2 Zero Trust Components
docs.text:
Figure 25.2. Zero Trust reference architecture (NIST SP 800-207) Identity Provider (IdP) Issues verified claims about user and device identity. Examples: Okta, Azure Active Directory, Google Workspace. Policy Engine (PE) Evaluates trust score based on identity claims, device health (MDM compliance, patch level, EDR status), and contextual signals (geolocation, time, behavioural baseline). Policy Administrator (PA) Translates the PE decision into a session token or access credential. Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) Proxies or brokers traffic; enforces the PE allow/deny decision. Examples: Cloud-based reverse proxy, ZTNA agent.

BeyondCorp: Google’s Zero Trust Implementation

Google’s BeyondCorp model (2014–) moved access control from VPN-based perimeter to device and user verification. The core insight: the corporate network is as untrusted as the public internet. Employee laptops must present a device certificate (managed by Google’s CA) and user identity token to the Access Proxy before reaching any internal service.

docs.title: 25.4 Network Segmentation
docs.text: VLANs Layer-2 segmentation; limits broadcast domains but does not prevent routed traffic unless combined with inter-VLAN ACLs. DMZ Architecture A perimeter network hosting publicly accessible services (web, email) behind an outer firewall; an inner firewall separates the DMZ from the internal network. Micro-segmentation Software-defined segmentation at the workload level; each VM or container has its own firewall policy. Service Mesh (Istio mTLS) Transparent mutual-TLS between microservices; every service has a certificate from a mesh CA; east-west traffic is authenticated and encrypted.

docs.title: 25.4.1 Microsegmentation in Practice
docs.text:
A traditional data centre relies on VLANs and perimeter firewalls to separate network zones, but once an attacker compromises a single host inside a VLAN, east-west traffic—server-to-server communication within the same network tier—flows freely. This flat internal network is the reason that ransomware can encrypt thousands of servers after a single workstation is compromised: the ransomware spreads laterally via SMB (port 445) or WMI with no firewall between servers in the same VLAN.

Microsegmentation replaces VLAN-based controls with workload-based policies. Instead of assigning a firewall rule to a subnet, you assign it to a workload identity—a VM tag, container label, or process signature. The policy is: “the payment-service workload may communicate with the postgres-primary workload on port 5432, and nothing else.” Any other connection—whether from a compromised adjacent workload or from the workload itself trying to reach the internet—is blocked by default.

Implementation options:

  • VMware NSX enforces distributed firewall rules at the hypervisor level; policy follows the VM regardless of which physical host or VLAN it migrates to. NSX’s distributed firewall processes traffic before it exits the virtual NIC, so there’s no traffic path that bypasses it.

  • Illumio Core installs a lightweight agent on each workload (physical server, VM, or container) that enforces allow-list policies locally and reports telemetry to a central Policy Compute Engine. Because policy enforcement is at the host, it works across heterogeneous environments—on-premises bare metal, cloud VMs, and containers in the same policy domain.

  • Cisco Tetration (now Cisco Secure Workload) uses network flow telemetry and machine learning to generate proposed segmentation policies based on observed communication patterns before enforcement is turned on—a critical feature for brownfield deployments where unknown dependencies would otherwise cause policy-induced outages.

The operational challenge of microsegmentation is the discovery phase: mapping every legitimate communication path before writing a deny-all default rule. Skipping this step and enabling enforcement too early causes unexpected application outages that erode trust in the programme. A phased approach— observe, propose, verify, enforce—is the only reliable path.

docs.title: 25.5 Threat Modelling: STRIDE
docs.text:
Definition 25.3 (STRIDE)

STRIDE is a mnemonic for six threat categories used to systematically analyse system components: Spoofing identity, Tampering with data, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege.

docs.title: 25.5.1 STRIDE Applied to a Web API
docs.text: Threat Example Mitigation Spoofing Forge or replay a JWT to impersonate another user Short JWT expiry; signature verification; token revocation Tampering Modify request body after signing HMAC request signing; TLS Repudiation Deny having made a destructive API call Structured audit log with user/IP/timestamp Info Disclosure Verbose error messages leak stack traces/SQL Generic error responses; structured logging DoS Unbounded query floods the API endpoint Rate limiting; query complexity limits Elevation IDOR: access another user’s resource by ID Ownership checks; object-level authorisation

docs.title: 25.5.2 Worked STRIDE Example: REST API with Database Backend
docs.text:
Consider a simple web API that accepts JSON over HTTPS, authenticates callers via JWT, and stores records in a PostgreSQL database. Walking each STRIDE category against this system produces concrete, actionable mitigations:

Spoofing. An attacker calls the API without a valid token, or replays a stolen token from a previous session. Mitigation: Require a signed JWT in the Authorization: Bearer header on every request. Use short expiry (15 minutes) with refresh tokens stored in HttpOnly cookies. Validate the signature against the public key from the issuer’s JWKS endpoint—never accept alg: none or HS256 with a predictable key. Maintain a token revocation list (or use short-lived tokens) for logout and account-takeover recovery. Tampering. The JSON body is modified in transit, changing a transaction amount or target account ID. Mitigation: TLS 1.3 prevents in-transit modification. For higher-assurance APIs, add an HMAC request signature over the canonical request body (Content-Type + body SHA-256 + timestamp), similar to AWS Signature v4. The server rejects any request whose signature does not match, regardless of TLS protection. Repudiation. A user denies having submitted a fraudulent transfer. Without logs, the API can’t prove otherwise. Mitigation: Write structured audit logs for every state-changing API call: authenticated user ID, source IP, hashed request body, resource modified, and timestamp. Ship these logs to an append-only, write-once storage tier (AWS S3 Object Lock, or a WORM appliance) so that neither the user nor a compromised application server can delete them. Information Disclosure. A database error propagates verbatim to the client: ERROR: relation "users" does not exist reveals schema. Mitigation: Catch all exceptions at the controller layer and return a generic 500 Internal Server Error with a correlation ID. Log the full exception internally. Configure the framework to suppress stack traces in production mode. Denial of Service. An attacker scripts thousands of unauthenticated POST requests per second against /auth/login, exhausting the database connection pool. Mitigation: Apply a token-bucket rate limiter at the reverse proxy (nginx limit_req_zone, API gateway throttling): 10 requests/second per IP with burst 20. Add progressive delays after three failed login attempts and account lockout after ten within one hour. Elevation of Privilege. The GET /api/invoices/{id} endpoint returns an invoice to any authenticated user if they guess the numeric invoice ID—a classic IDOR. Mitigation: Every database query must include an ownership predicate: WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = \(2</code>, where <code>\)2 is the authenticated user’s ID extracted from the verified JWT, never from the request body. Use UUIDs instead of sequential integers to prevent enumeration.

This analysis is conducted in a structured session with developers, architects, and security engineers during the Design phase of the SDLC. Each threat-mitigation pair becomes a tracked security requirement, verified during penetration testing before release.

docs.title: 25.6 Security Controls Classification
docs.text:
Security controls are classified by function and implementation type:

Preventive Detective Corrective Administrative Policy, training Audit, review Disciplinary action Technical Firewall, MFA IDS, SIEM Patch, quarantine Physical Lock, fence CCTV, alarm Fire suppression

A compensating control fulfils a security requirement when the primary control is not feasible (e.g., network-layer monitoring compensates for an unpatchable legacy system).

docs.title: 25.7 Hardening and Benchmarks
docs.text: CIS Benchmarks The Center for Internet Security publishes prescriptive configuration guidelines for OS, middleware, and cloud platforms at two levels: Level 1 (basic hygiene, minimal performance impact) and Level 2 (defence-in-depth, higher operational overhead). DISA STIGs Security Technical Implementation Guides from the US Department of Defense; mandatory for federal systems; more prescriptive than CIS. Automated Compliance Tools such as OpenSCAP (OVAL/XCCDF), Chef InSpec, and Puppet Bolt continuously assess and remediate drift from the baseline.

docs.title: 25.8 Secure SDLC
docs.text:
Security must be integrated throughout the software development lifecycle (SDLC) rather than applied as a post-deployment afterthought.

Secure SDLC Activities by Phase

Phase Security Activities Requirements Security requirements, abuse cases, privacy impact assessment Design Threat modelling (STRIDE, PASTA), attack trees, crown jewel analysis Development Secure coding standards, peer review, pre-commit hooks Build/CI SAST (Semgrep, Checkmarx), SCA (Dependabot, Snyk), secrets detection Test DAST (OWASP ZAP, Burp), IAST, fuzzing, manual pen test Release Security gate (fail build on critical findings), signing, SBOM Operations Patch management, SIEM, CSPM, vulnerability management

docs.title: 25.8.1 Security Guardrails in CI/CD
docs.text:
“Shift left” is the principle that security issues caught earlier in the development process cost orders of magnitude less to fix. The IBM Systems Sciences Institute estimated that a defect found at the requirements stage costs $100 to fix; the same defect found in production costs around $10,000. The implication is clear: embed automated security checks into every stage of the CI/CD pipeline so that issues surface when a developer still has full context, rather than weeks later during a scheduled pen test.

A mature CI/CD security pipeline includes all of the following as mandatory gates—a finding above the configured severity threshold blocks the pull request or deployment:

SAST (Static Application Security Testing). Semgrep and SonarQube scan source code for insecure patterns—SQL injection, XSS, hardcoded credentials, unsafe deserialization—without executing the code. Run as a PR check; fail on High/Critical findings. Semgrep’s rule registry includes OWASP Top 10 coverage for Python, Java, JavaScript, Go, and C/C++. Keep rulesets pinned to a version so results are reproducible. Secrets Scanning. GitLeaks and TruffleHog scan the git history and staged changes for secrets—API keys, private keys, connection strings, and OAuth tokens—using regex patterns and entropy analysis. Run as a pre-commit hook (client-side, before the secret ever reaches the remote) and again as a CI server-side check. A secret committed to a public repository should be considered compromised immediately, regardless of whether it was caught later— git history is public and search engines index it within minutes. SCA (Software Composition Analysis). Dependabot (GitHub-native) and Snyk scan dependency manifests (package.json, requirements.txt, pom.xml) against vulnerability databases (NVD, OSV) and open automated PRs with version bumps when a dependency has a known CVE. Configure severity thresholds: auto-merge Low/Medium dependency updates, require human review for High/ Critical. SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) generation using Syft or CycloneDX should be part of every release artefact. Container Image Scanning. Trivy and Grype scan container images for OS package CVEs and application dependency vulnerabilities before push to the registry. Add the scan step between the docker build and docker push stages. Use a distroless or scratch-based base image to minimise the OS package attack surface—a distroless Python image carries no shell, no package manager, and no utilities an attacker could repurpose. IaC Scanning (Infrastructure-as-Code). Checkov and tfsec analyse Terraform, Kubernetes YAML, CloudFormation, and Helm charts for misconfigurations—S3 buckets with public ACLs, security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0, containers running as root, missing pod security standards. Run on every PR that touches .tf, .yaml, or Helm templates. DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing). OWASP ZAP and Burp Suite Enterprise scan a running deployment in a staging environment for vulnerabilities that only manifest at runtime: authentication bypass, session fixation, CORS misconfiguration. Run against the staging environment on merge to the main branch, not on every PR (it requires a running service and takes longer).

The combined effect is a security control at every commit. A developer who introduces a hardcoded AWS secret sees a pre-commit hook failure within seconds; a dependency CVE surfaces as a Dependabot PR the same day the CVE is published; a container misconfiguration blocks deployment before it reaches staging. The cost of maintaining these pipelines is modest—a few hours to configure initially, then ongoing tuning to reduce false positives. The alternative—finding the same issues during a quarterly pen test—costs dramatically more in both remediation time and risk exposure.

docs.title: 25.9 Compliance Frameworks
docs.text: Framework Scope and Key Requirements ISO/IEC 27001 International ISMS standard; 93 controls in Annex A (ISO 27002:2022); risk assessment and Statement of Applicability required NIST CSF 2.0 Six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover; voluntary framework aligned to NIST SP 800-53 PCI DSS v4.0 Payment card data; 12 requirements; customised approach option SOC 2 Type II AICPA trust service criteria (Security, Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, Privacy); audited over observation period HIPAA US health data; administrative, physical, and technical safeguards; breach notification within 60 days GDPR (Technical) Encryption, pseudonymisation, data minimisation, privacy by design; 72-hour breach notification to supervisory authority

docs.title: 25.9.1 NIST CSF 2.0 Controls Mapping
docs.text: Function Example Controls Key Outcome Govern Risk tolerance, supply chain policy Accountability established Identify Asset inventory, vulnerability scanning Risk understood Protect MFA, encryption, patch management, training Access limited Detect SIEM, IDS, anomaly detection, audit logs Events visible Respond IR plan, playbooks, communication plan Impact contained Recover Backups, DR plan, lessons learned Services restored

docs.title: 25.9.2 Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM)
docs.text:
As organisations move workloads to AWS, Azure, and GCP, misconfigurations in cloud resource settings have become the dominant source of cloud security incidents—far more common than sophisticated attacks against patched software. An S3 bucket with public access, a security group that opens port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0, or an IAM role with : permissions can expose critical data with a single misconfigured checkbox.

Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) tools continuously evaluate every cloud resource configuration against security benchmarks and alert on deviations. They connect to cloud APIs (AWS CloudFormation, Azure Resource Manager, GCP Cloud Asset Inventory) and compare the actual resource state against:

  • CIS Benchmarks (CIS Amazon Web Services Foundations, CIS Microsoft Azure Foundations) — prescriptive configuration checks, e.g., “S3 buckets should not allow public ACLs”, “Multi-factor authentication should be enabled for all IAM users with console access”.

  • NIST CSF and SOC 2 control mappings — useful when cloud security findings need to be reported against an audit framework.

  • AWS Foundational Security Best Practices (AWS native, surfaced via AWS Security Hub).

Key CSPM platforms:

AWS Security Hub AWS-native aggregation hub that ingests findings from GuardDuty (threat detection), Inspector (vulnerability scanning), Macie (S3 data classification), and third-party integrations, scored against the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard. No additional agent required for AWS resources. Wiz Agent-less graph-based CSPM that models the entire cloud environment as a connected graph—resources, identities, network paths, and data stores—and identifies attack paths that combine misconfigurations. A typical Wiz finding isn’t “S3 bucket is public” but “EC2 instance has an IAM role that can access this public S3 bucket which contains secrets, and the instance is reachable from the internet on port 443 via a public load balancer.” Prisma Cloud (Palo Alto Networks) A broad CNAPP (see below) that includes CSPM, CWPP, and IaC scanning in one platform; strong compliance reporting for PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2, and GDPR.

It’s important to distinguish CSPM from adjacent categories that are often conflated:

  • CWPP (Cloud Workload Protection Platform) focuses on runtime protection of cloud workloads—EDR-equivalent capabilities for VMs and containers, detecting in-memory attacks, cryptomining processes, or anomalous system calls. Where CSPM asks “is this resource configured correctly?”, CWPP asks “is this workload behaving correctly at runtime?”

  • CNAPP (Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform) combines CSPM and CWPP into a single platform with a unified data model, enabling correlation between configuration-level findings and runtime telemetry. Wiz, Prisma Cloud, and Microsoft Defender for Cloud are examples of converged CNAPP offerings. The CNAPP model reflects the reality that a useful cloud security finding usually requires both dimensions: a container breakout is more critical if the host VM’s IAM role can write to a production database.

CSPM should be enabled from day one of a cloud deployment, not retrofitted. The marginal cost of running AWS Security Hub on a new account is negligible; the cost of remediating a data breach caused by a public S3 bucket that CSPM would have caught on day one is not.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 25.1

Perform a STRIDE threat analysis on the following architecture: a mobile banking application that authenticates users via OAuth 2.0 with an external IdP, communicates with a REST API over TLS, and stores transaction history in a PostgreSQL database. For each STRIDE category, identify at least one concrete threat and a corresponding technical mitigation.

Exercise 25.2

Your organisation currently uses a traditional VPN for remote access. Design a phased Zero Trust migration roadmap over 18 months. Include: (a) identity foundation (IdP selection, MFA rollout), (b) device posture assessment, (c) micro-segmentation of the three most critical application tiers, and (d) metrics to demonstrate improved security posture to leadership.

Exercise 25.3

Map the following controls to their ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A categories and to the corresponding NIST CSF 2.0 function: (a) encryption of data at rest with AES-256, (b) quarterly penetration testing, (c) automated patch deployment within 72 hours of critical CVE publication, (d) centralised SIEM with 1-year log retention, (e) annual security awareness training.

docs.title: Chapter 26: Cloud-Native Security
docs.text: Cloud-native architectures offer elastic scalability and rapid deployment but introduce distinct attack surfaces: misconfigured identity policies, exposed storage buckets, container escape paths, and insecure supply chains. Security engineering in the cloud requires understanding the shared responsibility model, identity architecture, container and orchestration hardening, and supply chain integrity.

docs.title: 26.1 The Shared Responsibility Model
docs.text:
Definition 26.1 (Shared Responsibility Model)

In cloud computing, the shared responsibility model delineates which security obligations rest with the cloud service provider (CSP) and which remain with the customer, depending on the service model.

Control Area IaaS PaaS SaaS Physical data centre CSP CSP CSP Hypervisor / network CSP CSP CSP Operating system Customer CSP CSP Runtime / middleware Customer CSP CSP Application code Customer Customer CSP Data classification Customer Customer Customer Identity & access mgmt Customer Customer Customer

Misconfiguration is the Customer’s Responsibility

Data breaches from public S3 buckets, permissive IAM policies, and exposed databases are customer-side failures. The CSP provides the tools; the customer must configure them correctly.

docs.title: 26.2.1 AWS IAM Fundamentals
docs.text:
AWS IAM controls who (principal) can do what (action) on which resource under what conditions. Policies are expressed in JSON and attached to users, groups, roles, or resources.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "ReadOnlyBucketAccess",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject",
        "s3:ListBucket"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::my-secure-bucket",
        "arn:aws:s3:::my-secure-bucket/*"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
IAM Roles for EC2/Lambda Instance profiles attach a role to a compute resource; credentials are rotated automatically via the Instance Metadata Service (IMDSv2). Prefer roles over long-lived IAM user access keys. Principle of Least Privilege Grant only the minimum permissions required for a task. Use IAM Access Analyser and the AWS IAM Policy Simulator to verify effective permissions. Confused Deputy Problem A service with broad permissions may be tricked by a less-privileged caller into performing actions the caller could not perform directly. Mitigation: use aws:SourceAccount and aws:SourceArn condition keys in resource-based policies. 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Deny",
    "Action": "s3:PutObject",
    "Resource": "*",
    "Condition": {
      "StringNotEquals": {
        "aws:RequestedRegion": ["eu-west-1", "eu-west-2"]
      }
    }
  }]
}

docs.title: 26.2.2 AWS Organizations and Service Control Policies
docs.text:
AWS Organizations lets you manage multiple AWS accounts under a single management structure called an organization. The real security power sits in Service Control Policies (SCPs)—JSON policy documents attached to an Organizational Unit (OU) or to individual accounts that act as guardrails on every principal inside that account, including the root user. SCPs don’t grant permissions on their own; they establish the maximum permissions ceiling. Even if an IAM administrator inside a member account writes a policy granting full : access, the SCP filter applies first and can deny specific actions before the IAM evaluation even runs. This makes SCPs the right tool for non-negotiable organisational controls rather than account-level IAM policies that an account administrator could later modify.

Two patterns show up in almost every enterprise AWS deployment. The first is preventing CloudTrail from being disabled: a single SCP applied at the root OU that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging, cloudtrail: DeleteTrail, and cloudtrail:UpdateTrail ensures no account—regardless of what the local IAM policies say—can silence the audit trail. The second pattern restricts IAM user creation in non-production accounts. When your organisation mandates federation through an IdP (Okta, Azure AD), long-lived IAM users are a policy violation; an SCP that denies iam:CreateUser in all accounts except the management account enforces this automatically without relying on each team to remember the rule.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyCloudTrailModification",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "cloudtrail:StopLogging",
        "cloudtrail:DeleteTrail",
        "cloudtrail:UpdateTrail",
        "cloudtrail:PutEventSelectors"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyIAMUserCreation",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "iam:CreateUser",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "aws:PrincipalOrgID": ["o-exampleorgid11"]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

One important nuance: SCPs follow an implicit deny model at the organizational boundary. If you apply a restrictive SCP that only allows specific services (an allow-list SCP), every service not listed is implicitly denied even if the local IAM policy permits it. Most enterprises use deny-list SCPs instead—they start with a FullAWSAccess policy and layer specific denies on top— because allow-list SCPs require enumerating every permitted service, which breaks as teams adopt new AWS services. Tag-based conditions work inside SCPs too, which lets you write guardrails like “deny terminating any EC2 instance tagged Environment=Production unless the request comes from the approved change-management role.”

docs.title: 26.3 Cloud Storage Misconfigurations
docs.text:
Capital One Breach (2019)

A misconfigured WAF EC2 instance had an over-permissive IAM role attached. An attacker exploited an SSRF vulnerability in the WAF to reach the EC2 Instance Metadata Service and retrieve the IAM role credentials. Using those credentials, the attacker exfiltrated over 100 million customer records from S3 buckets. Root cause: SSRF + overly permissive IAM role + absence of IMDSv2 enforcement.

Common cloud storage misconfigurations:

  • AWS S3: Block Public Access disabled; bucket ACL set to public-read; missing server-side encryption.

  • Azure Blob: Container access level set to Blob or Container (anonymous read).

  • GCP Cloud Storage: Bucket IAM includes allUsers or allAuthenticated Users with Storage Object Viewer.

Detection and remediation:

# Enable managed Config rule
aws configservice put-config-rule \
  --config-rule '{"ConfigRuleName":"s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited",
                  "Source":{"Owner":"AWS",
                    "SourceIdentifier":"S3_BUCKET_PUBLIC_READ_PROHIBITED"}}'

# Remediate with Auto Remediation -> AWS-DisableS3BucketPublicReadWrite

docs.title: 26.4 Container Security
docs.text:
Definition 26.2 (Container Security)

Container security encompasses the practices and controls applied to container images, registries, runtimes, and orchestrators to reduce the attack surface and limit the blast radius of a compromise.

# Use a minimal, pinned base image
FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:<digest>

# Run as non-root user (principle of least privilege)
RUN useradd -r -u 1000 appuser
USER 1000

# Copy only what is needed (avoid COPY . .)
COPY --chown=1000:1000 app/ /app/
WORKDIR /app

# No secrets in ENV or build args; use runtime injection
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "main.py"]

docker run \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --user 1000:1000 \
  myapp:latest

docs.title: 26.4.1 Image Scanning
docs.text: Tool Integration Key Feature Trivy CLI, GitHub Actions, CI/CD Fast; OS + application dependency CVE scan Snyk IDE, CI/CD, registry Fix advice; licence compliance Docker Scout Docker Desktop, Hub Native; real-time policy evaluation Grype CLI, Syft SBOM input SBOM-aware; EPSS scoring

docs.title: 26.4.2 OCI Image Registries and Registry Security
docs.text:
The Open Container Initiative (OCI) image format is the standard for container images, and where you pull those images from matters as much as what’s inside them. Public registries like Docker Hub are convenient but introduce several risks: Docker Hub’s rate-limiting policy (100 pulls per 6 hours for anonymous users, 200 for free accounts) drove most organisations to mirror images to private registries in 2020, and that operational decision also improved their security posture as a side effect.

Private registries—Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure Container Registry—give you control over who can push and pull, automatic vulnerability scanning on push, and immutable image tags enforced via tag immutability settings. ECR can block pushes if the image contains critical-severity CVEs above a threshold, acting as an admission gate before the image ever reaches a cluster.

The image pull policy in Kubernetes controls whether the node checks the registry for a fresh copy or uses a locally cached version. IfNotPresent (the default) reuses a cached layer if the tag already exists locally—which means a pod restarted after a security patch might silently continue using the old, vulnerable image if the tag (e.g., latest) hasn’t changed. Setting the pull policy to Always forces a registry check on every pod start, but it adds latency and increases registry load. The practical recommendation: pin images to their SHA-256 digest rather than a mutable tag, and set pull policy to IfNotPresent on the pinned digest—you get determinism without the registry round-trip overhead, and a changed image simply gets a different digest and therefore a different deployment manifest.

Registry mirroring for air-gapped or restricted environments deserves its own mention. In production environments with strict egress controls, nodes can’t reach Docker Hub or even public cloud registries. A mirror (Harbor, JFrog Artifactory, or a self-hosted OCI distribution server) proxies and caches upstream images inside the network perimeter. The containerd mirrors configuration in /etc/containerd/config.toml tells the container runtime to try the internal mirror before the upstream source. This pattern also lets you enforce a policy: only images that have passed your internal scanning pipeline appear in the mirror, so nodes can only pull approved images regardless of what a developer specifies in a pod spec.

docs.title: 26.5 Kubernetes Security
docs.text: Figure 26.1. Kubernetes security control layers

docs.title: 26.5.1 RBAC
docs.text:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: pod-reader-binding
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: monitoring-sa
  namespace: default
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

docs.title: 26.5.2 Pod Security Standards and SecurityContext
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secure-pod
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:latest
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: "500m"
        memory: "256Mi"

docs.title: 26.5.3 Secrets Management
docs.text:
Never Store Secrets in Environment Variables or Images

Environment variables are visible in /proc/<pid>/environ and in container inspection output. Secrets baked into images persist in layer history. Use external secret stores with runtime injection instead.

Options for Kubernetes secrets management:

Sealed Secrets (Bitnami) Encrypt secrets client-side with the cluster public key; store encrypted SealedSecret CRD in Git. External Secrets Operator Sync from AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, or HashiCorp Vault into Kubernetes Secrets at runtime. HashiCorp Vault Agent Injector Sidecar injects secrets as files into the pod filesystem; short-lived dynamic secrets per service.

docs.title: 26.5.4 Admission Controllers
docs.text:
Every object creation or modification request to the Kubernetes API server passes through the admission control pipeline after authentication and authorisation. Admission controllers are the last line of defence before a resource lands in etcd. Kubernetes ships several built-in controllers (LimitRanger, ResourceQuota, PodSecurity), but the most powerful extension points are the webhook-based controllers: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration.

A mutating webhook runs first and can modify the incoming object—injecting a sidecar container, adding default resource limits, or rewriting an image tag to a digest. A validating webhook runs after mutation and can only approve or reject; it can’t change the object. Both call an external HTTPS service that receives a JSON AdmissionReview object and returns an allow/deny decision with an optional patch (for mutating).

OPA Gatekeeper implements policy-as-code for Kubernetes. It registers itself as a validating webhook and uses two Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs): ConstraintTemplate (defines the Rego policy logic and the shape of the constraint) and Constraint (instantiates the template with specific parameters, e.g., which namespaces to enforce). Rego is a declarative query language—you express what must be true for a request to be allowed, not a sequence of imperative checks.

Kyverno takes a different approach: policies are expressed as Kubernetes YAML resources rather than a separate policy language. A Kyverno ClusterPolicy uses a validate/mutate/generate structure that reads like a Kubernetes manifest, making it more approachable for teams that aren’t comfortable writing Rego. The trade-off is expressiveness: Rego can express complex logic that would be verbose or impossible in Kyverno’s YAML DSL, but most common policies—require labels, enforce resource limits, disallow latest tags—are simpler in Kyverno.

The canonical example that every admission controller tutorial covers is blocking pods without resource limits. Without CPU and memory limits, a single misbehaving pod can starve other workloads on the node (the “noisy neighbour” problem), and in a security context, unlimited memory grants a compromised container unlimited headroom for its payload.

# ConstraintTemplate defines the Rego policy
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: requireresourcelimits
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: RequireResourceLimits
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package requireresourcelimits
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        not container.resources.limits.cpu
        msg := sprintf("Container '
                       [container.name])
      }
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        not container.resources.limits.memory
        msg := sprintf("Container '
                       [container.name])
      }
---
# Constraint enforces the template in the default namespace
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: RequireResourceLimits
metadata:
  name: require-resource-limits
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: [""]
      kinds: ["Pod"]
    namespaces: ["default", "production"]

apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-resource-limits
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-container-limits
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: [Pod]
    validate:
      message: "CPU and memory limits are required for all containers."
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - resources:
              limits:
                cpu: "?*"
                memory: "?*"

The practical difference between Gatekeeper and Kyverno shows up in your team’s skill set. If your platform team already writes Rego for other OPA policies (e.g., in Terraform Sentinel or Conftest), Gatekeeper is a natural fit. If they’re primarily Kubernetes operators who think in YAML, Kyverno has a shallower learning curve and ships with a library of ready-made policies for common controls.

docs.title: 26.6 Supply Chain Security
docs.text:
SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artefacts) A Google-originated framework with four levels of build provenance guarantees (L1: signed provenance; L4: hermetic, isolated build). SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) A machine-readable inventory of components and their versions. Standard formats: CycloneDX (OWASP) and SPDX (Linux Foundation). Required by US Executive Order 14028. sigstore / cosign Keyless container image signing using ephemeral keys and certificate transparency log (Rekor). Verify: cosign verify <image>. in-toto Framework for supply chain layout attestation: each step (build, test, sign) is attested by the appropriate functionary. 
# Generate CycloneDX SBOM with Syft
syft myapp:latest -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json

# Sign image with cosign (keyless, OIDC-based)
cosign sign myregistry.io/myapp:latest

# Verify signature
cosign verify \
  --certificate-identity-regexp=".*@myorg.com" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer="https://accounts.google.com" \
  myregistry.io/myapp:latest

docs.title: 26.6.1 SBOM in Practice
docs.text:
An SBOM without a vulnerability database behind it is just a list. The value of an SBOM comes from feeding it into a continuous vulnerability correlation pipeline, and that pipeline has several stages that are easy to describe but require tooling discipline to execute consistently.

The standard pipeline looks like this: generate the SBOM at build time (Syft from a container image or source tree produces CycloneDX JSON or SPDX), scan that SBOM against a CVE database (Grype consumes Syft SBOMs natively; Trivy does the same), then triage findings by reachability analysis. Reachability is the key step that most teams skip. A dependency on log4j-core 2.14.1 will light up scanners, but if your application calls no code path that uses the JNDI lookup feature, the CVE isn’t exploitable in that build. Tools like Endor Labs and Semgrep’s reachability analysis attempt to determine whether the vulnerable function is actually called from application code. This cuts the actionable findings from hundreds to tens.

The remaining fixable vulnerabilities—where a patched version exists, reachability confirmed—feed into ticket creation (JIRA, GitHub Issues) with SLA targets based on CVSS severity and your organisation’s risk appetite. Tracking over time matters: a vulnerability database growing without tickets being closed is a programme health problem, not a tooling problem.

VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) is a companion format to SBOMs, defined by CISA and implemented in CycloneDX and OpenVEX. A VEX document is a machine-readable assertion from the component supplier or integrator that a known CVE—present in a dependency’s SBOM—is not exploitable in the built artefact, with a reason code: not_affected, not_applicable (the vulnerable component isn’t included in the build), fixed, or in_triage. VEX lets a scanner like Grype filter out CVEs that the producer has already assessed and declared non-exploitable, reducing the noise that drives analyst fatigue. US Executive Order 14028 and NTIA guidance explicitly reference VEX as part of a complete SBOM ecosystem.

# Generate SBOM from container image (CycloneDX format)
syft myapp:1.4.2 -o cyclonedx-json > sbom-myapp-1.4.2.json

# Scan SBOM for vulnerabilities; output table sorted by severity
grype sbom:sbom-myapp-1.4.2.json \
  --only-fixed \
  --fail-on high

# Apply VEX document to suppress assessed-non-exploitable CVEs
grype sbom:sbom-myapp-1.4.2.json \
  --vex vex-myapp-1.4.2.openvex.json

# Track results over time: push to a vulnerability tracker
grype sbom:sbom-myapp-1.4.2.json \
  -o json | jq '.matches[] | {id:.vulnerability.id,
               severity:.vulnerability.severity,
               pkg:.artifact.name}' \
  >> vuln-tracking.jsonl

FROM cloudtrail_logs

docs.title: 26.7.1 Falco for Runtime Security
docs.text:
GuardDuty, Defender for Cloud, and SCC are excellent at correlating cloud API events, but they don’t see what happens inside a running container at the syscall level. That’s where Falco fills the gap.

Falco is a CNCF open-source runtime security project. Its sensor intercepts Linux system calls using either a kernel module or an eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) probe attached to the kernel’s tracepoints. eBPF is the preferred deployment mode in modern Kubernetes clusters because it doesn’t require a kernel module signed for the host OS, it runs in a sandboxed VM inside the kernel, and it carries less risk of crashing the node than a traditional kernel module.

Rules are written in YAML and pattern-match against the stream of syscall events enriched with container and Kubernetes metadata (container name, namespace, pod name, image digest). A rule specifies a condition (a Falco filter expression) and a output message template. The detection engine evaluates every syscall against all active rules with negligible overhead because the filtering logic runs inside the eBPF program, in kernel space, before the event even reaches user space.

The classic example rule—one that ships in Falco’s default rule set—is detecting a shell spawned inside a container. Legitimate application containers don’t need an interactive shell; if /bin/sh or /bin/bash starts inside a container whose parent process is not another shell, that’s a strong signal of post-exploitation activity (an attacker who achieved code execution and dropped to a shell for interactive reconnaissance).

- rule: Shell Spawned in Container
  desc: >
    A shell was spawned in a container. This is often indicative of an
    attacker gaining interactive access after initial code execution.
  condition: >
    spawned_process
    and container
    and shell_procs
    and not proc.pname in (shell_binaries)
    and not container.image.repository in (known_shell_spawning_images)
  output: >
    Shell spawned in container
    (user=
     container_id=
     image=
     shell=
     k8s_ns=
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [container, shell, attack, T1059]

An important characteristic of Falco’s design: it’s a detection-only tool. It generates alerts; it doesn’t block syscalls. Blocking at the syscall level requires a different technology (seccomp profiles, which deny specific syscalls at the kernel scheduler before they execute). Falco’s role is to fire an alert when a runtime rule matches; the response mechanism is a separate layer. In practice, teams wire Falco alerts to a response function—an AWS Lambda or Google Cloud Function triggered by the alert—that takes automated action: isolating the pod (removing it from the service’s selector labels so it receives no new traffic), capturing a memory dump for forensic analysis, or opening a PagerDuty incident. Some teams connect Falco to Falcosidekick, a fan-out service that routes alerts to Slack, Elasticsearch, S3, and a response function simultaneously.

# Example Lambda handler (Python): isolate pod on Falco shell alert
import boto3, json, subprocess

def handler(event, context):
    alert = json.loads(event['body'])
    if alert['rule'] != 'Shell Spawned in Container':
        return
    pod_name = alert['output_fields']['k8s.pod.name']
    namespace = alert['output_fields']['k8s.ns.name']

    # Remove pod from service selection by removing app label
    subprocess.run([
        'kubectl', 'label', 'pod', pod_name,
        '-n', namespace,
        'app-', '--overwrite'     # removes the 'app' label
    ], check=True)

    # Optionally cordon the node to prevent new scheduling
    node = alert['output_fields'].get('k8s.node.name', '')
    if node:
        subprocess.run(['kubectl', 'cordon', node], check=True)

    print(f"Isolated pod {pod_name} in {namespace}")

Falco’s rule library covers a wide threat surface out of the box: writing to /etc, /usr, or /bin from inside a container; outbound connections to unexpected IP ranges; ptrace calls that suggest container escape attempts; and loading kernel modules from user space. Custom rules are easy to add and should target your specific application baseline—if your web app container never makes outbound DNS queries except to the cluster DNS resolver, a rule alerting on any other DNS destination catches unusual C2 communication with low false positives.
